note: Manimekalai's councils warn that if the festival is forgotten, the spirit that relieved the king and the spirit that beats and eats wrongdoers bound in its noose will not stay.
teaches: The Silappathikaram presents the crossroads spirit as a standing marvel of Puhar, while the Manimekalai makes its presence depend on keeping Indra's festival, so the city's moral guard becomes something that can be lost by neglect.

note: The couplet's woman asks what would become of her if she forgot, since she knows no forgetting and even remembering burns; Madhavi's woman says to the adumbu and the swans, let him go, we will not forget those who forgot us.
teaches: In the Kural not forgetting is a helpless bind, since memory both burns and keeps her alive, whereas in the song it is announced as a choice with an audience, a reproach to the forgetter, so the pair shows the same refusal to forget used as a lament and as a charge.

gains.a: the stanza gains the couplet's inner cost, that the vow not to forget is also a burning she cannot escape
gains.b: the couplet's private bind gains a public turn, the same memory declared to witnesses as an accusation against the one who forgot

note: Tirumular makes the five dances the five acts done by grace; the Neelakesi cites the dance and the acts only as the opponent's shield, which 767-775 break.
teaches: The doctrine Tirumular offers as the heart of grace is the very one the Jain debater names in order to refute, and her answer (a god who is all is the author of every harm) is the objection Tirumular's dance never meets.

gains.a: the epic's brief list is shown to be a real Saiva teaching, the dance joined to the five acts, not a straw man
gains.b: the verse gains a hostile contemporary reading that treats the five acts as making god responsible for destruction and harm

note: In the opening sermon the sage tells the worshippers that a child's body comes from blood and its life from former deeds; here Neelakesi explains how the soul takes up the father's seed and the mother's blood and grows within the body.
teaches: The sage's bare division between a body from the parents and a life from former deeds is filled in by the debate with the mechanism of conception that lets the Jain deny any god a part in it.

note: Kural 358 says understanding is seeing the excellent so that the folly called birth departs; 724 calls birth a disease, names bad deeds eaten as its cause, and makes true understanding the cure.
teaches: Both make birth the evil and understanding the cure, but the Jain verse inserts the deed as the cause between them, so understanding ends birth only by ending the eating of past deeds.

gains.a: the Jain claim is seen to share its end and its means with a widely held rule, which strengthens its offer to the opponent
gains.b: the couplet's 'folly called birth' is given a causal account it does not state: births go on because bad deeds are being eaten

note: In the Kundalakesi debate Neelakesi said the Buddha knew only by seeing, hearing and reckoning (எண்ணியும் உணர்தலால்); her hymn now praises the Jina as the one who knew without reckoning (எண்ணாது உணர்ந்தான்).
teaches: The epithet in the hymn is a debating point turned into praise: the Jina is defined by exactly the mode of knowing she denied the Buddha, so the hymn carries the earlier argument into worship.

note: The Purananuru poet names the ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort as a deed so great that killing is no longer the living Chola's own fame; Manimekalai's opening makes the hanging-fort Chola the founder of Puhar's festival of Indra.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the epic taking a Sangam war-memory of the Chola line and turning it into a sacred charter, so that a city's yearly rite rests on an ancestor's feat rather than on the reigning king.

gains.a: the epic's unnamed founder gains a lineage: he is the ancestor the Sangam court already cited by this one feat
gains.b: the poem's bare allusion to the fort-breaking ancestors gains a story in which that ancestor is Indra's ally and the patron of a festival

note: Bharatan seized a stranger merchant with goods as a spy, showed him to the king and had him killed; in this life Kovalan, a stranger with an anklet, is shown to the king as a thief and killed without inquiry.
teaches: The former deed is the present crime with the roles reversed, so Kovalan suffers exactly the false accusation he once made, and the goldsmith takes the place he once held.

note: Both say that the two kinds of deed, good and evil, leave the soul: in the Kural, for those who love the Lord's true praise; in the Neelakesi, by the way the Jina taught under the asoka tree.
teaches: Sung in the middle of Neelakesi's own praise, the verse credits release from both deeds to the teaching the Jina gave, not to the praise itself, which the couplet makes sufficient.

gains.a: the hymn's claim that merit too must go is matched by an older Tamil statement that both deeds are bonds
gains.b: the couplet's 'true praise' (பொருள்சேர் புகழ்) is shown being read as praise of a teaching to be followed

note: The patikam tells that Kanchanan, taking her for Kayachandigai, approached her and killed the prince; here she chooses that form to keep the prince away.
teaches: The disguise she takes to be free of Udayakumaran is what brings Kayachandigai's husband upon him, so her flight from the prince is the cause of his death, which the patikam names and this kaathai does not yet show.

note: Aravana Adigal told Aputhiran's death by fasting as a sun that sets in the west to rise again, with an unquenched purpose of sustaining lives; the island goddess calls the same death a killing of his own life that led others to kill theirs.
teaches: The epic gives two endorsed voices opposite verdicts on one death, the teacher's passage to a sustaining birth and the guardian's charge of killing, and leaves both standing beside the king who is its fruit.

note: Sivavakkiyar mocks the planted stone called a god and asks whether it will speak while the Lord is within; the pillar deity grants that stone and wood do not speak but says deities the wise install in them stay and speak to men.
teaches: Both start from the same premise, that the stone itself is mute; they part over whether a power can be lodged in it, the epic answering yes for guardian deities of a city and the Siddhar answering that the Lord is found only within.

gains.a: a sharp statement of the sceptic's objection that the deity's account is built to meet
gains.b: evidence that the 'speaking stone' it mocks had a worked-out defence, the deity bound to its place, rather than naive idol worship

note: Akananuru 127 credits Cheralathan with driving off the sea-foe, cutting the kadamba and carving his bow on the Himalaya; the kuravai's closing blessing hails the king of the Kudavar who ruled Kolli and the Himalaya where the bow was carved.
teaches: A deed the akam poem ties to one named Chera becomes, in the epic's blessing, an epithet of the reigning king of the Kudavar without a name, which shows a Sangam memory turned into a dynastic title; the Tamil does not say the two kings are one.

gains.a: the blessing's 'bow-inscribed Himalaya' gains its Sangam source and reads as inherited fame, not a deed of the king now ruling
gains.b: the poem's single feat is shown surviving as a formula for the whole line in a later work

note: Naladiyar 370 makes the fresh flood (புதுப்புனல்) a type of what does not last: it ends when the rain ends; Paripadal 7.84-86 prays to the Vaiyai's flood that the bathing in it may never be left (நின் படிந்து நீங்காமை).
teaches: The same new flood that the ethical quatrain uses to prove that pleasures and loves dry up is, in the festival hymn, the object of a prayer for permanence, so the pair shows the didactic poet reversing the devotional value of the river by fixing on its ending rather than its yearly return.

note: The couplet says one who slipped by not guarding beforehand will grieve later over his own fault (தன்பிழை); Kovalan, now in Madurai, grieves that he grew heedless (பொச்சாப் புண்டு) and failed his parents and his wife.
teaches: The couplet makes late regret the heedless man's whole penalty and puts the fault in him alone, while the epic has the heedless man grieve and still lose his life, and lets him ask in the same breath whether karma rather than his own lapse has brought him here.

gains.a: Kovalan's confession gains a name and a rule: his is the heedlessness whose fruit is regret that comes too late
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where regret is not the end of the penalty, and where the one who grieves over his own fault also suspects a former deed

note: Aravana Adigal teaches that seeing that no thing has a self (எப்பொருளுக்கும் ஆன்மா இலை) is the nature of release; Neelakesi asks how release and relief of pain fit a teaching that there is no soul.
teaches: The Buddhist epic makes no-self the content of release, while the Jain epic treats the same doctrine as making release impossible, since for it someone must be freed; the two verses disagree on whether release needs a subject.

note: The goddess warns the prince to give up his intent on the ascetic girl; he does not, and is cut down by the vidyadhara Kanchanan as he goes to the girl in her disguise.
teaches: The warning threatened failing rain and perishing beings, but the fruit comes as one man's sword on the prince alone, so the cosmic stakes she named collapse into a private death.

note: The Kural's woman hears the herdsman's flute as evening's envoy and a killing weapon; the epic sets the herdsmen's music and the humming bee over an evening that grieves the parted and delights the joined.
teaches: Heard together, the two show that the flute's cruelty lies in the listener's separation, not in the sound, since the same pastoral music opens a night of delight for others in the epic.

gains.a: the epic's impartial evening gains the inside of one parted listener, for whom its music is a weapon
gains.b: the couplet gains a wider scene in which its deadly flute is, for other hearers, simply the sign of nightfall

note: In Kural 1130 the woman says he lives in her heart while this town (இவ் வூர்) says he is loveless and far; in Ainkurunuru 110 the friend says we call him ours while this town (இவ்வூர்) says otherwise, and asks fate to make it so.
teaches: Both set the lovers' word against the town's, but Valluvar's woman rests in her inner certainty while the Sangam friend turns to fate to make the bond public, so the couplet's private comfort appears in the older poem as a demand for marriage.

note: The Kural defines a land as one free of severe hunger, unceasing disease and destructive enemies; the hymn says hunger, disease and enmity perish wherever the Jina goes.
teaches: The three ills the Kural treats as a test of a well-governed land are, in the Jain hymn, ended by the presence of a saint rather than by the king, so the pairing moves the source of a land's welfare from rule to holiness.

gains.a: the hymn's list of marvels is seen to answer a standard Tamil measure of a good country, not just to praise
gains.b: the couplet's measure is shown being claimed by religious polemic for the Jina's presence

note: Purananuru 55.1-2 (மலைப் பெருவில் பாம்புஞாண் ... ஒரு கணை ... மூவெயில்) and Paripadal 5.24-25 (நாகம் நாணா, மலை வில்லாக, மூவகை ஆர் எயில் ஓர் அழல்-அம்பின்) give the three-forts deed in the same parts: mountain bow, serpent string, one arrow; both also turn on Siva's forehead eye.
teaches: The same tripura formula serves a puram poet as the vehicle of counsel to a Pandya king and a devotional poet as the prelude to Murugan's birth, showing that Siva's deed was common stock usable for statecraft and worship alike in the Sangam period.

note: The couplet says her eyes would not make him tremble if her bent brows would straighten and screen them; the song says she takes lives with her bending brows, as her brothers take lives with boats.
teaches: In the Kural the curved brow is the eyes' failed guard, which could save him by straightening, while the song makes the curve itself the killer and the killing a family trade, so the pair shows the same conceit shifted from a hope of rescue to a charge of hereditary guilt.

gains.a: the song's brow-as-weapon gains the couplet's sense that the brow's bend is a fault, கோடு, the word for a bent sceptre too
gains.b: the couplet's private plea gains a social frame, a fisher girl whose people kill for a living, so the lover's charge of murder is cast as inherited rather than chosen

note: The Kural says the two kinds of dark deed do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise; Neelakesi says those who strew flowers and hymn the Aptha lose both kinds of deed and reach the state of Siva.
teaches: The couplet leaves its Lord unnamed and its reward unstated, and the epic fills both, naming the Aptha by the marks just argued for and calling the reward release, which shows how a sect could read the Kural's opening chapter as its own.

gains.a: the verse's claim that worship removes both kinds of deed is seen to rest on a widely known couplet, not on Jain doctrine alone
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed Lord and unstated outcome are given one concrete reading in a sectarian debate

note: The Vaisheshika in Manimekalai 27 lists substance and quality as separate categories, substance bearing quality; Neelakesi says the quality is the qualified substance itself and the two are both different and one.
teaches: Against the Vaisheshika separation of substance and quality, the Jain refuses both their separateness and their simple identity, so the two schools disagree on whether a quality can be counted apart from its bearer.

note: Puram 186 says the world lives not by rice or water but by its king, who must know he is its life; the minister tells the king that if he leaves, his land will cry like an infant whose mother is gone (110 to 111).
teaches: The Sangam duty that a king know himself the world's life becomes, in a Buddhist epic, the argument that holds a king back from renunciation, so the poem's maxim sets a limit even on seeking release.

gains.a: a Sangam warrant that makes the minister's plea a statement of a king's duty rather than a courtier's flattery
gains.b: an application the poem does not foresee: the king's being the world's life binds him against leaving it for a higher world

note: The Akananuru remembers Cheralathan who carved his bow on the Himalaya and heaped tribute at Maanthai; the epic's Chera of the carved bow feeds Buddhist sages in a Vanji grove. The Tamil shares only the epithet of the carved bow and the Chera line, not a name.
teaches: Holding them together shows the epic borrowing a Sangam conqueror's epithet to give Vanji's Buddhism a royal founder, turning the king remembered for hoarded tribute into a king remembered for a gift to monks.

gains.a: the nameless king of the epic gains a Sangam identity as the bow-carving conqueror, which the epic leaves unstated
gains.b: the poem's image of the conqueror's hoard gains a later legend in which the same line gives food rather than piles treasure

note: The patikam sets as the epic's third moral that a former deed comes in wrath and makes its doer eat (ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும்); Kovalan's death is told in the same words (பண்டை ஊழ்வினை உருத்து).
teaches: The moral stated as a thesis at the outset is spoken again in its own words at the death, and in the same line as the king's bent sceptre, so the epic gives its first and third morals as two causes of one event.

note: With Arkkachandra (264) Neelakesi offered right vision as the path; with Parasaran (781) the defeated man concedes in his own words and she gives him that vision.
teaches: The Neelakesi ends its debates with a gift and not only a win: the same jewel of right vision closes the Buddhist and the Sankhya sarukkams, so conversion is the form a victory takes.

note: Verse 18 states that the wise neither grieve nor exult because what is due will come; verse 19 shows a man unmoved both by a king's pardon and by a plot to kill him, naming all of it the fruit of deeds.
teaches: The maxim of 18 is put to its hardest test in 19, a reprieve and a death plot, and 19 names the cause 18 left unnamed: deeds.

note: Patitruppattu 11 likens Cheralathan's sea-raid and felling of the guarded kadambu to Murugan cutting down Sur in the sea; the epic's herdswomen tell the same Chera deed and say he churned the sea, Vishnu's deed.
teaches: Both poets lift the Chera's kadambu raid into a god's sea-deed, but each picks the god of its own setting: the Patitruppattu's war poem chooses Murugan, the herders' kuravai chooses Maal, so the same royal memory is divinised differently by genre.

gains.a: the epic's bare 'the Chera who threw down the kadambu' gains the Sangam record of who did it and how it was praised, while the epic itself does not name Neduncheralathan
gains.b: the Patitruppattu's comparison gains a later witness showing the kadambu raid still famous enough to be sung by Pandya herdswomen beside the other two crowns

note: Kannaki bids the fire god go to the wicked (ஏவ); this kaathai opens by naming the fire as ஏவல் தெய்வம், the god under command.
teaches: The title the fire bears here carries over from her command, so the burning of Madurai is presented as a god's obedience to a woman rather than as divine wrath.

note: The Kundalakesi fragment lists exposure, fire, cold, begging and matted hair as mere words and calls living subdued the true penance; Mokkalan lists sun, rain, fasting and sleeplessness as profitless.
teaches: The Buddhist dismissal of mortification, stated in the fragment as a positive ideal of restraint, appears in the Jain epic only as a negative charge that it can then answer, so the Neelakesi keeps the attack and drops the Buddhist alternative.

note: In 203 Neelakesi told Kundalakesi that a power carried from moment to moment would be a sixth thing beyond the aggregates; in 513 she says the Buddha's store of consciousness is the soul under another name.
teaches: Across two opponents the Jain argument has one shape: any carrier the Buddhist adds to explain memory and continuity is called a soul, so the store-consciousness is met with the charge first made against Kundalakesi.

note: Maalathi carries a Brahmin household's dead baby to every shrine, Saathan says the gods give no boon to those without tapas yet hands her a child by becoming it; Gotami, a Brahmin's wife with a dead son, appeals to the gods' boons and every god of the Chakravala says none can give back a life.
teaches: The two epics tell the same story of a grieving mother at Puhar's shrines with opposite endings: a god supplies a living child by illusion in one, while in the other the gods together refuse even that, and the mother dies.

note: The brahmin promises that bathing in Bhavakaarini brings knowledge of one's former birth (பழம்பிறப் பெய்துவிர்); Kavunthi asks whether he does not see in this birth what was gained in past births (இறந்த பிறப்பின் எய்திய வெல்லாம் பிறந்த பிறப்பிற் காணா யோநீ).
teaches: The Jain ascetic answers the pilgrim's offer point for point, moving knowledge of past lives from a sacred pool to the reading of one's present life, so the chapter sets two routes to one end side by side without letting either deny the other.

note: The Silappathikaram's patikam sets as a moral that the deed of the past comes in wrath and feeds its fruit (ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும்); Manimekalai uses the same verb of the prince's former killing of a cook (உருத்து எழும் வல் வினை).
teaches: The pair shows the sequel taking its companion's moral from the frame into a mechanism: here the wrathful deed is named, traced across two births and two deaths, and offered to a mourner as consolation rather than as a verdict on a king.

note: The couplet says sulking is like salt, and drawing it out a little too long is like a little too much; Kovalan's sulk, begun at the shore, is here drawn out into a refusal of her letter.
teaches: Past the couplet's 'little too much' the quarrel stops being a spoiled sweetness and becomes a verdict on the beloved's whole nature, which is how a lovers' sulk turns into the epic's break.

gains.a: the refusal gains a measure by which it is an excess of an ordinary lovers' sulk rather than a reasoned judgment of Madhavi
gains.b: the couplet gains a case showing what the excess it warns of looks like, a rereading of all past tenderness as pretence, with a cost it does not name

note: Kavunthi's penance-given curse (தவம்தரு சாபம்) turns two scorners into jackals for twelve months; Viruchikan's curse binds Kayasandigai to hunger for twelve years. Both are ascetics' curses with a fixed term, but here the cursed woman names her own ripening deed as the cause and her husband calls the curse causeless.
teaches: Set beside the Silappathikaram, where the curse simply answers an insult, the Manimekalai makes the ascetic's curse an instrument through which the victim's own karma ripens, and lets one voice call it unjust, so the curse is no longer self-justifying.

note: Both tell of the husband of Karikal's line seized by the Kaveri flood at a festival; the akam poem leaves him taken, the epic has the sea bring him back to the wife who followed.
teaches: The Sangam memory of a lover lost to the river, which an akam courtesan uses as an image of a man taken away for good, is completed in the epic with a restoration won by the wife's steadfastness, turning a story of loss into an exemplum of chastity's power.

gains.a: the clipped allusion gains its back-story: the flood at Kazhar before Karikal in which the husband was seized
gains.b: the akam image gains a later ending in which the sea gives back what the river took, showing how the tale was retold as a chastity legend

note: Both recite the Chola line's ancestors, the king who entered the scale for the dove and the one who destroyed the hanging fort; the puram poem praises a Chola who withered the Chera's unwithering Vanchi, the epic has a Brahmin recite the same lineage in the Chera's own court.
teaches: The praise of the dove-king's line, which in the Sangam poem celebrates a Chola's victory over Vanchi, is spoken in the epic before the king of Vanchi as a pledge that the Chola's sceptre is sound, so the formula once used against the Chera now serves an alliance between cousins.

gains.a: Maadalan's assurance gains its source: a fixed Chola praise in which the dove, the fort and the just sceptre go together
gains.b: the puram formula gains a later use in which the rival it once mocked hears it as reassurance

note: The goddess told Manimekalai that Udayakumaran is her Rahula and that her mind has not left him; here she bows to him as her former husband and admits her heart goes to him.
teaches: The attachment the goddess predicted is admitted openly rather than denied, and Manimekalai turns the former husband's claim on her obedience into the occasion for her refusal.

note: The couplet says that if the sky fails, hunger stays and torments the wide world; the deity foretells the bowl of dharma that gives rain's plenty to a parched world.
teaches: Where the couplet treats hunger after drought as beyond remedy, the epic answers it with organized charity, the begging bowl standing in for the failed rain.

gains.a: a statement of the stakes: drought brings hunger even to a world ringed with water
gains.b: a remedy the couplet does not consider, feeding by alms when the sky fails

note: The Manimekalai's Jain says each thing is both lasting and passing and has arising, staying and perishing (தோற்றமும் நிலையும் கேடும்); 803 names the three as மும்மை.
teaches: A Buddhist epic's report and a Jain epic's own argument agree on the triad as the Jain signature, which shows the Buddhist account of this doctrine is faithful where the Jain uses it.

claims.gist: being worshipped by Indra does not by itself make one the supreme Lord
humans of the small island lands, wanting in qualities, do not attain the higher state even by great penance
when a god's door stays shut the king's justice has failed
a king answers for the wrongs his servants do in his name
awareness and pleasure arise from the combined elements as intoxication arises in liquor
when the combination breaks up, each element returns to its own kind and nothing survives
the four elements are built up from atoms, and smell and the other sense qualities belong to them
if there is no path, no merit and no fruit, arguing for that view is itself pointless
if wasting the body were meritorious, burning oneself, leaping from a height or wasting with disease would count as penance
one of right faith is free of the three follies and the eight prides and praises no false object out of love, fear or desire
preaching great compassion while eating fish and flesh is self-contradictory
the truth the Buddha saw is the void
hunger destroys birth, dignity, learning, modesty and beauty
giving to those able to repay is selling dharma; the true way is to end the hunger of the helpless
those who give food give life
drink, lying, lust, killing and deceit are what the wise renounce, and a life built on them is base
one generality cannot be present whole in endless separate things
the cave opens to one who keeps the hill god's feet in mind and walks round the hill three times
a woman of chaste family guards herself as maiden, wife and widow and worships no god but her husband
it is royal custom for a prince to bind a courtesan and silence her false talk
if all that is to come is already present, a woman's unborn daughter must already hold her own daughter, and so without end, which is absurd
after a moment perishes its powers pass into the next, as flower scent stays in a pot
hell-beings who thirst find nothing to relieve them
a deed of a former time flares up and brings death even on an infant
a wife who does not sulk when her husband unites with another shows the great chastity of a noble woman
atoms that occupy one and the same place can become many and take form without being divided
one is saved by cutting the chain of dependent arising
a strong deed, once sown like a seed, returns to its doer and cannot be put off when it clings
life stays in the body no longer than a lamp in a windy open place
souls are freed from the bundle of births only when the light of the Jina's spoken teaching reaches them
each god is to be worshipped with its own distinct rites by those who know the way
debaters of rival schools should part without hatred or quarrel even from those who reject their view
souls are of distinct colours and fixed great numbers
mahat is what gives rise to the sense of 'I' and 'mine'
only a sentient thing can bring a thought into being
one who eats flesh to fatten his body has no compassion
the aggregates form one inseparable whole
parts that are inseparable must be the qualities of one bearer, and that bearer is the soul
Makkali is the Lord
the Ajivika scripture is the nine books called Kathir
the subtle categories are five
the working of the categories is fixed
composite things are only names for collections, with no single thing there
one who names what he holds unreal speaks falsely every time he names it
to call a thing inexpressible is itself to express it, so the claim defeats itself
feelings and moral qualities are not made by the material elements
the Veda is self-existent, made by no one
one of Sudra birth has no competence to speak on the Veda
the omniscient's knowledge grasps many distinct things through their likeness and difference without fault
on the Buddhist account there would be neither this birth nor the next
a ripening evil deed draws its bearer to the place where it will come to fruit
those who are born meet growing suffering and those not born meet the greatest bliss
suffering comes from attachment and bliss is reached by those freed of it
the five precepts are the way to be saved

note: Neelakesi's fiery body enters another body like a shadow; Tirumular's light born in the womb spreads through the earthly body like a bubble in water, a shadow, and the eight take hold.
teaches: Writers of opposed schools both picture the subtle body that passes into a new one as a shadow, which shows they agreed rebirth needs a subtle carrier and differed only on what it is made of, the Jain fiery and karmic bodies or Tirumular's eight.

gains.a: the Jain doctrine of the subtle bodies is seen to have a Saiva counterpart, so the debate does not turn on whether a subtle body exists
gains.b: Tirumular's obscure bubble-and-shadow line gets a plain statement of a shadow-like body entering another

note: Kural 255 says hell will not open its mouth to release the flesh-eater; Neelakesi 97 shows the flesh-eater burning inside the fire's mouth, crying out.
teaches: The couplet's closed mouth of hell, read beside the epic, becomes a place one is held and burned in, and the epic shows that the Kural's verdict falls on the eater as a sinner in his own right, not only on the killer.

gains.a: the epic's charge against eating flesh gains the Kural's warrant that eating, not only killing, keeps one in hell
gains.b: the couplet's bare image of a mouth that will not open gains a picture of what is suffered inside it

note: The idyll names the courtesans' many deceiving lies and hidden embraces and their draining of rich young men, but lists them among the splendours of the city; the Kural likens the false embrace of women who sell themselves to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room.
teaches: The deceit the Kural turns into horror was already admitted, in the same terms of lying and false embrace, by the court poet, who still counted it as part of the city's wealth, so the moralist's chapter answers a practice that praise poetry had treated as a sign of prosperity.

note: The Buddhist teacher in the Manimekalai accepts only two means of knowledge, perception and inference; Neelakesi says a teacher who knew only through the senses and reasoning lacks subtle knowledge and his word is no scripture.
teaches: The same restriction to perception and inference that the Buddhist offers as rigour is, from the Jain side, the proof that its founder was not omniscient and so cannot ground a scripture.

note: The Manimekalai's drunk pleads with an unwashed Jain ascetic (மண்ணா மேனியன்) that his soul should not suffer in a filthy body; the Neelakesi answers that dirt on the body is nothing to correct, since adornment hinders meditation.
teaches: The unwashed Jain ascetic was a stock target in the Buddhist-Jain quarrel: the Buddhist epic mocks it through a drunkard's pity, and the Jain epic gives the reply, that the filth is the body's own and attending to it is the real distraction.

note: Both are Kayamanar's poems of the mothers left after an elopement: in 189 the foster mother wanders the house and says the town has lost its treasure; in 195 the birth mother claims her years of care and asks the diviner which house the pair will reach first.
teaches: Read together the two mothers' griefs differ in kind: the foster mother mourns a public loss, while the birth mother, conceding she has no claim on the youth, turns grief into a practical question about the return, which shows the elopement already moving toward an accepted marriage.

note: Vellaikkudi Naganar tells the Chola that the world blames kings when rain fails and bids him ignore such talk and guard the ploughmen; Senguttuvan names rain failing and a life wronged as the protector-king's two great fears.
teaches: The Sangam counsellor treats blame for drought as unfair public talk a just king can bear, while the epic king takes the same burden inward as fear and ranks one wronged life above drought, so that kingship itself becomes suffering.

gains.a: the king's lament gains a known royal topos, the king answerable for rain, against which his ranking of a wronged life above drought stands out
gains.b: the poem's advice to set aside blame gains a counter-voice: a king who, after seeing a Pandya die of one wrong verdict, finds the burden unbearable rather than ignorable

note: In kaathai 7 the goddess tells the prince that a bent sceptre unsettles the planets, the rain and the people's lives, and bids him drop his designs on the ascetic girl; here he recalls only a woman showing a sceptre and wonders if she was a god.
teaches: The warning that tied the prince's lust to the kingdom's rain reaches him only as an image he cannot interpret, which is what lets the courtesan laugh it away and sets up his ruin.

note: Kannaki's dream of a harm to the city with the king, which she would not speak of, is fulfilled in the burning of the Pandya's house and Madurai.
teaches: The harm she refused to name in her dream turns out to be her own act, so the omen foretold not only the city's fall but the part the dreamer would play in it.

note: The Naladiyar's ascetic's bowl (தவசி கடிஞை) is filled slowly at door after door by householders' small gifts; Manimekalai's bowl, held by a renunciant, never fails and only the takers' hands tire.
teaches: Set together, the two bowls reverse the flow between householder and ascetic: the quatrain's begging bowl is the image of a giver's merit filling, while the epic's is an ascetic's vessel that gives without end.

gains.a: the bowl's inexhaustibility is seen against the ordinary begging bowl it inverts, which the epic never needs to describe
gains.b: the quatrain's image of the slowly filled bowl gains its opposite, which shows that its point is about the giver's accumulation, not the bowl

note: The herders liken Kovalan and Kannaki to the dark god and the lamp of their clan who relieved his distress; in the next kaathai Maadari dances the kuravai of Krishna and Pinnai so that Kannaki may see it, to ward off a coming harm.
teaches: The herders' wonder at their guests becomes a rite: having seen the couple as Krishna and his consort, they dance that pair's kuravai to avert the harm their omens foretell, which has already fallen.

note: The preface to the Patitruppattu's fifth decade says Senguttuvan went through the forests to take a stone for the goddess Pattini, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed it in the Ganga; the Manimekalai names the stone, the Ganga crossing and the defeat of Kanaka and Vijaya.
teaches: The pair shows the stone-taking already fixed as the defining deed of this Chera in two different kinds of text, and shows the Manimekalai using that known deed only to date and dignify the city where its own Buddhist story continues.

gains.a: the epic's brief royal praise gains a second witness that its Senguttuvan is the Chera of the Sangam decade's preface
gains.b: the preface's one line on the Pattini stone gains the names of the defeated kings and the crowning detail that the epic tradition attached to it

note: Saathuvan lets the chief stop killing yet still eat beasts that die of old age; Neelakesi holds that flesh is itself a fault and that its renunciation by all would end the killing.
teaches: For the Buddhist story the wrong lies in the killing, so meat from a natural death is allowed, while for the Jain debater eating is wrong in itself because it is what keeps killing going; the two epics draw the line at different acts.

note: The Naladiyar says a husband cannot put away even a wife without good qualities; Neelakesi treats the bodhisattva's giving away of his wives as the act of a man no bond restrains.
teaches: Her charge depends on the household norm the quatrain states, that a wife is not the husband's to dispose of, and applies it to judge a renouncer's gift, which the quatrain never contemplates.

gains.a: the polemic's force is traced to a shared Tamil view of marriage rather than to Jain doctrine alone
gains.b: the quatrain's bond of marriage is shown to set a limit even on religious giving

note: The Thinaimalai man says the girl guarding drying fish turns weapon-eyes on him and it is he, not the fish, she guards; the vari says the goddess who afflicts those who see her driving birds from drying fish has taken a woman's form.
teaches: The same fish-guarding girl is a wry reversal of guarding in the akam verse and a goddess in disguise in the epic song, so the pair shows the neithal scene moving from the lover's joke to a performance piece of supernatural praise.

gains.a: the stanza gains its plain source scene, in which the girl's task and the man's capture are human and comic
gains.b: the akam verse gains a later form in which its girl is lifted into an anangu, showing how the stock scene was elevated in courtly song

note: Kural 225 ranks the strength to bear hunger below the strength to remove it; Aputhiran, who lives on begged food, grieves not at his own hunger but at finding no means to remove the travellers', and it is then that the goddess gives him the bowl.
teaches: Together they show the couplet's higher strength given to a man with no wealth at all: the epic makes the power to end others' hunger a gift answering grief, not a store of means, which the couplet's comparison of two strengths leaves unexamined.

gains.a: a rule that explains why the goddess answers his grief at not feeding others rather than his own need
gains.b: a case where the higher strength is wanted by one who has only the lower, so the couplet's ranking becomes a longing rather than a description of the rich

note: The pillar deity told Manimekalai that the prince's death came from his killing of the cook who broke the vessels meant for the sage Brahmadharma; Manimekalai now passes that revelation to the prince's mother.
teaches: The same account of a past killing changes use between the two kaathais: revealed to the lover as the reason for his death, it is retold to the mother as the reason not to hate the woman she blamed for it.

note: Kavunthi gave Kannaki as a ward to the herdswoman and charged her to bathe, dress and mother her; Maadari here receives her as a ward, has her bathed and settles her.
teaches: The ascetic's charge is carried out point by point, so the refuge fails not through any lapse of the guardian but on the very day she is kept as promised, and the harm comes from the city's justice, not the host's house.

note: Akananuru 238 names Nalli for rain-like giving of chariots and elephants to suppliants (மழைசுரந் தன்ன ஈகை) as a simile's backdrop; 150 tells one of his gifts in full, a chain from his chest given to a ragged poet in the forest.
teaches: The akam epithet compresses into a formula of chariots and elephants a fame that the puram poem shows was made of personal, unannounced gifts, so the akam poet's shorthand assumes hearers who knew stories like 150.

note: The couplet says a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon; the epic's moonrise says the moon's spot shows like a fault in the worthy.
teaches: The epic can use the couplet's moral as the familiar term of a comparison for the sky, which shows the saying was common enough to be turned round.

gains.a: The odd simile of a moon's spot shown like a worthy man's fault gets its source and its direction.
gains.b: The couplet is seen working as a known saying that a narrative poet could invert in passing.

note: The Alarpadu Kaathai ends with the goddess of Madurai appearing before (முன்) the pathini, unable to bear the fire; here she will not stand before her and appears behind her, being the Pandya's family goddess.
teaches: Read together, the goddess's first coming is driven by the fire, but her place behind Kannaki shows that the city's deity arrives as an embarrassed advocate of the guilty king's house.

note: On the road Kovalan, reading Madhavi's letter, says the fault was his own; before the king, Kannaki says ஊழ்வினை drove him to Madurai.
teaches: The pair shows the epic giving Kovalan's ruin two causes in two voices: his own confession of fault, made privately to clear the courtesan, and his wife's public appeal to former deeds, made to indict the king, so neither account stands alone as the poem's verdict.

note: In 583 Neelakesi objects that the lac colour put on the seed does not reach even the sprout, yet the Buddha says it settles in the flower; in 601 the Buddha replies that the power hides in between, hard to see, and appears in the flower.
teaches: The Buddha's defence of karmic transfer rests on an unseen passage, which is exactly what Neelakesi's empirical objection denied, so the dispute becomes one over whether what cannot be seen may be posited.

note: Puram 9 praises a Pandya who before battle bids cows, brahmin-natured men, women, the sick and the sonless take shelter; the Chola's dictum spares, after battle, men who have made themselves look like non-killers.
teaches: The old dharma of war spares people by what they are, but the epic shows warriors claiming that shelter by what they wear, and a king using the rule not to restrain himself but to belittle another king's captives.

gains.a: the Chola's taunt gains its ground: an old Tamil rule that war is not waged on those who do not fight
gains.b: the poem's list gains a hard case it does not foresee, defeated fighters who step into the spared class by disguise

note: Both kings open a northern march by moving sword and umbrella at a chosen hour: the Chola with his drum to find foes for his arms, the Chera toward the Himalaya for a stone.
teaches: The Chola went north wanting only enemies for his shoulders, was stopped by the mountain and left his tiger carved on it, while the Chera goes with a cause, a pathini and an insult to Tamil, and carries a stone away from the mountain, so the epic's second northern march gives a moral reason to the rite the first performed for glory alone.

note: Neelakesi sets out to debate in order to do compassion (தயா செய்தற் பொருட்டாக); in the debate she asks whether one who let his own calf die has compassion (தயா) for others.
teaches: The debate is a contest over who owns compassion: the Jain debater's mission is framed as தயா, and her attack denies the Buddha the same virtue.

note: The couplet bids one see the true thing whatever nature (தன்மை) a thing appears to have; the Buddhist teacher strips perception of name, class, quality and action and assigns them to inference.
teaches: On the Buddhist account the 'nature' the couplet looks past is largely the mind's own labelling, so seeing the true thing becomes a matter of separating bare perception from what inference adds.

gains.a: the technical definition of perception gains a moral aim: the true thing the couplet calls understanding
gains.b: the couplet's open word தன்மை gains one precise reading, as the class, quality and name the mind lays on what it sees

note: Kovalan meets a humped bull in the street and does not know it as an ill omen; in the next kaathai the herdswomen see the tears of their humped bull and say a harm is coming.
teaches: The same beast gives the same warning to two kinds of people, and only the herders, whose knowledge it is, read it, so the epic makes reading the omen a matter of birth and has the warning understood only after the harm is done.

note: Neelakesi first argues that a silent omniscient leaves his books without authority; in 685 she adds that if silence proved full knowledge, children, trees and mountains would share it.
teaches: The attack on the silent Lord has two steps: silence cuts off the scripture, and silence cannot serve as evidence of knowledge, so the Ajivika is left with neither a speaking teacher nor a proof of his teacher.

note: The couplet says the woman who wore anicham flowers with their stems will hear no good drums for her waist; Kovalan asks why her attendants loaded her with garland, musk and pearls, making her small waist suffer.
teaches: The epic takes the Kural's single joke of a waist too fine to bear flowers and spreads it over a whole toilette, moving the lover's praise from the secret meeting into the marriage chamber, where it is the husband who speaks it and the maids who are blamed.

gains.a: Kovalan's catalogue gains a known convention behind it, so its reproach of the attendants reads as praise in the established form of நலம்புனைந்துரைத்தல்
gains.b: the couplet gains a speaker and setting it lacks, a husband in the first days of marriage, showing the convention used outside the lovers' secret union

note: Both epics place in Puhar a spirit that seizes the wicked with its noose, beats them and devours them; in the Silappathikaram it punishes named sins, in Manimekalai it is one of the powers the festival keeps appeased.
teaches: The same noose-bearing spirit changes office between the two epics: a moral police against hypocrites and false witnesses in the first becomes, in the second, a power whose goodwill depends on the city keeping its festival.

note: Both heroines of the debate epics take another woman's form: Neelakesi takes a princess's shape to break a sage's vow, Manimekalai took Kayachandigai's shape to teach her former husband birth and death and end his karma.
teaches: The Jain and Buddhist epics use the same device of a borrowed body to opposite ends, one to bind a man in desire and one to free him from it, so the borrowed form itself is neutral and the intent decides.

note: Kundalakesi 4 calls nakedness, ash, fire and fasting mere talk and tapas a restrained life; the epic shows a naked fasting ascetic in the street, cared for unseen lives and begged to drink by a drunk.
teaches: The two Buddhist works keep their distance from bodily austerity by different means, argument in the fragment and street scene in the epic, and the epic allows the naked ascetic a real virtue, his pity for unseen lives, that the fragment's dismissal leaves out.

note: Kovalan's Kaveri proves her chastity by not sulking when the Chola unites with the Ganga; Madhavi's Kaveri walks as she does because her husband's sceptre never bends.
teaches: Sung back over the same river, the two stanzas put the burden of fidelity on opposite partners: Kovalan asks the wife to bear the husband's other union, Madhavi makes the river's grace the sign of a husband who keeps straight, so the exchange is a quarrel about who owes faithfulness.

note: The quatrain's old deed seeks out its own doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Kannaki laments a deed to be eaten that reached her husband through the king's fault.
teaches: Where the quatrain sends the deed straight back to the one who did it, the epic interposes a guilty king between deed and fruit, so karma and the ruler's fault both stand as causes of one death.

gains.a: Kannaki's 'deed that must be eaten' gains the quatrain's account of how a deed finds its owner
gains.b: the quatrain gains a case where the deed arrives through another's wrongdoing, which its image of the calf leaves out

note: Kural 872: take on the enmity of ploughmen whose plough is the bow rather than of those whose plough is the word. Thinaimozhi 17: the woman fears for her man passing the hamlets of those who live by ploughing with the bow, while her shoulders slacken because he left without grace.
teaches: The Kural ranks the bow-ploughmen as the lesser enemy, and the venba agrees in its own way: the bowmen are only a feared danger on his road, while the wound she actually bears, slackened shoulders, comes from his word, the promise and grace he withheld.

note: The hunters close their rite praying that the Pandya of Pothiyil wear the vetchi and ruin other lands; in Madurai the same king's sceptre fails and he falls dead before Kannaki.
teaches: The blessing asks for victory over others' lands, but the king's ruin comes from within his own court; the forest rite that hailed Kannaki as the goddess has, unknowing, blessed the king she will undo.

note: Neelakesi mocks a teacher who calls release emptiness (சூனியம்); the Idaikkadar Siddhar tells the soul that clinging to what became the void (சூனியமான அத்தை) is beyond compare.
teaches: The void that the Jain debater treats as an absurd account of release is, for a later Siddhar, the goal itself, so the word changes from a target of ridicule to a name of the highest state.

gains.a: the ridicule is seen to target a word that later Tamil mystics would claim for release
gains.b: the Siddhar's void is placed against an older debate in which calling release empty was a charge to answer

note: Manimekalai asks the Jain for his lord, his categories, their workings, and bondage and release; Neelakesi asks the Ajivika for his teacher, scripture, categories and their workings.
teaches: Both epics question rival schools by nearly the same heads, but the Jain examiner puts scripture in place of bondage and release, and her first attack (680) falls on the scripture, so the choice of heads already aims the refutation.

note: The akam heroine asks that, when this life turns into the next, the same man be her husband and she the one close to his heart; the goddess tells Manimekalai that exactly this has come about, her heart still bound to her former husband, and calls it seed falling on scorched saline ground.
teaches: The bond across births that the akam poem asks for as the highest pledge of love is, in the Buddhist epic, the very danger to the merit that would end births, so the same wish is fulfilled and judged a loss.

gains.a: The goddess's verdict is seen to overturn a fixed ideal of Tamil love poetry, not just a passing desire of the prince.
gains.b: The heroine's vow gets a sequel in which it is granted, and its cost, the turning of rebirth into a trap, is shown.

note: Manimekalai's disguise as Kaayasandigai leads Kaanchanan, Kaayasandigai's husband, to think the prince is courting his wife and to kill him; the pillar goddess then calls the death ஊழ்வினை and blames Kaanchanan.
teaches: The disguise that protects Manimekalai's vow becomes the means of the prince's death, and the epic assigns the death to past deeds while still holding the killer guilty, so her innocent act is one link in a chain of karma.

note: In Puram 72 the Sangam Pandya Nedunjeliyan of Talaiyalanganam curses himself, should he fail in his vow, to be a king whose people find no cool shade and spread his blame (குடிபழி தூற்றும்); the epic's Madurai spreads the blame of its king (மன்பழி தூற்றுங் குடி) and finds his cool umbrella breeding heat. The two kings share a title, not an identity: the epic's Nedunjeliyan is not the Sangam one.
teaches: The Sangam king's conditional self-curse, a boast of what will never happen, becomes in the epic a description of what has happened to a later Pandya, so the formula of royal disgrace moves from oath to fulfilment.

gains.a: the citizens' words gain the weight of an old Pandya oath that names exactly this disgrace
gains.b: the oath's imagined penalty gains a story showing a Pandya city actually blaming its king

note: Manimekala told the sleeping Sudhamathi that within seven days Lakshmi, her younger sister, would come knowing her own birth and Sudhamathi's; here Manimekalai rises from the seat knowing that birth.
teaches: The goddess's promise to a third person is kept before Manimekalai knows it was made, so the recognition at the seat is staged as the second prophecy fulfilled in the chapter, not a private vision.

claims.gist: nothing at all is pure
one who kills a man mistaking him for his enemy incurs no karma of killing
a death that one's deed causes is a killing whatever the doer took the victim to be
bodies in hell cut by blades rejoin like water
steady praise of the Lord's shrine is the best course
an evil mind leads to burning suffering and a worthy one to bliss, as lac on a pomegranate seed reddens its flower
wherever there is awareness and pleasure, a soul is joined there
hair and nails grow though they have no life, so growth does not prove that trees live
hair grows only while the soul dwells in the body
a reason that proves the opposite of the property to be proved is contradictory
a reason that undoes the intended specific character of the property to be proved is contradictory
the senses exist for the sake of another, the self, because they are aggregates, as beds and seats are
seeing the three kinds of suffering together is the noble truth
one who teaches that all is suffering cannot claim to give others joy
at the gods' entreaty in Tushita a Buddha will be born after 1616 years and his dharma will again fill the world
if inherence joined qualities from outside, any quality could be joined to any thing
what is wholly non-existent cannot come to arise
whatever is faultless in the other schools' words is already contained in the Jina's scripture
the mind (intention) alone is karma, and the bodily act is not karma
bodily action is karma too, not only the mind behind it
a being of five aggregates continues as a god or a hell-dweller according to wholesome or unwholesome deeds
all lovers who have quarrelled must reunite, for that is the love god's command
those who complete hard austerity are born again to enjoy a land of plenty such as Uttarakuru
the soul knows only matter that the senses reach, and what they do not reach does not exist
what lies beyond the senses is known only through scripture
a wife who does not sulk when her husband unites with another keeps a woman's lasting chastity
memory of past experience is not the effect of any perceptible element
the organs of action are counted as organs because they act
when pulse and water are cooked into one dish both undergo change, so neither alone can be said to persist unchanged
the dharma of compassion, taught, ends the suffering of the world
knowing objects does not bind karma unless the binding activity is present
what is called a person is five aggregates: form, feeling, consciousness, perception and formation
nothing abides; each thing perishes of itself at once, like the tip of a flame
the Buddha takes on suffering to remove the inescapable suffering of others, and this is his compassion
one who knows the states of birth and the nature of souls does not fear other beings, who are like housemates and kin
nothing is ever made known except through its qualities, so the soul need not be shown apart from them
the Veda has neither beginning nor end
birth is a disease and dharma is its unfailing medicine
if the one god is every creature, he is the doer of all their harms and so an evil god
the dharma taught by a teacher cures a being as medicine cures the sick
one who eats flesh without intending harm to any creature incurs no evil deed
the seller kills for the buyer's price, so the eater's lack of intent does not free him from the killing
if revered brahmin seers were born of a courtesan, a mother's lapse cannot debase her son
one not born of a proper brahmin union is unfit for Vedic study
being formless, the soul is held in the body as formless consciousness is
taking up austerity and hearing the dharma lead to the cutting off of becoming
souls suffer birth, aging, disease and death in a sea made of the evil deeds they themselves did
the Jina's teaching is the raft by which souls cross that sea
the Jain ascetic's feathers are gathered after they fall, harming no bird, which is unlike eating flesh
the horn's absence in the calf is the prior non-existence of a state, while the substance persists throughout
the birth of a meritorious king brings back the rain and ends hunger

note: The Kundalakesi praises the Buddha as one who kept nothing for himself and toiled only for others; Neelakesi takes the bodhisattva's gift of himself and his wives as proof of a man bound by nothing.
teaches: The same total self-giving is the Buddhist invocation's ground of worship and the Jain debater's first charge, which shows the quarrel was over whether others (a wife) can be given as one's own.

note: The Kural says those who have learned and seen the true thing reach the path of not coming back here; Mokkalan asks what makes non-return final, and Neelakesi answers that karma returns only through yoga activity, which the freed soul lacks.
teaches: The Kural names the path of no return without saying what keeps it closed, and the debate supplies a mechanism: return needs the inflow of karma through activity, which release has ended.

gains.a: The Jain answer is set against the general Tamil promise of a path of no return, showing which part of that promise it explains.
gains.b: The couplet's 'not coming back' is tested by the objection that a lasting freed self could be bound again.

note: In 516 Neelakesi tells the Buddha that sound travels until it reaches the ear; in 760 she tells the Sankhya that sound has form and so cannot belong to space.
teaches: The same Jain premise, that sound is matter, does the work against two opponents: it makes sound travel against the Buddhist and keeps it out of formless space against the Sankhya.

note: In 736 the Sankhya says the soul does nothing, has no quality, is eternal and present everywhere; in 765 Neelakesi uses that all-presence to deny that soul and nature ever newly join.
teaches: The opponent's own praise of the soul as everywhere present becomes the premise that undoes his account of creation by union, since a thing never absent cannot newly arrive.

note: Senguttuvan has the image of the pathini goddess carved from the Himalayan stone and installed in her shrine; the Manimekalai's shrine holds an image of both Kannaki and Kovalan, and the goddess in it speaks.
teaches: Where the Silappathikaram's royal shrine sets up Kannaki alone as a goddess of the realm, the Manimekalai makes the image a family one with the father beside her, fit for a daughter's prayer, which reshapes the cult toward the household the later epic cares about.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives seed, sprout and stalk all called paddy as the example of naming by continuity (தொடர்ச்சி); Neelakesi grants seed-to-flower continuity only because a long branch joins them without a gap.
teaches: The Buddhist example of continuity works only where the stages touch, and Neelakesi uses that condition to deny that it reaches across death to a new body.

note: Here the lute passes into Madhavi's hand in a bower set up for pleasure; in the next kaathai the songs she sings on it make Kovalan think her false, and, his ūzhvinai coming to fruit, he leaves her on the shore.
teaches: The instrument and the place prepared for the lovers' pleasure become the means and site of their parting, which the next kaathai assigns to karma acting through the lute's music.

note: 392 asks what bears arising, persisting and perishing; 403 applies the answer to the calf and the bull, whose horn arises while the substance persists.
teaches: The abstract triad of 392 to 393 is turned into a test case in 403, which shows what the Jain means by persistence: the animal's substance, not its horn.

note: Aathirai enters the pyre to go where her husband's deeds have carried him, but the fire will not touch her and a voice says he lives; Neelakesi 218 names the wife's death with her husband as the absurd end of praising futile death.
teaches: Neither epic lets a wife's death on the pyre stand as achieved virtue, the Jain by argument and the Buddhist by a fire that refuses her, yet the Manimekalai gives the karmic motive the Neelakesi's reductio leaves out.

note: Both give the Jain doctrine that a thing persists in kind while its form arises and perishes: the Manimekalai's Jain with gram cooked into a dish and the sprouting neem, Neelakesi with a gold pot remade as a crown, applied to the soul passing from man to god.
teaches: On arising, persistence and destruction the Buddhist epic's report of the Jains matches a Jain debater's own illustration, so here the polemical account is one the school would accept, and the Neelakesi shows it was aimed at the soul's rebirth.

note: The sage resolves to make her understand her own powerlessness (திறமின்மை); she ends by confessing she cannot touch him.
teaches: His plan is carried out without any act of his: her own failed terrors teach her the powerlessness he meant her to learn.

note: Neelakesi asks what cause brings the elements together, since they cannot join themselves; Tirumular sets unknowing maya beside the knowing soul and calls the making of elements and senses the fivefold work of grace.
teaches: Both texts deny that unknowing matter assembles itself into a knower, but where the Jain debater leaves the cause in the soul and its deeds, the Saiva verse gives it to grace.

gains.a: Neelakesi's open question gains the answer a rival theist school gives, showing which answer the Jain debater leaves unsaid.
gains.b: Tirumular's assignment of elements and senses to grace gains the opponent it presupposes: the materialist for whom the elements need no cause at all.

note: 255 mocks those who eat a creature's flesh once it has died; Kural 258 says those of faultless sight do not eat flesh that has parted from life.
teaches: The Kural's phrase 'flesh parted from life' already covers the Buddhist allowance for meat from an animal that died, so the Jain jibe can claim the couplet's authority against that defence.

gains.a: the sneer at eating the dead creature gains a stated principle that even flesh already lifeless is refused
gains.b: the couplet's wording is shown to answer a specific sectarian defence of meat from animals already dead

note: Kural 261 makes bearing pain one half of penance; Mokkalan argues that if wasting the body were good, burning or wasting with disease would also be penance.
teaches: The reductio bites only if the couplet's pain is pain one inflicts on oneself; if it is the pain that comes unsought, the Kural and the Buddhist agree, so the pairing shows that the couplet's word உற்ற decides which side it is on.

gains.a: Mokkalan's argument gains a precise target: a definition of penance in which enduring pain is half the whole
gains.b: the couplet's ambiguity about whose pain is meant is shown to matter, since a rival school's objection falls on one reading and not the other

note: Puram 264 tells of a hero-stone set up on gravelly ground, crowned with a red flower garland and peacock feathers, with the fallen man's name carved; the epic's kaathai named நடுகல் installs a stone from the Himalaya as a jewelled image with priests and daily rites.
teaches: The epic takes the hero-stone rite, raised by herdsmen for a fallen fighter, and gives it to a woman whose power is chastity, enlarging it with Brahmin sacrifice and a temple, so the old rite of the warrior becomes the founding of a goddess's cult.

gains.a: the kaathai's title gains its source in the rite it adapts: stone, garland, offering
gains.b: the poem's simple rite is shown transformed into temple worship of a pathini

note: The Manimekalai's teacher makes release the seeing that the links are sorrow, unstable and without self; the Neelakesi's Jain argues that momentariness would make release the mere perishing of each moment.
teaches: Set beside the Buddhist epic's own account, the Jain charge is seen to aim at a version of Buddhism the Buddhist teacher would not own, since there release is an insight gained by those who see impermanence, not the impermanence itself.

note: The opening sermon names standpoints (நயன்) among the doors through which the soul and its qualities are examined; 819 and 820 use the standpoints to settle the quality question and win the opponent.
teaches: The sermon's list of methods is not decoration: the standpoint it names is the very tool that ends the Vaisheshika debate, by making one and different two views of one thing.

note: 116 names the triple discipline as the medicine for the diseases of birth; 724 names birth as the disease, bad deeds as its cause and true understanding as its cure.
teaches: The sermon's medical scheme is not left in the opening: at the close of a debate it is the frame in which the defeated opponent is offered treatment rather than condemnation.

note: Manimekalai shows the prince an old woman's body and says flowers, sandal, cloth and jewels hide its flesh; the Neelakesi's sage tells the adorned woman herself that her bath, scents, jewels and garlands only cover filth with skin.
teaches: The Buddhist and Jain epics use one argument with the roles reversed: in the Manimekalai a woman ascetic cures a man's lust, in the Neelakesi a male ascetic rebuffs a woman's, and here the body he unmasks is itself a borrowed disguise.

note: The quatrain says not even ascetics (உறுவர்) can remove what must befall; the epic shows an ascetic who sees the couple's coming fate by his inner lamp and tells them the deed cannot be put off.
teaches: The pair shows the quatrain's limit on ascetic power from the ascetic's side: the Charana knows, does not grieve, and states the rule himself instead of trying to avert the fate.

gains.a: the Charana's silence about the couple's fate gains a reason: by the quatrain's rule his knowing could not change it
gains.b: the quatrain's general uruvar gains a named scene where a seer meets those whose fate he foresees

note: Kovalan tells Kannaki in their bridal chamber that the swan, beaten by her gentle gait, hid among the lotus pools; in the kaanal vari he tells the swan not to follow a fisher girl, whose walk it cannot match.
teaches: The same compliment Kovalan gave his bride is given, with Madhavi listening, to an imagined shore girl, so the pair shows how readily his praise moves from one woman to another, the very thing Madhavi then reads as a hidden meaning.

note: Naladiyar 37 says the gains of human birth are many and should be used for the world beyond; Neelakesi 86 says only the humans of the land of deeds can reach bliss by penance.
teaches: The quatrain treats human birth as one opportunity, while the epic splits humanity by land and says the gain of release belongs only to those born where deeds and penance are possible.

gains.a: the epic's cosmological sorting of humans gains an ethical point: it matters where one is born because only there can the human gain be used
gains.b: the quatrain's general 'gains of human birth' gains a limit it does not state, that not every human birth carries them

note: Both tell a king that the rulers before him, many and mighty, are all gone; Puram 363 concludes that he must renounce the whole sea-bounded world before death, Maadalan that he must perform a great sacrifice and rule for aeons.
teaches: The same proof from dead kings yields opposite counsel: the Sangam poet's impermanence ends in giving up the kingdom, the epic's brahmin's in a rite that keeps the king on the throne, so the argument alone does not decide between renunciation and ritual.

gains.a: Maadalan's sermon is seen to stop short of the conclusion the older poem draws from the same premise
gains.b: the poem's call to renounce is set against a counsellor who uses its argument for a royal sacrifice

note: The Kural likens the learned who cannot unfold their learning to scentless flowers; Neelakesi ranks a silent omniscient below any man who tells the good he sees.
teaches: The couplet faults those unable to expound, and the verse extends the fault to one who could speak and chooses not to, turning a rule about scholars into a test of a god.

gains.a: the verse's mockery gains a recognised Tamil norm that knowledge counts only when it is passed on, which the debate itself never states
gains.b: the couplet, which speaks of inability, gains a case of deliberate silence and a use of its standard in judging a religious founder

note: The Kural asks what a virtuous householder would gain by going the outside way; the Neelakesi's ideal land has virtuous householders and also those who leave home's troubles to wear away their deeds.
teaches: The Jain poet answers the couplet's question by naming a gain the household cannot give, the wearing away of deeds already done, while still praising the household's gifts and conduct.

gains.a: the verse's two kinds of people are seen as a reply to a known Tamil challenge to renunciation
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question is given a specific answer that it does not consider

note: Tirumular puts in fire-mouthed hell those who said 'kill, stab'; the Neelakesi puts there those who ate the flesh as well as those who killed.
teaches: A Saiva and a Jain text each carry the guilt of a killing beyond the hand that strikes, one back to the man who ordered it and the other forward to the man who eats, so between them the whole chain around a death is held to account.

gains.a: the Jain charge against the eater is seen as one case of a wider rule of shared guilt that a Saiva text also holds
gains.b: Tirumular's extension of guilt to the speaker gains its counterpart in the consumer, which he leaves to his next verse on flesh

note: Tirumular says merit and sin both come with one into birth and both must be cut at the root to reach the Lord; the Jain tale shows merit carrying a monkey to a human birth and then to a god's body that keeps the monkey's hand.
teaches: The god who still bears a monkey's hand makes visible Tirumular's point that merit, too, works by giving births: the reward of the gift is another body marked by the last one, which is why the Saiva verse ranks merit as a bond to be uprooted rather than a road to the Lord.

gains.a: the tale's god with the monkey's hand gains a reading as a sign that merit's fruit is still a birth, not only a proof of the gift's power
gains.b: Tirumular's abstract claim that merit binds gains a concrete image of a merit-made body that carries the history of its former birth

note: Tirumular describes the whole town wailing, renaming the dead man a corpse, burning him and bathing to forget; Manimekalai asks the queen whether she weeps for the body, since mourners themselves cast it into the burning ground, or for the life, whose next dwelling is set by deeds.
teaches: Tirumular's observation that mourners burn and forget the body they weep for becomes in the epic the first horn of a dilemma whose second horn turns grief for one life into pity for all lives.

gains.a: a plain picture of the mourners' contradiction that her terse question 'who cast him into the burning ground?' assumes
gains.b: a use for the observation: the Buddhist teacher draws from it an obligation of compassion, not only the impermanence the verse leaves the reader with

note: Kuruntokai 73 says the Kosar killed Nannan's fragrant mango tree and drove him from his land; the preface of the fourth ten says Narmudi Cheral beheaded Nannan of Peruvaayil and felled his gold-bearing vakai.
teaches: On a plain reading the two disagree on which tree was Nannan's guardian and who destroyed him, so either the name Nannan covers more than one chief or felling his guarded tree was a victory several conquerors claimed, and neither poem alone shows that the deed was told of more than one enemy.

note: The Kural's woman says the whole town reels in sorrow when evening spreads; the venba says the same moonlit night is cool to Madhavi with her lover and hot to Kannaki without him.
teaches: The parted woman's sense that the whole town suffers with her is set against a city where one night divides two women of the same house's story, which shows her claim is the projection of grief.

gains.a: the venba's neat sorting of two women gains the parted woman's own conviction that evening is a public calamity
gains.b: the couplet's town-wide sorrow is shown to be a single woman's view, since the epic's city is split by the same hour

note: Kural 314 says the punishment for those who hurt you is to shame them by doing them good; Neelakesi 138 says the sage made her, who came to kill him, bow by his virtues alone.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's punishment by goodness carried through to its end: the would-be killer is not only shamed but turned into a worshipper and, two verses later, an advocate.

gains.a: her confession gains the couplet's frame, in which his forbearance is a form of punishment and not passivity
gains.b: the couplet's counsel gains a case in which the wrongdoer was a deadly enemy and the result was conversion

note: Kudapulaviyanar tells the Pandya that food makes the body (உண்டி முதற்றே உணவின் பிண்டம்), so those who bind water to land give body and life, and bids him build tanks; the goddess uses the same phrase, the body is a lump of food, to give Manimekalai a mantra that cuts off her own hunger.
teaches: The same maxim drives two answers to hunger: the Sangam poet makes it a king's duty to feed a people by irrigation, the epic turns it into an ascetic's private release from hunger, the first step before the bowl that will feed others.

gains.a: The goddess's sudden afterthought at 90 is heard as a known saying about kings and food, which foreshadows Manimekalai's later role as feeder of the hungry.
gains.b: The poem's maxim is shown carried from the king's public works to a single renouncer's body, where the remedy is a mantra, not water.

note: The quatrain says sin cannot stand before austerity while merit lasts; the goddess says that when a former deed rises in wrath penance does not help those not upright.
teaches: Both limit what austerity can do, but the quatrain makes merit run out with time, while the goddess makes the bar moral: penance fails against a ripened deed for those who lack uprightness.

gains.a: the goddess's saying gains a measure: austerity does guard, but only on terms
gains.b: the quatrain's limit gains a second condition and a case, the ascetic-guarded couple who still meet the deed of a former birth

note: Kural 451 says the small take small company as kin; Thirikadugam names living as kin of the unlearned as a ruin that comes from ignorance.
teaches: The couplet explains who seeks low company (the small); the verse names why (ignorance) and what follows (ruin), giving the act a cause and a result.

note: 628 prevents pain by not desiring pleasure. 669 accepts pain for the sake of the pleasure that results. One asks you to stop wanting joy and the other to work for it.
teaches: They may differ in scope, since 628 speaks of how one meets pain and 669 of which tasks to take up, but neither verse says so.

note: The Naladiyar's fool hails a pot of filth as a woman because of its skin; the Neelakesi's men perish for a filthy body worm-filled under its cover.
teaches: The quatrain rests its case on disgust alone, while the sermon sets the same disgust beside the evil rebirth and the stained lineage, so the impure body becomes one of three reckonings a restrained man makes rather than the whole argument.

gains.a: the sermon's compressed image of the covered body is explained by the quatrain's fuller picture of skin hiding the openings
gains.b: the quatrain's single argument from the body's foulness is placed within a teaching of rebirth and family honour it does not state

note: Natrinai 34's friend tells Murugan that, knowing the sickness is not his seizure, he came to the veri house at the velan's call, and so, though a god, he is truly foolish (மடவை மன்ற); the kuravai ranks the god as more foolish than the velan if he comes.
teaches: The single daring address to the god in the Sangam poem becomes a graded series (the velan foolish, the god more so) sung inside a hymn to the same god's spear, so the mockery of his coming to the rite sits beside praise of his power without contradiction.

gains.a: the stanza's charge against the god is seen to be a received akam boldness, not irreverence peculiar to the epic
gains.b: the poem's address gains a setting in worship: the same girls who call the god foolish here have just sung his victories

note: Tirumular says silence of speech alone is mere muteness, true silence being the stilling of mind; Neelakesi says silence of speech proves nothing, since trees and mountains are silent.
teaches: Both deny that outward silence shows attainment, but they move the test in opposite directions: Tirumular inward to a stilled mind, the Jain debater outward to the teaching a knower must give.

gains.a: the verse gains a contrast showing that its attack on silence touches only silence of the tongue, not an inner stillness it never discusses
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's distinction gains a debater who uses the same point against a rival's mute Lord, showing that mere muteness was a live charge between schools

note: At their first meeting in the hall Manimekalai told the prince in words that the human body is a vessel of birth, age, disease and death; here she shows him an old woman's body feature by feature.
teaches: Manimekalai moves from stating the doctrine of the suffering body to making the prince look at one, which shows that she treats his desire as a failure of seeing that a statement did not cure.

note: The couplet sets not killing one creature above a thousand sacrifices; Champapathi calls 'killing is dharma' a false word and counts a mother's offer of her own life for her son's under it.
teaches: The epic extends the couplet's rule against killing to giving one's own life in exchange for another's, which the couplet, concerned with animals and sacrifice, does not consider.

gains.a: Champapathi's sharp refusal of a mother's offer is seen to rest on the ethics of not killing, not on want of pity.
gains.b: The couplet's rule is carried to the case of self-offering, where its scope is tested by a sympathetic petitioner.

note: Kural 356 says those who have learned and seen the true thing reach the path of no return; Neelakesi says those of any form who understand the Lord's scripture reach release in due order.
teaches: Both make understanding the road to release, but the epic names whose scripture it must be and adds that any being, even a demoness, may walk it, by stages.

gains.a: the epic's sectarian claim is set beside a general rule that learning and seeing truth free one from birth
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed 'true thing' is claimed by one school's scripture, and its learner is opened to beings of any form

note: The Silappathikaram's image in the court weeps without speaking (நாவொடு நவிலாது) when the king's sceptre bends; the Manimekalai's speaking image (நா உடைப் பாவை) proclaims a woman's innocence to the city.
teaches: Puhar's images serve as witnesses of justice in both epics, but one only weeps silently at a bent sceptre while the other speaks and clears a woman, so the pairing shows the speaking image as an active judge where the weeping one is only a sign.

note: Both use the tiger that will not eat prey that has fallen on its left side and goes hungry instead.
teaches: The Naladiyar uses the tiger's refusal as a model of one's own honour, while the Chola poet uses it to choose whom to befriend, so the image was a shared emblem of high-mindedness that each book bent to its own question.

claims.gist: a god who both destroys and creates gives no ground for clear understanding
each must wear out his own deeds to reach release; no other's compassion does it
even when ruined oneself, one should not plan the ruin of the worthy
the world and the scriptures both condemn the killer, and giving up killing benefits this life and the next
living beings are born into four states of birth, of which hell is one
the hell-earths lie below, borne up by three rings of wind
a cruel deed, come to ripeness, brought the father to a violent death abroad and the daughter to her present misery
a thing sinks in one respect and rises in another
worship of Murugan can bring a wished marriage and avert an unwanted one
the other schools' doctrines, once heard, prove to lack truth, after which one keeps to the Buddha's Pitaka path
the Lord worshipped by the Indras taught dharma, adharma, time, space, soul, matter, merit, sin, bondage and release
the prince's own ripened evil deed brought about his death, using the vidyadhara's hand
