making images of the Buddha earns merit for both the makers and the worshippers
the killer and the eater both incur the cruel deed
a husband's abandonment of his innocent wife was the work of strong karma, not her fault
the beauty praised in a woman's features is changed by age into its opposite
sacrifice drives away disease and demons
gods who delight in killing cannot remove the deed of the killer
existence and non-existence in respects are said only of real things, not of fictions like a hare's horn
a monk's way of taking food, cleaning his bowl, shaving his head and painting his eyes is fixed by the Vinaya's rules
substance and quality must be either the same or different, and either answer undoes the Jain account
killing animals in Vedic sacrifice, for spirits and gods, or as medicine inflicts the suffering of death on them
an insult to kings left unanswered brings disgrace on every king like the one insulted
a king who fails his war vow deserves to become a king whose sceptre terrifies his own subjects
resemblance and descent do not make the reaper the doer; he remains another
action is one with the substance that acts
action is a category separate from substance
the life does not divide and go separately when the body is cut into parts
a continuum left after the aggregates have wholly perished can carry nothing
the round of births has no beginning
a path is acceptable only if it shows how birth is cut off and how a deed's fruit fits the deed
a thing is annihilated in one respect, not annihilated in another, and both
one who harms another in the forenoon sees his own harm come in the afternoon
a chaste wife's steadfastness can make a tree, a flood and the sea give way to her
chastity is the one thing a wife cannot be without
where chaste wives live, the rain does not fail, plenty does not falter and the king's victory does not decay
a king should perform the great Vedic sacrifice, which opens the way the gods praise
dharma must not be put off to tomorrow, for life may leave today
release is emptiness
one who eats flesh has no compassion for other beings
the doer is only the doer and the reaper only the reaper
the fruit of good and bad deeds alike falls to those who did them
cognition is sixfold, arising when the five senses and the mind meet their objects, with no knower besides
the dharma she teaches is a raft that cuts off birth and brings bliss
a formless soul cannot be bound and a soul with form would be diminished, so the soul is untenable either way
the Buddha taught that staying in the household is a fault and one must leave home
one whose life belies the renouncer's guise cannot teach renunciation
a king's unbending sceptre shows in the ease and plenty of his land, as a wife's bearing shows a just husband
reviling ascetics who keep a strict rule of alms brings evil karma on the reviler
an evil deed, when it ripens, drives one to the very act that brings punishment
an ascetic's fast gives his word the power to lay a binding curse

note: The quatrain's ascetic's bowl (தவசி கடிஞை) fills slowly by alms at door after door; the guard reports a begging bowl (ஐயப் பாத்திரம்) that, taken into the prison, makes food flow for a crowd.
teaches: The quatrain uses the begging bowl as the image of slow accumulation in the giver, and the epic reverses its direction, making the ascetic's bowl the source that pours out, so in the Buddhist epic the mendicant is the giver and the city the receiver.

gains.a: The marvel of the one bowl gains the ordinary picture of a begging bowl it overturns.
gains.b: The quatrain's image gains a counter-case where the bowl's fullness belongs to the beggar, not the donor.

note: Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, blood, bone and skin and asks which of these is the garlanded woman; Neelakesi 128 lists the woman's beauties and says lovers, ascetics and jackals each see something else in them.
teaches: The quatrain dissolves the beloved into parts, while the epic keeps the parts whole and moves the difference to the viewer, so the two give two routes to the same detachment: analysis of the object and analysis of the gaze.

gains.a: the sage's three viewers gain the anatomical list that says what the ascetic and the jackal actually see
gains.b: the quatrain's question gains a speaker and an addressee, a sage telling it to the woman herself

note: Neelakesi says the Buddha's reasoning collapses into the void; the Siddhar tells his listener that all arising deeds are seen to be void, appearing without appearing in pure space.
teaches: For the Jain debater reaching the void is a reductio, for the Siddhar it is the seeing that frees; the same word marks defeat in one tradition and insight in the other.

gains.a: the Jain charge gains a witness that some Tamil teachers embraced the void as a goal, so the charge is aimed at a live position, not a straw one
gains.b: the Siddhar's void gains the objection it must meet, that a void reached by regress leaves nothing to know or hold

note: The opening called Neelakesi a demoness who took the great one's dharma and turned from violence; her last words say those of any form who understand the Lord's scripture reach release.
teaches: Her closing claim generalizes her own story: a demoness who learned the scripture is the proof that form and birth do not bar release.

note: Kural 225 ranks the strength of those who endure hunger, read by its commentators as ascetics, below that of those who remove it; here a goddess tells a girl who has just renounced that removing hunger is beyond praise and the true way of the world.
teaches: The epic dissolves the couplet's ranking of giver over ascetic by putting the bowl in a renunciant's hand, so the one who endures hunger becomes the one who ends it.

gains.a: the sermon's praise of the hunger-curer is seen as an answer to the Kural's ranking, not only a commonplace
gains.b: the couplet's opposition between ascetic and giver is shown not to be fixed, since a renunciant may be the giver

note: Kundalakesi's praise of her lord repeats, phrase for phrase, the invocation of the Kundalakesi: great from the first, thinking only good until the end, wanting nothing for himself, toiling for others.
teaches: The Neelakesi argues against the Kundalakesi's actual opening verse, so the surviving fragment is the text under attack and the debate is with a book, not an invented opponent.

note: The couplet says those born of good family do not slip (இழுக்கார்) in conduct; the goddess says those born in the Pandya line joined to conduct (ஒழுக்கொடு) suffer no fault (இழுக்கம்) even in untamed youth.
teaches: The couplet's rule about good birth is spoken by the dynasty's own goddess while she excuses its present king, so the epic shows the rule used as a family's defence at the moment its member has failed.

gains.a: the goddess's boast gains a recognised maxim behind it, which is why it carries weight against Kannaki's charge
gains.b: the couplet gains a test: the chapter itself tells of a king of that line who erred, so good birth does not guarantee what the couplet claims

note: The patikam names only the curse of Sangaman's wife from a former birth; the Katturai Kaathai tells that Kovalan, then Bharatan, a king's servant, seized Sangaman as a spy and had him killed, and that his widow Nili, finding no refuge, cried for justice.
teaches: Read together, the curse is seen to repeat its cause exactly: a merchant falsely taken and killed by royal order, a wife left with no ground to stand on, so Kovalan's death mirrors the one he caused and Kannaki's lament repeats Nili's.

note: The couplet ranks not killing one creature to eat above a thousand oblations; Maadalan ranks the sacrifice of dharma above the war-sacrifice in which the king has killed for fifty years.
teaches: Read together they make a three-step ranking that neither states: the Kural puts abstaining from killing above the Vedic rite, while the epic's brahmin puts the Vedic rite above the killing of war and offers it as the remedy for that killing.

gains.a: Maadalan's remedy is shown to rest on a ranking the Kural itself would not grant
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the oblation is urged as the cure for killing, not as its rival

note: The Kural pictures penance as pain burning the ascetic as fire burns gold; Neelakesi fears that the fullness of the sage's penance will burn her.
teaches: The fire of penance faces two ways: inward in the Kural, where it purifies the one who bears it, and outward in the epic, where the assailant feels it as a fire that would consume her.

gains.a: her fear is seen to rest on the same fire that the Kural says the ascetic has passed through
gains.b: the couplet's inward fire is shown to be imagined by others as a danger to them

note: The quatrain says an old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the pillar says the prince's ripened deed came here and took his life, and that Kanchanan's deed will reach him too.
teaches: The epic shows the old deed finding its doer across a change of birth and through a stranger's hand, which gives the quatrain's search image a path: the deed reaches the prince by way of another man's mistake.

gains.a: The pillar's statement gains the image of the deed as an active seeker, which explains why a chance misidentification could deliver it.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case in which one deed's arrival creates a new deed with its own doer, a chain the calf image does not show.

note: The goddess says Tarai and Virai were reborn beside Manimekalai because they worshipped at the Padapankaya hill when Aravanar bade them; Aravanar now tells that afterwards one died drunk under an elephant and the other leapt from a terrace.
teaches: Held together, the two accounts show the epic letting one act of worship outlast a drunken death and a suicide: the manner of dying does not cancel the merit, which is why the two women now stand beside the heroine.

note: Kural 920 groups double-minded women with drink and dice as the company of men Fortune has left; the queen turns the charge on the courtesan house itself, a life built on drink, lies, lust and deceit, and from which a courtesan's own daughter flees in fear.
teaches: The couplet sees the courtesan only as a danger to the man, while the epic shows the same house as a danger to the women born in it, so that renunciation is a courtesan's escape, not only a patron's.

gains.a: a short traditional judgment that frames the queen's list as the old ethical verdict on the courtesan's world
gains.b: a case from inside the courtesan's house, where the harm falls on its daughter, which the couplet's man-centred warning never considers

note: The Kural asks how one who eats another's flesh to swell his own can hold to compassion (அருள்); Neelakesi asks a monk who eats flesh so that his body thickens whether he has any compassion (அருள்).
teaches: The couplet's question, put to anyone, becomes in the debate a charge against a school that makes compassion its centre, so its force is to expose a contradiction inside a teaching rather than to state a general rule.

gains.a: the taunt draws on a rule Tamil readers already held, so it reads as a common standard and not only a sectarian one
gains.b: the couplet is shown aimed at a real opponent who claimed compassion while eating meat, which the couplet alone does not name

note: The sage foretells Rahulan's death by a glance-poison snake without a cause; the deity of kaathai 21 gives the cause, his killing of the cook, and says Lakshmi's loving refusal to leave him could not turn the deed aside.
teaches: Together the passages show the epic's karma working in two steps: the prophecy fixes the fruit as certain, and only later is the deed named, with the added point that a wife's devotion, even unto the pyre, does not share or lighten a husband's deed.

note: In the Arkkachandra debate she named the felling of living trees among sins that bring hell; here she argues against Mokkalan that trees really are alive.
teaches: The earlier charge that felling a tree is a sin rests on a premise the Buddhists deny, and this passage supplies the argument for it: healing, feeding and withering show the tree to be a soul one can wrong.

note: Senguttuvan rejects a stone from the Podiyil hill bathed in the Kaveri as unworthy of those born in his line of valour, and resolves that if the Himalaya's king will not give a stone to carve the great Pattini goddess, he will march north; the summary views the book as one with the king whose army fought with valour fitted to aram and reached the Ganga.
teaches: The king's own reason for the northern war was the honour of his line of valour, with the goddess's stone as its occasion, and the summary keeps exactly that reason and drops the occasion, so the book that began with worship for Kannaki is remembered as a Chera conquest called righteous.

note: The Buddha said continuity arising from a seed by potency is change, and that release is not other than this; Neelakesi replies that if each moment perishes entirely, release is that perishing and needs no austerity.
teaches: The Buddha's own phrase that release is not other than the change of the series is what lets the Jain equate nirvana with every moment's end, so the Buddha's wording supplies the premise of her reductio.

note: In 282 Neelakesi herself says the body lives by food and awareness by the body; in 357 she mocks the Buddhist claim that cold, heat and hunger keep dharma out of the mind.
teaches: The Jain debater grants that the mind needs a fed body but not that it needs a comfortable one, so her two arguments mark a line between sustaining the body and sparing it.

note: The teacher says bondage and release have their own causes and no one exists to grant them; Tirumular says grace put the soul into bonds and grace gives release.
teaches: The two name the same pair, bondage and release, and give opposite answers to who brings them about: the epic denies any giver, and Tirumular makes one grace the giver of both, so the Buddhist and Saiva accounts of release divide exactly at line 251.

gains.a: a named rival position, a giver of both bondage and release, that line 251's denial excludes
gains.b: a counter-position that shows Tirumular's claim that binding itself is grace is the very claim a causal account without a giver rejects

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of a king who rules by the sceptre; the ascetic credits Nagapuram's unfailing rain to Punniyarajan's birth, before any rule.
teaches: Where the couplet makes a land's rain the fruit of a king's just rule, the epic makes it the fruit of his former birth's charity, moving the cause of plenty from the sceptre to karma.

gains.a: the rule against which the ascetic's claim stands out as a claim about birth, not governance
gains.b: a case where the king's plenty precedes any act of rule, showing a second source of the link between king and rain that the couplet does not name

note: Idaikkadar says a roasted seed will not sprout and those without devotion will not reach the goal; Neelakesi says a burnt seed never sprouts and so the released soul is never born again.
teaches: The same roasted seed is failure for the Siddhar, the soul without devotion that cannot grow toward release, and success for the Jain, the soul whose karma is burnt so it cannot grow into rebirth, so the image's meaning depends on whether sprouting is birth or attainment.

gains.a: the Jain verse's image is seen to have a rival use in which not sprouting is a loss
gains.b: the Siddhar's terse image is set against the older doctrinal use it inverts

note: The quatrain mocks the fool who calls a body of nine oozing openings 'broad-shouldered one'; Sudhamathi answers the prince's love-poetry questions about Manimekalai with the same inside-out view of the body.
teaches: The epic stages the quatrain's cure as speech to a lover just after he has used the love-poem epithets, and then shows it failing: the sight of the girl reaches him before the words do.

gains.a: Sudhamathi's catalogue is placed in an existing ethics genre that answers love poetry's epithets one by one.
gains.b: The quatrain's sure contempt for the fool gets a test case in which the cure is spoken in time and still loses to sight.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says atoms never enter one another; in 713 the Jain's Ajivika says the same of souls, each with its own length and breadth.
teaches: The rule of non-penetration that the Buddhist account gives for atoms is, in the Jain account, also a rule for souls, and only there does it meet the objection of crowded bodies.

note: The epic calls the teacher whose seat this is the physician of the disease of birth (பிறவிப் பிணி மருத்துவன்); Arunagirinathar calls Murugan of Thiruttani the physician of the disease of becoming (பவரோக வயித்திய நாத) and asks his grace to cut birth's root.
teaches: The same title names two cures: in the Buddhist epic the physician heals by teaching dharma to those who have cleansed their minds, and his seat alone is left to be worshipped; in the Saiva hymn he heals by grace given to one who calls his name.

gains.a: The epithet at line 61 is shown to be a contested title, and the epic's choice to name no god while using it becomes visible.
gains.b: The hymn's physician-god is seen against an older Tamil use of the title for a teacher whose cure is a doctrine heard, not a grace received.

note: In the akam poem the wife refuses the bard sent to plead for her husband because he is a deceiving philanderer (மாயப் பரத்தன்); here the man refuses the go-between sent by the courtesan because her love is a dancer's art.
teaches: The epic stages a marutham refusal of the go-between with the roles turned round, so that the charge of false love the convention lets the wife bring against the man is brought by the man against the courtesan.

gains.a: the scene gains its genre: Kovalan's answer is a வாயில் மறுத்தல், and its harshness reads as a convention used against Madhavi
gains.b: the poem gains a view from the other side of the same convention, where the one refused is the woman and the charge of deceit is shown, later in the story, to be wrong

note: Perunkoppendu insists against the elders that her husband's pyre is to her a lotus pool; the sage tells Lakshmi as a plain fact that she will sink into Rahulan's fire, and the epic sends her, through that fire, to a new birth still bound to him.
teaches: The Sangam queen's choice of the pyre is her last word and her karpu's proof, while the Buddhist epic treats the same act as foretold and as no end at all: the bond she dies for carries into the next birth as the attachment that must be undone.

gains.a: Lakshmi's foretold death in the fire is set against a known Tamil model of the wife who chooses the pyre, which shows how flatly the sage reports it, without praise.
gains.b: The queen's claim that the fire and the lotus pool are one meets a work for which the fire leads not to union but to rebirth with the same longing.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai places the god at Erakam among Brahmins who chant the six-syllable mantra at the hours; the kuravai names Erakam with Senthil, Sengodu and Venkunru as hills the god never leaves.
teaches: The same shrine is claimed by the guide poem for a Brahmin rite and by the hill women for their kuravai, and their list differs from the six seats, so the roster of Murugan's hills was not yet fixed when the epic was made.

gains.a: the epic's four names gain a comparison that shows they are a distinct list, with Sengodu and Venkunru outside the six
gains.b: the guide poem's Erakam is seen also as a hill folk's god's seat, not only a Brahmin site

note: In the Silappathikaram Kannaki appears in the sky, declares the Pandya faultless and a guest in Indra's palace, and says she will not leave Murugan's hill; in the Manimekalai she foretells her own rebirth, her hearing of the Buddha and her release, while meanwhile working wonders for all.
teaches: The Buddhist epic does not deny the Pattini cult: it keeps Kannaki present and helpful as the earlier epic does, but makes that presence a long interval before a birth in which she must still hear the Buddha, so the goddess becomes a future disciple.

note: Kural 212 says wealth earned by effort exists to do good to the worthy; in Natrinai 186 the wife says her husband crossed the waste for wealth with a heart that strives for others.
teaches: The wife in the poem defends a painful separation with the Kural's ethic of earning in order to give, so the household rule appears here as the reason that made the paalai journey honourable in her eyes.

note: Kural 301 says restraint of anger counts only where anger can take effect; the line calls anger poor where it inspires no awe.
teaches: The couplet says restraining powerless anger is no virtue, and the line says indulging it is no gain, so together they show that anger without power is worth nothing whether held back or let loose.

note: 926 says that drinkers are eating poison. 1201 says love is sweeter than liquor because it delights even in memory, taking liquor's delight as the benchmark.
teaches: The book of love borrows, without judging, the pleasure that this chapter condemns.

note: The quatrain says the best renounce without delay after slowly considering that home, youth, wealth and strength do not last; Maasaathuvan gives his wealth away and renounces only when the news of his son's death makes life seem death.
teaches: The pair separates renunciation reached by reflection from renunciation forced by bereavement: the epic's fathers come to the quatrain's act by the road the quatrain hopes to spare, after the loss has already happened.

gains.a: the father's turning gains a measure: it is the right act done late, under grief rather than insight
gains.b: the quatrain's counsel gains a case showing what the delay it warns against costs, a house emptied before its master leaves it

note: In the idyll the old women seek an omen and hear a herd girl tell a distressed tethered calf that its mothers will soon come; in the epic the herd's own signs foretell sorrow and the herdswoman dances so that the cows' and calves' distress may pass.
teaches: Both read a calf's distress among the herds as a sign about an absent man, but the idyll's chance word promises a return and the epic's signs announce a death the herders do not yet know, so the mullai omen-scene is turned from hope to loss.

gains.a: the rite gains its convention: in mullai poetry an omen among the herds speaks of an absent husband, which lets the signs point at Kovalan without naming him
gains.b: the idyll's comforting omen gains a counterpart in which the same kind of sign foretells a husband's death and a rite fails to turn it

note: Mokkalan says that if self-torment were dharma, mutilation and impalement would be excellent; Neelakesi answers that he praises the bodhisattva for enduring having his flesh cut and his body split.
teaches: The Buddhist's own hero stories contain the very bodily sufferings he ridicules, so the reductio is turned on him: either the bodhisattva's endurance was folly or the Jain's is not.

note: The Manimekalai names the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness); Neelakesi says three of them are modes of knowing, leaving two.
teaches: Set beside the Buddhist's own list, the Jain attack is seen to aim at the split of consciousness from feeling, perception and volition, collapsing the person into a knower and form, which is the Jain soul and matter by another route.

note: The Kural asks how one who eats another's flesh can hold compassion; Neelakesi asks the same of a teacher said to be all compassion who eats flesh.
teaches: The couplet's general question becomes a charge against a named teacher's claim to compassion, so the Kural's link between flesh and compassion settles a dispute between schools.

gains.a: the Jain charge borrows the authority of an accepted ethical rule instead of a sectarian one
gains.b: the couplet's question is shown answering a concrete case: a teacher's compassion is measured by his food

note: The kadambu thrown down in the sea and the bow set on the Himalaya, epithets of the Chera line in the opening lines, return in the drum's proclamation.
teaches: The same two feats change use within one kaathai: at the start they adorn a king going to see the hills, at the end they are a threat sent to northern kings, which marks how far the news of the pathini has turned the pleasure trip.

note: Kural 335 urges good deeds before the hiccup stops the tongue; the sage of Kayankarai urges dharma before death that cannot be turned back (49 to 50), but adds that good deeds win only better births and that none escape birth except those who hear the coming Buddha.
teaches: The sermon separates what the couplet joins: haste in good deeds before death decides the next birth, but release waits on a teacher not yet come, so urgency to do good is not urgency to be free.

gains.a: a measure of what is shared Tamil ethics in the sermon, so that only its claim at 47 to 48 stands out as Buddhist doctrine
gains.b: a limit the couplet does not state: good deeds rushed to before death lead on to heaven or a human birth but do not end birth

note: In 72 the kings mock Neduncheliyan as a boy (இளையன் இவன்); in 78 the new warriors say 'the fighter is young' (பொருநனும் இளையன்) and are pursued to their fathers' town and killed.
teaches: 78 tells, through a court poet, the sequel that 72 vows in the king's own voice, so the anthology keeps both the vow and its fulfilment, and the taunt of youth becomes the hinge of the king's fame.

note: Paripadal 5 praises the spear that cut Sur's mango in the sea and split the crane-named mountain and says the velan's praises and veri are neither true nor false; the kuravai names the same crane-mountain killer and calls him foolish if he comes to the velan's rite.
teaches: Both texts hold the god's deeds fixed while keeping the velan's rite at a distance: the hymn suspends judgement on the rite, and the kuravai laughs at it, which shows that doubt about the diviner was compatible with full praise of Murugan.

gains.a: the friend's mockery gains a temple-hymn parallel that also refuses to vouch for the veri
gains.b: the hymn's guarded 'neither true nor false' is shown in a folk voice that goes further and laughs

note: Pattinappaalai's Thirumavalavan makes the northerners wilt among many regional conquests; the epic's Thirumavalavan marches to the Himalaya and brings back gifts from three named northern kings.
teaches: Read together, the two show a Sangam king's memory being enlarged: one line of the older poem about the north becomes a whole campaign whose trophies are buildings in Puhar, so the epic makes the conquest serve its picture of the city.

gains.a: the epic's past king gains a Sangam record under the same name, showing the episode draws on remembered praise
gains.b: the poem's brief line on the northerners gains a later tradition that turned it into a Himalayan expedition

note: The brahmin tells the traveller to recite the mantras of five and eight letters and bathe in the pool he wants, though better to fix the heart on the god's feet; the Siddhar asks those seeking a holy water where the bathing is, and says the holy water is the five letters within.
teaches: Both move from outer water toward an inner formula, but the brahmin keeps the pool and makes the letters its key while the Siddhar dissolves the pool into the letters, so the pair shows two stages of one turn from pilgrimage to recitation.

gains.a: the epic's rite gains a later voice that removes the pool it still keeps and shows where its own ranking of devotion over water could lead
gains.b: the Siddhar's attack gains an early literary witness of the practice it rejects, recitation of a letter-formula as the key to a sacred pool

claims.gist: money given to buy meat makes the giver one of the killers
the mind that grasps each letter perishes at once
understanding a word or a reckoning needs a knower that lasts across its parts
the Buddhist monk's garb serves to make him known to those who give flesh, and he desires flesh
if all is suffering, deeds and their fruits are all alike and no path is higher than another
the exclusion must be stated as a rule, not only shown in an instance
the exclusion must deny the property to be proved first and the reason after; reversed, it fails
by these rules one can examine an inference and know without doubt what in it is true and what false
the Buddhist doctrine cannot join a deed to its fruit at all
a village that sings the praise of the pathini gains the boon of seeing its lovers wed
the luminary gods are five, some circling the world mountain and some fixed
the elements do not keep one fixed direction of motion
a renouncer who keeps the household's labours for his robes has not renounced household life
the adorned body is flesh whose smell is hidden by flowers, paste, cloth and ornament, a deceit established by those of old
one who brings ruin on those who rely on him, heedless of sin, is no leader
names such as paddy or month are conventions for continuities and collections
mind arises and passes like a flash of lightning
ruin for the sake of the impure body leads to an evil rebirth and stains one's lineage
names and cognitions do occur for what does not exist
worship of the First Lord's twin feet washes away hard deeds
a misfortune such as a wrong union comes from the fruit of former deeds
the Brahmin's tending of the sacred fire brings rain
those who are born die and the dead are born again, and dharma brings worth as wrong brings suffering
the fruit of a deed must be eaten even when it arrives through the king's fault
if consciousness does not reach the object perception takes, consciousness has no object
a land's rain fails when the king's sceptre bends, when austerity fails, or when women's chastity falls short
a ruler's own austerity can bring a saviour to his stricken land
death takes ascetic and rich, infant and old alike
those who see the burning ground and still live revelling in wealth and drink without desiring dharma are the greatest fools
the Jina's endless knowledge is itself an inner instrument, so his knowing is not free of instruments
a separate inherence is needed to join qualities to their bearers
quality and bearer need no third thing to join them, and taken apart neither exists
everything that is spoken proceeds from one Lord by one rule
if all is one being, a debate between opponents has no point
alms received from a chaste wife are of the greatest worth
a wife's chastity brings the rain
a grave deed ripens through a sage's curse into suffering
evil deeds reach their doer and the dead are born again
wood, earth, stone and painted images do not themselves speak
deities installed by the wise in images at a city's places stay there and tell mortals what will befall
the omniscient's knowledge reveals the nature of all things together as the sun lights everything
bathing in the pool Punniya Saravanam gives the treatise of the king of the gods
bathing in the pool Bhavakaarini brings knowledge of one's former birth
bathing in the pool Ishtasiddhi gains whatever one wishes
the praise of the Lord brings about the auspicious state
instruments of knowing are karma and the partial knowledges karma produces; the Lord's complete knowledge needs none
giving up one's own life by fasting is killing, and the one who does it bears the deaths of those who follow him
a renouncer who eats what others have prepared does not share the fault of its preparing
whatever arises moment by moment is simply its own nature

note: 673 praises a Lord who neither ages nor greys; 694 answers with a sickness hotter than fire that came upon the god.
teaches: Against a portrait of a Lord without wrinkle or grey hair the Jain debater sets a single bodily event, showing that the debate tests a doctrine by its founder's body as well as by argument.

note: Naladiyar says craving enters by five gates, body, mouth, eyes, nose and ears, and whoever guards them reaches release; the teacher counts six gates, with the mind among them, and places craving three links after the gates.
teaches: The pairing shows two models of the senses: the quatrain makes the five gates the entry of craving and guarding them the path, while the chain adds the mind as a sixth gate and puts contact and feeling between gate and craving, so guarding the gates is not where the chain is cut.

gains.a: an ethical practice of guarding the gates that the chain's definitions do not state
gains.b: the mind as a sixth gate and the steps between sense and craving, which the quatrain's five gates leave out

note: 259 says only the mind counts and conduct is not evil karma; 261 answers that release needs mind and outward conduct to agree.
teaches: The debate's central point is here: the Jain refuses to let a pure intention excuse a deed, so the meat question becomes a question of whether karma lives in the mind or in the act.

note: The patikam traces the ruin to a curse of a former birth ripening; the fire god here says he held an old order to burn the city, while Kannaki claims the act as her own rage.
teaches: Read together, the burning is caused three ways at once, by a karmic curse, by a standing divine order and by the wife's own deliberate act, and the epic does not choose between fate and her choice.

note: Mullaippattu 1-6 likens the rain-cloud rising from the sea to Mal, who grew to measure the world; Kar Narpathu 1 likens the rainbow to the garland on the chest of Mal, coloured like the warring sea.
teaches: Both mullai poems open their rains with Mal, the god of the mullai land, so the land's god is the first image of its season; the later venba moves him from the rising cloud to the rainbow, making the sky his adorned chest rather than his growing body.

note: The Kural calls taking what does not last for what lasts the lowest understanding; Aravanar's model rule is 'whatever is made is impermanent', valid only in that direction.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the textbook rule shows impermanence as something proved from being made, with the warning that the converse fails, so knowing the passing is a matter of inference as well as of seeing.

gains.a: the stock example gains the moral weight the Kural gives to knowing impermanence
gains.b: the couplet's demand to see the passing as passing gains a stated form of proof and its limit

note: Both describe the making of a hero-stone: 264's name carved, red flower garland bound with maral fibre and peacock feather; Akananuru 269's names washed, turmeric, and a karanthai garland tied with fibre on the stone by the road.
teaches: The akam poet borrows the puram rite almost item by item to fill the heroine's fear of the road, which shows that the hero-stone was a fixed, widely known ritual whose details an akam audience would recognise as danger without being told.

note: Indra, to idle Aputhiran's bowl, sent rain until the land had no hungry; Aputhiran, reborn as Punniyarajan in the city of Indra's descendant, is a king since whose birth the rain has not failed.
teaches: The plenty that once mocked Aputhiran's charity by leaving no one to feed is now the sign of his merit as king, so the epic turns Indra's rival gift into the reward of the charity it tried to make useless.

note: The crescent is praised as founder of the Pandya line and as ruling the stars without swerving from its nature (பான்மையில் திரியாது); in kaathai 20 a Pandya, umbrella drooping and sceptre slack, calls himself the thief.
teaches: The epic's first word on the Pandya line is a praise of unswerving rule set over a scene of Kovalan's straying, and the later verdict turns that praise against its own king; the tension rests on reading the moon's constancy as the line's.

note: In 214 Neelakesi argues that a gift of flesh or an eye cannot join another's body and so helps no one; in 360 she argues that the gift of the body to a beast kills the many lives within it.
teaches: The Jain case against the bodhisattva's self-giving has two prongs across the debates: the gift is useless to the receiver and murderous to the small lives in the giver, so it fails both as charity and as non-harm.

note: The Kural says that a mind which examines (ஓர்த்து) and knows what is with certainty (ஒருதலையா) need not think of birth again; Aravanar closes with examine (ஆய்ந்து) and know without doubt (ஐயம் இன்றி).
teaches: The couplet names examination and certainty as the way out of birth but gives no procedure; the epic supplies one, and its technical word for certainty, ஏகாந்தம், is the couplet's ஒருதலை in Sanskrit dress.

gains.a: the fallacy list gains a stated end beyond winning debates, the certainty the Kural ties to release
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'examine and be certain' gains tests for when an argument has earned certainty

note: The couplet says women who obtain their husbands win great distinction in the world of the gods; the brahmin says men without a chaste wife do not enter it.
teaches: Taken together, the couplet and the brahmin's maxim make the wife and husband each the other's way to heaven, but the epic gives the maxim to a man urging a sixty-year-old to marry and then has Visakai deny it, so the reciprocal rule is shown as a pressure rather than a truth.

gains.a: The brahmin's maxim gains its counterpart in the couplet, which ties a woman's heaven to her husband.
gains.b: The couplet gains the reverse claim about men, and a scene in which that claim is answered.

note: The couplet says the sky withholds rain when the king bends justice; the Kanchi king names the bent sceptre as only one of three possible causes and cannot tell which holds.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's law into a king's anxious self-examination, and then sets it aside: the deity names no fault and sends a renunciant's bowl instead of a reform of rule.

gains.a: the king's question gains its source, the received rule that ties rain to the sceptre
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the rule cannot be applied, since the drought comes and the ruler cannot find his fault

note: The Kural says the loving belong to others even to their bones; Kundalakesi lists the Buddha's literal gifts of eyes, body, wife and child as proof of his compassion.
teaches: The couplet's figure of giving one's bones becomes in the birth-stories a literal record of bodily gifts, and the pairing shows where the figure turns contestable: once it includes wife and child, the Jain opponent can call it madness rather than love.

gains.a: the catalogue of gifts is seen as an extreme reading of a Tamil ideal of love, not a foreign oddity
gains.b: the couplet's hyperbole is shown being taken literally and so exposed to an objection it does not face on its own

note: The couplet likens a king's punishing the cruel to weeding a crop; the Chola king, at a beggar's request, empties his prison and makes it a house of dharma.
teaches: Held against the couplet, the epic's king does not deny that the cruel must be punished but turns the instrument of punishment itself into an instrument of charity, so the sceptre is shown by feeding rather than weeding.

gains.a: The king's act gains the standard view of royal punishment it departs from.
gains.b: The couplet's weeding image gains a royal alternative it does not consider, in which the prison is abolished rather than filled.

note: Verse 58's plan that the sage will drop his vow once she breaks his restraint in a woman's form meets its answer in 72, where every wile draws only the question of what these are to him.
teaches: Holding the plan beside its failure shows that the epic places the vow's safety in the sage's inner containment, the very மனநிறை she meant to break, not in avoiding the temptress.

note: The patikam's first moral is that dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship (அரைசியல் பிழைத்தோர்க்கு அறம்கூற்று); the bhutas name the same fault (கோமுறை பிழைத்த) as the cause of the city's burning.
teaches: The patikam promises death to the erring king; this unit extends the penalty from the king to his city and makes it a standing law the guardian spirits obey, which the moral as first stated does not say.

note: In 177 Kundalakesi reports that her teacher first taught the three scriptures and the five aggregates; in 477 the Buddha himself is shown dividing his teaching into Sutra, Vinaya and Shastra and then the aggregates.
teaches: The Neelakesi climbs from report to source: the doctrine Neelakesi first met second-hand from a nun is now spoken by the Buddha in person, so the debate that follows is staged as a refutation at the root.

note: Kural 319 says hurts done to others in the forenoon come back to oneself in the afternoon, of themselves; Neelakesi argues that the fruit of deeds falls to the doers themselves (செய்தார்கள் தாம்).
teaches: The couplet's 'to oneself' (தமக்கு) is set within one day of one life, while the debate asks whether the same self is there across births to receive it.

gains.a: Neelakesi's claim gets an ethical rule everyone grants, so its denial looks like a denial of morality itself
gains.b: the couplet's returning harm is stretched across births, where the identity of the one it returns to becomes a question

note: Both use the sea of births: the Kural's பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல், crossed by reaching the Lord's feet; the Neelakesi's sea of the souls' own evil deeds, crossed on a raft the Jina made.
teaches: The Jain hymn fills in what the couplet leaves open: the sea is made of the swimmer's own deeds, and the Lord's part is to build the raft, not to hold the swimmer.

gains.a: the hymn's raft is seen answering a Tamil formula in which reaching the god is the only way across
gains.b: the couplet's bare verb 'reach the feet' is shown to admit a reading in which reaching means following a path one must travel oneself

note: In the dream kaathai Devanthi read Kannaki's dream as the fruit of a vow broken in a former birth and prescribed a bath in the tanks; here she says she heard the dream and did not grasp what it would bring.
teaches: The friend who once explained the dream by past karma and a ritual remedy now confesses she misread it, so her earlier karmic diagnosis is shown to have been the wrong kind of answer to a warning of the future.

note: Kural 1083's lover learns that Death has a woman's form; the epic says Death took a woman's form because the king's just sceptre forbade its killing.
teaches: The Kural's conceit of the deadly beauty is a lover's discovery, while the epic gives it a political cause, the sceptre that holds Death in check, so a love-figure is turned into praise of the king.

gains.a: the epic's wonder gains the Kural's established conceit of Death in a woman's grace
gains.b: the couplet's figure gains a reason inside a just kingdom, why Death must disguise itself

note: The Buddha said the deed exists and its fruit exists but there is no doer; Neelakesi answers that if the fruit comes later down the line, the deed itself must last until then.
teaches: Granting deed and fruit while denying a doer moves the lasting thing from the agent to the deed: the Jain shows that the Buddha's karma needs a persistence somewhere, and the debate is over where to put it.

note: The kuravai ends praising the Pandya's victorious drum and asking the god to remove the herd's distress; the woman who led it comes back from the river with news of the Pandya's guards killing an innocent man.
teaches: Set side by side, the herdswomen's blessing on the king's victory is overtaken within lines by the report of his injustice, so the rite meant to avert evil omens is shown failing at the very moment it is completed.

note: Madhavi ranks first among pathini women those who give up their lives when their husbands die; the cemetery holds brick shrines for women who died together with their husbands, sorted by varna beside ascetics and kings.
teaches: The death Madhavi praises as the highest kind of chastity ends, in the goddess's tour, as one more class of memorial in a field whose lesson is that no death is exempt.

note: In the bridal chamber Kovalan calls Kannaki gold and doll (பொன்னே, பாவாய்) for her beauty; in Madurai, after she has followed him, he calls her gold, creeper and doll of modesty for the steadfastness that brought her with him.
teaches: The same endearments return with a new ground: the words that praised her body in the chamber praise her chastity and endurance on the road, so the pair traces Kovalan's turn from admiring Kannaki's beauty to recognising her virtue.

note: Kovalan devises a remedy for his ruin, to trade with the anklets in Madurai, and in the same line the narrator says the deed was driving him; the couplet says fate gets there first even when one plans another way.
teaches: The pairing shows fate overtaking a plan by using the plan itself: Kovalan's scheme to recover is the very road by which the deed reaches him, a case the couplet's bare 'it gets there first' does not picture.

gains.a: a rule that explains why the narrator credits Kovalan's sensible plan to the deed (line 78)
gains.b: a concrete mechanism: the counter-plan becomes fate's vehicle rather than being outrun by it

note: Both use fire for the belly. 947's fire is a measure to observe, and 227's is the disease of hunger that won't touch one who shares food.
teaches: One is the eater's problem and the other's cure is ethical, which widens what 'not falling ill' means.

note: Offered bathing and Kama's shrine as a way to keep her husband, Kannaki says it is not worthy; the couplet praises the wife who worships her husband rather than a god.
teaches: The scene shows the couplet's wife as one who refuses a rite offered for her own good, at the cost of the remedy, and that the refusal is framed as dignity (பீடு), not as doubt about the gods.

gains.a: the rule that explains Kannaki's refusal without making her a sceptic about the tanks
gains.b: a lived test in which the wife turns down divine help for her marriage at the moment she most needs it

note: Here the narrator gives Kovalan's break with Madhavi to his ripening deed; when he returns to Kannaki he gives his ruin to his own play with a deceitful woman (சலதி) and is ashamed.
teaches: The same break has two causes in two voices, karma in the narrator's and Madhavi's deceit in Kovalan's, so the epic lets its hero blame the woman while its own frame says the fault came from his past deed.

note: Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the eight-qualitied one is as useless as a sense organ without its power; the kuravai asks what ear it is that has not heard Thirumaal's praise, and goes on to the eye and the tongue.
teaches: The couplet's simile, an organ without its function, becomes in the kuravai a definition carried through ear, eye and tongue, so the claim that the body's parts exist for worship is spelled out organ by organ and bound to one named god.

gains.a: the epic's refrain gains a recognised ethical form: it is the Kural's argument that an organ is defined by its proper act, applied to devotion
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed god and single organ gain a sung extension, where the same test is applied to each sense and given a sectarian object

note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; offered heaven's reward, Aputhiran laughs that heaven is a place where no one does dharma or gives, and asks what its king could give him.
teaches: The couplet's hypothetical, giving is good even without heaven, becomes in Aputhiran's mouth a judgment that heaven is worse than earth for a giver, because there is no hunger there for giving to meet.

gains.a: a statement of the principle on which his laughter rests, that giving is valued apart from any reward
gains.b: an argument the couplet does not make: heaven is not merely unnecessary to giving but excludes it

note: The hunters pay for victory with blood at the goddess's feet; the Kural ranks not killing above a thousand oblations.
teaches: The conflict is about what an offering is worth: the hymn makes killing itself the price that buys the goddess's favour, while the couplet holds that no offering outweighs one life spared; it holds if the throat-blood of line 144 is a slain creature's.

gains.a: the hymn's blood price gains a measure from outside the cult, one by which the payment is a loss
gains.b: the couplet's comparison of oblation and abstention gains a live case where the offering is not ghee but blood

note: Both hold that heaven belongs to the round of deeds; Tirumular frees the soul from heaven, hell and earth by grace, while the seers have Kovalan freed by hearing the Buddha's dharma after he has eaten his deed.
teaches: The two agree that heaven is no escape from karma and part exactly on the way out: Saiva release is given by grace, while the Buddhist release comes after the deed is spent and the teaching heard, with no giver.

gains.a: the seers' prophecy gains a rival account of release that makes plain it involves no god
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a named case, Kovalan in heaven still owing his deed, of the soul turned through heaven by karma

note: The couplet says crushing foes comes through tapas if the ascetic so intends; Sudhamathi warns the prince that Manimekalai's fated austerity carries a curse for an arrow.
teaches: The couplet's power of tapas is invoked here as a shield for a girl who has barely begun austerity, and the prince's shrug at line 21 shows the threat carrying no weight until it is backed by practice.

gains.a: Sudhamathi's warning is read as an appeal to a recognised Tamil belief that tapas can harm an enemy, not an empty boast.
gains.b: The couplet's claim gets a case where the power is asserted on another's behalf and fails to deter, which the couplet's confident statement does not consider.

note: The couplet calls those whose work is killing base in the eyes of the discerning; the vari tells the fisher girl that her elders live by killing lives in the sea and she by killing lives in men's bodies.
teaches: The ethics book brands killing for a living as base, while the coastal song takes the fishers' killing as the plain inheritance of a family and makes it a compliment, so the pair shows a whole people's livelihood that the Kural's judgment would fall on and that the poetry of the shore never questions.

gains.a: the stanza's easy wit about killing gains an ethical weight it does not register: by the Kural's standard the father's trade is base work
gains.b: the couplet's judgment gains a concrete people it would condemn, the fishing families the epic sings with admiration

note: The couplet says harm done to others comes back on the doer of itself; the deity applies this to a killing done in zeal to serve a holy man and denies that the service exempts it.
teaches: The couplet does not ask whether a good motive changes the return of harm; the epic answers that it does not, and names the excuse it rejects, that the master served will protect his servant.

gains.a: a general rule against which the deity's denial of the pious excuse is measured
gains.b: a test of whether intention to serve dharma can stop harm from returning, which the couplet leaves open

note: Kural 484 says even the world comes to hand (கைகூடும்) if one weighs the time and acts by the place; the line says gain coming to hand (கையுறல்) for one who does not know the time is false.
teaches: The couplet makes knowing the time enough for even the greatest gain, and the line makes it necessary for any gain, so together they give timing both halves of a condition: without it nothing comes to hand, with it even the world can.

note: Thuvathikan foretold that her bowl of dharma would give rain's plenty to a parched world; here the bowl feeds Kanchi and the rain returns.
teaches: The fulfilment shows the epic treating feeding as the cause of rain, reversing the usual order in which rain must come before there is food to give.

note: Devanthi's friend born on the Himalaya and bathed in the Ganga and the blessing's doll born of the mountain king are the same Himalaya stone, spoken of as Kannaki.
teaches: The Himalaya origin is given to Kannaki twice, once in a friend's grief and once in a royal blessing, and the second, with its echo of the mountain king's daughter, shows the woman of Puhar being absorbed into the figure of the great goddess.

note: Kural 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life rather than shame for life; Madhavi says that by staying alive after hearing of her lover's suffering she gave up her shame.
teaches: Read against the couplet, Madhavi's confession places her among those who kept life at the cost of shame, so the shame the town sees in her tapas already lay in her survival, and her renunciation becomes the answer of one who has failed the rule rather than a new disgrace.

gains.a: the general rule that makes her confession intelligible: the couplet says why outliving the news of Kovalan's suffering counts as giving up shame
gains.b: a person who has failed the rule and lives on, which shows a way of answering lost shame, by tapas, that the couplet's choice between shame and death leaves out

note: The herders' omens fall in the cowshed (the cattle's bells drop, the cows tremble); the queen's fall in the court (the falling umbrella and sceptre, the trembling gate bell).
teaches: The same wrong is signalled first in the house of the victim's hosts and later in the king's own house, each through the things of its own life, so the omens move from the cowshed to the throne as the consequence nears the king.

note: The couplet says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre rightly; Aravanar asks whether the king of heaven or the just-sceptred king has failed, and says want has come though the Kaveri flows. The link holds on the reading that the questions at 46-47 clear both.
teaches: The epic grants the Kural's premise that a just king brings plenty and still finds hunger in his land, so hunger becomes a want no sceptre cures and the place where the renouncer's bowl, not the king, must act.

gains.a: The rhetorical questions at 46-47 are explained: they answer the Kural's doctrine that want betrays a bent sceptre, which is why the speaker must clear the king before calling for the bowl.
gains.b: The couplet's promise of plenty under a just king gains a counter-case where both god and king are blameless and the people still hunger.

claims.gist: things (or the soul) are without qualities
keeping precepts makes no sense for one who denies qualities
the aggregates are form, three kinds of feeling, six kinds of consciousness, perception and twenty formations
a tree that heals where it is cut shows life as a wounded body does
a cognition arises and is itself what suffers, while another thing is confused
the renouncer's duty is to complete contemplation, and for that he needs nothing but food
the five kinds of earth, water, fire, wind and life are the whole of what exists
particularity is a separate category
particularity is only the thing's own quality
all sensible qualities except sound belong to the earth-kind
an element with no sensible quality could be known by no means of knowledge
if the continuity is a real thing, the teaching that nothing lasts loses its meaning
every means of knowledge other than perception is a form of inference
a sound reason is either an effect of what is inferred or of the same nature as it
those who break a hard-sworn oath are without virtue
the Jain Lord's categories arose from his own mind and do not match things as they are
the hell-beings are the worst of all births and their suffering is hard to bear
a substance and its kinds are one with nothing besides
the Buddha did not know all things, since he knew only through the senses, hearing and reasoning
only the word of one with complete and subtle knowledge can count as scripture
all things are impure
the hardship of bodily austerity is futile
the king's fall came because his former deed arrived
a just king's line never needed the bell rung by those wronged
her suffering came from a deed of old
a king who gives up his life for a wrong done under him is to be praised
the Jataka tales are fabrications of a one-sided teacher
there is no substance standing apart from its qualities
a released soul that still knows, persists and takes outer objects keeps the grounds of evil karma
loss and arising belong to the modes of a substance, which differ while the substance remains
one who avoids killing, lying, theft and others' wives and curbs the craving for wealth reaches the world of the gods
a reason that turns the subject itself into its opposite is contradictory
a reason that proves the absence of the subject's specific character is contradictory
existence is neither substance, quality nor action, because it is distinct from the being of each, as generality and particularity are
a clan becomes the first of clans through a daughter born in it who bears the goddess's form
a substance persists while its modes, like milk, curd and buttermilk, arise and perish, so it has the threefold nature of arising, perishing and lasting
a quality other than its thing cannot be called that thing's quality
all cognitions arise by way of will
if every will needs a prior will, there is an infinite regress
a teacher who gave his body in former births for its merit must account for how the doer reaps
if virtuous gods can show the three times, the Lord wiser than the three worlds knows them
the five senses arise each from one of the five elements
a living soul exists
the king's sceptre has strayed from rightness, and the king's error is what has robbed her of her husband
the sun knows all that is done in the world and can bear witness to a man's innocence
suffering common to all is of two kinds, harm from outside and disease of the body
a thing and its nature always come together as one, leaving nothing for inherence to join
a wife may follow her dead husband into the place his deeds carry him
a woman whom even fire will not kill is held by her own evil deeds
a curse laid in grief by one wronged makes the wrongdoers suffer the same sorrow
when a former deed rises in wrath, penance does not help those who are not upright

note: The cow that licks, suckles and guards the abandoned infant here is the cow in whose womb Aputtiran is reborn after he dies on Manipallavam.
teaches: The mother who would not pity her child is replaced across two births by the cow, which first nurses him and then bears him, so the name 'cow's son' that the brahmins throw at him as an insult becomes literally true and honoured.

note: Both pledge a herd girl to the man who, unafraid of the black bull's fury, takes it (காரி கதன் அஞ்சான்); in the Kalittokai her kin give her to the catcher, in the epic no bull is penned.
teaches: The epic keeps the bull-catch pledge word for word but drops the contest, so a herders' marriage custom survives as the names of dance roles in a rite against ill omen.

gains.a: the pledge gains its origin in a real contest in which a girl's kin give her to the man who takes the bull
gains.b: the custom gains a later life, recited over girls as a ritual formula with no bull and no catcher

note: Kundalakesi gave the Buddha's gifts of wife and child as proof of his compassion; Neelakesi tells the Buddha that those who take such gifts cannot be shown not to be thieves.
teaches: The gift offered as proof of compassion is answered not only as the giver's folly, as in 207, but as a wrong done through the receiver, since a wife and children were never the giver's to give.

note: To the killer Kanchanan the same deity said that karma took the prince's life yet his own cruel deed would not leave him; to Manimekalai it says the prince's death is the fruit of his own killing.
teaches: Together the two speeches show the epic's karma as a chain in which every link is also a fresh wrong: the victim's old deed ripens only through a new killing whose doer is held to account in turn.

note: In kaathai 20 the pillar image tells Kanchanan that ripened karma took the prince's life; here the ascetic tells the king that the prince's evil deed itself struck him by the vidyadhara's hand.
teaches: The killing is told twice as the work of karma, but the deity also tells Kanchanan his act was a cruel deed that will follow him, while the ascetic, speaking to the father, leaves the killer's guilt out, so the same explanation is shaped by who hears it.

note: 121 says giving is easy and knowing due rank (வரிசை அறிதல்) is hard; 140 shows the lord of Nanjil, 'knowing rank' (வரிசை அறிதலின்), answering a request for rice with an elephant.
teaches: Read together, the two poems show that வரிசை cut both ways: 121 wants the patron to rank the recipient, 140 praises a patron who ranked by his own greatness and so overpaid, so the measure of a gift could be the giver's standing as well as the receiver's worth.

note: The Manimekalai's Vedic logician lists comparison, scripture, presumption and other means beside perception and inference; the Neelakesi's teacher lists memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and scripture.
teaches: Both lists keep inference and scripture, but the Jain list admits memory and recognition as valid knowledge and leaves out comparison and presumption, so the count of means is itself a point of difference between the schools the epics stage.

note: Saathan's rule that gods grant no boon without tapas uses the couplet's own word செய்தவம், and then he grants Maalathi a child she has not earned.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the tale shows that the rule linking tapas to its reward is the god's to state and also the god's to override, so grace in the epic stands beside the merit rule rather than inside it.

gains.a: the general law behind Saathan's line 17, which shows his gift to Maalathi as an exception to it
gains.b: a scene where the law is spoken by a god to a woman without tapas and then not applied

note: In 499 she tells the Buddhist that nothing is ever known except through its qualities; in 802 she tells the Vaisheshika that a quality other than its thing cannot be called its.
teaches: The same principle that a thing is reached only through its qualities is used first to prove a bearer exists and then to deny that the bearer can stand apart from what it bears.

note: The couplet says that when the king bends justice the sky withholds rain; the goddess gives the same chain with the planets inserted between sceptre and rain, and aims it at the heir's desire for a nun.
teaches: The pair shows the rule's reach being widened: what the Kural ties to judging wrongly the epic applies to a prince's private lust, so the sceptre is bent by desire, not only by a verdict.

gains.a: The goddess's warning is grounded in a known rule of kingship, which shows she argues from ethics shared beyond her own creed rather than from her power.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which the wrong is not a judgment and the wrongdoer not yet king, which tests how far its bending of justice extends.

note: The queen of Bhoothapandiyan refuses the widow's life of alli food and the gravel bed and chooses the pyre; Kannaki asks whether she too must waste away like the widows who keep those observances.
teaches: Both widows refuse the observances of kaimmai, but the Sangam queen turns to the pyre while Kannaki turns to the sun and the king, so the epic moves the wife's refusal of widowhood from death beside the husband to a demand for justice.

gains.a: the lament gains the Sangam measure of what the widows' observances were and that a high-born wife could reject them
gains.b: the poem's choice between widowhood and the pyre gains a third way, a widow who rejects both to accuse the king

note: Purananuru 34 cites dharma as granting expiation (கழுவாய்) for killing cows, destroying unborn children and wronging elders, but none for ingratitude; in Neelakesi 148 the demoness asks expiation for her sins and is told to teach the Jina's path.
teaches: Both assume that grave wrongs admit expiation, but the Sangam maxim treats it as a provision of dharma with exceptions while the Jain sage turns it into a lifelong mission of persuasion.

gains.a: the sage's command gains the older Tamil idea of a fixed expiation, against which its novelty shows
gains.b: the maxim's list of expiable wrongs is shown to admit a case, killing and the will to kill, met by teaching rather than rite

note: Tirumular says the Lord who made birth for joy shut it in the suffering of the bond; Aravanar says the born meet growing suffering, the unborn great bliss, and suffering comes from attachment.
teaches: Both trace suffering to a binding, attachment or the bond, but they disagree about birth itself: for the Buddhist teacher birth is the suffering and not being born is bliss, while for Tirumular birth was made for joy and the bond was laid on it by the same Lord; the conflict holds on reading இன்பப் பிறவி as birth made for joy.

gains.a: a theist account in which a maker lays the suffering on birth, which shows that Aravanar names no maker and makes attachment alone the cause
gains.b: an opposed claim that birth is itself suffering, which shows that the verse's birth made for joy is a position taken, not common ground

note: Both kuthirai maram poems name the young rider with one formula: நோக்கினர்ச் செகுக்கும் காளை (302) and எள்ளுநர்ச் செகுக்கும் காளை (303).
teaches: The epithet for the young horseman was a fixed frame with a free slot for his victims, those who look at him or those who mock him, so two poets of the same thurai shared a stock line and varied only whom it threatened.

note: Tirumanthiram 1616 makes Siva the renouncer who dwells in the burning ground and cuts off the births of those who renounce; Neelakesi 141 praises the ascetic who in the burning ground uprooted all his own karmas.
teaches: The same dwelling place holds two answers to who ends rebirth: in the Saiva verse the god of the burning ground cuts the renouncer's births, in the Jain hymn the renouncer there uproots his karma himself, a disagreement that turns on reading பல்வினையும் பறிப்போய் as his own karma.

gains.a: the hymn's self-won release is set against the Saiva alternative it implicitly excludes
gains.b: Tirumular's burning-ground renouncer-god is shown to answer a rival model in which no god is needed

note: The couplet warns men off women who weigh the gain and speak of virtue; Chithirapathi describes dancers who take many gains with sweet speech and leave like bees, and tells the prince to bind such a woman.
teaches: The couplet's advice is to avoid the profit-weighing woman, while the courtesan who describes the same woman advises the prince to seize her, so a portrait meant to protect men becomes a licence to coerce a girl who has left that life.

gains.a: The courtesan's self-portrait gains the weight of a recognised moral description, which makes her case for force seem like common sense.
gains.b: The couplet's type gains a case where the woman so labelled is no longer what the label says, showing how the description outlives the conduct.

note: Tirumular says a land where Brahmins make the oblation dusk and dawn does not decline and its king prospers; here the Brahmin bhuta of the unfailing three-fire life leaves Madurai because its king erred.
teaches: Tirumular makes the Brahmins' rites the protection of king and land, while the epic makes the king's justice the condition of the guardian of those rites staying, so the two run the dependence in opposite directions.

gains.a: the Brahmin bhuta's departure gains its weight: it withdraws what the Saiva text holds to be the land's very safeguard
gains.b: the verse gains a limit: in the epic even the guardian of the three fires cannot keep a city whose king has done wrong

note: The couplet says the அந்தணர் are the virtuous, because they wear cool kindness toward every life; Sudhamathi's Brahmin father, turned off by Brahmins and Jain monks alike, cries for any அறவோர் and is answered by a Buddhist monk, called மறையோன் at 68.
teaches: The epic tells the couplet's redefinition as a story: those who hold the title by birth or by vows fail the dying man, and the title of one who knows the sacred lore passes to the stranger who shows kindness to him.

gains.a: The cry அறவோர் உளீரோ gets the couplet's measure of virtue, kindness to every life, which explains why the monks of spotless form fail it.
gains.b: The couplet's definition by conduct is shown working against real holders of the status, and across a sectarian line the couplet does not name.

note: Kural 351 says a base birth comes from the confusion that takes the unreal as real; Aravanar puts ignorance first in the chain of birth and defines it as trusting hearsay that a hare has horns.
teaches: The couplet names unreal things taken as real without saying which; the epic gives the error a mechanism, hearsay preferred to what is seen, and a place, the first of twelve links, so the couplet's one step to birth becomes a chain.

gains.a: an older Tamil statement that ignorance is the root of birth, which shows the Buddhist chain speaking in a known idiom
gains.b: a definition of its மருள் by a stock example of an unreal thing (the hare's horn) and a causal sequence from error to birth

note: Both have women parted from their lovers at evening (காதலر்ப் பிரிந்த, nearly the same half-line), and both liken their breath to air blown in a smith's furnace.
teaches: The epic takes a Sangam paalai heroine's evening lament nearly verbatim and turns it from one woman's crisis into a class of Puhar's women, one entry in a survey of the city's nights.

gains.a: the epic's brief list gains the depth of a full lament, the friend, the fear of death in the evening, that its two lines only gesture at
gains.b: the Akananuru poem gains evidence that its furnace image and half-line had become stock diction a later poet could cite as a type

note: In 7 the poet asks readers not to scorn his work, since people take even a bird's cry as meaningful; in 885 Neelakesi counts the omen of bird cries among the things the elements cannot explain.
teaches: The poem leans twice on the common trust in bird-omens, once to defend itself and once to defeat the materialist, which shows how much of its case rests on what the world already accepts.

note: Both list the five aggregates; the Manimekalai's teacher names feeling நுகர்ச்சி and formation பாவனை, the Neelakesi's Kundalakesi names them உழப்பு and செய்கை.
teaches: The Jain poet reports the aggregates accurately in substance, but naming feeling as pain (உழப்பு) and adding the flame of momentary perishing loads the list toward the points he means to attack.

note: 338 wishes love to last like the Porai's Kolli; 209 tells how Kari killed Ori and gave Kolli to the Cheras, who set a goddess image there.
teaches: Read with 209, the hero's figure of permanence is a hill that changed lords by a killing, so what the poet makes lasting is the hill itself, not any house that held it.

note: The quatrain says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounce in childhood; Visakai points to Dharmadattan's grey hair and turns him not to renunciation but to giving.
teaches: The quatrain offers only two paths, early renunciation or clinging to youth; Visakai, who has kept a vow of chastity since youth, shows a third for the grey-haired householder: shared charity without marriage.

gains.a: Visakai's appeal to his grey hair gains the quatrain's standard of what the wise do before it comes.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the one who saw age coming chose a vow and charity rather than the robe.

note: The brahmin likens the summer that turns mullai and kurinji into paalai to a wide land that has lost its royal order when its king bent with his officers (கொற்றவன் கோடி); the couplet says that if the king bends justice the sky will not pour rain.
teaches: The couplet states that a bent king dries the sky, and the brahmin's simile reads a drought landscape as the look of a misruled kingdom, so the waste Kovalan crosses already pictures the bent sceptre waiting in Madurai.

gains.a: the simile gains a doctrine that makes the drought the fruit of misrule rather than only a likeness of it
gains.b: the couplet gains a picture of what its rainless land looks like: forest and hill twisted out of their nature into waste

note: Both show a wife at her husband's wounded chest at the edge of night; the Puram wife reads the omens and dreads the widow's life, while Kannaki asks who will name the deed and blames the king.
teaches: The Sangam lament by the wounded body looks ahead to widowhood, but Kannaki's lament at the same scene turns outward into a charge against the king, so the old mourning form becomes the opening of a plea.

gains.a: Kannaki's lament gains the old shape of the wife's watch by the wounded husband, against which its turn to accusation shows
gains.b: the Puram wife's private grief gains a counterpart in which the same scene is made public and political

note: The couplet says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from the difference in deeds; the vari credits a girl's penance with her glory and then declares her birth-clan, the bow-wielding hunters, the clan among clans.
teaches: The song agrees that distinction comes from a deed, the girl's penance, but hands that distinction straight back to the birth-group, the move the couplet's rule forbids, so the pair shows how a low-ranked clan claims rank through one daughter's merit rather than by denying that birth confers it.

gains.a: the hunters' boast is shown to rest on a deed and not on birth alone, and to turn that deed into a clan's rank
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a case that tests it, where an individual deed's distinction is claimed for a whole clan of a lowly calling

note: Kural 948 tells the physician to find the disease, then its root, then the remedy, and act; 723 says the teachers' instruction does the same for the suffering of many beings.
teaches: The Kural's method of the physician becomes, in a Jain debate, the method of the religious teacher, so that a rival doctrine is treated as a disease to be diagnosed rather than an enemy to be beaten.

gains.a: the debater's appeal to teachers gains a known, stepwise method that any listener can check her diagnosis of the Ajivika against
gains.b: the couplet's clinical rule is shown to carry over to the cure of births, a reach its place in the chapter on medicine does not claim

note: After the northern battle the Chera is hailed as one who made a field of dharma (அறக்களஞ் செய்தோன்) having finished the field of war; Maadalan tells him he has made only the war-field sacrifice and never the dharma-field one.
teaches: The epic sets the battlefield hailed as a field of dharma against a brahmin's verdict that the same wars were sacrifice of the wrong field, so the king's highest praise and his counsellor's rebuke use the same two words to opposite ends.

note: 381 makes six assets (army, people, wealth, ministers, friends, fortress) the mark of a lion among kings. Parimelazhagar's 'others' in 661 are exactly army, fort and friendship, which he says don't count as firmness.
teaches: The list of assets is empty without the mind that uses them.

note: The Puhar book opens hailing the moon, the sun and Puhar for resembling the Chola's umbrella, wheel and line, and closes wishing Puhar to live like the morning sun and the evening moon.
teaches: The book is framed by the same sun, moon and city, but at the opening the heavenly bodies are praised as likenesses of the king, and at the close they are the measure of the city's own life with the king gone from the comparison, matching a summary that names the Chola line but no Chola.

note: The kuravai girls call Murugan's kurava wife their own clan's daughter; Thiruppugazh 1000 tells Valli guarding the hunters' millet from her platform and Murugan entering the field.
teaches: The epic's hill women claim Valli as kin and pray to Murugan as an in-law of the clan, while the later devotional song keeps the millet field and the hunter girl but makes the story a model of the god's grace to the devotee, so the kin claim comes first and the theology after.

gains.a: the clan claim gains a view of what the Valli story would later carry in devotion
gains.b: the song's millet field and hunter girl are seen rooted in a hill people's claim to the goddess as their daughter

note: Tirumular says the king whose task is to protect cows, women, the virtuous and the holy goes to endless hell if he fails them; in the burning Madurai the cows and the virtuous are protected not by the king, who is dead, but by the fire itself.
teaches: The two list the same protected beings, but the Saiva verse punishes the failing king after death while the epic transfers his duty of protection, in this life, to the wronged wife's fire.

gains.a: the fire's sparing gains a recognised code: these are the beings any king is bound to protect
gains.b: the verse gains a case where the duty survives the king's failure and is fulfilled by another power, which its threat of hell does not consider

note: Both are vanjinam vows in the conditional form 'if I do not, may I', one by a Pandya Nedunjeliyan before battle, one by Kannaki against a Pandya; the epic's king is not shown to be the Talaiyalanganattu victor of the puram poem.
teaches: The puram king stakes his own name as a just king on winning, while Kannaki stakes her name as a pathini on unmaking a king, so the epic turns the royal oath-form against the royal house and makes a widow's virtue the thing pledged.

gains.a: her vow gains the recognised form and force of the warrior's pledge, which explains the kaathai's name
gains.b: the puram oath-form gains a use outside war and kingship, showing that its penalty of being called a cruel king could be fulfilled by another's vow

note: Against Kundalakesi (201) Neelakesi used the thread running through a garland for what carries knowledge from moment to moment; against Mokkalan (419) she says the soul's being stays through austerity, vows and divine birth.
teaches: The continuity argued against Kundalakesi for memory within one life is here stretched across births, because the reward of penance needs the same soul to arrive in heaven.

note: The Neelakesi's hell has no one to relieve the sufferer (பரிபவரும் இல்லையே); Arunagirinathar asks Murugan to come at speed when Death would drop him into the seven hells, so that his sins go.
teaches: The two answer opposite ways whether anyone can stand between a sinner's deeds and hell: the Jain sermon says no one can, the Murugan song asks that the god do exactly that; the conflict holds if பரிபவர் means one who relieves or rescues.

gains.a: the Jain hell's lack of a rescuer is seen as a stance against the hope of divine rescue that Tamil devotion voices
gains.b: the devotee's plea is seen against a doctrine for which such a plea has no one to hear it

note: The couplet asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep on the beloved's soft arms; the epic likens the newly married couple to those who enjoy in Uttarakuru the fruit of completed austerity.
teaches: Both weigh a couple's joy against a heavenly world, but the couplet ranks love above heaven while the epic makes the couple's joy itself a heaven earned by past austerity, and so something that can be used up, which is how the epic prepares its turn from pleasure to karma.
