gains.a: the epic's simile gains a contrast: love here is not set above heaven but counted as heaven's wage, a measure of merit rather than a rival to it
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question gains an answer it does not give, that the beloved's arms may be a heaven only for as long as the merit behind them lasts

note: The couplet says nothing is stronger than ஊழ், which arrives first even when one devises (சூழினும்) another way; the patikam says the ஊழ்வினை comes in wrath and makes one eat it, through the finely made (சூழ்வினை) anklet.
teaches: The couplet's fate outruns any plan, and the epic gives the plan a body: the anklet Kovalan meant to sell to start life again becomes the instrument of the fate it was meant to escape, and the epic adds that fate comes in anger and feeds its fruit, which the couplet does not say.

gains.a: the epic's moral gains a sharper claim about scheming, that devising against fate is itself overtaken, which explains why Kovalan's fresh start ends in his death
gains.b: the couplet's abstract race between fate and plan gains a concrete object, the anklet, and an emotional colour, the wrath of the returning deed

note: The decade preface on Senguttuvan, son of Nedunjeralathan by the Chola Manakkilli, says in one phrase that he went north wanting a stone for the goddess pathini and bathed it in the Ganga; the epic's prose gives the same parentage and campaign, and adds the Aryan kings' taunt and the stone carried on their heads.
teaches: Held together, the two show the Sangam colophon tradition already knew a Chera king's northern stone for a pathini, and the epic turns that bare record into a cause and a ritual: the stone becomes a goddess only after it is won by humbling the kings who mocked Tamil kingship.

gains.a: the epic's prose gains an outside witness for the king's parentage and his stone-seeking campaign, so the cult is set in remembered Chera history
gains.b: the preface's terse phrase கடவுள் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள் gains the story of whose stone it was and why the king went for it

note: Kural 256 says no one would sell flesh if the world did not kill to eat; Neelakesi says that if all renounced flesh no one would go near killing, and that the teacher who teaches dharma earns its merit.
teaches: The couplet blames the eating world for the killing; the debate adds that a world's eating follows its teachers, so a teacher who permits flesh carries the demand argument's guilt.

gains.a: Neelakesi's bare 'if all renounced it' gains the Kural's market reasoning that links each buyer to the killing
gains.b: the couplet's faceless 'world' gains a concrete cause of its habits, the teacher whose word makes flesh-eating dharma

note: Neelakesi says that if only perception and inference counted there could be no medical treatise; the Kural's chapter on medicine states the three humours on the authority of the learned in the books (நூலோர்).
teaches: The Kural's deference to the medical books for the three humours is just the kind of text-borne knowledge the Jain debater cites: neither the patient's sight nor his inference gives it.

gains.a: the debater's appeal to medicine gets a Tamil instance in which a moral book takes medical doctrine on its authors' word
gains.b: the couplet's passing reference to நூலோர் is seen to carry a view of knowledge that a rival school in Tamil denied

note: The couplet says this woman is herself the cure for the sickness she brings; the vari asks whether the sickness her face and eyes gave can be cured only by her breasts.
teaches: The song splits the couplet's paradox across the body, the eyes and face causing the sickness and the breasts curing it, which shows how a later lyric turned the Kural's single riddle into a scene of parts.

gains.a: the stanza's closing guess gains a known paradox behind it, that the beloved breaks the rule of medicine by being both cause and cure
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete setting and a division of roles within the woman's body that it leaves unstated

note: Kural 275 says the hidden conduct of those who claim to be free of attachment brings many evils; 258 charges monks who swell attachment while seeming free of it.
teaches: The Kural leaves its 'many evils' unnamed; the Neelakesi names them as a ghost's birth or dark hell, turning a moral warning into a doctrine of rebirth.

gains.a: the charge of hypocrisy is anchored in a recognised rule about false renouncers
gains.b: the couplet's vague cry of evils is filled in with the specific rebirths a Jain expects for such conduct

claims.gist: if kings take up the dharma of grace, nothing else is needed to remove the world's faults
dharma for all living beings is nothing but food, clothing and shelter
becoming is the accumulation of karma
each link arises with the one before it as its support: ignorance supports action, action consciousness, and so on
a teacher who permits flesh-eating leads himself and his disciples into the fiery hell
trees are living beings, as their changes with the seasons show
a giver who knows the asker is a god gives without risk of death, so the gift is no sacrifice
a dissimilar example from which neither property is excluded fails, whether it exists or not
when a quality perishes the substance changes with it
when the source has perished, what arises after it has nothing in it
a part cut from one body cannot become part of another, so a gift of flesh or an eye benefits no one
the Buddhist teachers' doctrine ruined the idea of release
a deed done even without intention reaches its doer and bears fruit
a deed done without intention bears no fruit at all
a thief armed with these arts can be seen by no one, by night or by day
one cannot hold both that the aggregates exist and that form, feeling, perception and formation do not
there is a person (pudgala) besides the aggregates
youth does not last
the soul passes between the bodies of gods, humans, beasts and hell-beings, going by the deeds it did, as a dancer changes costume
the supreme self is the one that enjoys and sees
perfection and knowledge belong to every soul, not to one supreme self
the Buddhist relation of the truths to the aggregates meets the same dilemma of identity and difference
worship of the Buddha's footprints in one birth brings its fruit in the next, as rebirth beside the one who led the way
the teachings of the various other schools are false words
the human body is a lump made of food, so hunger rules it
rules for eating and shaving are not themselves the path of dharma
the quality has no reality apart from its bearer, and the bearer is one with its quality
right faith is unturning trust in the eight things beginning with God, joined to longing for bliss
an old deed drives its doer to his end
wealth earned by dharma and spent in the way of the virtuous does not run out
present suffering is the fruit of one's own old deeds
beings come to the womb by good or bad deeds, and the ripening deed brings joy or sorrow
the bad deeds are ten: three of the body, four of speech and three of the mind
those who do the ten bad deeds are born as animals, ghosts and hell-beings
those who avoid them, keep the precepts and give are born as gods, humans and Brahmas
the Ajivika god is free of disease
an omniscient who does not tell what he knows is lesser than an ordinary man who shares the good he sees
the supreme knower keeps silent and does not teach what he knows
a soul as large as the body cannot be contained within the body
the soul extends through the whole body and is contained within it
under a king whose sceptre is just, Death cannot do its work openly
the gods need and eat the flesh offered in sacrifice
the gods have no bodily hunger for meat, so the slaughter offered to them is pointless
animals with all five senses, hearing the last, are many in kind by legs and gait and fill sea and islands
faulty examples are of two kinds, by similarity and by difference, each in five forms
the omniscient's knowledge does not depend on the senses and does not proceed in sequence
bondage and release arise from their own causes, and no one exists who can grant them
desire, anger and delusion are the cause of all that has been taught
clinging is cut by seeing things as impermanent, sorrowful, selfless and impure; hatred by friendliness, compassion and sympathetic joy; delusion by hearing, reflection, cultivation and insight
adornment and enjoyment hinder meditation, so an ascetic need not clean away the dirt of the body
filth belongs to the nature of the human body
the sin of killing follows only when the killer's mind reached the one who died
hardships such as exposure, fasting and sleeplessness bring no benefit

note: The Vanji ascetics foretell that the sea will take Kaveripattinam; in kaathai 25 the sea swallows it by the Manimekala goddess's curse and the ascetic and the mothers go to Vanji.
teaches: The flood of Puhar is given two causes in the epic, a prophecy the seers already knew and a goddess's curse on a negligent king, so foreknowledge and a moral cause sit together without either cancelling the other.

note: In 127 the sage gives Neelakesi the nectar of dharma as the medicine for birth; in 722 she tells the Ajivika she was a demon until a great one gave her that medicine.
teaches: The cure first given to the demoness becomes the debater's own credential: she argues not only from doctrine but from her own conversion, offering the opponent what she was given.

note: The Valayapathi fragment says not to accept a dharma joined with killing; Neelakesi applies that rule to the Veda, which she says forbids killing and yet permits limitless killing in sacrifice.
teaches: The fragment's maxim gets a named target: the dharma joined with killing is the Vedic sacrifice, and the Neelakesi adds that such a dharma fails even by its own rule against killing.

note: The Manimekalai names the mind's three bad deeds as coveting, anger and wrong view; 529 says pride, deceit and greed are as evil as anger and the Buddhists leave them uncondemned.
teaches: Set against the Buddhist epic's actual list, Neelakesi's charge turns out to be a clash of classifications: she measures a list of ten deeds against the Jain four passions, anger, pride, deceit and greed.

note: In 387 Neelakesi gives Mokkalan the threefold nature of arising, perishing and lasting; in 803 she offers the same three to the Vaisheshika.
teaches: The one triad is aimed at opposite errors: against the Buddhist it adds lasting to momentary things, against the Vaisheshika it adds perishing to eternal substances.

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out the one who did it as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Manimekalai says the cruel deed ripened so that her father went to a foreign land and died by the sword, and that it casts 'us' into misery.
teaches: The quatrain's deed that hunts down its own doer explains how karma found Kovalan far from home, yet the daughter's 'us' lets the same ripening fall on her too, which the one-doer rule does not allow, so the pair opens the question whether a deed's fruit can be shared by kin.

gains.a: a stated rule that the deed seeks out its own doer, against which her claim to share her father's ripening becomes visible as a widening
gains.b: a case in which the deed finds its doer in a strange land, and a survivor who counts herself in its fruit, a limit the calf image leaves untested

note: Puranan likens his Lord's ungraspable form to the rainbow; Neelakesi makes the rainbow the type of a caused thing, born of sun on rain.
teaches: The same rainbow serves the Ajivika as a sign of a form beyond grasping and the Jain as proof that such a form is produced, so the simile decides nothing until its cause is asked.

note: Manimekalai hears the prince's chariot with fear and asks what to do; in the next kaathai, after he has gone, she confesses that her heart followed the stranger who had scorned her.
teaches: The crystal wall kept her body from his hands but not her heart from him, so the flight here and the confession after it show the girl's renunciation is not yet secure.

note: Kural 362: if one must desire, desire not to be born, and that comes by desiring not to desire; the patikam closes with Manimekalai, having heard the dharma, vowing that becoming be cut off (பவத் திறம் அறுக என ... நோற்றதும்).
teaches: The Kural allows one desire, for birthlessness, and reaches it by turning desire on itself; the epic makes that one desire a vow kept with austerity after hearing a teacher, so the end the Kural states as inner paradox is reached in the epic through instruction and practice.

gains.a: the heroine's closing vow is seen to be the single desire the Kural permits, not a lapse from desirelessness
gains.b: the couplet's wish for birthlessness gains a path, a teacher's dharma and a vow, which the couplet does not name

note: The Sankhya of 735 counts twenty-five principles that need no maker; Tirumular's Lord makes the twenty-five within the womb for each birth.
teaches: The Saiva verse keeps the Sankhya tally of twenty-five but puts a maker over it, the one element both the Sankhya and its Jain critic do without.

gains.a: The Neelakesi list gains evidence that its twenty-five were common coin in Tamil doctrine, later taken up into a theistic account of embodiment.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's bare 'twenty-five' gains its named members and its Sankhya origin, so a reader can see what the Lord is said to assemble.

note: Both picture a public hall (பொதியில்) fallen to ruin, its pillar abandoned by its god; in Purananuru 52 it is the fate of lands the Pandya conquers, in Akananuru 307 a dove clings to it with its mate.
teaches: A ruined hall abandoned by its god was a stock picture of a conquered land, and the akam poet turns it round: even in that ruin a pair of birds keeps faith, which makes the hero's leaving harsher.

note: Mokkalan says that to declare a thing inexpressible is self-contradiction; the Manimekalai's Buddhist teacher counts keeping silent before an ill-formed question as a proper kind of answer.
teaches: The Buddhist in the Jain epic attacks the Jain mode of the inexpressible with an argument his own school, as the Manimekalai presents it, would have to face, since it too treats not saying as an answer.

note: The Maduraikkanchi lists in Madurai's four streets (நால்வேறு தெருவினும்) the shell-cutters, gem-borers, goldsmiths, gold-assayers and cloth-sellers; the epic closes its tour with the gold-assayers, cloth street, grain street and the four streets (நால்வேறு தெருவும்).
teaches: The epic follows the Sangam catalogue of Madurai's trades down to the four streets, but where the Sangam poem lists them as the plenty of a victorious Pandya, the epic shows them through a stranger about to be condemned by one of these trades, so the inherited praise of the city becomes the setting of its fall.

gains.a: the epic's tour gains a source and a measure: it is the classic praise of Madurai, which makes its turn toward ruin a turn against a known tradition
gains.b: the Sangam catalogue gains a later reading in which the gold-assayers it lists among the city's glories include the trade that will bring about the city's burning

note: Thuvathikan foretold the drought in Kanchi and that she would bring rain there with the bowl; Kovalan's father now gives the same charge and asks whether she did not learn it from Thuvathikan.
teaches: A goddess's foretelling becomes a human teacher's command, so her mission to Kanchi rests on two witnesses, one divine and one from her own family.

note: The brahmin warns of a goddess on the hard way who appears gently and holds travellers back; at the pool Kovalan recalls that the wondrous brahmin said a deluding goddess haunts the forest (மயக்குந் தெய்வமிவ் வன்காட் டுண்டென) and unmasks her with a mantra.
teaches: The pilgrim's road knowledge, which Kavunthi had set aside as unneeded for the cave, is what saves Kovalan in the forest, so the chapter does not let either guide be simply right.

note: In Kovalan's sarthu vari the shore girl asks how simple folk could know that men who broke their oaths before the sea-god are without dharma; in Madhavi's, she asks how they could know that girls' slipping bangles proclaim the men who married them in secret.
teaches: Both songs use the same refrain of feigned simplicity, but Kovalan's names the man's broken oath as the wrong while Madhavi's shows the cost landing on the woman's body, whose loosening bangles make the secret public, so the exchange moves blame from the oath to its visible price.

note: Arunagirinathar lumps Buddhists with the followers of Kapila and Kanada as clamouring disputants whose books cannot give the teaching; here a Buddhist teacher takes apart arguments of the Sankhya and the Vaisheshika by formal logic.
teaches: The pair shows the same quarrel from inside and outside: what the devotee hears as noise of books, the epic presents as a disciplined refutation, and it is the Buddhist the devotee counts first among the noisy.

gains.a: the epic's refutation gains a later Saiva verdict that its whole contest misses the point
gains.b: the song's list of disputants gains a working example of how those schools actually argued against each other

note: The voice in the burning ground names the merchant Chandradattan and his ship; at the end of the tale Saathuvan comes home on Chandradattan's ship, as foretold.
teaches: The prophecy that stopped Aathirai's death is kept only after Saathuvan has converted his captors, so the voice in effect promised a return that his own learning and argument had still to earn.

note: The patikam says the Pandya did not inquire because the time of the deed's ripening had come; Kannaki addresses him as தேரா மன்னா, the king who did not inquire, and says ஊழ்வினை drove her husband to Madurai.
teaches: The patikam makes karma the reason the king failed to inquire, but Kannaki uses that failure as her charge against him while giving karma only as what brought Kovalan to the city, so the epic keeps karma and royal fault as two causes and assigns blame only to the second.

note: The defeated Kundalakesi names Arkkachandran of Ujjain as her teacher (227); 233 opens the next sarukkam on Arkkachandran in Ujjain.
teaches: Each defeat in the Neelakesi names the next opponent, so the chain of debates is built by the losers' own testimony of who taught them.

note: The Kural says to be spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and all else is show; Neelakesi denies that the mind alone is the deed and argues that action always goes with it and is karma too.
teaches: A mind-first ethic that the Kural states as praise of sincerity becomes, between Buddhist and Jain, a disputed claim about where karma lies, and the Jain side refuses to let the act fall away.

gains.a: Neelakesi's argument is seen to cut against a widely accepted Tamil maxim, not only against Buddhist doctrine
gains.b: the couplet's stress on the mind is shown to carry a doctrinal risk, the excusing of the act, that the Kural does not address

note: Kovalan asks whether his ruin is illusion or a strong former deed (வல்வினை கொல்லோ); at his death the narrator answers that his former deed came in wrath (பண்டை ஊழ்வினை உருத்து).
teaches: The question the victim cannot answer is answered by the narrator only over his body, so the karma he half suspects is confirmed only when it can no longer be acted on, and he had meanwhile blamed himself.

note: Tirumular says the wise gave up logic and disputation (தர்க்க வாதம்) and gained release by reciting the Veda; Aravanar, who folds scripture into inference, ends his teaching of dharma with the rules of disputation.
teaches: The two give opposite answers to whether argument leads toward release: for Tirumular it is what the wise leave behind, for the Buddhist teacher it is the discipline that sorts true from false before doctrine is heard.

gains.a: the epic's logic lesson gains a named Saiva rejection of the very method it teaches
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal of argument gains a full example of the argument he dismisses, from a school that grants the Veda no separate authority

note: The town lists the arts set down for dancing women that Madhavi mastered; Silappathikaram 3 opens on her seven years' training in dance, song and beauty for her first performance before the king.
teaches: The training that the earlier epic presents as the making of Madhavi's fame becomes in the town's mouth its argument against her leaving that life, so the courtesan's accomplishments bind her to her trade as a claim others hold on her.

note: The quatrain says a harlot's love goes out like a lamp when the money is gone; Chithirapathi says courtesans leave a drained flower like bees and leave men like Fortune when their merit ends.
teaches: The moralist's charge against the courtesan is spoken in the epic by a courtesan as her house's rule, and she uses it to forbid her daughter's grief and renunciation, so the faithlessness the quatrain condemns turns out to be enforced on the women themselves.

gains.a: Chithirapathi's boast is shown to be the very account outsiders give of her profession, which she presents as her own code.
gains.b: The quatrain gains the cost to the woman who tries to leave the life it describes, which its warning to men never considers.

note: The patikam states that a former deed comes in wrath and makes its doer eat its fruit; here the narrator uses the same words (ஊழ்வினை, உருத்து) for the moment Kovalan leaves Madhavi.
teaches: The first time the narrative names the patikam's third moral at work, the deed ripens not in a crime or a court but in a lover mishearing a song, so the epic's karma enters the story through a private misjudgement long before Madurai.

note: In 259 the monk says nothing exists but the mind and evil conduct is not evil karma; 541 states the Buddhist rule that a killing needs knowledge and intention as well as a death.
teaches: The earlier boast that only the mind counts becomes a precise five-part rule here, and the precision is what lets Neelakesi build cases of mistaken identity in which a man dies and no killing is counted.

note: The herdswomen dance the kuravai of Mayavan, his elder brother and Pinnai to ward off the omens before Kovalan's death; the Chola king sees that same kuravai in birds whirling in his pleasure grove.
teaches: Across the two epics the one divine dance is first a rite of fear performed by herdswomen over coming disaster and then a pleasantry of a king at play, while Kovalan's daughter works in his prison, so the image measures how far the court stands from the suffering it governs.

note: In the Silappathikaram the goddess of Madurai tells the grieving Kannaki she will see her husband within fourteen days, but only in a god's form; here the grieving Lakshmi is told a goddess will show her husband in a later human birth.
teaches: The two epics answer the same plea of a widow to see her husband again in opposite ways: the first through a heavenly reunion after death, the second through a new birth in which the man shown is the one she must learn to leave.

note: 339 says death is like sleep and birth is like waking from it, as an image of impermanence. 1216 wishes waking away altogether, for the sake of staying with her lover.
teaches: If the two were read together, her wish would come close to a wish not to be reborn, though nothing in the verse says this.

note: The Manimekalai's Vaisheshika gives the same six categories (பொருள், குணம், கருமம், சாமானியம், விசேடம், கூட்டம்) and is left unanswered; Neelakesi's opponent gives them in 785 to 788 and she answers them from 791.
teaches: The six-category list was a fixed set piece of Tamil accounts of the schools, and the two epics differ in what they do with it: the Buddhist epic records it and moves on, the Jain epic makes each category a target.

note: Tirumular says the undiscerning take the moon in clouds and in a pot of Ganga water as many, though it is one; Neelakesi asks who ever said the moon differs in each water, to show the Lord's one knowing present to all things.
teaches: Both use one moon in many waters, but the Saiva verse makes the many appearances one reality, while the Jain keeps the many things real and makes only the knowing single.

gains.a: The Jain image is seen to stop short of the oneness the same figure carries in Saiva teaching.
gains.b: Tirumular's moon is shown to be a shared figure the Jains used for knowledge, not only for the one Lord in many bodies.

note: Kavunthi asks whether anything rare is out of reach for those who never swerve from truth and protect living beings, against the brahmin's pool that grants every wish; the couplet says austerity is pursued because it gains whatever is wished as it is wished.
teaches: Kavunthi uses the Kural's promise that discipline gains every wish against a pool that also grants every wish, and grounds that discipline in truth and non-harm, so the couplet's motive of attainment becomes an argument for ethics over pilgrimage.

gains.a: Kavunthi's rhetorical question gains a stated rule that a disciplined life yields whatever is wished
gains.b: the couplet gains a rival, the wish-granting pool, which shows what its claim for austerity competes with

note: The Kundalakesi fragment says filth pours from every opening of the body, so no fragrance is to be found in it; the Neelakesi says dirt on the ascetic is simply the human body's nature.
teaches: The Buddhist poet's own premise, that the body is filth through and through, is the ground of the Jain reply: if the body is foul by nature, washing it cannot make it clean, and mocking the unwashed ascetic contradicts the Buddhist's teaching on the body.

note: Kovalan's midnight dream at Madurai has Kama casting his flower arrows on the bare ground and Madhavi giving Manimekalai before the dharma-one of the Bodhi; in the last kaathai Devanthi reports both as done, Kama flinging his bow and arrows on bare ground as Madhavi gives her daughter at the Bodhi.
teaches: The dream Kovalan feared as a sign of coming harm is fulfilled after his death in its other half, his daughter's renunciation, so the poem treats the dream as true in every part and lets the bad omen and the good one come out of a single night.

note: Uthiyan Cheral's great feast (பெருஞ்சோறு) is praised in Purananuru 2 as a king's gift; here the crowd at that feast becomes a simile for hills crowding on the desert track.
teaches: An akam poet could assume his hearers knew a king's famous feast well enough to turn its crowd of eaters into a picture of a landscape, which tells us how far puram fame was common knowledge.

note: 126 calls Malaiyaman Kari lord of a land of palmyra groves (பெண்ணையம் படப்பை நாடு); Akananuru 35 names Kari of the long chariot, lord of Kovalur, and the great river Pennai (பெண்ணையம் பேரியாறு) at his ford.
teaches: The mother's lament in Akananuru 35 places her daughter's flight on the river of Kari's land, so a puram patron's territory supplies the akam poem's geography, and the shared பெண்ணையம் suggests that 126's phrase may name the river land rather than palms alone.

note: Pisasakan says the world has always been only the combining of elements and those who say otherwise are deluded; at the sarukkam's end he says he accepts birth, demons and all she said.
teaches: The epic stages the materialist's claim to permanence of his view in order to reverse it within the same sarukkam, so the debate ends in a conversion rather than a mere victory.

note: The couplet asks why those who welcome good fortune grieve when it turns; Aravanar tells a king who has lost both queens not to grieve, since it is the fruit of old deeds.
teaches: The couplet grounds equanimity in consistency toward one's own fortune; the epic's monk grounds it in karma and speaks it to a mourner, showing the same counsel turned from self-discipline into consolation for another's loss.

gains.a: Aravanar's curt consolation gains the Kural's argument from consistency, which keeps it from sounding like indifference
gains.b: the couplet gains a hard case: bereavement, where the counsel must be said by one person to another

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika puts all of a life into the moment of conception; 709 shows that this would put a woman's daughter's daughter, and so on, into the first womb.
teaches: Holding the two together shows what the Jain thinks the doctrine costs: if a life is complete at conception, so are all lives to come from it, an infinite nesting the bare report never faces.

note: The Kural says no one would bring meat to sell if the world did not kill to eat; Neelakesi tells the monk who calls buying meat fair that by paying the fishermen daily he wants killing always.
teaches: The couplet's market argument is turned on a particular defence, that meat bought or given is clean of killing, and shown to cover the buyer who pays day after day, so steady demand makes him a party to each killing.

gains.a: Neelakesi's argument is seen to rest on a principle already stated in the Tamil ethical canon
gains.b: the couplet's general demand-and-supply claim is applied to the Buddhist rule of meat accepted from others, a case it does not name

note: In kaathai 14 Indra's gift of plenty left Aputhiran's bowl with no takers and his hall silent; here Aravanar says want has come again despite the Kaveri and forbids laying the same bowl aside.
teaches: The bowl's worth is shown to depend wholly on there being hunger: plenty once made it useless and drove its keeper to death, and now a season of want is the reason it must come back into a girl's hands.

note: The sermon lists the deaths of beasts in Vedic sacrifice among the many sufferings death brings; the debate takes the same slaughter and argues who bears its karma.
teaches: What the sermon offered as an item of compassion for the victim becomes in debate a question of moral accounting for the sacrificer, so the poem moves from pity for the beast to the sacrificer's own liability.

claims.gist: knowing belongs to the soul's own nature wherever the soul is
a soul that knows nothing after it departs could not be shown to exist
alms placed in the hands of great ascetics yield growing fruit, as seed sown with the right water, soil, season and tools
the true scripture is the word of the lord who knew without being taught
all things are comprised in the nine categories
one who does penance without fault has no use for a begging bowl
flesh of a creature that has already died may be eaten
if mind and action are separate, the Buddhist cannot say what the experience of a deed's fruit follows from
the Lord's greatness is that the eight seeds of karma are burnt away, not mere absence of birth
there are only two means of valid knowledge, perception and inference
perception is bare awareness, free of name, class, quality and action, which are reached by inference
inference from an effect to its cause, as from smoke to fire, does not err, while inference from cause or co-presence can
the cause's perishing and the effect's arising are simultaneous, like the two ends of a balance beam
knowledge of all times at once would be knowledge of what does not exist
if self-torment were dharma, self-mutilation, hanging, burning and impalement would be excellent
water that rises into cloud and falls again does not simply move downward by nature
tormenting the body in order to conquer the senses is a fault
the Buddhists' own tonsure and rules are bodily discipline of the same kind
the materialist would need a further, sixth element to account for mind
a teaching that all is suffering with no joy leaves no reason to teach or keep conduct
a compassion that ceases at the teacher's release while beings still suffer was not real compassion
a past deed at its term drives a man to the place of its fruit
losing inherited wealth to a deceitful courtesan brings a man shame
the dharma the Buddha taught has declined, so the way to release is nearly closed and the way to evil births lies open
even in the decline good dharma can still be attained, though by few
what comes to be, how, how much and when are all fixed beforehand
language distinguishes action, quality and form words, so the things they name are distinct
self-wounding and other extreme mortifications are of no use
birth yields nothing and austerity yields fruit
the four classes are ordained from the beginning
a scripture that says both of these is confused
atoms never enter one another, and each sinks or rises by its own nature
a doctrine that admits no change gives no cause for sinking and rising
if speaking proves passion, every bodily movement proves it too, and a being without movement could not be called alive
the formless aggregates cannot combine by contact as material things do
a trace cannot pass between two moments that never exist together
one who denies the soul cannot say who it is that holds a view
a newborn's knowing to seek the breast shows knowledge not produced by the elements of this birth
a deed done in another's name does not pass to that other
a soul not other than the body in place cannot be the one that reaches heaven for its alms, so meritorious deeds lose their point
those who did good reach the golden world, and those whose hearts are full of love go where their attachment leads
the fruits of virtue and of wrongdoing both ripen
the born die and the dead are born, and this is the ancient order of life, nothing new
the king was born by the grace of Siva, the rider of the bull
five subtle elements arise between the principle of self and the gross elements
to hold that a thing does not become another and yet that milk becomes curd is self-contradiction
the mind perishes entirely together with what it knew
if nothing of the mind remains, no one is left to know its perishing
if milk persists in the curd, the curd should be called milk
the Buddha conquered Mara and, not desiring heaven, strives for the dharma of others
once a life departs it goes to a new birth according to the deeds done
the saying that killing is dharma is a false and wretched word
a life given in place of another's does not keep that other alive
a king's warfare can be waged in keeping with righteousness

note: Thirikadugam names three seeds of the month's three rains: the priests' virtue, the king's just rule, and the wife who follows her husband; the Neelakesi gives its land three rains a month from its own known goodness.
teaches: The three-rains formula, which Thirikadugam ties to the conduct of priest, king and wife, appears in the epic as a landscape convention that explains away the missing palai tinai, its moral causes left unspoken.

gains.a: the epic's claim of three rains is seen to carry an implied moral order the verse does not state
gains.b: the quatrain's formula is shown travelling into poetic description, where it serves the tinai scheme rather than ethics

note: The quatrain says that knowing people still do blameworthy things because of deeds done before; the epic calls Virai's drunken death and Tarai's fall the ripening of a cruel deed.
teaches: The epic applies the quatrain's explanation to a death and then, at 46 to 48, names the drink and the leap, so a past deed is the cause behind the act while the act itself stays on the record.

gains.a: the epic's bare phrase வெவ் வினை உருப்ப gains a stated mechanism: the old deed works by producing the fault itself
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract puzzle gains a named case in which the blameworthy act is fatal and its doer is reborn

note: Both are the hero's words to his heart under the same occasion (அல்ல குறி), both liken the girl to the treasure the old Velir guarded at Pazhi, and both turn on எனினும் அஃது ஒல்லாய்.
teaches: The repeated opening under one thurai shows a fixed formula for the spoiled night meeting, the Velir's hidden gold at Pazhi standing for the guarded girl, which 258 then ends in the heart's ruin and 372 in a run of similes for its swinging.

note: The Kural asks what is stronger than fate, which comes first whatever one devises; Neelakesi attacks a fixity that sets in advance what comes, how, how much and when.
teaches: The couplet claims fate outruns human contrivance, but the Jain attack shows that the vulnerable step is the further claim that every particular of an outcome is already fixed, which the couplet does not make.

gains.a: the verse gains a contrast showing that its target is the total fixity of every detail, not every Tamil teaching of fate's strength
gains.b: the couplet gains a measure of how far its claim stops short of the Ajivika determinism that the Jain debater thought refutable

note: The Naladiyar quatrain calls the life a dancer (கூத்தன்) who leaves the skin bag, after which the body's fate does not matter; Maadalan's soul is like dancers who do not stay in one costume but go by their deeds into the bodies of gods, men, beasts or hell-beings.
teaches: The quatrain uses the dancer to make the abandoned body worthless, while the epic follows the dancer to its next costume, which its deeds choose, so the same figure moves from indifference to the corpse to anxiety about the next birth.

gains.a: Maadalan's simile gains a known ethical use of the dancer image to test against
gains.b: the quatrain's dancer gains a destination: the epic says where the performer goes after leaving the costume

note: 741 allows that a ruler may fear and protect himself behind walls. 775 counts even a blink before a spear as flight.
teaches: The chapter on the state and the chapter on the warrior hold different standards for fear, and both are the Kural's.

note: 33 likens the sage to the earth in patience and Meru in strength; in 49, as Neelakesi prepares her terrors, he resolves to let her frighten him as she will and to teach her.
teaches: The epithet of patience becomes the sage's whole strategy against the demoness: he does not resist her terrors but outlasts them, and turns the trial into a chance to teach.

note: Tirumular tells the devotee to take refuge in the shade of the one God's feet so that the sea of deeds will not reach him; Neelakesi, a Jain convert, prays at the Jina's feet that her old deeds may end.
teaches: A Jain convert and a Saiva poet both bring their deeds to a Lord's feet in prayer, so the difference between Jain release by wearing deeds away and Saiva release by grace is not visible in the act of worship but only in the doctrine behind it.

gains.a: the epic's prayer gains a Saiva statement of what refuge at the feet is supposed to do, against which the Jain hymn's silence about how the feet end deeds stands out
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a rival tradition that uses the same act of refuge at the feet without his one all-pervading God

note: Maadalan told how a poor man who bore false witness against a chaste wife was caught in the noose of the devouring spirit, which would not take Kovalan's life in his place; among the poem's closing commands is never to bear false witness.
teaches: The command against false witness is the one rule in the final list that the poem had already shown punished on stage, by a spirit that refused even a willing substitute, so the bare imperative carries the weight of a remembered scene in which no one could pay another's penalty.

note: In Akananuru 117 the foster mother says the girl did not think of the nochchi or her playmates when she left; in Natrinai 184 the mother cannot bear to see the nochchi and the terrace where the girl played.
teaches: The pair shows the same household shrub on both sides of the elopement: forgotten by the daughter who has gone, and unbearable to the mother who stays, so the left-behind play things measure how unequal the parting is.

note: Sudhamathi tells the prince the girl is given to fated austerity; in kaathai 18 he reports that a golden woman appeared to him at night with a sceptre and told him to forget the girl who had taken up tapas.
teaches: The warning comes twice, first from a woman he brushes aside and then from a divine figure, and the prince repeats the second to Chithirapathi without obeying it, so his ruin is shown as a refusal of a warning he understood.

note: The Naladiyar quatrain, in its chapter on youth not lasting, says that since merciless Death roams looking for his people one should take provisions for the journey in good time; the epic's last lines say youth, wealth and body do not last and bid the hearers seek a true companion for the land they will go to.
teaches: The epic folds the Naladiyar's three opening themes, wealth, youth and body not lasting, into one line and draws the same conclusion of provision for the journey, but sets it after a list of concrete deeds, so the provision is named as truthfulness, not killing, giving and the rest rather than left as a figure.

gains.a: the epic's closing line gains from the quatrain the image of Death as a hunter who takes even the unborn, which is the urgency behind உளநாள் வரையாது
gains.b: the quatrain's undefined provisions (தோட்கோப்பு) gain a list of the deeds that make them up, given just before in the epic's commands

note: In the Ainkurunuru the wife begins to push away her husband's chest, broad as the Kaveri's full flood, in sulking; in the vari the Kaveri herself is the wife who never sulks at the Chola's other unions.
teaches: The Sangam marutham gives the Kaveri's flood to the straying husband and lets the wife sulk at it, while the epic song makes the river the wife and her not sulking the highest chastity, so the same river image moves from licensing the wife's oodal to forbidding it.

gains.a: the stanza's demand for a wife without oodal stands out against the older convention in which the wronged wife's sulking was expected and even loved
gains.b: the quatrain's playful river-chest gains a later reading in which the river is no longer the husband's breadth but the wife's patience

note: The sermon promises that in the land of deeds penance drives out dark karma and brings the highest bliss; 807 argues that this needs deeds to be qualities of the soul itself.
teaches: The promise of release in the sermon rests on a metaphysics the later debate supplies: only if karma inheres in the soul can penance change the soul and free it.

note: Kural 34 makes a spotless mind the whole of virtue; the Uvavanam seat shows that a flower laid without intention goes nowhere, as proof that a deed without intention bears no fruit.
teaches: The couplet puts the mind first in judging virtue; the seat pushes that principle to the disputed case of the unintended act and makes it a point on which schools divided, which the couplet never has to face.

gains.a: a general ethical statement, free of any school, behind the Buddhist side of the dispute
gains.b: a hard case, the deed done without any thought, that tests how far the mind-first rule reaches

note: The sage foretold that Rahulan would die of the serpent's venomous gaze within sixteen days and that Lakshmi would burn with him; Manimekalai now uses that death to ask the queen why she did not weep for the same life then.
teaches: The prophecy of a death in the former birth becomes, in this kaathai, the ground of an argument against grief: the same life has died before unmourned by its present mother, so her grief is for this body only.

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre rightly; the minister says rain returned to Savakam after twelve years when the king was born, before he wielded any sceptre.
teaches: The epic moves the cause of a land's plenty from the king's rule to his birth, that is, to merit carried from a former life of giving, so a king can bring rain before he governs at all.

gains.a: a Tamil rule that makes the minister's report a claim about kingship rather than a bare wonder
gains.b: a case its link between rain and right rule cannot explain: rain that follows a king's coming and precedes his rule

note: Maadalan says Madhavi's seaside song crushed the crowns of Kanaka and Vijaya; the earlier unit is the moment she takes up the yazh in a sulk to answer Kovalan's songs.
teaches: The scene of a lovers' misreading of each other's songs on the beach turns out, in Maadalan's riddle, to be the first link in a chain that ends in a northern war, so the poem asks the reader to see a small private quarrel and a campaign as one sequence of cause.

note: Both epics use one formula for death by fasting: Kavunthi 'gave up her life by the vow of not eating' (உண்ணா நோன்போ டுயிர்பதிப் பெயர்த்ததும், 27:83) asking whether the couple's deeds had struck at her too; Aputhiran dies by the same vow (உண்ணா நோன்போடு உயிர் பதிப் பெயர்ப்புழி, 95).
teaches: The twin epics give the same fasting death opposite fruits: Kavunthi's ends a life overtaken by others' karma in grief, while Aputhiran's is a passage to a birth in which his purpose of feeding goes on.

note: The quatrain mocks debaters who do not know how to make what they learned reach the hearer; the teacher's false theses are exactly theses that cannot reach the hearer, because he does not grant their terms or already holds the conclusion.
teaches: The epic gives the quatrain's complaint a precise form: an argument fails not only by poor delivery but when its subject or conclusion is foreign or already granted to the one it is aimed at.

gains.a: the technical rules gain an ethical frame, as the duty of a speaker to the one he addresses
gains.b: the quatrain's 'not knowing how to make it reach' gains named cases showing what such a failure is

note: Saathan says gods give no boon to those without tapas; the goddess of Madurai later says that when a former deed comes in wrath, tapas does not help those not upright.
teaches: Together the two divine sayings set limits on tapas from both sides: without it no boon, and with it no shield once an old deed has ripened against one who was not upright.

note: In Akananuru 297 the man on his way for wealth sees a wildcat's fluffy kitten following its mother like stars round the moon; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 40 the heroine hears that on his road the spotted wildcat watches for prey for its kitten.
teaches: Each lover sees the wildcat with its young on the wealth road from his or her own side, the man as the household he leaves behind and the woman as the provision he goes to win, so the creature gathers both halves of the paalai argument about leaving for wealth.

note: Kalittokai 104 ends its herders' kuravai by praising the god of the ancient bright discus and wishing that the world take the one word of the Pandya with the thunder-loud drum; the epic's kuravai to the discus-holder (கதிர்திகிரி, line 99) ends in the same wish for the Pandya's drum.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam mullai close, god first and then the Pandya's drum, but moves the kuravai from the joy after the bull-catch to a rite against ill omens, so the inherited blessing now carries dread rather than celebration.

gains.a: the epic's close is shown to be a set form of the Madurai herders' kuravai, not Ilango's invention, which makes its irony a turn on a known convention
gains.b: the Kalittokai's conventional wish for the Pandya is shown to be one that a story could test: the epic sets it on the day the same dynasty's justice fails

note: Madhavi's stanza tells of a shore lord who looked at the crab with its mate and at her and then went away, leaving her senseless; at the kaathai's end Kovalan, hearing her songs as aimed at another, lets go of her and leaves.
teaches: The persona's lament for a lover who left after seeing a scene of union is followed, within the evening, by the singer's own lover leaving her, so the pair shows Madhavi's song turning from a role into her situation.

note: The couplet says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by right; the epic's fame says that in the just Pandya's land even beasts, serpents and thunder spare those who depend on it.
teaches: Held together, the two show the claim that nature answers a just sceptre turning, in the epic, into a traveller's reason to trust a stranger king, a reputation the story then puts to the test with the travellers' own lives.

gains.a: the border praise gains its doctrinal ground: the fame rests on the Kural's teaching that a just reign orders nature itself
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its promise is taken as a guarantee by outsiders and so becomes something a king can betray

note: The king pledges to drive out the losers that day; in 228 the beaten Kundalakesi is drummed out of the city gate.
teaches: The penalty the debaters agreed to at the start is carried out exactly, so the debate is framed as a binding royal trial and not a mere exchange of views.

note: The couplet holds that giving is good even if there were no higher world; the charana proves the worth of a gift by showing the god it produced, with the monkey's hand still on him.
teaches: The Kural deliberately cuts giving loose from any reward in a higher world, while the Jain tale makes a visible heavenly body the evidence for the gift's worth, so the pair separates two defences of giving, one that needs no world beyond and one that rests on it.

gains.a: the tale's proof by reward is set against a view that does not need the proof, which shows how much its case rests on the heaven it displays
gains.b: the couplet's hypothetical 'even if there were no higher world' gains a concrete rival: a contemporary teaching that answers the hypothetical by producing the higher world as witness

note: Kavunthi assures Kovalan that, unlike the dice-ruined king who left his wife in the forest by strong karma, he has a life never parted from his wife; in the Pandya's court Kannaki says her husband came to Madurai driven by ஊழ்வினை and was killed.
teaches: The nun's karma, invoked to show that Kovalan's lot is better than the exiled king's, is the same force Kannaki names when she stands parted from him for ever, so the consolation becomes the epic's irony: the karma Kavunthi uses to excuse a parting is already moving toward a worse one.

note: The two summaries share their opening lines word for word (aram, maram, the old city, festivals, the gods' visits, food, the unfailing sky), with the Vaigai for the Kaveri; the Madurai summary ends by viewing its book as one with the Pandya Nedunjeliyan who died on his throne with his chaste queen, the Puhar summary names no king.
teaches: Because the praise of righteousness and unfailing rain is a fixed frame granted alike to the Chola line and to the Pandya whose verdict burned his city, the epic's judgment of a kingdom lies not in that praise but in what each summary sets at its centre: for Madurai a king who died of his own wrong, for Puhar no king at all but its arts.

note: Tirumular says those who give up killing, theft, lust and lying reach Siva's feet and its bliss; Aravanar counts the same sins among ten and says that leaving them, with precept and giving, wins only birth as god, human or Brahma.
teaches: The same abstentions are release in the Saiva verse and only a better birth in the Buddhist sermon, which places release in knowing the twelve links rather than in conduct; the pair shows that the two schools agree on the list and disagree on what it buys.

gains.a: a rival claim that abstaining from the great sins reaches the highest, which sharpens the epic's limit on what good deeds can do
gains.b: a finer count of the sins by body, speech and mind and a denial that abstention alone ends birth, against which its promise can be weighed

note: Aputtiran begs with an ordinary bowl to feed the helpless and eats the leftovers; in the next kaathai, unable to feed travellers who come in the rain, he is given the inexhaustible bowl by Chinthadevi.
teaches: The divine bowl goes to someone already living as a beggar who feeds others before himself, so the epic presents it as answering an alms-giving done with nothing rather than as the source of his charity.

note: The Naladiyar answers a beautiful woman's appeal by dissecting the body into entrails, blood and bone and asking which part is she; the Neelakesi's sage meets a full display of wiles with one question, what are these to us.
teaches: The Naladiyar's dissection is a method for one still tempted, while the sage needs no method; and since this beauty is a demoness's borrowed shape, the Naladiyar's question of where the woman is in the body has, here, a literal answer: nowhere.

gains.a: the sage's bare dismissal is shown to stand where a quatrain needs a whole argument
gains.b: the quatrain's rhetorical question gains a scene in which the alluring body truly belongs to no woman

note: Kural 225 ranks the strength of those who bear hunger below the strength of those who remove it; in the patikam the renunciant who begs with a bowl is the one who ends Kayachandigai's hunger-fire.
teaches: The Kural sets the one who endures hunger and the one who relieves it as two kinds of strength in rank, while the epic gives both to one person, a begging ascetic whose bowl feeds others, so its Buddhist renunciation removes the Kural's ranking rather than falling under it.

gains.a: the bowl scene gains a standard from the ethics books by which the heroine's begging is a higher strength than ascetic endurance, not a lower one
gains.b: the couplet's contrast between enduring and removing hunger is shown not to be exclusive, since a renunciant can hold both

note: Pattinathar searches hair, skin, blood, bone and worms for the 'I', finds it nowhere, and says that only when the Lord's grace came did he see himself; the Neelakesi praises an ascetic who knows himself other than the body by his own steadfast penance.
teaches: Both hold that the self is not the body, but the Saiva poet reaches that knowledge only by grace while the Jain sage reaches it by enduring, so the shared insight hides a disagreement about how it is won.

gains.a: the Jain claim gains a sharp contrast that shows it needs no god for the knowledge of the self
gains.b: the Siddhar's turn to grace is shown to be a choice, since another school claimed the same insight without it

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says gain, loss, birth and death are all mixed in at conception and the fate laid down before makes what comes; 707 tests that claim on breasts, teeth, hair and nails that a newborn lacks.
teaches: The Buddhist epic lets the Ajivika's 'all is set at conception' stand and walks away; the Jain epic takes it as a claim about the body and refutes it by the parts that visibly appear later.

note: The prince describes Manimekalai quoting old wisdom (முதுக்குறை முதுமொழி எடுத்துக் காட்டி) as the goads that tamed him; in kaathai 20 Kaanchanan sees the disguised Manimekalai doing the same and takes it for a wife's flirting.
teaches: Her act of teaching is read twice as desire, once by the man it is meant to turn away and once by the jealous husband, and the second misreading is fatal.

note: Among the ancestors Maadalan cites are the king who took a four-Veda man's poem and sent him to the upper world, and (lines 144-146) the one who struck Agappa and bathed in Ayirai and the two seas; the third decad's preface and colophon give Palyanai Selkezhu Kuttuvan these feats and the brahmin poet's reward of heaven through sacrifices.
teaches: The Sangam tradition's sacrifice that sent a brahmin poet to heaven becomes Maadalan's precedent for the sacrifice he urges on the king, yet the same preface says that king went away to the forest, and the epic's counsellor leaves out the renunciation and keeps only the rite.

gains.a: Maadalan's allusions gain the stories behind them: the poet Gautamanar, his reward and the king who gave it
gains.b: the preface gains a later reading in which its king's sacrifice is remembered and his going to the forest is not

note: The Kural ranks abstaining from one killing above a thousand sacrifices; the Neelakesi lists the Vedic sacrifice among the deaths that make a beast's birth a suffering.
teaches: The couplet weighs sacrifice and abstention as merits for the actor and leaves the rite standing as a lesser good; the Jain sermon removes it from the scale of merit by counting it as a harm to the slain beast.

gains.a: the sermon's charge is seen as a sharpening of an older Tamil ranking that already put non-killing above the rite
gains.b: the couplet's comparison is shown to be open to the harder reading that sacrifice is itself a killing, which a Jain teacher draws

note: Tirumular praises the lord who swallowed the poison and shares half his body with the lady; the hunters give the poison-swallowing to the goddess herself.
teaches: The hymn moves Siva's defining act of grace to his consort through the shared body Tirumular names, and makes it the ground on which a goddess who eats the pitiless hunters' offerings still grants grace.

gains.a: the hymn's attribution gains its basis: the goddess is the half of the poison-eater's body
gains.b: Tirumular's half-body formula gains a use outside Saiva devotion, where it lets a forest goddess claim Siva's deed

note: Tirumular bids refuge in the shade of the feet of the one God present in all ten directions, so that the sea of deeds will not reach; Aravanar goes to worship the footprints of the First Lord on one hill because they wash away hard deeds.
teaches: Both texts make worship of feet dissolve karma, but the Saiva feet are everywhere because their Lord is, while the Buddhist feet are a print left on a particular hill by a teacher of the past, so the shared gesture rests on opposite accounts of where the cleansing power lies.

gains.a: the epic's footprint worship is shown to use a devotional idiom the Saiva texts also use, against which its relic-and-place character stands out
gains.b: Tirumular's claim that the feet are in every direction gains a contrast with a rival tradition whose sacred feet are fixed in one place

note: The Vaisheshika says generality gives being (உண்மை) to substance, quality and action; here the argument that being is other than substance, quality and action is shown to make being nothing.
teaches: Read together, the units show the Buddhist teacher taking the Vaisheshika's own words for being and showing that its category, argued as the Vaisheshika argues it, empties itself.

note: The Manimekalai praises the Buddha as one who does not pity his own life and protects others' lives; Neelakesi takes the same countless lives of self-giving as evidence of countless sins.
teaches: The mark by which the Buddhist epic defines its teacher's dharma is exactly what the Jain debater reinterprets as karmic debt, so the two schools disagree over what suffering for others means.

note: Both letters are sent through Vasantamalai with the same formula for Madhavi's state (பசந்த மேனியள் படர் ..., line 68 here; 13:67-68), and in both she writes with her own hand.
teaches: The repeated wording marks the second letter as a rerun of the first, so the reader can see that what changes between a refused and an accepted letter is Kovalan's state, not Madhavi's message.

claims.gist: reality is exhausted by twenty-five categories, from the soul and the unmanifest down to the five elements
toddy, lying, theft, killing and lust are the five things to be shunned
lust is hardest to throw off, and who shuns it has shunned all evil
those who do not renounce lust suffer in unbearable hell
a sickness of love that a man gave is not the god's doing, and no rite of the velan or of the god can cure it
an evil deed, through the anklet, caused what befell her husband
arising by succession down a line answers the objection and is the strength of the Buddha's path
though some of its divisions fail, the aggregates are real and so the mental states exist
worship offered from belief in a god and giving driven by desire are faults
a magnet moves iron without life, so change from a cause does not prove that plants live
a deity who has granted a child must be repaid with the vowed blood offering
one who has put away desire and hatred does not grieve even when he foresees another's suffering
monks who call themselves pure and others impure have ignored their own teacher's truth
if the one reborn is the same man his sorrow never ends, and if not, the good he did is wasted
a compound is named after the constituent that predominates in it
a hostile intention binds karma even when the deed falls on someone other than its target
true learning is curbing hatred, relieving the hunger and want of others, grasping the truth that ends sorrow and keeping love for all creatures
likeness, partiality and descent each leave the thing another
a soul leaving the dead body with only its karma-body cannot gain a new body unless one is set in the mother's
a subtle fiery body enters the new body as a shadow does
the goddess abides as the light in the hearts of Hari, Hara and Brahma
giving one's body to be eaten kills the many lives within it, and is no better than poisoning common water to cure one man
a lord defined by having no birth and no forgetting is no better than a stone
one who studies the meaning the Trustworthy One gave in the scripture cannot fail to know
nothing that has a name and a cognition is wholly non-existent
if the city forgets the festival, the guardian spirit that removed the king's distress will bring affliction on it
a spirit binds the wicked of the city with its noose, beats them and devours them
the elements come together of themselves to make awareness
the joining of the elements needs a cause beyond the elements
if the person who acted perishes with the act, no one remains to receive its fruit, and doing dharma is in vain
only the killer, not the eater of sacrificial flesh, bears the sin
those who eat the flesh share the killer's deed
a thing becomes its effect only through its own proper causes, not anything from anything
conduct joined to faith and knowledge is either complete or partial
food given to the hungry is the medicine that saves life
the other teachers spoke only from what each partly knew, and their teachings are false
the Jina's knowledge burns away the whole chain of deeds
a woman's judgement is folly
a true pathini's vow can end a kingdom and destroy its city
a king who gave up his life for his own wrong verdict is free of fault and received among the gods
nothing endures beyond the moment
a doctrine of momentariness cannot establish any thesis, including the four truths
the four truths become plain to one only when the fitting cause has ripened
those who heed the charanas' teaching and turn to dharma, lay givers among them, reach the final world of unending joy
a man's former deed rose up against him and brought his killing through a petty man
the Buddhist rule allows a man to take as partner a hermaphrodite, an animal, a courtesan or a lifeless thing
a single grasp of all things either erases their differences through a common quality or cannot hold unlike things together
taking a woman's garland and wearing it is the marriage the ancients described
one who shuns intoxicating liquor as harmful must for the same reason shun flesh
the Veda is a made work, not eternal, because it shows action and novelty
because it is joined with killing, the Veda leads its followers to an evil state of birth

note: The Manimekalai's teacher says the first Jina (in Buddhist usage, the Buddha) taught only two means of knowledge, perception and inference; Neelakesi answers that on that rule there could be no medical treatise that cures disease.
teaches: The Buddhist rule of two means of knowledge, stated as doctrine in one epic, meets in the other a counter-case from medicine, showing that the dispute over scripture as a means of knowledge was argued in Tamil from practical knowledge, not only from revelation.

note: The couplet says all living beings join hands to the one who does not kill and refuses flesh; the epic shows lay votaries worshipping the stone seat set for the flesh-renouncing Charanas even when none is there.
teaches: The couplet's hyperbole of universal worship becomes an institution in the epic: a built seat honoured in the ascetics' absence, which then becomes the place where a Charana actually appears at line 161.

gains.a: the empty seat gains its reason: the refusal of flesh is what earns such worship
gains.b: the couplet's worship gains a concrete form, a lay cult of the renouncers' seat

note: Both have warriors at the bhuta's altar in Puhar crying that the victorious king take victory (கொற்றம் கொள்க) with a thunder voice as they offer bali; the Silappathikaram stages it as the festival's central rite, the Manimekalai lists it among the night noises a grieving woman hears.
teaches: Set side by side, the same offering formula moves from the heart of a royal festival to one sound among drunk shipwrights and mantra-men, which shows how the later epic pushes the blood rite to the margin of its story.

note: Villavan Kothai credits Senguttuvan with making the sea-fenced land Tamil (இமிழ்கடல் வேலியைத் தமிழ்நா டாக்கிய); the Patitruppattu preface uses nearly the same phrase of his father Imayavaramban.
teaches: The minister applies to the son the formula the preface gives the father, so the Chera line's fame works as a shared inheritance that the campaign for the stone is said to renew.

gains.a: the minister's praise gains its source, a formula of the Chera line rather than a fresh boast
gains.b: the preface's phrase gains a later use as an argument that the northern kings will yield without war

note: Sudhamathi's sermon on the body did not reach the prince before the sight of the girl; here the goddess reports that his gaze has not abated and sends the women into refuge.
teaches: The epic marks the failure of the sermon on the body as a fact the plot acts on: after argument fails, protection becomes a matter of place and then of flight.

note: Neeli's curse in the former birth is the deed the prose says rose up against Kovalan (வினையுருத்து); the prose also names the goldsmith and the king.
teaches: The retelling at Vanchi keeps the goddess's karmic explanation but sets it beside the petty man and the king as agents, and beside Kannaki's reviling of dharma, so the karmic cause is told without excusing the human ones.

note: The Chola of the puram poem entered the scale with his own body to save a dove from a hawk; the Chera here gives the Brahmin gold measured against his own weight fifty times over, just after the Brahmin has praised that very dove-king.
teaches: The scale in which a Chola ancestor weighed his flesh against a bird becomes in the Chera's court a scale in which the king's weight is matched in gold for a messenger, so the body-as-measure moves from self-sacrifice to royal gift.

gains.a: the weighing gains the Tamil memory of the royal scale, which makes the gift an answer to Maadalan's praise of the dove-king
gains.b: the dove story gains a later royal practice in which the king's body is weighed for giving, not for suffering

note: The goddess hails Manimekalai for recovering her former birth at the Buddha's seat; here that knowledge of the former birth, in which she held to giving and the precepts, is what she brings to her taking of refuge.
teaches: Read together, the two show that the memory of a former birth is not the end of her awakening but its qualification: what she recovered on Manipallavam is cashed here as the two practices that make her fit to take refuge and hear the doctrine.

note: The Kural defines a land as one that goes on without crushing hunger, unceasing disease and destructive enemies; the drummer ends the proclamation by wishing that hunger, disease and enmity leave the city.
teaches: What the Kural states as the mark of a true land, the epic's city asks for once a year as a festival blessing, showing that the freedom from the three ills was felt as a gift to be renewed by rite, not a settled condition.

gains.a: the herald's closing wish gains a political measure: these three ills are exactly what decides whether Puhar is a land at all
gains.b: the couplet's definition gains a public voice and an occasion, a drum proclamation in which the city itself asks to meet it

note: Devanthi urges Kannaki to bathe in the sacred tanks and worship to win her husband back, and Kannaki refuses; the Bhuta tells Maruthi that worship of gods is what cost her the rain.
teaches: The Manimekalai's Bhuta supplies the doctrine behind Kannaki's refusal of the tanks in the Silappathikaram: a pathini's power rests on not turning to gods, so Kannaki's refusal is part of what makes her word able to burn Madurai.

note: The goldsmith declares that the anklet fits none but the queen; in the court Kannaki's anklet, broken, shows gems where the queen's holds pearls.
teaches: The craftsman's expert verdict, the only evidence against Kovalan, is shown false by the anklet itself, so the case is undone by the very object it was built on.

note: The Kural's woman asks the bewildered evening whether its mate is as hard as hers; Madhavi's heroine asks whether this bewildering evening (மருள்மாலை) exists in the land of the man who left.
teaches: Both put to evening a question that is really about the absent man's hardness, and the epic sets that question in a performance before a lover who is present, showing how the convention can be heard as a personal charge.

gains.a: the epic stanza gains a known form, the address to evening, which marks it as a conventional lament rather than Madhavi's confession
gains.b: the couplet gains a dramatic setting in which its question is sung aloud and misheard, with consequences for the singer

note: The couplet calls relieving the destitute's ruinous hunger the place where a man of wealth should store it; Aravanar likens laying aside the hunger-ending bowl to the gods keeping back their leftover nectar, and calls it unfit.
teaches: The couplet keeps a giver's profit in view by making charity a kind of saving, while the epic's bowl has no owner to profit and treats any keeping back as the gods' hoard, so feeding the hungry is pressed past prudence into a duty with no return.

gains.a: Aravanar's rule against laying the bowl aside gains a contrast with the ethics book's view of charity as a store for the giver, which shows how far the bowl's keeper is from any owner's interest.
gains.b: The couplet's banking image gains a case with no depositor at all, a bowl whose holder gains nothing, which exposes the self-regard the image keeps.

note: In kaathai 7 the goddess says Kovalan named the child after her and that she told Madhavi in a dream that the child would be a great ascetic; here Aravanar gives the reason for the naming, the goddess's rescue of the Bodhisattva ancestor.
teaches: Read together, the name Manimekalai is a debt of the family line to a goddess who serves a future Buddha, so the renunciation foretold at her birth is the line's old bond coming due.

note: Neelakesi argues that the ascetic's staff and bowl would be wasted unless a soul survives the body; Tirumular says garb put on the body is not for the soul and falls away with the body.
teaches: Both tie ascetic dress to the body-soul question but draw opposite lessons from it: for the Jain debater the gear presupposes a soul, for Tirumular it cannot reach the soul at all, so outward penance is evidence in one text and irrelevance in the other.

gains.a: the epic's argument gains its limit: the Saiva text denies that outward marks bear on the soul it presupposes
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal of garb gains a context in which garb was used as proof of the soul against a materialist

note: Tirumular says that even burning one's bones as firewood and frying one's flesh does not reach the Lord without melting love; Mokkalan says cutting wounds and leaping from mountains serve no purpose.
teaches: Both reject bodily extremity as the way, but Tirumular keeps it as a measure that love surpasses while Mokkalan declares it simply useless, so the Saiva verse still honours the ascetic's pain where the Buddhist does not.

gains.a: Mokkalan's list gains a Saiva witness that self-torment was a recognised extreme to be gone beyond
gains.b: Tirumular's hyperbole is seen against a debate in which such acts were literally practised and literally attacked

note: Purananuru 39 praises the Chola who made the Chera of the Himalaya-carved bow fall and withered வாடா வஞ்சி; the epic's king enters வாடா வஞ்சி and the drum boasts of the carved bow.
teaches: The epithets 'unwithering Vanchi' and 'the bow carved on the Himalaya' are the Chera line's own glory in the epic and the measure of a Chola victory in the Sangam poem, so the pairing shows one stock of Chera fame used by both its owners and its enemies.

gains.a: the proclamation gains the knowledge that its boasts were stock epithets that rival poets also used
gains.b: the poem's paradox of withering the unwithering city gains the Chera's own use of the same name for a city at the height of its power

note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists killing, theft and lust as the three evil deeds that arise in the body; 539 takes that very grouping and asks who does them if the mind is not there.
teaches: The Buddhist epic sorts deeds by the door they go out through and counts the mind's three faults separately, so the Jain objection works only by reading a classification of doors as a claim that the body acts without mind.

note: 283 line 6 names the assembly hall of the Kosar (கோசர் அவைக்களத்தானும்); Akananuru 262 names the town-elder Kosar (ஊர்முது கோசர்) who blinded Anni Mignili's father.
teaches: Both poets know the Kosar as a body that sits in judgment, an institution in the puram fragment and the source of a borrowed story in the akam poem, so the Kosar's council was famous enough for an akam speaker to cite it as a known wrong.

note: Neelakesi's first charge against the Buddha is that he does not count eating flesh a fault; the couplet argues that flesh is sold only because people eat it.
teaches: The couplet supplies the reason a Jain debater can blame the flesh-eater who kills nothing: the eating is what causes the killing, so silence on eating is silence on killing.

gains.a: the bare charge in the verse gains the argument by which it is pressed later in the Neelakesi
gains.b: the couplet's market argument is seen aimed at a school's actual position in Tamil debate

note: The Buddha counts six cognitions at the six doors; Neelakesi asks how the five not occurring can be known to exist, and says their hidden existence licenses a soul.
teaches: Counting six kinds of cognition already assumes something that holds the unused ones, so the Buddhist's own enumeration is made to imply the abiding knower he denies.

note: 45 tells two quarrelling Cholas that their fight will delight other kings; 58 tells a Chola and a Pandya that if they never break their union the whole earth will be theirs.
teaches: The two poems state one calculation from opposite sides, division gives the gain to outsiders and union takes it from them, so together they show Sangam poets thinking of alliances between crowns in terms of who profits.

note: Kural 284 says that a love grown in stealth yields at harvest a sorrow that does not die; Manimekalai tells the queen not to think that the harsh suffering of those who live by stealth is for thieves alone, since these ways bring sorrow to all who live in the world.
teaches: The couplet assigns undying sorrow to the thief; the epic refuses to let a listener file that sorrow under a class of criminals and extends it to a queen whose fault was deceit, making the rule about theft a rule about all concealment.

gains.a: a known rule on the fruit of stealth, which gives force to the phrase she will not let the queen keep at a distance
gains.b: a scene in which the couplet's reader is warned against using it to sort the guilty from herself

note: The Manimekalai's Jain says time makes the short occurrence called கணிகம் and the long one of கற்பம்; Neelakesi throws the same two words at the Buddhist who denies time while using them.
teaches: The pair கணிகம் and கற்பம் was the Jain definition of time, so when Neelakesi mocks the Buddhist for speaking of moments she is pointing out that the word for his momentariness belongs to a doctrine of time he rejects.

note: Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker lets primal nature unfold and withdraw by itself and names no creator; in the Neelakesi's Sankhya sarukkam the opponent defends a Lord of five acts, with the dance first.
teaches: The two polemical epics give the same school different shapes: the Buddhist account keeps Sankhya godless, while the Jain account hangs a Saiva-style lord on it, so neither can be read alone as what the Tamil Sankhyas held.

note: In the dream kaathai Saathan, having grown up as Maalathi's child and married Devanthi, shows her his ageless youth, tells her to come to his shrine and leaves, and she keeps worship there to win him back; in the last kaathai Maadalan retells this and the god returns by possessing her.
teaches: Devanthi's long worship to get her husband back is answered, but not as she asked: the god returns as a voice that takes over her body to reveal others' former births, so the husband she waited for comes back only as an oracle.

note: Both give the same Jain list, opened with the same epithet (இந்திரர் தொழப்படும் இறைவன் in the Manimekalai, இந்திரர்கள் தொழப்படுவான் here) and framed by the same questions of lord, categories, their workings, bondage and release.
teaches: The Jain categories circulated as a fixed formula that both sects' epics quote; the Buddhist epic lets a Jain recite it and moves on, while the Jain epic puts it in a Buddhist's mouth so that its defence can follow.

note: Madhavi hands Kovalan the yazh and he chooses the songs; at the kaathai's close the narrator says his old deed came to fruit over the yazh music and he left her.
teaches: The pairing shows the narrator placing the first turn of the story's karma not in a crime or a curse but in a lute passed between lovers at play, so the moral of the patikam that past deeds come to fruit begins with a song chosen for pleasure.

note: The image addresses Sudhamathi with இரவிவன்மன் ஒரு பெரு மகளே, துரகத் தானைத் துச்சயன் தேவி and promises that Lakshmi will come knowing both births; returned from the island, Manimekalai addresses her mothers with the same lines and names them Tarai and Virai.
teaches: The prophecy is fulfilled in the very words of the image, now in the girl's mouth, and the later scene supplies what the image left out: Madhavi too was a sister, Tarai.

note: The couplet defines the woman who guards herself, tends her husband, keeps their good name and does not flag; Kannaki hid her grief before his parents and followed him without gainsaying him though his conduct was unworthy.
teaches: The couplet does not say what such a wife owes a husband who wrongs her; Kannaki's answer is to name his fault and follow him all the same, so the epic shows the couplet's tireless wife carried into the ruin her husband makes.

gains.a: Kannaki's hidden grief and silence before her in-laws gain a name as keeping the household's good name, part of what defines the wife in the couplet
gains.b: the couplet gains the hard case it leaves open, a husband who has failed her, and one answer to it

note: The goddess foretells that Manimekalai will hear the false words of the many schools and gives her a mantra to take another form; in kaathai 27 she goes among the reckoners of Vanji in an ascetic's borrowed form and questions them one by one.
teaches: The debate chapter is set up as a test prepared for in advance: the disguise exists because the goddess expects no one to tell a young girl the truth, so the schools are heard under a mask chosen against their condescension.
