note: In 163 Neelakesi resolves to bring down the Buddha's path because he does not call eating flesh a fault; in 335-337 she argues it point by point against Mokkalan.
teaches: The charge stated in one line at the outset of her debates turns out to need a long argument against particular defences, that the killer was hidden, the animal not marked out, and the meat paid for.

note: The venba says the old deed drove Kovalan out of Puhar before dawn; the quatrain says an old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows.
teaches: In the quatrain the deed seeks the doer; in the venba the doer is moved toward the deed, so together they show karma working from both ends, the deed seeking and the doer being sent.

gains.a: an image for why the venba gives the deed the active verb கடைக்கூட்ட
gains.b: a narrative case where the search ends by bringing the doer to a distant city, not by the deed arriving at his door

note: Given audience by the Chera, Nariveruuthalaiyar asks for nothing and tells him to guard the realm with grace and love; offered jewels, land and treasure, Neelakesi refuses them and tells the king to keep to the path of dharma.
teaches: The visitor who turns a king's favour into counsel persists from bardic to religious poetry, but the counsel shifts from ruling with grace to following a doctrine, and the refusal of gifts becomes a renouncer's mark.

gains.a: Neelakesi's scene is seen as a known Tamil form, the counsel given in place of a gift
gains.b: the Sangam form of counsel to a king is shown carried into a sectarian epic where the adviser wants nothing

note: 270 explains poverty as too little austerity, which is something people could change. 377 says enjoyment is only as the apportioner apportioned.
teaches: The same fact gets a moral cause and a fatal one.

note: The Siddhar says he has resolved to beg from any caste and lacks nothing; Aputtiran, driven from caste with stones in his bowl, begs from every house to feed the helpless and eats what is left.
teaches: Begging across caste lines is the Siddhar's chosen freedom and his sufficiency, while for Aputtiran it is what is left after caste expels him, and he turns it outward to feed others, so the same act carries renunciation in one and charity in the other.

gains.a: The epic beggar's stripped life is seen as close to a renouncer's, though he claims no renunciation.
gains.b: The Siddhar's self-sufficiency is seen to leave out the feeding of others that the epic puts at the centre of begging.

note: The patikam opens with Ilango living at the eastern-gate shrine after giving up kingship; in the last kaathai the goddess tells why: when a man said he bore the mark of a future king, he looked at him in anger and put away the earth's burden to end Senguttuvan's distress.
teaches: The poet's renunciation, stated without cause in the first line of the poem, is explained only in its last unit and by the goddess herself, so the poem's frame makes the poet's giving up of a throne one more past act whose meaning the pathini reveals, like the former births of the mothers.

note: Both compare a courtesan's love to a river that fails with the rain; the Naladiyar's மாரி அறவே அறுமே and வாரி அறவே அறும் lie close to the Valayapathi's lines 3 and 1.
teaches: The Naladiyar gives only the ending, love cut off when income ends, while the fragment makes வாரி mean both flood and income and adds the rise, so the love is shown swelling with the wealth as precisely as it dries.

note: Kural 5 says both kinds of deed, born of darkness, do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise; 807 says good and bad deeds and their fruits are qualities of the soul, or birth and release mean nothing.
teaches: Both count good deeds with bad as what binds, but the Jain debater asks what clinging is: a deed can cling or fall away only if it is a quality of the soul, which the couplet takes for granted.

gains.a: the verse's technical argument is tied to a plain moral teaching that both good and bad deeds bind
gains.b: the couplet's image of deeds clinging gets a stated account of what the clinging is, which it does not give

note: In 821 darkness perishes as the disciple understands the three and remembers the Lord's feet; in Tirumanthiram 2293 the malas leave like evening darkness before a flame by grace.
teaches: Both texts end bondage with darkness dispelled, but in the Jain verse the remover is the disciple's own knowledge and remembrance, while the Saiva verse gives the work to grace.

gains.a: the Jain verse's silence about any act of the Lord stands out once set beside a text where the Lord's grace does the work
gains.b: the Saiva image of grace as flame is set against a release with the same image and no giver, which shows grace is its distinctive claim

note: The Manimekalai's Vaisheshika closes his account with inherence joining quality and bearer, and the Buddhist epic lets it stand unanswered; 815 attacks that very relation with a regress.
teaches: Read together, the two epics show which Vaisheshika category the rival schools found weakest: the Buddhist work records inherence as the school's last word, the Jain work makes it the first thing to fall.

note: Kannaki states the forenoon-afternoon law of returning harm, in other words than the couplet's, as her warning to the Pandya's house.
teaches: The couplet's தாமே says the harm returns of itself with no agent, but the epic puts the law in the mouth of the woman who will herself bring the harm back that same day, so the impersonal return of a deed is shown working through a wronged person's act.

gains.a: her threat gains the standing of a known moral law rather than private revenge
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the returning harm has a human executor and falls on a whole city, not only on the doer

note: Tirumular says that as a madman is cleared by medicine, he was made clear when Nandi gave grace; Neelakesi says she, once a demon, was made clear by the dharma a teacher gave her.
teaches: Both use the same image of madness cured, but the cure differs in kind: for the Saiva it is the Lord's grace that stops his doing, for the Jain a teaching she must take in and keep.

gains.a: the Jain convert's cure is shown to be teaching without a gracious god, which is what sets it apart from the nearest Saiva parallel
gains.b: Tirumular's grace-as-medicine is seen against a rival in which the medicine is doctrine and the patient does the work

claims.gist: rebirth and ghosts are real
memory carried from infancy to old age shows a lasting knower
the great forgive those who wronged them when they come and confess
worship of the Bodhi sage's feet removes the deeds that follow one and leads to the faultless path
ending the hunger of living beings is a dharma whose end is the same for men and for gods
the doctrines of the other schools are not sound and deserve no assent
by the reverse of the chain all sorrow without end ceases
one who praises the bodhisattva's endurance of cutting cannot consistently condemn the hardships of penance
the world begins when soul and nature come together
effects exist in their cause before they appear
rebirth can be explained by examples where an effect arises at a distance without anything passing over
in each such example the cause still exists while the effect appears
chastity's power can consume a king with his house and army and drive a city's gods away
a king who has bent his sceptre restores just rule by giving his life for the fault
souls pass through a long fixed course of births that runs its course regardless of their acts
the doer perishes, but the continuum running on from him receives the fruit of his deed
the fruit of a deed arises in the same moment as the deed
if a deed's fruit comes later down the series, the deed persists until then
fire and the soul by nature move upward, wind sideways, water and earth downward
each moment perishes wholly and a different cognition arises after it
the body and its life come from wind
the soul is other than the five elements
on reflection nothing endures
the substance is the bearer of its lasting and passing qualities and is not apart from them
a strong deed of the past came upon her and brought the loss of her husband and the ruin of Madurai's kingship
a woman like her is a greater deity for the clan than any other and should be taken as its god
granting acting souls beside non-acting ones destroys the thesis that the soul does not act
cognitions do not all arise at once because will is lacking
a single will governing all cognitions would be a bearer of qualities, a soul under another name
feeling is not a separate aggregate but an outgrowth of activity
the five aggregates arise together and perish within one moment
the arisings of a thing form an unbroken continuity (santana), as a flame, the wind or a stream does
the flame, the wind and the stream are not examples of bare succession, since something real persists in each
the Jain counts of five extended existents, six substances and nine categories contradict one another
one who bears false witness is seized and devoured by the spirit
a good life may not be taken in exchange for a sinner's, for that would cost the higher state
suffering not explained by the good deeds of this life is the fruit of deeds of a former birth
wherever there is mind there is action, so action cannot be excluded from karma
what a true seer foretells comes to pass
the deed of those one has guided may rise against oneself
renouncers strive to end the rebirth of the born body
when the cause for awakening has not ripened in one birth, it comes to pass in a later birth
the Manimekala goddess's word cannot undo Indra's curse on the city

note: Devanthi blames a vow Kannaki broke to her husband in a former birth; the goddess of Madurai later traces the disaster to a curse on Kovalan's former self, who had Sangaman killed.
teaches: The poem offers two former-birth causes for the same ruin and gives the authoritative one to a goddess, so the friend's guess that the fault was the wife's own is left standing as a mistaken reading.

note: Both use ஒறுத்தல், punish. 314 says to punish wrongdoers by shaming them with kindness; 550 says that the king punishing the worst of them with death is simply weeding a crop.
teaches: The word keeps its form while the ethics of person and state divide.

note: The epic's line 21, வளம்தலை மயங்கிய நனந்தலை மறுகும், is the Pattinappaalai's line 193 on the same city's streets of mingled wealth.
teaches: Pattinappaalai uses the line to close a map of goods arriving from every mountain and sea, while the epic attaches it to a census of Puhar's own craftsmen and traders, so the borrowed praise moves from what flows into the port to who works in it.

gains.a: its catalogue is anchored in an older poem's praise of the same streets, which tells the reader this is the canonical Puhar
gains.b: the older line gains a list of the people behind the wealth, whom its own poem leaves out

note: 256 parodies 'all is suffering' as a greedy monk's complaints; the Manimekalai teacher gives suffering as the first truth and clinging as its cause.
teaches: The parody works by dropping the cause: the Buddhist epic ties suffering to clinging and its end to non-clinging, which the Jain song omits so the doctrine sounds like grumbling.

note: The Silappathikaram gives Madhavi's descent from the maiden cursed to earth when Urvasi's dance failed before Indra as the pedigree of her art; Chithirapathi counts the same heavenly dancers, Urvasi of her own line, to measure her shame now that Madhavi begs.
teaches: The curse-myth that certifies the courtesan's art in the first epic becomes, in the second, the yardstick by which the courtesan house judges a daughter's renunciation as the worst fall of the line.

note: Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker calls the person the one awareness that knows all; Neelakesi takes the seer and enjoyer as the opponent's own words and gives that knowing to every soul.
teaches: Where the Buddhist epic only records the person as one knowing awareness, the Jain epic uses the same attribute to argue that the Sankhya has already granted a knowing soul in every being.

note: The couplet ranks not killing one creature above pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices; Neelakesi says the sacrifice itself is the killing and its heavy deed falls on those who perform it.
teaches: Read beside the Jain charge, the couplet's comparison is seen to be the mild form of an argument the debater presses to the end: the Kural weighs sacrifice against abstention, Neelakesi denies the sacrifice any merit at all.

gains.a: Neelakesi's charge gains a widely shared ethical maxim that already ranks abstention above sacrifice, so her conclusion looks like its extension rather than a sectarian novelty
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the oblations it sets aside are themselves animal killing, which sharpens its comparison into an indictment

note: Kural 340 asks whether the life lodging in the body has no home of its own; Neelakesi 140 praises the sage who, while rain beat on him and poisonous creatures crawled over him, knew himself to be other than the body.
teaches: The couplet's doubtful question about the soul's lodging becomes in the epic a settled conviction that is practised: knowing the self is other than the body is what lets the ascetic bear the body's torments.

gains.a: the sage's endurance gains the couplet's image of the soul as a lodger, which explains why bodily suffering does not touch him
gains.b: the couplet's question gains an answer from a school that holds soul and body distinct and turns that into discipline

note: Neelakesi says the Buddhist has no space of measureless extent; the Manimekalai's teacher of logic names both 'one who says space is unreal' and 'one who says it is real' as parties to an argument, without taking a side there.
teaches: The Buddhist manual treats the reality of space as a disputed thesis between parties, while the Jain debater fixes the denial on the Buddhist and draws its cost, that the world then has no edge.

note: Kovalan, infatuated, knows no letting go (விடுதல் அறியா விருப்பினன்) once he buys the garland; in the Manimekalai, Madhavi tells how Aravana taught her that the great sorrow of the born comes from attachment (பற்றின் வருவது) and gave her the five precepts.
teaches: The sequel's Buddhist teaching names as attachment the cause that the first epic's narrator only shows as an infatuation that cannot let go, so the garland scene becomes the case the doctrine later diagnoses, told to the woman who sold the garland.

note: The Kundalakesi's invocation praises its lord as one who kept nothing for himself and laboured only for others' good (பிறர்க்கே உறுதிக்கு உழந்தான்); Neelakesi 222 mocks the monkey-king's self-offering, which saved no one, as no greatness.
teaches: The dispute is not whether the Buddha gave himself away but whether labour for others counts when, as the Jain argues, it profits no one; the Buddhist praise rests on intention, the Jain rebuttal on result.

note: The Kural calls it the lowest folly to take what does not last for what lasts; Mokkalan and Neelakesi dispute whether a thing can both last and not last.
teaches: The couplet assumes things fall cleanly into the lasting and the passing, and the debate shows that division itself was contested, the Jain holding one thing lasting in substance and passing in its modes.

gains.a: the debate's technical question is tied to a Tamil moral warning about mistaking the passing for the lasting
gains.b: the couplet's simple contrast is shown to stand on a metaphysical choice the schools did not share

note: The patikam's third moral is that the deed of the past comes in wrath and makes one eat its fruit; the last kaathai states the law of births in full: the good reach the golden world, the loving go where their attachment leads, the fruits of virtue and wrong both ripen, and the born die and the dead are born.
teaches: The poem opens with karma as a vengeance that falls on Kovalan and closes with karma as an even law that also rewards and that lets love carry the mothers to rebirth beside the pathini, so the frame turns the threat of the opening into a consolation by the end.

note: Kural 91 defines sweet words as moist with love and free of deceit; 536 argues against a rule that gentle speech is good by citing the soft-spoken plotter.
teaches: The Kural's definition already builds in the guard Neelakesi says the Buddhist rule lacks: speech counts as sweet only when it is without deceit, so her gentle conspirator would not qualify under it.

gains.a: the objection gets a ready answer in an older definition, which shows the rule can be repaired rather than discarded
gains.b: the couplet's clause படிறிலவாம் is shown to do real work, excluding exactly the soft-spoken plotter a debater raised

note: The Kural says penance can crush one's foes if one so intends; the sage, attacked by Neelakesi, intends instead to make her see her powerlessness and come to the dharma.
teaches: The power the Kural grants penance against enemies is here held back and turned to converting the enemy, which is what the Kural's 'if one so intends' leaves open.

gains.a: the sage's restraint is seen as a choice not to use a power the Kural says penance has
gains.b: the couplet's condition எண்ணின் gains a case where the ascetic, able to destroy, chooses not to

note: The Manimekalai says the chain of becoming has no I and no mine, no going and no coming; Neelakesi says whatever carries traces across the moments is a soul, like the thread in a garland.
teaches: The point of disagreement is located exactly: both accept that something continues from moment to moment, and they differ only on whether that continuity needs a thread, a soul, running through it.

note: 256 mocks 'all is suffering' as a greedy monk's complaints; 556 draws its practical consequence, that with no joy anywhere one may as well walk into fire.
teaches: The poet attacks the first truth twice in two tones, as a lazy monk's grumble in the Arkkachandra debate and as an argument against the Buddha himself that the doctrine would remove every reason for conduct.

note: Kovalan blames a deceitful woman for the poverty that shames him; the couplet ranks double-minded women with drink and dice as the company of those Fortune has left.
teaches: Kovalan speaks the couplet's judgment of himself, but the closing venba and the narrator put his ruin down to the old deed, so the epic lets the Kural's verdict on courtesans stand as a ruined man's account rather than as the cause.

gains.a: a standard of the age against which Kovalan's blame of Madhavi sounds conventional and self-excusing
gains.b: a speaker who applies it to himself in the moment of loss, while the story he is in names another cause

note: The Ainkurunuru friend asks whether it is a kindness if the old velan of an unerring tradition casts his beads and says the girl's sickness is Murugu; the epic's old wise woman of the clan's ancient duty, possessed, declares Kannaki divine and Kannaki calls it confusion.
teaches: In the akam convention the possessed diviner of an old line is the one who gets it wrong, mistaking love for a god's seizure, while in the epic the possessed old woman's word is the true one and the hearer's doubt is the mistake, so the pairing shows the epic reversing the Sangam irony about divination to make it carry prophecy.

gains.a: Kannaki's dismissal of the speech as பேதுறவு reads as a known stance, the akam scepticism toward the diviner, which the story will overturn
gains.b: the friend's mockery of the unerring velan gains a later counter-case where the same kind of possessed elder speaks truly

note: 233 refuses the dawn report of spear wounds on the chest of Evvi, leader of the bards' families; Akananuru 115 uses the bards who, in the battle where Evvi fell (எவ்வி வீழ்ந்த செருவில் பாணர்), broke off the curved necks of their lutes, as a simile for konrai pods on a desert path.
teaches: The akam poet assumes his hearers know that bards mourned Evvi by breaking their lutes, so the death the puram poet cannot bring himself to believe became, in the akam tradition, a fixed public memory usable as a passing image of curved pods.

note: The goddess told Lakshmi that the dharma of the meal Saathusakkaran ate would not leave her and would end her births; here Manimekalai names this bowl as that meal's fruit (105-106).
teaches: The prophecy's fruit arrives first not as release but as a means of further giving, so in the epic merit ripens into the power to make more merit before it ends births.

note: The Kundalakesi fragment calls the body a deed-made thing where swarms of worms small and grown feed and live; Neelakesi says the many lives within the bodhisattva's body die when he gives it to the beast.
teaches: The Buddhist verse uses the body's teeming worms to teach disgust for it, while the Jain debater uses the same teeming body to charge the Buddhist hero's gift with mass killing, so one image serves renunciation on one side and non-harm on the other.

note: The quatrain says a small act of virtue that reaches worthy hands spreads like a banyan from a tiny seed; the goddess says Lakshmi's meal to a sage will not go to waste but will cut off her births, and also that the giver herself, as a seed of dharma, could be lost on barren ground.
teaches: The epic agrees that a gift to the worthy grows, but changes its harvest from a covering shade of merit to the end of rebirth, and adds that the giver's own attachments can still waste what the gift has sown.

gains.a: The goddess's claim at 41 is placed within an ethics-book teaching on giving to the worthy, which marks how far its promised fruit goes beyond that teaching.
gains.b: The quatrain's growth image is shown to depend on the giver as well as the receiver, a condition it does not state.

note: The Kural promises the sky to those who have left doubt and become clear; the teacher describes two sound-looking proofs of opposite theses that together leave only doubt (சங்கயம்).
teaches: The epic shows a doubt that more argument cannot remove, since each side's reasoning holds, so the clarity the couplet praises cannot come from matching proofs alone.

gains.a: the stalemate fallacy gains its stake: doubt is what the Kural says bars the way to the sky
gains.b: the couplet's 'leaving doubt' gains a precise case of doubt that reasoning itself produces

note: Kannaki bids the fire spare Brahmins, the virtuous, cows, chaste wives, elders and children and go to the wicked; here the flame spares the side of the virtuous, the cows and calves escape, and the warriors' quarter burns.
teaches: The exemptions she named are carried out street by street, so the fire is shown as a discriminating judgment rather than a blind disaster, and the warriors' quarter is put among those she called the wicked.

note: The Kural says understanding is seeing the true thing in whatever thing, of whatever nature; Neelakesi says no thing has ever been made clear except through its qualities.
teaches: The Jain makes the couplet's 'whatever its nature' into a method: the true thing is reached through its qualities, not by stripping them away, which is why she can claim the soul is known by knowing and seeing.

gains.a: the debater's rule about qualities gains the Kural's claim that seeing the real thing is what understanding is for
gains.b: the couplet gains an answer to how the true thing is to be seen, which it leaves open

note: The fifth kaathai shows Puhar's warriors and women making offerings at the guardian bhuta's altar that Indra sent; here the vidyadhara tells why it was sent: a Chola guarded Amaravati against the asuras and received the bhuta and the five halls as Indra's gift.
teaches: Read together, the townspeople's worship and the outsider's origin story show the festival as heaven repaying a Chola's service, which the city's own rite does not explain.

note: Innaa Narpathu 31 says singing to an untuned lute is very painful; Thirikadugam says song not measured to the beat is painful to hear.
teaches: One verse faults the pitch and the other the beat, so together they show the period held music to two measures, tuning and time, either of which failing makes song painful.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) as what is spoken of as a person; Neelakesi names feeling, cognition, perception and action (உழப்பு, அறிவு, குறி, செய்கை) and says they belong to one being.
teaches: The Jain debater accepts the Buddhist list of the four mental aggregates term for term and disputes only whether they have one owner, so the quarrel over the self is about ownership of the aggregates, not about what they are.

note: The goddess cites a saying that fire will eat Madurai and its king on a fixed day of Aadi; the fire god says he had a command long before (பண்டே) to burn the city on the day the pathini was wronged.
teaches: Two separate voices, the omen and the fire god's standing order, make the burning predetermined, so Kannaki's act is shown as the trigger of a sentence already fixed.

note: The patikam states as a thesis that the deed of the past comes in wrath and makes one eat it; the Tirumanthiram says that by Siva's grace deeds do not cling (வினை சேரகிலாமை).
teaches: If the patikam's line is read as admitting no release, the two give incompatible accounts of whether a past deed must be eaten, and the epic offers no grace that could stop it, since even the gods appear only to honour Kannaki after the deed has run its course; the Tirumanthiram puts grace before the fruit.

gains.a: the epic's moral gains its sharpest contrast, which shows that its karma is unmediated: no god in the patikam intervenes before the fruit
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's claim gains a rival from the same language and land in which deeds do cling and must be eaten, so its grace is seen as an answer to a live view

note: The venba gives Madurapathi the powers of Lakshmi, Saraswati and the slayer of Mahisha; the next kaathai shows her body half dark and half gold, lotus in one hand and sword in the other.
teaches: The venba's union of gentle and warlike goddesses is drawn in the next kaathai as a body divided down the middle, so the reader sees the city goddess's double nature first named, then pictured.

note: The Manimekala goddess gave Manimekalai mantras to take another form, travel the sky and end hunger, warning that people would not tell a young woman the truth; here the form-changing mantra defeats the queen's plot.
teaches: The pair shows why the goddess's gifts were defensive: the mantra of another form, given against those who would not trust a young woman, is first used to save her from a slander about her body.

note: Aravanar told her that she would not take up the teaching until the events caused by her had come to pass; now, after the prison, Aputhiran's land and the tour of the schools, she asks him for it.
teaches: The long middle of the epic is framed as the waiting time Aravanar named, and her request now marks that the conditions he set have been met.

note: Kalittokai 11 closes its argument that the man will return with the omens at home: the lizard chirps on the good side and her lovely eye throbs on the left (உண் கண்ணும் ஆடுமால், இடனே). Thinaimalai 80 ends on the same left-eye omen, with the same closing word இடம்.
teaches: Kalittokai 11 reaches the throbbing left eye only after a long proof from the man's own words, while the venba rests the promise of return on the omen alone, which shows the left-eye sign was a recognised closing proof that could carry a whole short poem.

note: Manimekalai's Buddhist teacher gives the hare's horn as the case of what has no arising at all; Neelakesi's Buddhist uses the hare's and donkey's horns to show that some things are non-existent outright.
teaches: The Jain epic's Buddhist argues with the same stock example the Buddhist epic teaches, so here the polemic reproduces Buddhist doctrine fairly before Neelakesi answers it in 405.

note: The Naladiyar calls the meat-eater's belly a burning ground for beasts and birds; the Neelakesi places its flesh-eating demon hosts and a goddess's shrine inside a real burning ground.
teaches: The quatrain's metaphor joining flesh-eating and the cremation ground becomes the Neelakesi's literal scene, so the epic's first quarrel over flesh is staged where eating bodies and burning them meet.

gains.a: the burning-ground description is shown to carry an ethical charge against eating flesh, not only horror
gains.b: the quatrain's figure is shown worked out as a setting for the doctrinal fight over offerings

note: The Kural says all pains rest on those who caused pain (நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம்); Neelakesi applies the rule to the Buddha's pain-bearing gifts and says he must himself suffer what they caused.
teaches: Applied without limit, the rule that pain returns to its causer condemns even the giver who bears pain for others, and only a theory of what makes a deed evil can stop that.

gains.a: Neelakesi's charge rests on a maxim Tamil readers already accept, so it reads as consequence rather than spite
gains.b: the couplet meets a hard case it does not consider, pain caused in the act of helping others, which forces a choice about whether intention excuses it

note: The city sees Kannaki weeping beyond bearing (அல்லலுற் றாற்றா தழுவாளை), the very condition the couplet names as the force that wears away a king's wealth.
teaches: The couplet's tears work slowly as an abrasive on wealth, but the epic makes one woman's tears the moment the people themselves declare the sceptre bent, the first step to the city's burning.

gains.a: the citizens' grief gains a known rule that such tears are a weapon against the ruler
gains.b: the couplet's general 'those who suffer' gains a single witnessed scene in which a whole city reads the tears as a verdict on the king

note: Kannaki shamed the Pandya with the Chola whose gate bell's tongue trembled for the cow; the goddess replies that the Pandya kings' ears heard the Veda's tongue (மறைநா) and never the bell's tongue (மணிநா).
teaches: The goddess turns Kannaki's proof of the Chola's justice into evidence for the Pandya: a line whose bell no one ever had to ring needed no such exemplar, so the dispute over the king's justice becomes a dispute between two dynasties' records.

note: The old Pandya asks whether his sceptre has bent, admits his rule strayed through ignorant men and makes amends; Nedunjeliyan, shown the gem, says he is the thief and dies.
teaches: Both kings confess the fault as their own, but the ancestor's confession comes before any death and repairs it with land, while Nedunjeliyan's comes after and can only be paid with his life: the difference is when the king inquires.

note: Tirumular's grace-power descends as the guru when good and bad deeds are balanced and the soul becomes Siva; the epic's Manimekalai, after births of compassion, becomes a disciple and is saved by cutting dependence herself (சார்பு அறுத்து உய்தி).
teaches: Both put a teacher at the threshold of release, but in Tirumular the teacher is grace that ends the soul's own agency, while in the epic the great one only gives dharma and the disciple does the cutting, so they disagree over who acts in release.

gains.a: a sharp contrast that shows how far the epic keeps release in the disciple's own hands
gains.b: a Buddhist counter-model of the teacher-disciple bond without descent of grace

note: The Kural's first couplet says the world has the primal Lord as its first; the Neelakesi argues no creator can be first without an endless regress of makers.
teaches: Kural 1 says the Lord is first but never that he made the world, so the Jain regress argument against a creator leaves the couplet standing, which shows why Jain readers could keep it.

gains.a: the epic's attack is shown to be aimed at a maker, not at every claim that a Lord comes first
gains.b: the couplet's simile of the first letter gains a test that sets first apart from creator

claims.gist: as with paddy and cane, the later growth is neither the seed nor other than its line
the five kinds of sense-knowing must belong either to the elements severally or to a further knower
a cruel deed, when it ripens, brings death and ruin, and those it strikes are reborn among their former kin
no merit comes to the giver
killing carries no sin
one who denies the fruit of deeds has no reason to prefer austerity to the household life
a thing exists in its own nature and not in another's, and is inexpressible only in that all its aspects cannot be said at once
a wife who dies before seeing her husband's grief gains fortune in heaven
a stone from Pothiyil or the Himalaya, bathed in the Ganges or the Kaveri, becomes the goddess
mind is the soul joined with bodily form, not a separate substance
time is twofold, so it is not a single substance
an enemy who came to kill is overcome by virtue, not by force
nothing that exists perishes and nothing that does not exist comes to be
the lac analogy fails because the lac is a thing beyond the seed, and nothing beyond the five aggregates is admitted to carry a deed
high and low birth is not a real difference, since the senses find none between persons
an eye that has not seen Maal is no eye
cognitions that occur one at a time point to a single knower
a wife's fiery vengeance for a husband wrongly killed is not cruelty
the way of the scripture cuts the many deeds that cling to the soul through its entanglement with the body
the bali is a debt the hunters owe the goddess, not a gift they may withhold
birth and its sequels are diseases caused by eating the fruit of bad deeds
true understanding is the cure that ends the suffering of births
the world comes forth from the union of soul and prakriti
two things that can neither act and know together cannot produce by joining
a true wife bears the affliction that befalls her husband
no god can be present in the city of a king who has erred with the sword
a former deed comes in wrath and turns a man against the woman he loves
the Jina has passed beyond death, desire, aging and birth
the seven hells open into eighty-four hundred thousand dwellings
the beings of hell are neither male nor female
a husband may refuse to live on the food of a wife who has done a grave wrong
a wrong deed's sin is removed by gifts made as the Brahmins' law books prescribe
if everyone renounced eating flesh, no one would kill for it
those who teach dharma gain dharma by the teaching
every path of penance that ends birth is taught in the scripture of the Purvas
every true god is a name of the Tirthankara
unless kings do justice, the chastity of renowned women does not shine
a king does not live on once his sceptre bends
kings' fierce anger does not cool until their vow is fulfilled
the self is present throughout the body, so whoever takes a living half is the giver's killer
a body without awareness is a corpse, and to give a corpse is no gift
one should trust the god and honour those who trust
one should give up eating flesh and killing living beings
one should give gifts and keep austerities
one should not kill a kindness done, nor keep evil friends
one should never bear false witness
one should fear another's wife and protect lives in distress
liquor, theft, lust, lies and idle company are to be shunned
youth, wealth and the body do not last, so one must seek a companion for the world one goes to
the soul takes up the parents' seed and blood, settles within the body and grows with it
a trace that itself perishes needs a further trace, without end
the just sceptre of a line whose ancestor gave his flesh for a dove cannot bend, even in hard times
humans are of five kinds, and the first kind live in a land of enjoyment
of the six categories the first three possess being and the last three do not
substance, quality and action are separate from each other
either the scent went over and so did not perish, or it did not go and the smell is not there
awareness is nothing but a property of the elements gathered together
the Jina taught the way by which both good and evil deeds are separated from the soul

note: Before the debate the king promised to send the loser out with shame (174); in 228 the townspeople drive Kundalakesi out of the gate with drums and insults.
teaches: The expulsion is the execution of a stake both debaters accepted with joy beforehand, so the shame is the contract of the debate rather than the mob's cruelty.

note: Kannaki says she does not know the cruel deed behind her loss; the patikam's goddess tells the grieving pathini it was a curse laid in a former birth by the wife of Sangaman.
teaches: The heroine laments in ignorance of the cause the poem's frame has already disclosed, so the reader judges her accusation of the king knowing a second cause she does not.

note: The elder lady sets Kannaki up in a household for charity and the hosting of guests; in Madurai Kannaki says she has lost giving to the virtuous, tending Brahmins, receiving ascetics and welcoming guests.
teaches: The household the second kaathai founds for its charity and hospitality is named, duty by duty, as what Kannaki has lost, so the pair shows her grief in Madurai as the loss of a household's dharma, not only of a husband's company.

note: Gotami, mourning her son at the burning ground, begged the goddess to take her life for his and was told a life gone goes by its deeds; the queen, mourning her son, is taught the same and her grief is quenched.
teaches: The epic answers a mother's grief twice with the same doctrine but to opposite ends: Gotami, refused, dies beside her son, while the queen, taught to turn her love to all lives, is cleared and bows to her son's supposed enemy.

note: Both are royal vows in the conditional form whose penalty is the king's own sceptre turning cruel to his people; the Chera's line almost repeats the Pandya's.
teaches: The Pandya's vow names only his own subjects as the sufferers of a failed king, while the Chera's sets the choice out plainly, a sceptre that makes either foreign kings or his own people tremble, showing that the vow form took the king's power to terrify as fixed and staked the people's peace on a war abroad.

gains.a: the Chera's penalty clause is shown to be the old vanjinam formula, குடிபழி தூற்றும் கோலேன் ஆகுக, carried almost word for word into குடிநடுக் குறூஉங் கோலேன் ஆகென
gains.b: the formula gains a use against an insult reported from far away by ascetics rather than spoken to the king's face, so the vow answers a rumour of scorn

note: The Kural says griefs keep hold of those who keep hold of attachment; the teacher's truths say sorrow is caused by birth and clinging, and release, which is joy, by not clinging.
teaches: The Kural's one-verb picture of grip and grief becomes the second truth, and the epic adds its mirror, release as joy caused by not clinging, so the couplet's warning is shown to be half of a four-part formula.

gains.a: a Tamil saying in which the grip one keeps and the grip of sorrow are one act, which the formula's dry causal statement lacks
gains.b: the positive half the couplet omits: that not clinging is the cause of release, named as joy

note: In kaathai 14 Aputhiran hears that rain has failed in Savakam and sets out to carry his bowl there; here the cow's sage foretells, in Savakam itself, a protector born to make the rain abound and guard lives (மழை வளம் சுரப்பவும் மன் உயிர் ஓம்பவும்).
teaches: The errand the shipwreck cut short is fulfilled by rebirth: Aputhiran reaches the rainless land not as a beggar with a bowl but as its rain-bringing king, so the epic moves his charity from alms to kingship across a death.

note: The Vedic logician in the Manimekalai defines perception as fivefold sense knowledge; the Neelakesi's teacher counts as perception also avadhi, manahparyaya and kevala, knowledge without the senses.
teaches: The two epics define the same first means of knowledge incompatibly: for the logician perception ends at the five senses, for the Jain it reaches up to omniscience, which is what lets the Jain claim an all-knowing teacher as a source of valid knowledge.

note: In Puhar Kovalan blamed his ruin on sporting with a deceitful woman and the shame of lost wealth; in Madurai he blames his own heedlessness, bad company and disobedience to his parents.
teaches: Between the two confessions the blame moves from Madhavi to himself, so the road to Madurai is shown changing his account of his fall even as it carries him to his death.

note: The Kural likens the body-life bond to a bird leaving its nest; Neelakesi holds the soul joined with the body it has taken and makes it the one who sees and knows there.
teaches: The Kural's bird stresses how loosely the life sits in the body, while the Jain debater insists the soul fills and works the body as its knower, so the same separability is put to opposite uses.

gains.a: The verse's soul is set against a familiar image of a life that merely lodges in the body and leaves.
gains.b: The bird-and-nest image is shown to leave open what does the knowing while the bird is in the nest, which the debate answers.

note: Bhutikan dismisses Neelakesi as a Sudra woman with no competence in the Veda; five verses later the poet names her by her learning (புலமையினாள்) as she argues from the phonetics of the Veda itself.
teaches: The poet answers the Brahmin's caste taunt not with a counter-taunt but by showing the Sudra woman doing the grammarian's and logician's work on the Veda, so the debate's form refutes his premise before its content does.

note: The Silappathikaram ends Kannaki's story with her ascent in the gods' car with Kovalan; the Manimekalai says that this heaven only defers the evil deed, and that release waits for the Buddha at Kapilai.
teaches: Read together, the apotheosis that closes the first epic becomes a way station in the second: a Buddhist sequel re-reads the pathini's reward as a heaven still bound by deeds.

note: Verse 37 holds up the farmer who ploughs, sows and waters as the model of provision; verse 42 shows the ploughman who toils without seed as the fool.
teaches: The farmer's image cuts both ways in the fragment: what matters is not the labour, which both farmers do, but whether the seed of austerity was sown.

note: The king's own sentence, யானோ அரசன் யானே கள்வன், and his death are what Kannaki now rewards by declaring him Indra's guest.
teaches: Read together, the scenes show the self-condemnation as the act that wins the king heaven: the confession that he was the thief is what makes him faultless in the goddess's word.

note: The couplet says a fate of loss makes a man foolish; the epic shows Kovalan, his deed ripening, take a sung convention for a confession and leave.
teaches: The epic supplies the mechanism the couplet only asserts: ripening fate does its work by making a man misread what is in front of him, here a song in an assumed voice, so the folly is the means of the loss.

gains.a: the epic's ஊழ்வினை gains a precise maxim for how it works on Kovalan, through a loss of judgement rather than an outside blow
gains.b: the couplet's abstract 'fate that makes foolish' gains a concrete case of what the folly looks like and what it costs

note: In 393 Neelakesi told the Buddhist that the quality is the qualified thing and that she holds them both different and one; 804 states the same thesis against the Vaisheshika.
teaches: One Jain thesis faces opposite errors: against the Buddhist, who keeps only qualities, she stresses the bearer; against the Vaisheshika, who splits quality from bearer, she stresses their oneness.

note: In 64 the sage sees privately that the woman before him is a demon's daughter, not a princess; in 88 he lets it show in one word, நுமர் (your kin), among the demon class of the Vyantara gods.
teaches: The sage's knowledge of her true form, held silent in 64, becomes a tool of teaching: he names her kind inside a list of gods, so the cosmology itself unmasks her, and then defers it to keep her listening.

note: The Ainthinai Aimpathu heroine begs the crab not to walk over the tracks of her lover's chariot so she can look at them her fill; Madhavi's woman tells the tide that it has already broken up every trace of that path.
teaches: The Sangam heroine still holds the wheel-track and pleads with a small creature to spare it, while in the song the sea has already wiped it out and she can only ask what to do, so the pair shows the same last trace of the lover first guarded and then lost.

gains.a: the stanza gains the older poem's sense of what the track meant, all that is left to look at
gains.b: the quatrain's plea gains its sequel, the loss it feared, done not by a crab but by a tide no one can beg

note: The couplet asks what learning is worth to those who do not bow at the good feet (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர்) of the one of pure knowledge; the close says kings who do not bow at the good feet (நல் தாள் தொழார்) of Poraiyan find it hard to live, and Kannaki too praises Senguttuvan.
teaches: The close moves the Kural's phrase for bowing to the god's feet onto a living Chera king and makes the penalty for not bowing the loss of life rather than of learning's fruit, while the deified Kannaki joins the praise, so the epic ends by turning a devotional formula into a political one.

gains.a: the closing boast gains the weight of the formula it borrows: bowing at the good feet is the Kural's posture before the god
gains.b: the couplet's phrase gains a case of its wording transferred from the god to a king, which shows how its language of worship could be turned to royal praise

note: Tirumular says the wise gave up disputation (தர்க்க வாதம்) and gained release by reciting the Veda; Neelakesi appeals to the Apta's scripture as what leaves nothing unknown, but does so as a move in a debate.
teaches: Both rest final authority on a scripture, but the Saiva verse sets scripture against argument while the Jain debater uses scripture as the ground of argument, so the two disagree about whether debate serves the scripture.

gains.a: the Jain appeal to scripture is seen as one way to end a dispute, which a rival tradition takes as reason to give up disputing
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal of argument is seen as a choice, since another scriptural tradition put argument at the centre of its practice

note: At the wedding night Kovalan asks why her admirers decked her with other ornaments besides the flawless auspicious one (மறுஇல் மங்கல அணியே அன்றியும் பிறிதுஅணி); alone at evening she delights in no ornament but the auspicious one (மங்கல அணியின் பிறிதுஅணி மகிழாள்).
teaches: The husband's compliment that she needs no ornament but the marriage one comes true literally as the mark of his desertion, so the poet builds her abandonment out of his own flattery.

note: The Kural says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from the work one does; the Neelakesi praises a land where the four varnas each keep the path given to them.
teaches: A Jain poet could honour the Kural's ethics and still count the hereditary varna order as a land's virtue, so the couplet's levelling of birth was not read by him as rejecting the order, only as asking each to keep its duty.

gains.a: the verse's praise of varna order is seen against a Tamil claim that ranks by deeds, not birth
gains.b: the couplet's ambiguous செய்தொழில் is shown open to the reading of a fixed hereditary duty

note: In the Silappathikaram, when Madhavi gives her daughter to the dharma, the king and city grieve as men who have dropped a gem in the sea and the ascetics speak kind words; Chithirapathi says such a turn earns a courtesan only laughter.
teaches: Held together they show that the courtesan's renunciation has two publics: the city mourns the loss of beauty while the courtesan house reads the same act as ridicule, so neither epic's report of the town's reaction can be taken alone.

note: Akananuru 371: a twist-horned stag whose mate was shot will not drink the little water of the pool (சில்நீர் உண்ணாது) and lies stricken; the man crossing alone sees it and thinks of his love's eyes. Aimpathu 38: the stag feigns drinking the pool's little water so the doe may drink.
teaches: Held together, the two stags at a pool of scant water show the paalai poets making the stag's not drinking the sign of love both while the mate lives and after she dies, and Akananuru 371 bears out the friend's hope in 38, since there the traveller does see such a stag and his thoughts turn home.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain debater says release is blocking the way good and bad deeds come in and wearing out past deeds; Neelakesi names that way as yoga activity and uses it to deny that a freed soul could be rebound.
teaches: The inflow that the Buddhist epic's summary only mentions becomes, in the Jain epic, the answer to the charge that a released soul could fall back into bondage.

note: Kural 280 says neither shaven head nor matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 261 says the outward guise is false unless mind and conduct agree.
teaches: Both discount the guise, but for different reasons: the Kural makes conduct the test of renunciation, and the Neelakesi uses that same test against a monk who makes the mind the only test.

gains.a: the argument that the guise means nothing without matching conduct is given an older authority
gains.b: the couplet's dismissal of outward marks is shown not to support a mind-only view, since its test is still what one does

note: Madhavi lies down saying that though he will not come in the evening she will see him in the morning (காலைகாண் குவம்); in the next kaathai Kovalan comes instead to Kannaki's door (கடைத்தலையான் வந்துநம் கோவலன்).
teaches: The morning Madhavi waits for is the morning Kovalan returns to his wife, so her hope and Kannaki's dream are the two ends of one night, and the courtesan's loss is the wife's recovery.

note: Brahmadharman foretold that Rahulan would die of the snake's poison glance; the pillar deity now names the deed that set his deaths in motion: the cook he killed in anger at the sage's meal.
teaches: The prophecy of kaathai 9 gave only the event; paired with this unit it shows the epic withholding a cause for twelve kaathais and then placing it inside an act of service to the very sage who made the prophecy.

note: The invocation praises the god whose word removes the suffering of souls; the sermon names that word's content as a medicine of three parts the soul takes.
teaches: The invocation's claim that the god ends suffering by his word, not by intervening, is made concrete here: the cure is a discipline the hearer takes, so the god's role stays that of teacher.

note: In Kuruntokai 111 the mother takes the velan's word that Neduvel caused the girl's sickness, and the friend wants the lover to come so the household may see a great laugh (பெருநகை); here the friend's refrain is இதுநகையாகின்றே over the same mistake.
teaches: The laugh at the mother's misreading, a friend's private aside in the short poem, becomes the sung refrain of a public round dance, which shows the old akam situation turned into communal performance.

gains.a: the epic's refrain gains a source: the joke on the velan was an established akam situation, not the hill girls' invention
gains.b: the short poem's single laugh is shown as a convention strong enough to carry four stanzas of a festival song

note: Saathuvan argues that the departing life enters the body its deeds put on, as a reason for the Nagas to do good; Tirumular bids the reader seek the way by which, leaving this body, one does not enter another.
teaches: The same passage of the life into a new body is good news in the epic, a reason to act well for a better world, and the thing to be escaped in Tirumular, so the pair shows that a merchant's ethics of rebirth stops short of the release both traditions put beyond it.

gains.a: Saathuvan's argument gains the reminder that a good rebirth is still a rebirth, which the epic leaves to its later teaching
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a reasoned account, from the corpse and the dream, of the entry into another body that it simply assumes

note: Tirumular calls killing, theft, lust and lying sins as great as mountains, whose giving up leads to Siva's feet; the ascetic names toddy, lying, theft, killing and lust as the five to be shunned and threatens hell to those who keep lust.
teaches: Two traditions share nearly the same list of sins but use it differently: Tirumular makes their giving up a path to Siva's feet, while the ascetic names no god, singles out lust as the one that contains the rest, and uses the list to warn a king of hell.

gains.a: The ascetic's list gains a parallel that shows how far it is shared across schools.
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a godless version of the same discipline, where shunning is an end in itself and its failure leads to hell rather than away from Siva.

note: Kural 349 says that when attachment ends it cuts off births; Aravanar says suffering comes from attachment, bliss to those free of it, and that birth itself brings growing suffering.
teaches: The couplet ties the end of attachment to the end of rebirth but sets no value on birth; Aravanar's lines add that birth is itself suffering and offer a bereaved lay woman five precepts as the way in, not the renouncer's clean cut.

gains.a: a bare causal statement, attachment to rebirth, against which the teacher's added judgment that birth is suffering stands out as the Buddhist addition
gains.b: a scene where its renouncer's rule is given as consolation to a grieving woman still in the world, with lay precepts as the first step

note: Saathuvan argues from the insensible corpse and the dream journey that a life leaves the body and enters another fitted by its deeds; the materialist of kaathai 27 holds that awareness ends when the elements part, that inference is no means of knowledge, and that a next world of fruits is a lie.
teaches: The materialist's challenge is met eleven kaathais before he states it, by a merchant using exactly the inference the materialist refuses to accept, so the pair shows that the epic's case for rebirth stands or falls on whether inference counts as knowledge.

note: The pillar says the prince died by his own former deed; in the next kaathai the deity tells Manimekalai that deed: in a former birth he cut down a cook with a sword for spoiling a meal for the sage Brahmadharman.
teaches: The bare claim of ripened karma is given its content one kaathai later, and the content matches the form of the death, a sword for a sword, so the epic makes its karma traceable rather than merely asserted.

note: 409 uses high and low birth as a working scale, even to overturn it. 972 denies the scale at the root: birth is the same for all beings, and only deeds differ.
teaches: The two arguments against birth rank are different in kind.

note: Madhavi listed the ways of the pathini: die at once with a sigh, enter the blazing fire as if it were a cool pool, or wear down the body in vows; Aathirai takes the second way, and the fire will not have her, and she leaves it like a woman coming back from a bath (16:46).
teaches: Madhavi's list assumes the fire completes the pathini's choice, but Aathirai's fire refuses her, so the epic shows that a pathini's power can overrule even her own resolve to die and makes Madhavi's simile of the cool pool literally true.

note: Pattinattar counts the begging bowl (இரந்துண்ணும் ஓடு) among the renouncer's wealth without lack; Neelakesi says the bowl is costly, easily lost and useless to one who does penance without fault.
teaches: The begging bowl, emblem of renunciation for the Saiva poet, is for the Jain debater a possession that burdens: whether renunciation keeps even a bowl divides the traditions.

gains.a: Neelakesi's attack on the bowl is seen against a living ideal that prized it, so its edge against Buddhist practice is clearer
gains.b: the Siddhar's praise of poverty is shown to keep a possession that a stricter rule would give up

note: Pattinattar lists the five fires, lying in water, plucking hair and going without food and says his devotees reached release without them; Mokkalan lists sun, rain, fasting and sleeplessness as bringing no gain.
teaches: Buddhist debater and Saiva poet reject the same austerities for opposite reasons: for Mokkalan pain has no power to free, for Pattinattar the god's name frees without it, so a shared rejection hides a disagreement about what does the freeing.

gains.a: Mokkalan's attack is seen to belong to a wider Tamil rejection of mortification, not only to anti-Jain polemic
gains.b: the poem's list of austerities, which includes plucking the hair, is seen as the Jain practice a Buddhist also attacked, so its claim of a better way enters an existing quarrel

note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; Deepathilakai calls the feet of the Lord of dharma on Samantam the ship of dharma that frees from the great sea called birth (23-25).
teaches: The Buddhist epic takes the Kural's unnamed Lord and his feet as the Buddha's footprint on a named peak and turns swimming into being carried by a ship, so the couplet's open theism becomes a pilgrimage relic served by the gods.

gains.a: Deepathilakai's image is shown to rest on the Kural's opening chapter, giving the Buddhist claim the Kural's wording of release
gains.b: the couplet's இறைவன் is shown open to sectarian claiming, read here by a Buddhist work as the Buddha

note: Kural 261 defines tapas as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life; Sirupanchamoolam 31 keeps both, adds three more, and says penance so made is sweet, not lowly.
teaches: The couplet defines penance by two ethical acts; the verse keeps them, turns bearing pain into forgetting it, and meets an objection the couplet does not raise, that penance degrades the one who does it.

note: The Puram poem tells Killivalavan that giving, conquest and justice are not his own fame, since his line already holds the king who entered the scale for the dove and the ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort; the ammanai answers its riddle with the Chola who destroyed the hanging forts and names no living Chola.
teaches: Read together, the Puram poet's warning that the ancestors' deeds swallow a living Chola's fame comes true in the epic, where Chola praise sung at the Chera court consists of nothing but those ancestral deeds and the city of Puhar.

gains.a: the riddle's answer gains its old standing: the hanging fort was already the Chola line's inherited title in the Sangam praise of a named king
gains.b: the Puram poem's claim that ancestral glory outshines the present king gains a later case in which the line is remembered only by it, in a rival kingdom's women's game

note: In the next kaathai Manimekalai, remembering her former birth as Ilakkumi, recalls the sage's word that on a day of grave sorrow the goddess Manimekala would come, lift her up in the dark night and set her on an island in the south.
teaches: The waking that she meets as abandonment and a strange rebirth is the foretold step of a prophecy she has not yet remembered, so the epic makes her terror on the shore the unknowing half of a plan the reader learns only afterwards.

claims.gist: dancing the kuravai that Mayavan danced among the herds will drive away the distress the omens foretell
the gods worship Maal as the ultimate reality
giving one's blood to a demon is a great gift
dharma and adharma are superfluous, since sea, land and space suffice for things to move and rest
dharma and adharma fix the limit of the world within which souls and matter can move
gifts of one's flesh, eyes and head meet no real need, since no living person asks for them
taking another's thing in the belief that it is one's own is not theft
vyantara spirits frighten people with such displays
there is no one who knows, acts and enjoys the fruit
merit and giving make no sense without one who knows, acts and enjoys
one who has seen the truth should take up the renouncer's discipline of eating from the hand and the final fast
devotion to the Jina's feet brings one to the state where suffering is removed
a mother who sets a beautiful young daughter to hard tapas is cruel and lacks decency
ageing, growth and decline by degrees cannot be shown if each moment perishes wholly
if arising, persisting and perishing are qualities, the substance that bears them must be something else that cannot be named
whoever understands the Lord's scripture, of whatever form, attains release in due order
a person is a continuity (சந்தானம்) arising by potency, as sprout and branch from a seed
release is not other than the course of this continuity
swellings and heat in a tree are changes of a living body, as they are in ours
to call a thing both lasting and passing incurs the faults of both
refusing a thing's being both lasting and passing in different respects is one-sidedness
traces persist as the pathiri scent stays in a new pot after the flower is gone
as the scent outlasts the flower, the soul outlasts the body
one whose austerity is given by fate has a curse for a weapon and is beyond desire
the scriptures other peoples recite are derived from the Jina's teaching
lovers who let time divide them, or who forget their partners when apart, deserve to have love take their lives
penance that can be broken by being seen by women is not firm penance
the Buddha appeared to make dharma flourish in a world that had lost understanding, as a sun rises on darkness
on the festival day the gods leave heaven empty and come to dwell in the city
the gods grant no boon to those who have done no tapas
prakriti is made of three opposed qualities, and its products appear when one exceeds the others
animals live in constant fear of one another
two faculties that take the same object are not two
the Ajivika categories cannot be overthrown by rival schools
fault, deed and fruit are suffering and unstable, and no thing has a self
seeing them so is the nature of release
a thing has both a nature and an action, so the soul can be established from its nature
the seed-to-flower continuity holds only because an unbroken branch joins them, and no such link joins a dead man to a god
a child's body comes from the parents' blood and its life from its own former deeds, so no deity gave it
anger that destroys a city is a sin whose fruit must be suffered, even when the anger was provoked
heaven won by good deeds lasts only until their merit is spent, and then the evil deed still comes to fruit
beings driven by good and evil deeds are born and die again through many births
a deed makes karma by what it brings about, not by the intention alone

note: The couplet says only those who reach the Lord's feet cross the great sea of births; Aravanar says those who hear the Buddha's dharma pass beyond painful birth and vows to praise the Bodhi Lord's feet in every birth.
teaches: The epic names the couplet's unnamed feet as the Buddha's but moves the crossing onto hearing his teaching, and its worshipper expects many more births before that hearing, so the feet become a lifelong devotion rather than the crossing itself.

gains.a: Aravanar's vow gains a reading against the Kural's opening chapter, which shows how much of the shared idiom a Buddhist could take over
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed Lord gains a test case: a reader of another faith who fills the name and changes the means

note: The venba's மூதை வினை is unnamed here; the goddess of Madurai later names it as the curse of Sangaman's widow on Kovalan's former self.
teaches: Read together, the venba sets the deed moving with no content and the later speech fills it in, so the departure from Puhar is the first step of a debt whose terms the reader learns only after the death.

note: The Kural says wealth that comes without grace and love should be let go; the hunters name themselves graceless takers of wealth by wounding and ask the gracious goddess to eat their due.
teaches: Where the couplet tells the getter to let graceless wealth roll away, the hymn shows a community whose living is exactly such wealth offering a share of it to a goddess of grace, who is asked not to refuse it; the tension rests on reading the due as paid from the plunder.

gains.a: the hunters' self-description gains the ethical name for what they live by: wealth that comes without arul
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a case where graceless wealth is not let go but sanctified by offering

note: The Neelakesi's sage counts four states of birth (நாற்கதி); Aravanar in the Manimekalai counts six kinds of living beings: humans, gods, Brahmas, hell-beings, animals and ghosts.
teaches: The rival epics disagree even on how many destinies there are, so a reader comparing their karma teaching must first map the Jain four gatis onto the Buddhist six realms.

note: The Kural says the evil disease called hunger will not touch one used to sharing his food; Aathirai fills the inexhaustible bowl saying 'may the disease of hunger be cut off from the whole earth'.
teaches: The couplet promises that sharing guards the sharer from the disease of hunger, while Aathirai's gift, poured into a bowl that never empties, aims to cure the disease for everyone, so the pair moves from the giver's safety to a cure for the world.

gains.a: Aathirai's phrase பசிப் பிணி gains the couplet's account of hunger as a disease that sharing keeps away
gains.b: the couplet gains an image of sharing that no longer protects one household but is meant to empty hunger from the earth

note: The Buddha denies any doer behind the deed; the quatrain says an old deed seeks out the very one who did it, as a calf finds its mother among many cows.
teaches: The quatrain's comfort that a deed finds its own doer depends on there being a doer who lasts, which is exactly what the Buddha's thesis denies, so the proverb takes a side in the Jain-Buddhist debate.

gains.a: the Buddha's thesis gains an everyday image of the persisting owner it rejects, showing what ordinary moral talk would lose under it
gains.b: the quatrain gains an opponent who makes explicit that its calf image assumes a lasting self

note: The Pattinappalai's speaker, in the poem for Karikal, swears he will not leave his long-haired woman even if given all of Puhar; the epic, invoking Karikal's festival, seats Kovalan beside Madhavi on Puhar's shore, where before evening he will leave her (silappathikaram:7:286-300).
teaches: The idyll's vow that no city outweighs the beloved is tested on the very shore it praised, and the epic's lover fails it amid Puhar's full splendour.

gains.a: Kovalan's coming desertion is measured against a famous Sangam refusal to leave a woman for Puhar, which sharpens its cost
gains.b: the idyll's hyperbole gains a narrative counter-case showing that leaving was the choice it imagined refusing

note: The couplet says the wife who worships her husband rather than a god can command the rain; the venba takes its words and says the gods themselves worship such a wife.
teaches: The epic reads Kural 55 through Kannaki's end: the wife's power over nature becomes a claim on the gods, who now worship her, and the reward follows the burning of a city rather than a gift of rain.

gains.a: the venba gains the authority of the couplet's own words for its praise of Kannaki
gains.b: the couplet gains a case that tests it: its pathini wields fire and destruction, not rain, yet is still praised in its words

note: Tirumular bids the seeker hold to the Lord's feet, by whom strong deeds perish, and says the Lord will set him among the gods; Aravanan calls the Buddha's footprints on the hill the feet that destroy faults, and the next unit says the sisters who worshipped there were reborn beside Lakshmi.
teaches: Both give the feet power over past deeds, but the Saiva feet belong to a Lord who acts now and places the soul, while the Buddhist feet are the trace of a teacher who left long ago, and their fruit comes from the worshippers' own act ripening in the next birth.

gains.a: The footprint hill is seen as a Buddhist answer to the feet-devotion of Tamil theism, with the giver of grace replaced by a place and a remembered teaching.
gains.b: The verse's agent, the Lord who sets the soul among the gods, stands out as the thing a rival tradition does without while keeping the image of the feet.

note: Kannaki's 'he who relieved the distress of the bird' repeats the Purananuru's praise formula for the Chola's ancestor (புள்ளுறு புன்கண் தீர்த்த).
teaches: The epic takes a genealogical compliment that a Sangam poet paid a Chola king and turns it into a legal precedent that a Chola woman holds against a Pandya, showing the ancestor-legend working as a standard of justice across kingdoms.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain debater says each thing is both lasting and passing and takes on origination, persistence and destruction in every moment; in 420-421 Mokkalan calls this self-contradiction (milk becomes curd), and Neelakesi answers that change runs only by a thing's own causes.
teaches: The Buddhist epic sets out the Jain both-lasting-and-passing doctrine unanswered, while the Jain epic shows the Buddhist charge against it and the reply, so together they show the doctrine and where it was attacked.

note: Pattirakiriyar longs to go about without caste, as the agama of Kapila says; Neelakesi argues that high and low birth is unreal because sight, smell, taste and touch find no difference.
teaches: Both reject caste, but on different grounds: the Siddhar appeals to a scripture, while the Jain debater appeals to perception against scripture, which shows that an anti-caste position need not rest on any text.

gains.a: Neelakesi's argument gains a later Tamil voice reaching the same rejection of caste, which shows her point outlived the debate
gains.b: the Siddhar's verse gains a reason from the senses that does not depend on Kapila's unidentified agama

note: Both scenes bring a death before a king with the same approach formula (கோயில் மன்னனைக் குறுகினர்/குறுகினள் சென்று): Kannaki to the Pandya, the ascetics to the Chola.
teaches: Kannaki uses the audience to accuse the king of her husband's death, while the ascetics, bringing a father news of his son's death, hide the body and wrap the news in blessing and old stories, so the same entrance shows two ways of telling a king a truth he is implicated in.

note: The couplet says the king who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself (தானே கெடும்); the Pandya, having failed to examine, dies by his own sentence.
teaches: The epic takes the couplet's 'perishes by himself' literally, as a king's own verdict on himself, and adds what the couplet does not allow for: that the ruin can be read as redeeming the rule it ends.

gains.a: the unit's claim that the death showed a straight sceptre gains a rule behind it: a non-examining king's fall is self-caused, not an enemy's work
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which self-caused ruin is chosen and becomes the king's one act of justice, which a bare 'he will perish' cannot show

note: When Aputhiran's hall fell silent in plenty, rakes, libertines and idlers (விடரும் தூர்த்தரும் விட்டேற்றாளரும்) took it over with dice; here the same rakes and libertines (விடரும் தூர்த்தரும்) crowd round Manimekalai as she enters the street with the bowl.
teaches: The town's idlers mark both ends of the bowl's story: they fill the hall when the bowl is useless and gather in pity when it returns, so the bowl's renewed use is first met by the very crowd that had displaced it.

note: At the moat the flowers weep and the flags wave as if saying 'do not come'; in the palace the queen dreams of the umbrella and sceptre falling and the gate bell shaking.
teaches: The pair shows the epic sending warnings to both sides of the coming wrong, to the strangers at the walls and to the queen in the palace, and having neither heeded, so the catastrophe is foreseen in nature and in sleep yet still unfolds.

note: The Charana taught Kavunthi that the strong deed comes back to face its doer; here she asks whether the couple's deed has risen against her too and dies by fasting.
teaches: The doctrine she heard says a deed returns to its own doer, but the nun who led the couple treats their deed as falling on her as their guide, so the epic shows a Jain ascetic acting on a shared responsibility that the Charana's rule of individual return does not name.

note: Parimelazhagar uses Indra to illustrate both verses: 25 for the failure that shows the ascetic's power, and 144 for greatness lost through another's wife.
teaches: This is one story serving two chapters in the commentary, though neither verse tells it.

note: The Madurai herdswomen's book opens on the Pandya whose fish is written on the brow of the Himalaya with the tiger and the bow written beside it; the Vanchi swing song sings the king of the bow who holds the fish and the tiger and rules from the Yavana land to Kumari.
teaches: The two songs claim the same three emblems for different kings: Madurai sets the Pandya's fish first with the Chola and Chera signs beside it, and Vanchi folds fish and tiger into the Chera's bow, so the epic's praise of the three crowns is a set of rival boasts that its songs leave standing side by side.

note: Bhuthapandiyan's queen Perunkoppendu rejects the elders and chooses the pyre after her husband; the Chera queen grants the Pandya queen who died with her king heaven, but chooses Kannaki for worship.
teaches: The Sangam queen's death after her husband is the summit of a wife's virtue in its own poem, while the epic, granting such a death its heavenly reward, ranks above it the wronged wife who survived to accuse a king.

gains.a: the queen's verdict gains the Sangam model of the widow's chosen death that it puts in second place
gains.b: the poem gains a later judgment in which following one's husband in death is honoured yet ranked below the pathini's wrath

note: Maadalan's list of the king's victories runs close to the wording of the fifth decad's preface on Senguttuvan: சிறுகுரல் நெய்தல் வியலூர், இடும்பின் புறத்து இறுத்து, the nine kings beaten at the gate in standing battle, the sea driven back, the Aryan beaten at the Ganges.
teaches: The preface's bare record of conquests, which names the pathini's stone only as its occasion, becomes in the epic the praise a brahmin recites to cool the king's anger just before telling him that such conquests pass, so the same list serves first as glory and then as the premise of a sermon on impermanence.

gains.a: the epic's list gains an independent Sangam witness for the same campaigns in nearly the same words
gains.b: the preface's terse கடவுள் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள் gains the story of who the pathini was and what the stone became

note: The Kural asks what a householder living in dharma gains by taking the outside way; the Neelakesi grades conduct as complete or partial.
teaches: If the partial conduct is the householder's, as Jain usage suggests, the sermon accepts the household as a path of dharma but ranks it below renunciation, which is just the ranking the couplet's question refuses.

gains.a: the sermon's bare division into two grades is seen to answer a Tamil claim of the householder's equal standing
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question is shown meeting a rival that grants the household dharma yet calls it incomplete

note: The second decade's preface credits Imayavaramban Nedunjeralathan with carving the bow on the Himalaya; the epic's Aryan kings recall the day bow, tiger and fish were all carved there, and say no such kings are left.
teaches: The epic widens one Chera's boast into the shared emblem of the three Tamil crowns and makes the memory a reproach, so the son's campaign is shown as the redeeming of a glory the north said had lapsed.

gains.a: the taunt's 'day the bow was carved' gains a named Chera, Senguttuvan's own father, as its author
gains.b: the preface's single deed gains a later afterlife as a standard that northern kings could throw back at his heirs

note: Neelakesi charges that the Buddha does not count enduring austerity a vow; the Kundalakesi fragment calls bodily mortifications, nakedness among them, mere words, and puts tapas in restrained living.
teaches: The Buddhist fragment confirms the position the Jain debater attacks but shows it as a relocation of austerity into conduct, not the plain denial of austerity the charge describes.

gains.a: the Jain charge is seen against the opponent's own words
gains.b: the fragment's list of empty practices is shown to have a Jain target that the Neelakesi takes up

note: The Manimekalai's teacher describes release as the reverse chain in which birth and all its sorrow cease; Neelakesi says the released soul, like a burnt seed, never sprouts but abides eternally with eight qualities.
teaches: Both epics define release as the end of birth, but the Buddhist account has nothing that remains while the Jain account insists a soul abides, which is exactly what Mokkala's question in 457 asks.

note: The Kundalakesi invocation praises its lord as one who kept nothing for himself and laboured only for others' good; Neelakesi calls the stories of the Buddha's self-giving the doings of the deluded and possessed.
teaches: The Buddhist poem makes self-giving the very definition of its lord, so the Jain reply that such giving is madness strikes at the ground of the rival's devotion and not at a side issue.

note: The Kural says outer purity (புறந்தூய்மை) comes by water and inner purity by truth; Neelakesi lists water, betel and the tooth-stick and says that if outer cleaning purified the mind, courtesans would be the purest.
teaches: The couplet's two-part rule is turned into a reductio: Neelakesi supplies the absurd case that proves outer and inner purity are separate, and aims it at monks who tend their robes.

gains.a: Neelakesi's jibe gains a recognised rule behind it, so the courtesan example reads as proof rather than insult
gains.b: the couplet gains a counter-example that shows why water cannot reach the mind, which it states without argument

note: Purananuru 35.14-21 tells Killivalavan that his sky-touching umbrella is not to keep off the sun but to shelter suffering subjects, under a sceptre like aram itself; Paripadal 3.74-76 says the god, with grace as umbrella and aram as sceptre, made the twenty-one worlds a single shade with no second shade.
teaches: The puram poet has to argue the king into reading his umbrella as protection, a meaning the king may fail, whereas the hymn makes protection the umbrella's very substance in the god and takes over the royal boast of one shade with no rival, so the pair shows divine kingship and the counsel to kings using one ideal to measure each other.

note: The Purananuru poem says rice and water are not the world's life, the king is, and he must know it; the goddess says the king's swerving kills life through the failing of rain, so the standing of being the beings' life is lost.
teaches: The epic turns the poem's title into a conditional one that a king's own fault cancels, and routes his power over life back through the rain the poem had set below him.

gains.a: Lines 11-12 are read against an old formula of kingship that the goddess is citing in order to take away.
gains.b: The poem's claim that the king, not water, is the world's life gains its limit: in the epic the king governs life only by way of the rain.
