note: The wedding women bless Kannaki never to be parted from her lover nor loosen her embrace; two kaathais later Kovalan buys Madhavi's garland, cannot leave her and forgets his home.
teaches: The blessing names the very loss the story brings within two kaathais, so the wedding song works as an unknowing forecast, and the separation reads as a reversal of a rite performed with fire and Veda.

note: Akananuru 6 calls Tittan of Uranthai the great giver who brings the wealth of rain (மாவண் தித்தன்); 80 asks Tittan to witness the hero's victory 'whether he grants or not' (நல்கினும் நல்கான் ஆயினும்).
teaches: The akam poet uses Tittan's fame as a giver as a byword, while 80 makes his grace toward one man uncertain, so the same chief appears as a public giver and as a withholding judge whose favour must be won.

note: Kural 19 says that if the sky gives no rain, neither giving nor austerity will last; Indra's abundant rain leaves Aputhiran's bowl idle for want of takers, and the hall of giving becomes a gambling den.
teaches: Rain is the condition of giving in the couplet, but the epic shows that rain in full measure can end giving too, since giving needs someone in want, so plenty sustains the giver's means and destroys his occasion.

gains.a: the Kural's rule that giving depends on rain, against which Indra's rain reads as a pointed reversal
gains.b: the other limit of its rule: too much of what makes giving possible makes it pointless

note: The sermon told Neelakesi the fixed beings are of five kinds; here she defends that teaching against a Buddhist by calling trees fixed beings (தாவரம்) that everyone knows to be such.
teaches: The doctrine she received as a convert's lesson becomes the first ground she must hold in open debate, and she defends it by appeal to common usage rather than to the sage's authority.

note: The patikam announces as the epic's third moral that the deed of former birth comes in wrath and feeds its fruit (ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும்); Kavunthi says the hard deed feeds its fruit and that the unlearned are bewildered when the evil deed comes in wrath (உருத்த காலை).
teaches: The moral Ilango states from outside the story is first spoken inside it by a nun who uses it to console Kovalan for a hardship already past, so the reader hears the thesis as comfort just before it becomes the account of his death.

note: The pillar image tells Kanchanan he has done a cruel deed whose fruit will not leave him; the king says the vidyadhara did what the king should have done.
teaches: The same killing is a cruel deed with consequences in the deity's eyes and a royal duty done by another's hand in the king's, so the epic sets karmic judgment and royal justice side by side without reconciling them.

note: The couplet's highest wife commands the rain; here the chaste wives who bring down the rain themselves worship Aathirai, whom fire would not burn.
teaches: The epic places a rank above the Kural's summit of wifely power, and grounds it not in daily worship of the husband but in a wife's readiness to die for a husband who had deserted her for a courtesan.

gains.a: Aathirai's praise gains a fixed measure, the rain-bringing wife, against which her rank can be stated
gains.b: the couplet gains the sign that its power is not the highest, and that it can be tested against a husband who did nothing to deserve it

note: Madhavi lies with a helpless heart (கையறு நெஞ்சமொடு, line 116); her second letter ends asking Kovalan to take away the helpless heart (கையறு நெஞ்சம் கடியல் வேண்டும், 13:91).
teaches: The phrase carries one night's grief into the later letter, showing that what Madhavi asks of Kovalan there is to undo the state this refusal left her in.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists impermanence, suffering, no-self and impurity as marks to contemplate in order to cut attachment; Neelakesi names the same four as qualities the Buddhists lay on the aggregates.
teaches: The four marks the Buddhist teacher gives as a meditation for release are read by the Jain debater as predicates of a bearer, so the Buddhist list is turned into evidence for the substance-and-quality relation Mokkalan denies.

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its own mother among many cows; Mathurapathi's word traces a killing done as Bharatan in Kalinga to Kovalan's death in Madurai, and says the former deed does not fail to come.
teaches: The pair shows how far the calf can walk: the quatrain gives the deed a homing instinct, and the epic gives it a road across a birth, a kingdom and a change of name, with a widow's curse as the means by which it finds Kovalan.

gains.a: the epic's account of a curse crossing births gains a plain maxim that explains why the curse cannot miss its man
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract seeking deed gains a named case with a route, an agent (Neeli's curse) and a distance of a whole lifetime

note: The Paripadal fragment asks whether Madurai's fame can ever prove false as long as the Vaigai flows; the epic calls the Vaigai the never-failing (பொய்யா) creeper of the clan and has her hide her tears for the wife the city will wrong.
teaches: The Paripadal makes the flowing Vaigai the pledge that Madurai's fame cannot fail; the epic keeps the river unfailing but makes her the first to know that the city's justice will fail, so the pledge passes from the city to the river alone.

gains.a: the epic's 'never-failing' river gains the old pledge it echoes, which shows what the river's hidden grief is a grief for
gains.b: the fragment's confidence gains a story that separates the river's constancy from the city's fame

note: Kural 355 calls understanding the seeing of the true thing in a thing whatever its nature; 819 says thing and quality are one from one standpoint and different from another.
teaches: The couplet separates a thing's nature from its truth and asks us to see through to the truth; the Jain standpoint doctrine holds that the separation itself depends on where one looks.

gains.a: the standpoint method is set against a widely held definition of understanding, showing what it adds: a rule for when nature and thing are to be told apart
gains.b: the couplet's split between a thing's nature and its true being is shown to be one possible view, not the only one

note: The Puhar book tells how Thirumavalavan went north, was stopped by the Himalaya and carved his tiger on it; the ammanai sings a king who stamped his tiger on the northern mountain while the eight mountains of the quarters watched, and ruled all eight directions under his umbrella.
teaches: Set beside the narrative, the song shows the epic's praise turning a halt into a triumph: the mountain that ended Valavan's march becomes a witness, and one carving on one peak becomes rule of the eight quarters.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists a thesis that goes against one's own words (சுவசன விருத்தம், 'my mother is barren') among the false theses; 743 says the Sankhya's admission of acting souls destroys his own thesis (மேற்கோள்).
teaches: What the Buddhist manual gives as a textbook fault with a toy example, the Jain debater springs in a live debate, showing how the logicians' catalogue of faults was used as a weapon between schools.

claims.gist: space is a substance, known by its quality of sound
a reason found equally in similar and dissimilar cases proves nothing
nothing endures, and to teach this is the path
one who denies all endurance cannot consistently offer a remedy afterwards
virtue and the guilt of killing and theft belong to the doer as his own qualities
qualities are separate from the substance that bears them
the Veda contains precepts that contradict each other
killing in the sacrifice has no limit and brings gain
withering and coming to an end are marks of life in plants as in animals
a wife left by her husband loses the householder's duties of giving to the virtuous, tending Brahmins, receiving ascetics and welcoming guests
all is suffering
if sound touched the ear it could not be heard as far away
the body exists by food and awareness by the body
time is not a real thing
one who denies time cannot speak of moments, aeons or the stages of a life
hidden wrongdoers, the false ascetic, the unfaithful wife, the treacherous minister, the adulterer, the false witness and the backbiter, deserve to be seized and killed
the principles of reality are twenty-five
the formless, the non-world and the insentient are categories of their own
youth, the body and wealth do not last
sons do not win heaven for a man; only great virtue is a lasting companion
a deed's power passes unseen through the continuum, as a seed's lac colour passes hidden through the tree to the flower
animals arise by several modes of birth and wander from body to body consuming the fruit of their own deeds
the Buddha's scripture, examined closely, does not hold together
quality and substance are joined by a separate relation of inherence
a relation that joins things must itself be joined, so inherence leads to endless regress
if relation alone gave things their being, both relata and everything else would become empty
a Lord who is everything and destroys his creatures destroys himself, which is madness
burning anger turned on those who have taken the guise of penance wins no honour
the omniscient one knows the objects of the senses without perceiving them through the senses
if the four opposed elements are present in each other, each loses its nature and its use
the goddess takes up the raider's vetchi, and her will shows itself in omens over the enemy's land
a well-ordered land has each of the four varnas keeping to its own given path
a chaste wife dies at her husband's death, or enters the fire, or wears down her body in vows to rejoin him
the daughter of a great pathini must be given to tapas and not to the courtesan's trade
the cause of sorrow is birth and clinging; the cause of release, which is joy, is not clinging
what is spoken of as a person is five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, formation and consciousness
the world comes forth from nature and is drawn back into it at dissolution
taking the begging bowl is unfitting for a dancing courtesan and earns only ridicule
right conduct, right knowledge and right vision lead to lasting, unfailing bliss
an evil deed that has ripened must still be eaten even by one reborn among the gods for former merit
austerity kept under a former Buddha's Bodhi bears fruit in a later birth
release is reached by hearing the Buddha's dharma
eating flesh that another has killed binds karma to the eater whatever his intention
the trace perishes in the flower and arises in the pot, and is found everywhere
a girl's wasting is the god's seizure and the velan's rite will cure it
when a king errs in the order of rule, his city is due to be consumed by fire
no one relieves the suffering of the beings in hell
if the omniscient never spoke, the books in his name are the words of passion-bound souls and have no authority
a soul that does nothing could not be the teacher of the principles, and the claim contradicts what is seen
the eight of the octad are the four elements with colour, taste, smell and touch

note: The sage foretold that on a day of sorrow Manimekala would lift her in the dark night and set her on an island in the southern quarter (தென் திசை மருங்கில்); kaathai 6 tells it in the same words: at midnight the goddess carried her south and left her on Manipallavam.
teaches: Read back from this prophecy, the abduction of kaathai 6 that seemed a goddess's rescue from the prince is shown to be an appointment fixed a birth earlier, which turns chance into the ripening of a cause.

note: Madhavi described the pathini widows who die, enter fire as a pool or waste themselves in vows, and confessed she had lived on; Chithirapathi repeats the same figures and phrase to say a courtesan was never bound to any of them.
teaches: The same list of widow's deaths serves the daughter as a measure she has failed and the mother as proof that their caste is exempt, so Madhavi's renunciation is attacked from below as well as judged from above.

note: Naladiyar 20 urges keeping Death's stealth in mind and taking provisions in time; Thirikadugam names not reflecting on Death's certain coming as one of three things that lead to hell.
teaches: The quatrain makes remembering death prudent; the verse makes forgetting it a sin with a penalty, so heedlessness is turned from folly into guilt.

note: The couplet says enmity, sin, fear and blame never leave the man who crosses into another's home; the ascetic says such men die when their evil deed ripens, and adds those who set their hearts on women ascetics.
teaches: The couplet's offence is entering a married woman's home; the epic extends it to desire for a renunciant woman, who has no husband's home to violate, and makes death, not lasting disgrace, the outcome.

gains.a: The ascetic's general charge gains the Kural's account of what such a man carries while he lives.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case beyond the married woman, the woman of penance, which its home-centred wording leaves out.

note: Chithirapathi vowed that she would have the prince carry Manimekalai off in his golden chariot; here the prince himself plans to set her in his golden chariot.
teaches: The courtesan mother's plan becomes the prince's own wish in the same image of the golden chariot, so the reader sees the abduction as her design working through him rather than a whim of his alone.

note: The Kural says a joyless birth comes from the confusion that takes what is not real as real; the teacher names ignorance first of twelve links that end in birth and defines it as holding hearsay clear, as that a hare has horns.
teaches: The pairing shows that the Kural's மருள் can be given a precise epistemic fault, trusting report over what has been established, and that for the Buddhist teacher this confusion reaches birth only through ten links between, which the couplet's direct cause compresses.

gains.a: a Tamil ethical precedent that already makes confusion about the real the cause of birth, so the first link reads as more than a Buddhist technicality
gains.b: a concrete instance of the unreal taken as real, the hare's horn believed on hearsay, where the couplet names no example

note: Puranan says the Lord kept silent because speaking would cast him back into wandering; Neelakesi repeats his words and turns them, so that silence would make any silent man a lesser Lord.
teaches: The refutation works by repeating the opponent's own verse almost word for word, so the reader sees how a Neelakesi debate argues: the rival's premise is restated and pushed to an absurd consequence.

note: Kundalakesi will not speak without a great prize for the winner; in 230 the winner, Neelakesi, refuses every gift the king offers and asks only that he keep to dharma.
teaches: The stake Kundalakesi demanded turns against her twice: she suffers the loser's penalty, and the victor shows by refusing the prize that the Jain side did not argue for gain.

note: Deepatilakai tells Manimekalai that in a famine Indra's rain brought plenty and saved the brahmin about to eat dog's flesh; here Indra's rain, sent as a retort to Aputhiran, leaves his bowl idle and his hall to gamblers.
teaches: The epic gives Indra's rain two faces, the mercy that ends a famine and the spite that ends a giver's work, and in both tellings sets the human hand that feeds above the god's plenty, which Deepatilakai's praise alone does not show.

note: At 63 she bears a form made to be desired so as to shake his penance; at 128 the sage answers that the same limbs are three different things to the lustful, the ascetic and the jackal.
teaches: The sermon on the body is a direct reply to the disguise: the form chosen to excite desire is answered by showing that desirability lies in the seer, so the trick fails at its root.

note: The couplet says none but those who reach the feet of the அறவாழி அந்தணன் can cross the other seas; the goddess praises the Buddha's feet marked with the thousand-spoked wheel (ஆயிர ஆரத்து ஆழி), whom Sudhamathi has just called the one who turned the wheel of dharma (அறக் கதிர் ஆழி, 76).
teaches: The same words, அறம், ஆழி and the lord's feet, name the Buddha's wheel of dharma in the epic, which shows that ஆழி in the couplet's epithet could be heard as wheel as well as sea, and that a Buddhist hearer would find the Buddha in a verse that names no one.

gains.a: The goddess's praise of the feet is set in the Kural's opening frame, where reaching the feet is the way across.
gains.b: The couplet's unnamed epithet is shown in use for a named founder, which opens a second sense of ஆழி that the sea reading alone hides.

note: Madhavi says Manimekalai will be brought to great tapas and never to the courtesan's trade; at the close of kaathai 30 Manimekalai takes up tapas and vows to end the course of births.
teaches: The mother's claim made for her daughter in the third kaathai is fulfilled only in the last, and by the daughter's own vow after hearing the whole doctrine, so the epic runs between a claim made over Manimekalai and her own assent to it.

note: The sage Viruchikan cursed Kayasandikai to twelve years of burning hunger; Kanchanan comes to Puhar because the twelve years are over and she has not come home.
teaches: The twelve-year term set in the curse is what brings the husband to the city on the very days Manimekalai wears his wife's form, so the curse that seemed to end with her cure sets up the killing.

note: The couplet says those whose knowledge is refined by good sense do not sink into the common charms of women who are everyone's; the epic says that in the net of the dancers' glances even ascetics' hard-won wisdom turns to something else.
teaches: The Kural makes refined knowledge a protection against the courtesan, and the epic's street denies the guarantee by naming ascetics among those caught, so the pair shows the rule holding only for the wise who stay away, not for any wisdom that walks into the street.

gains.a: the epic's hyperbole gains its edge from the rule it breaks: the ascetic's fall matters because wisdom was supposed to protect
gains.b: the couplet gains a limit: its protection is a claim about who abstains, and the epic shows a learned art that even the disciplined are said to fall before

note: The benediction likens the Chola's bounty to the rain pouring from above; the couplet makes rain itself depend on the king's not bending justice.
teaches: Read against the couplet, the opening simile of rain and royal grace is not mere flattery but the old belief that the sky's giving follows the king's justice, which the epic will put to the test when a Pandya's crooked verdict brings fire rather than rain on his city.

gains.a: the simile gains a causal ground: rain and royal grace are linked because a just king's realm is the one the sky waters
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a ceremonial setting, sung at a wedding as praise rather than stated as a warning

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says the atoms never enter one another, yet move, sink and rise; Neelakesi takes the same premises and demands the cause of sinking and rising.
teaches: The two polemics report the same Ajivika premise, atoms that never enter one another and yet sink and rise; the Buddhist leaves it, while the Jain shows it leaves motion without a cause.

note: Natrinai 23's friend says the girl's thinness is hidden by her bangles and her loose hair excused by play, but her eyes cannot hide love; Kural 1271 has the man tell her that though she hides it, her kohl-lined eyes go beyond her control and have something to say.
teaches: The Natrinai supplies the test behind Valluvar's claim by sorting the signs of love into those an excuse can cover and the eyes, which none can, so the couplet's 'though you hide' turns out to name a practice of concealment the older poem lays out part by part.

note: The patikam opens with the hill kuravar telling Ilango of the one-breasted pathini taken to heaven before their eyes; the vari has desert hunters' priestess first naming Kannaki divine.
teaches: Both the frame and the first sign within the story put Kannaki's divinity in the mouths of forest and hill folk, before any king or sage acknowledges it, so the pairing shows the epic consistently letting the people of the wilds be the first witnesses of the pathini.

note: The spirit's first victims are those who hide behind penance (தவம்மறைந்து ஒழுகும்); Kural 274 likens hiding in penance to a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds.
teaches: The Kural shows why the false ascetic's concealment is dangerous, that it lets him prey on others, but names no penalty; the epic imagines a city where the concealment is publicly broken and punished with death, setting a sanction beside the couplet's diagnosis.

gains.a: the spirit's list gains the couplet's reason why the hidden ascetic is the worst of wrongdoers
gains.b: the couplet gains a civic answer to the hidden hunter, a power that sees through the bush

note: The Neelakesi's Buddha says the reaper is neither that nor other; the Manimekalai's teacher draws from the nayas a middle that is 'neither that nor what is not that' (அதுவும் அன்று அது அலாததும் அன்று), and that there is no doer apart from the doing.
teaches: The formula the Jain poem gives the Buddha is the one the Buddhist epic itself teaches, so Neelakesi's excluded-middle reply in 645 strikes the school's own middle way, not a caricature.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika counts the soul as a category apart from the four atoms, the one that knows; 715 presses an opponent who gives the soul form.
teaches: The Buddhist report keeps the Ajivika soul apart from matter, so the Jain's charge that it has form and can be sliced like a pumpkin is aimed at a version the other report does not give.

note: In the Venil kaathai Vasantamalai reports that Kovalan refused Madhavi's letter and Madhavi lies sleepless saying she will see him at dawn; the goddess in Vasantamalai's form tells him Madhavi turned in anger, condemned her calling, tore her pearls and dismissed her maid.
teaches: The illusion is built on the one unfinished thread in Kovalan's past, the refused letter, so the forest goddess tempts him with his unresolved bond to Madhavi rather than with a stranger's charm.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain lists dharma, adharma, time, space, soul, atoms, deeds, bondage and release; 729 has the Jain debater close by giving the three-times-three categories.
teaches: A Buddhist's account of Jain doctrine mixes substances with the path, while the Jain epic hands the convert the nine categories as one fixed count, which shows how each side reckoned the Jain list.

note: Kannaki cites the Chola who put his own son under the chariot wheel to shame the Pandya; the Chola king here fears it will be said that in that king's line an evil-doer was born.
teaches: The memory Kannaki used to accuse another king becomes a weight on the Chola's own line: he accepts his son's death as justice, but his first thought is to keep the stain on Manu's line from other kings, so the ancestor's example breeds concealment as well as justice.

note: Kural 55 says the wife who rises worshipping her husband commands the rain; Paripadal 20.88-89 has onlookers tell a wronged wife that worthy women praise and bow to their husbands even when the husbands slight them (கேள்வரை ஏத்தி இறைஞ்சுவார்).
teaches: The Kural offers the wife's worship of her husband as a source of power over nature, but the Paripadal shows the same ideal used in a quarrel to silence a wife whose husband has given her bangle away, so the couplet's praise of devotion could serve in practice as counsel to put up with a man's straying.

note: Aravanar tells Manimekalai that after she has heard the other doctrines he will teach her fully; in kaathai 27 she goes among the schools in Vanji and asks the Vedic logician his doctrine.
teaches: The survey of schools in kaathai 27 is set up here as a stage of instruction the teacher prescribes, so the rival doctrines are heard as preparation for the Buddhist teaching, not as free inquiry.

note: 183 says that it is better to die than to live by backbiting, because it is a false kind of life. In 1141 backbiting is what keeps someone else alive.
teaches: The same act has a very different moral look from the side of its target.

note: Both speak of the two deeds (இருவினை) and their ending: the Jina taught the way they part; Tirumular says that when they balance, grace-power comes as the guru and one's own doing ends.
teaches: On the same pair of deeds the Jain hymn gives the teacher only the role of telling the way, while Tirumular makes the guru a descent of grace that ends the soul's own agency.

gains.a: the hymn's silence about grace becomes visible as a position once set beside a text that makes grace the agent
gains.b: the Saiva doctrine of the balanced deeds is seen against a release in which no power descends and the soul does the work

note: Naladiyar 313 describes people who rush to debate on the strength of a word, talk at length and do not know when they are beaten; Neelakesi tells the Buddhist he does not know words and prattles many words like a ghost.
teaches: The Naladiyar's type of the endless talker becomes a charge thrown by one debater at another, which shows the description used as a weapon in debate as well as a moral portrait.

gains.a: Neelakesi's insult is placed within a known ethical type, the speaker who does not know when he is beaten
gains.b: the quatrain gains a scene where its charge is made by a party to the dispute, which shows that calling the other side a prattler is itself a debating move

note: Mokkalan says the Jina's categories came from his own mind without knowing things as they are; Neelakesi answers that, since no fault has been shown and the Lord's word is truth, the categories stand.
teaches: The debate turns on the source of authority: the Buddhist attacks the categories by their origin in one mind, and the Jain defends them by the teacher's nature, so neither touches the categories themselves.

note: The Silappathikaram brings evening on Puhar with the earth weeping as if her king were lost, lamps lit by women, the cowherds' mullai flute, and evening 'came and encamped' (மாலைவந்து இருத்தென); the Manimekalai's evening on Puhar has the lamps, the mullai flute and evening that came and encamped (வந்து இறுத்தனளால்) as a woman widowed in battle.
teaches: The sequel reuses its parent's evening on the same city almost item by item but moves the grief from an earth that has lost her king to a woman who has lost her husband and goes home to her kin, so the evening of Kovalan's daughter carries the bereaved woman's figure that the first epic gave to the land.

note: In 574 the Buddha said deed and fruit exist but there is no doer; asked now who reaps, he gives a fourfold denial: not the doer, not another, not both, not no one.
teaches: Pressed on the reaper rather than the doer, the no-doer thesis has to become a tetralemma, so the denial of a self costs the Buddha the power to name who receives karma.

note: The Jain debater in the Manimekalai says release is to block the inflow of both good and bad deeds and wear out past ones; the Jain charana of the Silappathikaram tells a gift whose merit leads to a god's birth.
teaches: Held together, the Jain doctrine stated in debate and the Jain tale told for lay hearers show the two levels of the same teaching: the doctrine counts good deeds among the bonds, while the tale for householders displays the heavenly birth that good deeds bring, and Kavunthi reserves release itself for those who turn to dharma (line 197).

note: Neelakesi says we will wear out our own deeds and go; Tirumular says that when the two deeds stand balanced, grace comes as the guru and ends one's own doing.
teaches: The Jain debater denies that another's compassion can release, and Tirumular makes release depend on a grace that ends one's own agency, so they answer oppositely who removes karma.

gains.a: the Jain self-reliance is shown to be aimed at any doctrine of release by another, not only the Buddhist one
gains.b: Tirumular's grace is seen as one side of a live dispute in which a rival denies any outside agent of release

note: The objection in Neelakesi 316 is that if pleasure and pain are the fruit of deeds, the pain of penance is too; the Kural defines penance as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life.
teaches: The Kural's definition of தவம் as bearing the pain that comes takes away the force of the objection: if penance is endurance of what arrives, it does not matter that the pain is old karma's fruit.

gains.a: the epic's objection meets a Tamil definition of penance that already answers it
gains.b: the couplet's உற்றநோய் is shown to bear on a live dispute about whether penance's pain is only karma ripening

note: The couplet says that crushing foes and raising those one loves come by tapas if one so intends; Kavunthi's penance gives her curse its hold and her word of release its power.
teaches: The epic shows both halves of the couplet in one act of one ascetic: the same tapas that turns the mockers into jackals sets the day they become human again.

gains.a: the phrase தவம்தரு சாபம் gains its doctrine: the curse is a use of the power tapas confers
gains.b: the couplet's 'if one intends' (எண்ணின்) gains a case where the ascetic does intend, and is then moved to limit what she intended

note: 741 quotes 736's words எத்திறத்தின்னுஞ்செய்யான் and turns them on the teacher: a soul that does nothing cannot be the master who teaches.
teaches: The refutation works by quotation: the Sankhya's description of the soul, repeated word for word, is shown to cancel the act of describing it.

note: The Naladiyar calls liberality milk a cow yields gladly to its calf, against the base who yield only when squeezed; Manimekalai wants the bowl to flow at the hungry's faces as a mother's breast flows at her newborn's (114-118), and Deepathilakai says it flows only for those who feed from compassion (120-121).
teaches: The epic turns the quatrain's distinction between glad and forced giving into a property of the vessel itself, which will not yield to a giver whose gift is not compassion.

gains.a: the mother's-breast simile and the bowl's condition are seen to rest on an old ethics image of giving as lactation
gains.b: the quatrain's moral distinction gains a story in which the manner of giving decides whether anything is given at all

note: Kundalakesi lists her lord's gifts of eyes, flesh, body, wife, land, child and heaven (205); the king's verdict in 224 calls those birth-tales fabrications of a one-sided teacher.
teaches: The debate is settled not by refuting each gift but by the king reclassifying the whole catalogue as fiction, so the Buddhist's chief proof of compassion is turned into the proof of one-sidedness.

note: The couplet honours the wife who worships her husband and no god; Chithirapathi describes the families whose women worship no god but the man who took them, to say Manimekalai is not of them.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's ideal working as a boundary of birth: women outside the families it describes are declared fair game, so praise of the chaste wife becomes an argument for coercing a woman who has chosen celibacy.

gains.a: Chithirapathi's argument rests on a standard of womanhood the audience already reveres, which is why it can persuade a prince.
gains.b: The couplet gains a reading of its exclusions: it says nothing of the women it leaves out, and here they are claimed as the prince's to take.

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Neelakesi says a deed of killing done for the gods ripens in the killer as poison in the one who eats it, whoever it was meant for.
teaches: The quatrain's claim that a deed finds its own doer becomes in the debate a weapon against transferred merit, showing that the proverb rules out offering one's deed to gods or ancestors.

gains.a: Neelakesi's argument gains a common proverb that already states her premise, so her opponent must deny popular wisdom to escape it
gains.b: the quatrain gains a disputed case, sacrifice offered for another, in which its calf image does real argumentative work

note: The pathiri scent left in a new pot appears in the Kundalakesi debate, where Neelakesi used it to argue a soul outlasts the body, and here as the Buddha's own example of the trace.
teaches: The same pot of scent is read two ways in one epic: against Kundalakesi Neelakesi took the lingering scent as proof that something outlasts its source, and against the Buddha she denies it can show a trace passing between moments that never coexist.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain speaker says dharma pervades everything and makes things move (பொருள்களை நடத்தும்); Neelakesi calls the reading 'we move by dharma' a quibble and says dharma lets things move as the sea lets a ship go, without pushing.
teaches: A Jain debater rejects as a misreading the very wording a Buddhist epic puts in a Jain's mouth: dharma is a condition of motion, not a mover, a distinction the Buddhist report blurs.

claims.gist: a reason found in some similar instances and in all dissimilar ones leaves the thesis open to doubt
a reason found in all similar instances and in only some dissimilar ones is likewise inconclusive
a being with a body and sense organs is born and caused, like a rainbow that arises from sunlight on rain
the Lord's form is like a rainbow that cannot be grasped
action gives rise to experience and experience to action, so neither is karma without the other
words have no real objects
one whose words refer to nothing real has no knowledge
that a work's author is not remembered does not show it has no author
no one is known to have made the Veda, so it has no maker
great attachment to possession, which cannot let go, drives kin to war
the Dharma seat on which the sage preached makes former births shine clear
the faults of speech are many more than four, including private talk with a woman and teaching pleasures
an example fails if one party denies it exists, and fails too if, granted, it lacks the properties
hands, feet, the two excretory organs and speech are organs
an organ is that which has an object and a knowledge of it
no Jain holds that an evil deed once done turns into pleasure
what does not exist cannot perish, as a crow's tooth has no size
things are not produced but only made manifest
a reason that is in doubt cannot ground a firm conclusion
nothing is more precious than the life of a living being
a vow to her husband broken in a former birth causes a wife's present lack
women who bathe in the Soma and Surya tanks and worship at Kama's shrine enjoy their husbands here and are reborn in the land of enjoyment
a god who is both doer and sufferer of every act gains nothing by acting
there is a way by which all painful karma is burned away
the Buddha lives not for himself but belongs to others, and turned the wheel of dharma from compassion so that beings may reach bliss
the Buddha has passed beyond Kama
a courtesan has no chastity, no austerity and no protection of caste, but sells herself for wealth
the directions arise relative to an observer, so no substance called direction is ever seen
a mixture cannot produce a thing of a nature none of its parts has
one and the same thing both is and is not, in different respects
the first lord of the dharma wheel taught out of compassion that all living things, beasts too, should live together without fear
the Buddha's footprints on the hill destroy the faults of those who worship them
knowing is the quality proper to soul, as burning is to fire
since things are eternal, the effect already exists in its cause, as the palm in its seed
if the tree were already in the seed, the hand holding the seed would hold the tree
the Buddha, having fulfilled the perfections, knew the four truths and the twelvefold dependent arising and how it ceases
worship of the Buddha's shrines saves one from birth in a state of suffering
hearing the Buddha's dharma with a loving mind brings the mind of renunciation and release from birth
when cold, heat and hunger beset the body, the mind cannot hold to dharma
a limb has both its own prior nature and a nature from relation
since a body cut and burned after death feels nothing, something that felt has gone out of it
in dreams the life travels far while the body stays, so the life can leave the body
the departing life enters the body that its own deeds have fitted to it
there are never two cognitions at once
the six cognitions exist together
right and left exist only by relation and have no being of their own
the Pandya's sceptre harms none of its people, only kings who refuse to bow
those born in a noble line joined to good conduct do not fall into fault even in untamed youth
cognition produces activity and activity produces feeling, so the aggregates are cause and effect, not simultaneous
gods who cannot end their own suffering cannot end that of others
if all things are impure there is no ground to choose clean over foul

note: Pathirakiriyar asks when he will see the bones within as white bones and himself lowered like a cast-off corpse; the king digs up his own former body, bones held together as if coated in white lime, and is bewildered.
teaches: The epic grants literally the sight the Siddhar longs for, one's own body as white bones, and shows that the sight alone does not free: the king is bewildered until Manimekalai tells him what it is for.

gains.a: a frame in which seeing one's own corpse is a discipline of release, against which the king's bewilderment is a failure to read it
gains.b: a test of its longing: the sight given in full, without the knowledge that would make it freeing

note: The patikam's third moral, ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும், reappears with the same verb ஊட்டும் in the Charana's sermon on the strong deed that will not go.
teaches: The poet's announced moral is put into the mouth of a Jain sage within the story, who adds what the patikam does not: that the Jina's word can end the births the deed feeds.

note: Maduraikkanchi's dawn in Madurai has the Brahmins chanting the Veda, the elephants fed and the horses in their stalls (பணைநிலைப் புரவி); the epic's travellers hear the same dawn, the Vedic chant and the stalled horses' neighing among it, from outside the walls.
teaches: The epic reuses the Sangam catalogue of Madurai's dawn, phrase for phrase in places, but moves its hearer from the king the idyll counsels on impermanence to the strangers whom the city will destroy, so the idyll's warning that such splendour passes is carried out on the city itself.

gains.a: the catalogue gains its pedigree: Madurai's dawn is a set piece of the Sangam city, heard in the epic as the city's settled glory
gains.b: the idyll's counsel that wealth and splendour do not last gains a story in which this very Madurai, with its stalled horses and chanting Brahmins, is burned

note: The couplet says the six-duty men forget their books if the guardian does not guard; the sages charge the Chera to guard the Veda-keepers of the Himalaya, which lies outside his kingdom.
teaches: The couplet ties the Brahmins' learning to their own king's protection, and the epic stretches that duty across the border, so that a king marching to punish northern kings is made guardian of the northern Brahmins, and he keeps the charge in victory (lines 248-250).

gains.a: the sages' charge gains a reason: without a guardian the Veda-keepers' learning fails, so the Chera's protection keeps the northern Vedas alive
gains.b: the couplet gains a case beyond the king's own realm, where the guardian of learning is an invader and the protection is owed to the enemy's Brahmins

note: Sudhamathi warns that no man who sees the weeping Manimekalai could turn away; in the next kaathai Ettikumaran's glimpse of her faded face entering the grove sends the prince after her.
teaches: The warning is fulfilled by exactly the beauty it named, a face dimmed by grief rather than adorned, so the renunciant's sorrow, not her old trade, is what draws the prince into the story.

note: The proverb verse tells of the young Chola who tied on grey hair and judged a case (உரைமுடிவு) to prove that a family's craft comes half-known; Sudhamathi names the same act (உரை முடிவு காட்டிய உரவோன்) to shame his heir.
teaches: The proverb says the line's judgment is inborn, and the epic turns the same story against the line's heir, who must be lectured by a woman, so the inherited craft is invoked because it is missing.

gains.a: The allusion at 108 is fixed to a known story whose point is wisdom in youth, which sharpens Sudhamathi's rebuke of a youth acting unwisely.
gains.b: The proverb's claim that a family's craft comes by birth meets a heir of the same line who lacks it.

note: The couplet says that for those who have gained the power of tapas even leaping past Death becomes possible; Champapathi, the old ascetic goddess, shows her power by proving that no god can give back a life.
teaches: The power over death that tapas earns, in the epic, stops at the one who earned it: even the oldest ascetic goddess and all the gods cannot pass it to the dead.

gains.a: Champapathi's display of power is seen as a demonstration of a limit, not a failure of her tapas.
gains.b: The couplet's 'even' is given a firm boundary: tapas may carry one past death but cannot bring another back.

note: Before her first debate Neelakesi bows at the Arhat's shrine; at the end of this one she sends the defeated Ulokan to praise the Lord's shrine.
teaches: The debates begin and end in worship at the Jina's shrine, so winning an argument is framed as bringing the loser to the place the debater started from.

note: The closing lines recall the evil dream (இடருற்ற தீக்கனா) in which Kannaki saw a false word laid on her husband in a great city.
teaches: Kannaki goes to the king remembering the dream that foretold the false charge, so the dream that was dismissed now becomes her warrant for the confrontation it did not foresee.

note: Against Kundalakesi she argued that if nothing of the first moment is in the next, knowing fails, and if something is, it is a soul; here she shows the two moments never exist together for a trace to pass.
teaches: The dilemma put to Kundalakesi about what a trace carries is sharpened into a point about time: before asking what the trace holds, the Jain asks when it could cross, and finds no instant shared by the two moments.

note: Neelakesi asks what could bind a soul that is pure and changeless; the Tirumanthiram makes soul and bond both beginningless, so the soul was never first pure and then bound.
teaches: The Jain question to the Sankhya, what first bound a pure soul, is the question the Saiva verse avoids by making bondage as old as the soul, at the price of a soul that was never pure until the Lord draws near.

gains.a: The Neelakesi's question gains a known school's answer, showing that one reply to it is to deny the soul ever had a pure beginning.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's 'beginningless' gains a reason: it closes off the debating question of how a pure, unchanging soul could fall into bondage.

note: The couplet makes sulking love's salt, good in right measure and spoiling only when overdone; the stanza calls not sulking at all, even at the husband's other union, a woman's great chastity.
teaches: Where the Kural sets a measure for oodal, the epic song sets it at nothing and names that karpu, so together they show the measure of sulking turning from a matter of love's taste into a test of a wife's virtue.

gains.a: the stanza's praise gains a standard to be measured against: by the couplet it asks for no salt at all
gains.b: the couplet's measure gains its limit case, a song that would remove sulking entirely from a wife's part

note: The couplet says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and the brahmins forget their books; the king says that without the guardian's guarding there are no ascetics' vows and no women's chastity.
teaches: The king adapts the couplet's list of what fails without a guardian to ascetics' vows and women's chastity, the two things his son violated, so the general rule becomes the reason he must count his own son's death as just.

gains.a: The king's maxim gains the couplet's frame of the guardian's duty, which shows it as a known rule rather than a private excuse.
gains.b: The couplet's list gains vows and chastity, and a case where the guardian's duty runs against his own son.

note: Aravanar tells Manimekalai she will not take up the teaching until the events her presence causes have happened; seventeen kaathais later she asks him for the true doctrine and he begins with the two means of knowledge.
teaches: The deferral is kept: the epic withholds its doctrinal core until its heroine has fed the hungry, emptied a prison and heard the other schools, so experience is made the condition of hearing the Buddha's logic.

note: The Vaisheshika counts space among the nine substances; the teacher judges examples built on space under both views, that it is a thing and that it is not.
teaches: The pairing shows the logic lesson deliberately leaving the schools' quarrel over space unsettled: a proof is faulted on either view, so the method does not depend on deciding the rival's ontology.

note: Both epics give the Ajivika fire rising, water sinking and wind moving; 717 adds that the soul rises with fire, and 718-720 attack the whole scheme.
teaches: Two hostile witnesses agree on the Ajivika theory of natural motions, which makes it likely a real doctrine; the Jain adds the soul to it because a rising soul is what he can refute.

note: The couplet's wife commands the rain; Kannaki commands the fire god, who waits on her word.
teaches: Where the couplet's wife who worships no god has the rain at her word, the epic shows a god coming in person to take her orders, and the power that brings rain turned to burning a city, so the same claim for the chaste wife's word is shown in its most destructive extent.

gains.a: her command over the fire gains a known doctrine behind it: the chaste wife's word moves the elements
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case showing that the power it grants is not only beneficent and can set a god to destroy

note: The couplet ranks the strength of those who endure hunger below that of those who end others' hunger; an ascetic here names ending hunger as the one dharma equal for men and gods and calls it the dharma of tapas.
teaches: The epic answers the couplet's ranking by giving the higher strength to a renunciant: with the bowl, the one who has left the household can feed others instead of only enduring hunger, and feeding becomes the ascetic's own discipline.

gains.a: Aravanar's claim gains the Kural's prior ranking of feeding above endurance, which explains why he can call feeding a form of tapas
gains.b: the couplet's opposition between ascetic and feeder gains a case where one person holds both roles

note: 553 argues that if all is suffering there cannot be four truths; the Manimekalai's teacher gives four truths in which the fourth is joy, which is release caused by not clinging.
teaches: The reductio holds only against a Buddhism that calls everything suffering without exception; the Buddhist epic's own fourth truth (இன்பம் வீடே) is the exception, which shows the Jain argument aimed at a version the Buddhist teacher would not accept.

note: Both cook a battlefield meal on hearths of crowned heads stirred with bangled arms (முடித்தலை அடுப்பு, தொடித்தோள் துடுப்பு), and both set it beside the king's care for Vedic Brahmins.
teaches: The puram poem makes the battlefield cooking the Pandya's own rite beside his completed Vedic sacrifices, and the epic gives the cooking to demons who call the field an அறக்களம் and then has the king order the fire-keeping Brahmins protected, so the epic keeps the old pairing of war-rite and Vedic rite and adds the name of dharma to the slaughter.

gains.a: the demons' feast is recognised as the formal battlefield sacrifice of the Pandya praise poem, not loose description of gore
gains.b: the puram image gains a later life in which the cooks are demons and the field is named a field of dharma, showing the formula become a convention that could be given to any Tamil conqueror

note: Sudhamathi's sermon on the body born of deeds failed to turn Udayakumaran once he saw Manimekalai; the goddess now reveals that he is her husband of a former birth and that her heart, too, still clings to him.
teaches: The failure of the grove sermon is given a cause in karma after the fact: the pull between the two was not mere sight but a bond carried across births, which is why words could not break it and a goddess had to carry her away.

note: 52: the shore is like a king who rises without haste, so fix a day. 53: the shore is like a king who has risen and will not settle, so come before our kin move.
teaches: One image of the shore as a royal army is given opposite tempos, unhurried and restless, to argue first for deliberation and then for urgency, which shows the poet using the image to set the pace of the plea rather than to carry a fixed sense.

note: The Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker counts speech, hands, feet and the two excretory organs among the twenty-five principles; 756 denies these are organs, since they have no object and no knowing.
teaches: Set beside the plain Sankhya list in the Manimekalai, Neelakesi's mockery shows exactly which item of the count she treats as weakest: the organs of action, which fail her test that an organ must know something.

note: Kural 230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even death is sweet when giving is out of reach; alone on an uninhabited island with no one to feed, Aputhiran will not keep his own life with the bowl, gives it away and starves himself to death.
teaches: The epic takes the couplet's hyperbole literally: a giver cut off from anyone to give to chooses death, and refuses even the means of life that giving had put in his hands.

gains.a: a general rule that turns his fast from despair into a judgment on a life without giving
gains.b: a case where the couplet's ranking is acted on, together with the refusal to turn a giving-vessel to one's own use, which the couplet does not state

note: The brahmin says men without a chaste wife do not enter the world of the gods however much good they do; Visakai says sons do not give that world and only great virtue is a companion.
teaches: The same phrase, புத்தேள் உலகம், is used for opposite conditions within twenty lines: the brahmin makes a wife necessary, Visakai makes virtue sufficient, and the narrator sides with her by counting their charity above the stars.

note: Kudapulaviyanar tells the Pandya that those who give food give life and urges him to build tanks; the disguised girl tells the Chola her bowl is life-medicine for embodied beings and asks him to give the prison to the righteous.
teaches: Both poems set a counsellor before a king to teach that feeding is giving life, but the Sangam poet asks for waterworks that bring fame and the other world, while the epic's beggar asks the king to give up a prison, so the duty to feed passes from royal works to a renouncer's bowl the king only endorses.

gains.a: The girl's plea gains a Tamil royal precedent for the claim that food is life.
gains.b: The poem's counsel gains a later scene where the one who feeds is not the king, which shifts who holds the life-giving power.

note: Both turn on the same word. In 594 wealth seeks out அசைவிலா energy. In 371 அசைவின்மை is itself produced by a fate of gain.
teaches: The causal arrow reverses, so the question becomes whether steadfastness is one's own at all.

note: The patikam's opening frame names three morals the poem will show (dharma as death to the erring king, the praise of the pathini, the past deed that comes to fruit) and calls the poem a பாட்டுடைச் செய்யுள்; the closing summary describes the finished work by its land, its akam and puram matter, its three aims and its music, dance and song forms, and repeats none of the morals.
teaches: The two frames of the epic describe it in different terms, the opening as a story built to prove three moral claims and the close as a compendium of Tamil poetics, music and dance, so the work presents itself at the start as an argument and at the end as an art, and the morals are left for the story itself to carry.

note: The prince praised Manimekalai for setting out 'wise old sayings' (முதுக்குறை முதுமொழி) as part of her allure; Kanchanan sees her setting out the same wise old sayings to the prince and takes it as a lover's talk.
teaches: The same words of wisdom are read by both men as courtship, the prince as charm to be won and the husband as proof of betrayal, so her teaching is misheard twice in the way most fatal to each hearer.

note: Deepathilakai says Aravanan will tell Manimekalai the bowl's nature (52); in the next kaathai Aravana Adigal says she has the bowl and gives the one dharma common to men and gods, curing hunger.
teaches: The goddess hands over the object and defers its meaning to a human teacher, so the epic places authority over the bowl's use with the Buddhist monk rather than the island's deity.

note: Both use the new pot that takes the scent of pathiri flowers: the Naladiyar for the unlearned who gain sense from the learned, the Neelakesi for the Buddhist example of traces that persist after the flower is gone.
teaches: A homely image of borrowed fragrance served Tamil writers for transmission without identity, and the Jain debater shows that the image cuts both ways, since a scent that outlives its flower can be claimed for an enduring soul.

gains.a: the Neelakesi's turn of the image is seen to work on a figure already proverbial in Tamil ethical verse
gains.b: the quatrain's simile is shown to carry a philosophical question it leaves unasked: whether what is passed on is something that lasts

note: Verse 20 lists not stealing, not gambling and not befriending the black-hearted among five abstentions; verse 27 says the friend of outsiders picks up toddy, theft and gambling.
teaches: Verse 20 puts bad company beside theft and gambling as one more abstention; verse 27 shows it as their cause, so the book's ban on bad friends is a ban on the way the other vices are learned.

note: Neelakesi says deeds move the soul to its next birth as the wind turns a whirligig; Tirumular says the subtle breath in the soul carries it as wind carries a flower's scent.
teaches: Both answer what carries a soul between bodies with an image of wind, but for the Jain the wind is the deed itself, needing no other mover, while for Tirumular it is the vital breath at the appointed moment, so the same image names karma in one and breath in the other.

gains.a: the whirligig image is set against a Tamil alternative it leaves out, breath as the carrier
gains.b: Tirumular's image is seen as one answer to a question a rival school answered with deeds alone

note: The quatrain says an old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the patikam has a deed of a former birth in Singapuram find Kovalan in Madurai, and says it has run its course for both of them (நுங்கட்கு).
teaches: The quatrain's deed seeks the one who did it, but the epic's curse reaches across a birth and a country through the word of the victim's widow and falls on the doer's wife as well, so the pair shows the epic widening the quatrain's single doer into a household.

gains.a: Saathan's report gains a general law stated without story, that a past deed actively seeks its doer, which makes the goddess's word an instance and not a private verdict
gains.b: the quatrain gains a case showing how the seeking works, through a curse spoken by another, and that it can fall on one who did not do the deed

note: Aravana Adigal told Manimekalai that Aputhiran died with an unquenched purpose of sustaining lives and was born from a cow's womb to rule Savakam; here Manimekalai tells that king that, bewildered by wealth, he knows neither that birth nor the cow's womb of this one.
teaches: Rebirth carried Aputhiran's purpose into a king's body but not his knowledge of it, so the purpose has to be handed back to him by one who heard his story from outside.

note: Aravanar told her that events would happen in the town because of her and that only after they had happened would she take up the teaching; the last lines show her hearing dharma and vowing to end becoming.
teaches: The pairing shows that the epic frames its whole middle, from the prison to the debates of Vanji, as a foretold delay, so that this lesson fulfils a prophecy made eighteen kaathais earlier rather than starting a new episode.

note: 242 announces that Arkkachandra should hear the deceits (சலம்) bound up with the Buddhist vows; 249 ends the list by asking whether such a rule is not deceit (சலமதோ).
teaches: The frame word shows that verses 243 to 249 are one indictment, so obscure items like the courtesan and Simhadatta verses belong to a single charge of sophistry rather than to separate anecdotes.

note: Manimekalai's teacher lists modes of usage that rest on what is not (இல்லது சார்ந்த வழக்கு), and pairs cognition with the hare's horn; Neelakesi's Buddhist insists that names and cognitions occur for what does not exist.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the Buddhist claim in 412 rests on a worked-out doctrine of usage, which is what Neelakesi's reply in 413 must deny by appeal to scripture.

note: The decade's preface says Senguttuvan went for the stone of the goddess pathini, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed the stone in the Ganga; the kaathai tells the expedition at length. The epic here does not name the king's parents, so the identity rests on name and deed.
teaches: The preface compresses the campaign to a stone sought, one Aryan lord defeated and a bathing in the Ganga, while the epic gives the war a cause in an insult to Tamil, names two kings Kanakan and Vijayan, and brings the army over the Ganga on allies' boats, so the two show a shared tradition of the pathini's stone told with different enemies and routes.

gains.a: the epic's campaign gains an independent notice in the Chera decade's preface, showing the stone for the pathini was part of the Chera king's remembered deeds
gains.b: the preface's bare clause கடவுட் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள் gains its story: why the stone was sought, from whom it was taken, and that the god was Kannaki

note: Both epics give the Sankhya twenty-five, but the Neelakesi counts the unmanifest and the five subtle elements while the Manimekalai counts the five sense objects and thought (சித்தம்) and leaves primal nature outside the list.
teaches: Two rival polemics hand down different lists under the same count of twenty-five, so the Tamil reports of Sankhya were not one fixed table and neither epic's list can stand for the school by itself.

note: The venba's 'queen of the king' and the speaker 'of harsh deeds' recur at the opening of the next kaathai, where Kannaki addresses the queen and calls herself கொடுவினை யாட்டியேன்.
teaches: The next kaathai's opening supports reading this venba as Kannaki's words to the queen, and shows the threat 'see what I will do' carried into the vow against the city.

note: Pattinappaalai says the Kaveri does not fail even when the star goes south and the sky withholds rain; Madhavi's stanza says the Kaveri's unceasing help that sustains life is the grace of the ruler of the wheel.
teaches: The idyll makes the river's reliability its own, a guarantee standing even against a failed sky, while the epic song moves that same unfailing gift under a ruler's grace, so the pair shows the Kaveri's bounty passing from a fact of the land to a token of the king.

gains.a: the stanza's ஒழியாய் gains its older ground, the Sangam guarantee that this river does not fail when the rains do
gains.b: the idyll's praise of the river gains a later reading in which its constancy is no longer self-standing but credited to the sun-like Chola

note: The Buddha calls the five aggregates a soul only as five fingers are called a hand; Neelakesi says the fingers' unity needs a bearer, or else they are five things.
teaches: The Buddha's chosen example becomes the Jain's evidence: an analogy for a mere name is turned into a case of qualities that need one substance.

claims.gist: where there is bondage it is the soul that suffers
suffering belongs to the bodily aggregate and to no self
either every element is conscious, or the unity of knowing requires a soul
sound is the quality of ether
sound gives no ground for positing the Vaisheshika's ether
an action that arises from seeing, knowing and desire implies one bearer of all these qualities
wives and children are not goods that may be given away, and whoever takes them so is a thief
a deed of the past drives a person's departure on the path that leads to its fruit
there are no ghosts and no rebirth
a deity summoned by mantra truly comes and possesses
there is a person who persists, as one Buddhist assembly recites
all wanting is coveting, a fault of the mind
if every wanting is coveting, the teacher's own composing of his teaching is coveting
a cause that never meets its effect cannot produce it
an example that lacks the reason's property cannot support the proof
an example that lacks the property to be proved cannot support the proof
an inference for others needs only thesis, reason and example; application and conclusion are contained in the example
a soul with no action and no contact with nature cannot be the cause of seeing and experiencing
the supreme one's teaching shows the way to cut the cycle of births and reach the auspicious state
the one heap of the body is analysed into five aggregates
valid knowledge is perceptual or non-perceptual, and perception includes, beside sense-and-mind knowledge, the supersensory avadhi, manahparyaya and kevala
the deed of a former birth rose in wrath and parted Kovalan from Madhavi
Kovalan was without fault and the king erred in killing him
one who loses a person given into her keeping has failed in her trust
the Veda names persons and fits the present age, so it is recent like any song
a woman who stays alive on hearing of her beloved's suffering has given up her shame
a courtesan, who lives on many men's gifts, owes none of the pathini's deaths or vows at her lover's death
the ten perfections are what bring bodhisattvas to buddhahood
conduct and vows are the means by which one becomes a Siddha
right faith has eight limbs, from freedom from doubt to steadying the wavering, love of fellow believers and spreading the dharma
one who toils for others with no gain to himself is paying off his own past sin
the Buddha removes the distress even of those who are strangers to him
the Lord neither speaks nor eats nor ages, and his form is unseen like a rainbow
an effect that arises across a gap with nothing passing over would appear everywhere at once
calling meat pure removes the deed of eating it
no restraint can hold once desire has taken hold
if the fixed order is the sole cause, there is no room for any separate effect of one's own doing
countless aggregates follow one another without interval
an unbroken series of aggregates cannot end in the teacher's complete extinction
the one who debates cannot be identified with any of the five elements
when a thesis and its contrary are each backed by a reason that looks sound, neither is established and both end in doubt
the contradictory reason is of four kinds, by the property or the subject, in its bare form or in its specific character
the Bodhisattva who perished was reborn as a god in the Tushita heaven
rebirth as a god cannot be claimed unless the continuum joining the dead man and the god is shown
darkness falls under none of the five kinds, so the five do not exhaust what exists
compounds made of atoms are infinite in number
the virtuous bear the wrongs of those who hurt them as a mother bears her nursing infant

note: In 307 Neelakesi answered that deeds carry the soul between births as wind turns a whirligig; in 748 she tells the Sankhya his soul, whether it goes or not, cannot be carried, and that its twofold deeds are its companion.
teaches: The image of deeds moving the soul that answered Mokkalan becomes the dilemma that sinks the Sankhya: only a soul that acts and is acted on can be carried by its own deeds from birth to birth.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 167 gives the attending gods as a sum (நால்வேறு இயற்கைப் பதினொரு மூவரொடு); Paripadal 8.4-7 names the same thirty-three group by group: twelve, two who speak of medicine, eight, and eleven from the lord of Aathirai.
teaches: The guide poem's 'eleven times three of four kinds' is spelled out in the Paripadal as four counted groups, showing that the Vedic thirty-three were known in Tamil by their divisions and that both poets made Murugan the one they attend.

note: The brahmin hails a Pandya who, when the thundering clouds withheld rain, bound them and made the harvest unfailing (மழைபிணித் தாண்ட மன்னவன்); the couplet says rain and harvest gather together in the land of the king who rules by the sceptre's nature.
teaches: The couplet makes rain the natural consequence of just rule, while the epic's praise makes the king compel the clouds, so the same belief appears once as a law and once as a dynastic feat that this epic will test when the Pandya's sceptre bends.

gains.a: the praise gains a stated rule by which the dynasty's rain-making can later be judged as a duty rather than a marvel
gains.b: the couplet gains a royal legend showing its abstract link between sceptre and rain told of one named line of kings

note: In Puhar's evening the women parted from their lovers sigh like a smith's bellows (ஊதுஉலைக் குருகின் உயிர்த்தனர்); here Kannaki, parted from Kovalan by his death, sighs like the bellows (ஊதுலைக் குருகின் உயிர்த்தனள்) amid a burning city.
teaches: The same formula moves from the passing grief of lovers apart for a night to a widow's grief that has set a city alight, so the forge in the image becomes a real fire.

note: The Jain in Manimekalai 27 gives gram cooked into கும்மாயம் as his example of a kind that persists while a form passes; in Neelakesi 390 to 391 the Buddhist attacks that very example and Neelakesi defends it.
teaches: The cooked-gram example is shown to be a fixed Jain teaching case known to both sides, so the Buddhist epic's report of Jain doctrine matches what the Jain epic itself has to defend.

note: The Patitruppattu poem names Neduncheralathan as the king who went against his foes on an island in the sea and cut down the kadamba at its root (கடம்புமுதல் தடிந்த); the swing song sings the guardian who cut the kadamba at its root (கடம்பு முதல் தடிந்த) and the emblem of the bow, and names no king.
teaches: The pair shows the Patitruppattu's title for one Chera king passing into the epic as an unnamed dynastic refrain, so that in Senguttuvan's court a deed the Sangam decade credits to Neduncheralathan is sung as the house's own.

gains.a: the swing song's unnamed guardian gains an identity: the phrase is the title of Neduncheralathan in the Chera court poetry
gains.b: the Patitruppattu's title gains evidence of its afterlife, as a stock phrase of the Chera line sung by women at play rather than a bard's praise of one patron

note: Ainkurunuru 154's woman can only call the town a liar and ask what she can do; in Kuruntokai 34 the friend says the town would not believe their denials (மறுப்பத் தேறலர்) and is silenced only by the sweet news that the lord will marry her.
teaches: Read together they show that in the neythal love story gossip cannot be ended by calling it false, since the town does not believe denials, and the only cure the poets allow is marriage, which turns the lying town into one that rejoices.

note: The Murukatruppadai hails Murugan among his titles as son of the banyan god, son of the mountain's daughter, and child of Kotravai of victorious war; the vari heaps on Kotravai herself the names of Gauri, Shiva's emblems and the title of Mal's younger kin.
teaches: The Sangam guide poem joins Kotravai to the Saiva household through her son, listing her beside the mountain daughter as Murugan's mother, while the epic's hunters make Kotravai herself absorb Gauri, Shiva's emblems and Vishnu's kinship, so the pair shows the war goddess of the wilds drawn into the great gods' family by two different routes.

gains.a: the epic's fusion of names appears as the later step of a joining already begun in the Sangam praise of Murugan as Kotravai's son
gains.b: the bare title கொற்றவை சிறுவ gains the full portrait of the mother it names, with her mount, weapons and the cult that worships her

note: Kaathai 27's Sankhya speaker gives the person as one, pervading and eternal awareness; here the argument for that person from the senses serving another is shown to prove a composite self.
teaches: The epic answers the Sankhya two kaathais later without denying it outright: its own proof for a partless self, followed through, yields a self with parts, so the refutation is internal.

note: On entering the Pandya land the travellers rely on the fame that the Pandya's straight sceptre keeps even beasts and thunder from harming those who depend on it; in the court the same Pandya, having killed Kovalan, finds himself the thief and his sceptre bent.
teaches: The pairing shows the epic letting the travellers stake their lives on a king's reputation for protection and then making that king's failure fall on exactly the stranger who trusted it, so the praise of the sceptre at the border is the premise his own verdict on himself overturns.

note: 263 mocks the Buddha's void release for giving nothing to hold to; Siddhar 1777 bids the seeker cling close to that which became the void.
teaches: Whether a void can be a goal one holds is exactly where they part: for the Jain debater the void offers no support, for the Siddhar it is the one thing to grasp.

gains.a: the debater's objection is shown to rest on taking the void as mere absence, which another Tamil tradition denies
gains.b: the Siddhar's call to cling to the void is set against the strongest objection to it, that no one desires an empty release

note: Both have a vidyadhara fly down from the sky to see Puhar's festival for Indra; in the Silappathikaram he brings his beloved as a spectator, in the Manimekalai Marutavegan seizes a brahmin girl and abandons her.
teaches: The heavenly visitor whom the first epic uses as an admiring eye on Puhar's festival becomes in the second a seducer who strands a girl there, so the same festival that showed Madhavi's art is now a danger to an unguarded girl.

note: Neelakesi quotes the quatrain's first line, 'even if ruined, do not plan the ruin of the worthy', against a teacher who ruined himself for others and taught flesh-eating.
teaches: The quatrain's counsel to forbearance becomes a test of a rival teacher: self-ruin does not excuse doctrine that harms others.

gains.a: the debater's charge rests on a saying the assembly already accepts, so it needs no Jain premise
gains.b: the quatrain's line is shown circulating as a proverb that a debater can cite against a whole school

note: The quatrain says the best of people reflect on impermanence, disease, old age and death and do their real work; Manimekalai says she understood the body's birth, ageing, disease and death and chose dharma.
teaches: The same reflection that the quatrain treats as a private discipline of the wise is here a defence a woman must speak aloud to a man pursuing her, and she doubts he will listen.

gains.a: Manimekalai's Buddhist reason is shown to rest on a reflection the Tamil ethical tradition already commends, not on a doctrine peculiar to her school.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a scene where the reflection must be argued before someone who does not share it, which its address to the wise leaves out.

note: The narrator states as event that at the jewel seat Manimekalai came to know all her former births (பழம் பிறப்பு எல்லாம் ... உணர்ந்ததும்); in kaathai 27 she asks whether no one has known a former birth, and the materialist answers that such knowledge is the delusion of those led by a god or by dreams. The tension holds on the reading that 281-283 are the materialist's.
teaches: The materialist's dismissal names exactly the route by which the patikam says her knowledge came, a goddess carrying her to an island, so the epic lets the one school it answers attack the very ground of its heroine's conversion.

note: Maadalan tells how Kovalan named Madhavi's daughter after the sea goddess who saved his ancestor with the words வந்தேன் அஞ்சல் மணிமேகலை யான்; here the goddess, speaking the same words, adds that on that naming night she told Madhavi in a dream that the child would be a creeper of tapas.
teaches: The pairing shows the Manimekalai turning a name given in gratitude for merit of giving into a vocation for renunciation, revealed only now by the goddess herself.

note: The Kundalakesi calls covering or stripping the body, ash, cold, fire, alms and matted hair mere words, and true tapas a subdued life; Neelakesi asks whether the Buddhist rules of eating, shaving and kohl are dharma.
teaches: Both schools use the same test, that outward discipline is not the path, and each turns it on the other: the Buddhist verse includes the Jain's nakedness among empty forms, and the Jain debater counts the Vinaya's grooming among them.

note: Kaathai 1 has the assembled sages warn that if the festival is forgotten the guardian spirit will bring harm; here a king searching for his lost son forgets the festival, and the curse follows.
teaches: The warning of the first kaathai turns out to name the cause of Puhar's end, and the lapse comes not from neglect but from a father's grief, so the city falls through the king's love rather than his vice.

note: The couplet is a woman's admission that the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint; the prince asks whether any restraint exists once desire takes hold.
teaches: The same claim that in the Kural is a woman's confession of her own defeat becomes, in a prince's mouth, a licence to press on a woman who refuses him, so the epic shows how the love-book's lament can serve as an excuse.

gains.a: The prince's maxim is recognised as borrowed from the love poets' woman's voice, which shows how far he has moved it from its place.
gains.b: The couplet's resignation gets a test: said by the stronger party about another's body, the same words stop being a confession and become a threat.

note: Just ten verses apart, this one ends the section on renunciation by promising a nature that can't be shifted, once craving goes. 380 asks what is stronger than fate, which gets there first.
teaches: The Kural moves from the highest claim for human release straight to the strongest claim against human power.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher names the five aggregates simply (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness); the Neelakesi's Buddha gives them with numbered subdivisions, three feelings, six consciousnesses and twenty formations.
teaches: The Buddhist epic gives the aggregates as a short list within the four truths; the Jain epic's Buddha gives a scholastic count, so the polemic attacks a more technical Abhidharma than the one the Buddhist epic chose to teach.

note: The Manimekalai's Sankhya soul is the knowing awareness, without the three qualities, one, pervading and eternal; the Neelakesi's has the same marks but adds that it does nothing and yet experiences.
teaches: The Buddhist and the Jain reports agree on the soul's marks, but only the Jain report foregrounds the pair 'does nothing' and 'experiences', which is exactly the pair it then sets against each other in 740-745.

note: The Sankhya speaker of kaathai 27 tells every stage of the world as வெளிப்பட்டு, becoming manifest; here 'because it is produced' is a reason a Sankhya does not accept, since for him things are manifested, not produced.
teaches: The pairing shows that the epic's logic lesson is built on the doctrines Manimekalai heard in Vanji, so the account of the schools in kaathai 27 is accurate enough to be used as the test case here.

note: 252 says the monks call all things impure yet bow at their own defiled master's feet; 558 says they call their own recitation, conduct and food pure.
teaches: The charge of inconsistency grows from the monks' worship of their teacher to their whole daily practice, so the 'all is impure' doctrine is shown to exempt everything its holders do.

note: In 857 the materialist says the five elements become eye, nose, tongue, body and ear with their five objects; in 879 Neelakesi tells him to give up that very thought and sets up the soul.
teaches: The materialist's derivation of each sense from an element is the exact point Neelakesi chooses to deny, so the soul she proves is defined against a sense apparatus made of matter.

note: Both open on Venus straying south as the sign of drought and say the Kaveri still brings its flood.
teaches: The epic borrows the Pattinappalai's drought omen for the Kaveri on the road out of Puhar, so the couple's departure from the city is set in the same praise that once opened a poem about the city's wealth.

gains.a: the epic's omen list gains its source and sense as a Chola praise-formula for the river
gains.b: the Sangam formula gains a later use in a travel scene, where it marks the plenty the travellers are leaving behind

note: The Sankhya speaker holds the person to be the one eternal awareness that knows all; the teacher says no thing has a self and makes awareness (உணர்வு) a link conditioned by action.
teaches: Held together they show where the Buddhist answer to Sankhya lies: not in denying awareness but in making it the third link of a chain, born of action and ceasing with it, so the eternal knower of kaathai 27 is answered three kaathais later.

note: The couplet gives the wife who worships her husband power over the rain on her own; the ancients' saying quoted here makes the glory of famous women's chastity depend on kings doing justice.
teaches: The couplet's chastity commands nature unaided, but the epic's closing saying makes its public glory wait on the king's justice being tested, so the pathini's power is tied to a failure of the sceptre.

gains.a: the saying is set against the best-known claim for a chaste wife's unaided power
gains.b: the couplet gains a condition the Kural does not state: chastity's power shows itself through the state's justice or injustice

note: The goddess told Sudhamathi, as Veerai, Tharai's younger sister, that in seven days Lakshmi would return knowing her birth; Madhavi cries that the seventh day has come and Manimekalai arrives to name Tharai and Veerai.
teaches: The promise and its keeping frame Manimekalai's island journey as a timed rebirth-recognition, and Madhavi's near loss of faith on the last day sets the goddess's truthfulness against a mother's fear.

note: Kural 559: if the king bends justice the sky bends and withholds rain; the epic's image weeps when either the king's sceptre or the judge's reading bends.
teaches: Both make a mute power answer a bent justice, but the Kural's answer punishes the whole land through the rain while the epic's image only grieves, and the epic adds a second culprit, the judge who twists the law-book, which the couplet does not consider.
