gains.a: the weeping image gains the Kural's claim that a bent sceptre has consequences beyond the court
gains.b: the couplet gains the point that justice can be bent by the king's judges as well as by the king

note: The Kural tells the healer to find the disease, its source and the means that subdue it; the Neelakesi sermon classifies suffering as disease in 109-113 and then names its remedy.
teaches: The sermon follows the physician's order the couplet sets down, diagnosis by kinds before the cure, and applies it to the disease of birth, so the Kural's medical rule serves as the shape of a religious argument.

gains.a: the sermon's long classification of harms is seen to have a purpose, the diagnosis that must precede the remedy
gains.b: the couplet's method is shown at work outside medicine, governing how a teacher reasons about suffering itself

note: Manimekalai's Ajivika says atoms never enter one another (ஒன்று ஒன்றில் புகுதா); Neelakesi's says they combine and part but one does not enter another.
teaches: Two hostile accounts state the same tenet in nearly the same words, so it is likely the Ajivikas' own, and the Jain debater singles it out for attack (698) where the Buddhist narrator lets it pass.

note: Both give the rite of laying a king who died of sickness on darbha grass and cutting him with a sword with the words 'go where the warriors go' (செல்வுழிச் செல்க in both); Avvai uses it to praise Athiyaman's battle wounds, Vasanthavai to console and rebuke a queen whose son died in neither war nor old age.
teaches: Held together they show the rite outliving its Sangam use as praise: in the epic it becomes the standard by which a dead prince is found wanting, so that the warrior code is used to stop a mother's grief rather than to honour a king.

gains.a: the Sangam source of the custom, which shows that Vasanthavai is quoting an old royal code of the warrior's death and not inventing a comfort
gains.b: a later witness that the rite was remembered as a royal custom and could be turned from praise of the wounded against a prince who died without honour

note: In 393 Neelakesi tells the Buddhist that quality and bearer are both different and one; in 800 she tells the Vaisheshika that they need no third thing to join them.
teaches: Her 'different and one' answers two opposite opponents: the Buddhist who keeps qualities without a bearer, and the Vaisheshika who keeps a bearer so apart from its qualities that it needs a joining category.

note: In kaathai 27 the Sankhya speaker describes the person as awareness itself; here 'the soul has consciousness' is the stock example of a thesis whose subject a Buddhist does not accept.
teaches: The doctrine Manimekalai heard laid out without reply in kaathai 27 returns as a lesson in debate, answered not by a counter-argument but by the rule that a debater cannot assume a soul his opponent denies.

note: Both liken the opening kodal cluster to a snake's raised hood in the rain-fed woodland; in Akananuru 154 the returning man sees it from the chariot, in Kar Narpathu 11 the friend points to it as the sign of his quick return.
teaches: The same flower-image is seen by the man on the road home and offered by the friend at home as a promise, so the shared stock of mullai images lets the two halves of a separation read the same sign in the same season.

note: The venba's challenge to the queen to see what the woman of harsh deeds will do is made explicit as a vow to destroy the kingdom and Madurai.
teaches: The vague threat that closed the plea becomes a sworn vow with a condition on her own chastity, so the step from grievance to destruction is taken as an oath, not as a sudden fury.

note: Kural 706 has crystal show the colour of what is near it, as the face shows the heart; the Sankhya, in Neelakesi's report, uses crystal beside a coloured thing for a soul that only seems changed.
teaches: The same crystal runs opposite ways: in the Kural its borrowed colour is a true sign of what lies within, in the Sankhya it is a mere appearance over a soul untouched, which is why Neelakesi can call the image an evasion.

gains.a: The Neelakesi verse gains a common Tamil use of the crystal image, in which borrowed colour reveals rather than hides, against which the Sankhya use looks like special pleading.
gains.b: The Kural couplet gains a sense of the image's other use, where crystal's colour is denied any truth, showing that its own reading of the face as a reliable sign is a choice.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika gives earth as hard, water cool, fire burning and wind moving, borne by eternal atoms; the Neelakesi's Buddha gives the same four marks with functions, borne by octads of momentary form (478, 485).
teaches: Across two polemical epics the marks of the elements are common ground; what the schools dispute is the bearer, eternal unchanging atoms for the Ajivika against momentary eight-fold clusters for the Buddhist.

note: In the previous kaathai the king gave Maadalan gold to his own weight, counted as ஐயைந்து இரட்டி; here Maadalan says he is not one who seeks rich gifts.
teaches: The counsellor's disclaimer comes after the largest gift in the story, so the epic leaves the reader to weigh whether the sermon is disinterested, without itself saying so.

note: Devanthi, whose husband is a god, keeps worship at his shrine to have him back; the couplet sets worship of a god against worship of a husband.
teaches: Devanthi's case dissolves the couplet's either-or, since her god is her husband, and so throws Kannaki's refusal of the shrine in the next unit into relief as a choice the couplet's terms describe exactly.

gains.a: a measure for Devanthi's piety as the reverse of the couplet's wife, which prepares the contrast with Kannaki
gains.b: a case the couplet did not foresee, a wife whose husband is himself the god she worships

note: The patikam's first moral is that dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship; the first venba after the Pandya's death calls this the saying of many assemblies, that dharma is death to wrongdoers, and turns it on the queen as well.
teaches: The patikam narrows the saying to kings and claims it as the poem's own thesis, while the venba gives it back to common opinion and extends it to the queen who dies with the king, so the pair shows the poem's moral both resting on a proverb and making it a rule of kingship.

note: The couplet says do aram without saying 'later'; Maadalan says if the king says 'we will do aram tomorrow', life may leave today, and the aram he means is the Vedic royal sacrifice.
teaches: The epic keeps the couplet's urgency but narrows aram from the whole of virtue to one rite performed by priests for a king, showing how the ethical maxim could be recruited for a particular religious practice.

gains.a: Maadalan's urgency gains the authority of a general rule about not deferring virtue
gains.b: the couplet's unspecified aram is shown filled with one school's content in a court setting

claims.gist: the body does not last, as no great king of the past remains
wealth does not last, as the fall of the conquered kings shows
suffering arises only from one's own evil deeds
the Buddha's sufferings for others were the fruit of a former deed done out of attachment
both good and evil deeds come back to their doer, so one should turn to good dharma
the bending of a just king's sceptre can be the fruit of another's former deed
on the Buddhist account another reaps what the doer did, and the doer never reaps it
qualities are both one with and different from the substance that bears them
the Lord who dances, destroys, creates, withdraws and grants release is beyond the faults charged against him
a tongue that does not say Narayana's name is no tongue
the god praised in the kuravai will take away the distress fallen on the cattle
without a lasting self the doer of a deed and the enjoyer of its fruit would be different persons
a single generality resides in every thing of its kind
the buyers' demand for flesh is what makes the hunter kill, so the killer is not the only culprit
conduct is shown in restraint, forbearance and the other virtues, twofold penance and the endurance of hardship
some things, like the horn of a hare or donkey, never arise, so their non-existence is not a matter of standpoint
a release that is a place would be one more destination like hell and heaven
the birth the Buddhist describes cannot be taken as a real principle
pleasure and pain are the effects of good and bad deeds
on that view the pain of penance undertaken later is itself only the fruit of deeds
a cow, which nourishes all people with its milk out of kindness, should not be harmed
the goddess of victory walks before the raider's bow when he goes for the enemy's cattle
the courtesan's guise brings great sorrow to the daughter who takes it up
one whose words have brought death to others should cleanse himself in the Ganga
those who worship the Aptha with flowers and praise lose both kinds of deed and reach release
saying a thing is not this is not saying it does not exist
memory and knowledge are carried from moment to moment by traces
whatever carries the traces through the moments is a soul, as the thread runs through a garland
a man's former deed comes in wrath and brings his death
when an innocent man is killed at the king's order, the king's just sceptre has bent
the five aggregates, with nothing binding them into one, are as unreal as a crow's teeth
moving beings have from two to five senses, and creatures like the snail have only two
penance founded on the Vaisheshika principles is false penance
the real things are the supreme self, root nature and the evolved nature that is not the root
the world is nothing but the elements, and talk of a soul yields only fruitless dispute
a thing that lasts cannot act, and a thing that perishes is replaced by a new one, so a thing cannot be both
dharma is the force that drives moving things
dharma is the medium without which nothing moves, not the mover itself
there are nine substances: five elements, direction, mind, time and soul
action is the movement of a substance
saving another from death at the risk of one's own life wins the form of the gods
those who love a person but have not done the dharma that leads upward are reborn near the one they love rather than going to the upper world
one who gives up the burden of a kingdom becomes king of an endless bliss beyond the reach of thought
the cause ceases as the effect arises, like the two ends of a balance beam
arising and perishing need one continuing thing to happen in, as the beam's ends need the beam
a blameless wife whose husband was wronged by a king may rightly turn her anger on the king's city
the burning of the city on the day the pathini was wronged had been ordained beforehand
Brahmins, the virtuous, cows, chaste women, elders and children must be spared when a city is destroyed, and only the wicked struck
one who has come to know her former birth is not deluded
a person is made of five aggregates
feeling, perception and volition are modes of knowing, so the aggregates reduce to knowing and form
a king who has made only the sacrifice of the battlefield, never the sacrifice of dharma, has left his duty undone
that a fruit held here does not exist in a distant town is a truism, not a hidden truth

note: The couplet calls a fort that which cannot be taken by siege, storm or work on those inside; Madurai's gate is lined with every engine against attack as Kannaki passes through it.
teaches: The epic fills Madurai's walls with the defences the Kural's fort requires at the very moment it lets in the woman whose wrong will burn the city from within, so the pair shows a danger the couplet's three threats do not name: an injustice of the king's own that no engine on the wall can repel.

gains.a: the list of engines gains a measure: by the Kural's standard the city is a perfect fort, which sharpens the irony of its fall
gains.b: the couplet's account of impregnability gains a case where the fort is lost through no siege at all, but through the king's own wrong

note: Kural 55 says the wife who rises worshipping her husband and not a god can bid the rain fall; here the pathini, who held to her husband alone, has become the god whom chaste wives worship, and the hill women ask her to keep their hill fruitful.
teaches: The couplet's power of the chaste wife's word passes, after her death, into a cult in which other chaste wives worship her, so the woman the couplet exempts from worshipping a god is herself made one.

gains.a: the epic's deification gains a basis in a stated ethical claim about the chaste wife's power over rain and plenty
gains.b: the couplet is tested at its edge: its own ideal, once dead, becomes an object of the worship the couplet set her free from

note: Kural 251 asks how one who eats flesh to swell his own can hold to grace; 472 grants the Buddha the greatest self-giving, even of his wife, and still faults him for not forbidding flesh.
teaches: Grace in the Kural is lost by the eater; the Neelakesi adds a teacher's grace lost by silence, so that a life of total giving can still fail the test if it leaves others free to eat flesh.

gains.a: the charge against the Buddha gets the Kural's rule that grace and flesh-eating cannot go together
gains.b: the couplet's test is extended from the one who eats to the one who teaches and does not forbid

note: In the grove the prince asked whether any restraint holds once desire takes root; here evening pursues him 'with an aspect that destroys restraint' and he leaves burning and sighing.
teaches: The prince's line that no நிறை survives rooted desire was his licence to pursue; two kaathais on, the same loss of restraint is drawn as a beast that hounds him away from her, so his excuse becomes his torment.

note: Against Mokkalan she said the scent in the sherd belongs to the flower, whose particles stay there and carry it; here she grants pot and flower coexist but denies that successive moments do.
teaches: Her earlier answer explains why the pot example cannot help the Buddha: the scent passes only because flower-matter is physically present with the pot, and no such co-presence exists between a perished moment and the next.

note: Kannaki told the Pandya that Kovalan came to Madurai driven by former deeds; here Madari cries that Kovalan was blameless and the king erred, and Maadalan puts the parting under karma.
teaches: Kannaki in her plea names both karma and the king's failure to inquire, and this report splits those causes between witnesses, the Brahmin naming karma and the herdswoman naming the king, so the epic keeps both explanations alive in the story's aftermath rather than letting either replace the other.

note: The patikam's line for kaathai 27 is that she asked them to state the faultless truth and heard (கேட்டதும்) the schools' doctrines; kaathai 27 lays the schools out one by one and she answers only the materialist.
teaches: The patikam's own word for the chapter of the schools is hearing, not defeating, which supports reading most of kaathai 27's accounts as reported views left for the Buddhist teaching of the later kaathais to answer.

note: The patikam's hill kuravar report to Ilango that they saw a pathini taken to heaven under a vengai; this unit is the hill women's own telling of that sight.
teaches: The frame says the epic began from the hill folk's report; the kaathai shows that report already as a cult with drums, incense and a prayer for the hill's wealth, so the poem's source is presented as a worship before it is a story.

note: At the burning Kannaki declared to the gods that she was without fault (குற்றமிலேன் யான்); under the vengai she laments that she is a woman of fiery deeds (தீத்தொழி லாட்டியேன் யான்).
teaches: Kannaki's own judgment of the burning reverses once the goddess has shown her the former deed, so the epic lets its heroine see her vengeance as a deed with its own weight just before it raises her to heaven.

note: Madhavi recounts Kannaki twisting off her breast and setting the king's city aflame; Silappathikaram 21 tells the act.
teaches: Madhavi retells the burning as the deed of the mother she assigns to Manimekalai, so the earlier epic's vengeance becomes a lineage by which a courtesan's daughter is claimed for tapas instead of her mother's trade.

note: Kannaki's image says the two went to the gods by former good deeds, the evil deed will still come, and they will wander until the Buddha appears at Kapilai; the Vanji seers foretell the same and add that Kovalan's merit came from austerity under an earlier Buddha's Bodhi.
teaches: The second witness confirms the first and supplies its missing cause, so the couple's heaven is traced to a past Buddhist austerity, not to Kannaki's chastity alone.

note: The couplet's man says he never knew Death before and now knows it in a woman's warring eyes; the vari's man says he did not know Death lived in the shore grove, and had he known he would not have come.
teaches: Both men learn Death in a woman's eyes, but the Kural's man ends in recognition while the song's ends in the wish never to have come, so the pair separates knowing love's danger from wanting to have avoided it.

gains.a: the stanza's refrain gains a contrast that shows its regret as a choice: the couplet's speaker accepts what he now knows
gains.b: the couplet's moment of discovery gains a sequel in which the knowledge comes too late to act on

note: The quatrain warns that merciless Death stalks and takes even the child while its mother wails; Gotami wails over her son and asks whether a spirit took him, and Champapathi answers that no spirit takes a life, only the boy's former deed.
teaches: The epic gives the quatrain's wailing mother a voice and an answer, and the answer removes the stalking agent the quatrain imagines: what takes the child is his own deed, with fright as its occasion.

gains.a: Champapathi's denial of a killing agent stands out against the ethics book's ready personification of Death.
gains.b: The quatrain's figure of Death as a thief is shown to be one account among others, which a Buddhist epic replaces with karma.

note: The goddess gave Manimekalai a mantra to change her form so that no one would dismiss her teaching as a young girl's; here she uses it to take Kaayasandigai's form and hide from the prince.
teaches: The power given for teaching rival schools is first used to escape a pursuer, so the epic's protection of her celibacy and its preparation for debate run through the same gift.

note: The Neelakesi's monk says evil conduct is not evil karma if the mind is pure; the Manimekalai's Buddhist teacher counts killing, theft and lust of the body among the ten evil deeds that lead to hell.
teaches: Set beside a Buddhist epic's own list of bodily evil deeds, the monk's mind-only defence shows itself as the Jain poet's construction of Buddhism, not the doctrine a Tamil Buddhist text teaches.

note: The couplet says that if the ruler bends justice the sky, bending its rain, will not pour; the summary credits the Pandya land, whose king bent justice in this book, with a sky that never fails to pour new rain.
teaches: Read against the couplet, the summary's line of unfailing rain claims for the Pandya land the very sign the Kural withdraws from a bent sceptre, so the epic's punishment for the bent sceptre falls on the king's own life and the city by fire rather than on the rain, and its stock praise of the land survives the verdict intact.

gains.a: the formula line about rain gains a political charge: under the couplet it is a claim that the king ruled justly, which the book itself has refuted
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which the bent sceptre is answered by a different penalty than drought, the king's death and his city's burning, which limits the couplet's rain as the only sign of misrule

note: 196 asks how perishing can be known if the mind perishes wholly with its objects; 562 asks how a teacher who says nothing stays can establish any thesis, the four truths included.
teaches: Neelakesi uses one argument against momentariness in both debates, first against the knowing of perishing and here against the stating of doctrine, so the self-refutation of the momentary becomes the Neelakesi's standing reply to Buddhism.

note: The first signs, milk that will not set and a weeping bull, come on the morning after Kovalan has been cut down at the king's word.
teaches: Read after the killing, the omens are no forecast but the herd registering a death its keepers have not heard of, so the reader holds the meaning the characters lack.

note: Tirumular says joy and sorrow are settled by former deeds and that those who see their joy and still do not give know no dharma; Manimekalai sees the prosperous enjoying the fruit of dharma sown (108-109) while the hungry stand ragged at their gates.
teaches: A Saiva and a Buddhist text agree that karma explaining who is fed does not excuse withholding, and the epic adds that the giver's own gift is the deed that will return as a means of giving.

gains.a: the unit's view of the rich at their gates is seen to be shared doctrine across the schools, not a Buddhist peculiarity
gains.b: Tirumular's argument gains a case in which the deed of giving returns, the bowl that is the fruit of a past meal

note: In Akananuru 51 the man tells his heart that wealth won by parting is not worth having and he will stay and hold her; in Kalittokai 18 the woman tells him the same and adds that even sharing one cloth, the united live the only true life.
teaches: The case against the wealth journey is made from both sides, and the woman's version goes further by accepting poverty outright, which the man's version never has to face.

note: Tirumular says souls that know what truly is go to grace and release is becoming one with Siva; Neelakesi says understanding the Lord's scripture brings release in due order, with no grace and no union.
teaches: Both put knowledge first, but in the Saiva verse knowledge leads to grace and union with God, while in the Jain verse the Lord gives only the scripture and the soul reaches release by its own understanding.

gains.a: the Jain claim is sharpened by a rival account that needs grace and union where it needs neither
gains.b: the Saiva sequence of knowing, then grace, then union, stands out against a release reached by knowledge without a giver

note: Puram 189 measures every man's need, king or hunter, by one measure of food and two cloths and concludes that wealth's use is giving; Manimekalai tells the king that dharma for all lives is nothing but food, clothing and shelter.
teaches: The Sangam measure of human need, used to tell a rich man to give, becomes the entire content of a king's dharma toward every life, and the king at once extends it to other kingdoms.

gains.a: a Sangam ground for reducing dharma to three material needs, so the definition reads as a measure of need and not a slight on doctrine
gains.b: a widening of its argument: what each person needs becomes what a king owes all lives, in his land and in others'

note: Both put the renouncer in the burning ground with the same verb: காட்டகத் துறைவான் in the Neelakesi, உறைவது காட்டகம் in the Tirumanthiram.
teaches: The burning ground was the renouncer's accepted dwelling across sects, but for Tirumular its dweller is Siva himself, whom renouncers imitate, while the Jain sage enters it as a stranger in a goddess's shrine whose offerings he will end.

gains.a: the sage's choice of dwelling is seen as a recognised mark of the renouncer, not only a test of courage
gains.b: the verse's image of the god in the burning ground is shown claimed by a rival tradition that gives the place no divine owner

note: The couplet says it is not the spear but the unbending sceptre that gives a king victory; Madhavi's paired stanzas say the Kaveri's grace shows first her husband's unbending sceptre, then the strength of his spear.
teaches: The Kural ranks the sceptre above the spear and removes the spear as a cause, while Madhavi's song sets them side by side as equal signs of one prosperous river, so the pair shows the court song keeping the force the ethical couplet sets aside.

gains.a: the stanza's turn from sceptre to spear gains a measure: the Kural shows the spear stanza is the one an ethicist would refuse
gains.b: the couplet gains a contrary witness, a praise-song that will not drop the spear when it praises the just king

note: 349 has rebirth cut only when பற்று is gone. On Parimelazhagar's reading, 506 won't trust anyone without பற்று.
teaches: The same absence is liberation in Aram and a security risk in Porul.

note: The couplet likens a king's killing of the cruel to weeding a crop; the royal bhuta's office is to put down cruel deeds (கொடுந்தொழில் கடிந்து), and the Pandya killed Kovalan as a thief under that office.
teaches: Held together, the two show the licence to kill wrongdoers, which the Pandya invoked, being the very office whose guardian spirit now abandons his city, so the Kural's weeding image is shown to depend on the king knowing which are the weeds.

gains.a: the royal bhuta's charter gains a pointed sense: its duty of putting down the cruel is the duty the Pandya misused
gains.b: the couplet gains its failure case, a king who weeded out an innocent and whose own guardian spirit then left

note: The couplet says nothing shames the tongue more than begging, even water for a cow; Aputtiran, the cow's son, begs from house to house to feed the blind, the deaf and the lame.
teaches: The couplet holds that even the worthiest cause cannot make asking honourable, while the epic makes begging on others' behalf its hero's virtue and the ground of the divine bowl; the conflict depends on reading the couplet's cow example as covering begging for another's need, which it seems to.

gains.a: Aputtiran's begging stands out as a choice made against a known ethic of shame, not mere want.
gains.b: The couplet's limit case meets a story that answers it by honouring a beggar for others' sake.

note: Kaathai 14 says he left his body on Manipallavam with the intent to sustain unappeased lives and arose from a cow's womb in Savakam; here the cause of that womb is that his unwavering heart never let go of the cow that had guarded him (ஒல்கா உள்ளத்து ஒழியான் ஆதலின்).
teaches: Read together, the two passages give rebirth two causes at two levels: compassion for all lives decides the land and the work, while a personal debt of gratitude decides the very mother, so a private bond shapes the birth inside a universal vow.

note: Kovalan's father is introduced as the master of great wealth who pours out his riches for others; in the Manimekalai Manimekalai finds him in a Buddhist monastery (பள்ளி) as one who has taken up great austerity (மா தவம்).
teaches: The merchant whose giving is praised at his son's wedding ends as a renouncer, so the pair traces in one man the passage from the householder's generosity to the renunciation the Manimekalai holds higher.

note: The Kural says one who denies what the world holds to exist will be set down on earth as a demon; the materialist who denies ghosts is named Pisasikan, the ghost's one, and the demoness claims him as son once he takes the dharma.
teaches: The epic plays the couplet's sentence out and reverses its sting: the denier is indeed reckoned of the demons, but as their adopted kin through dharma rather than as an object of scorn.

gains.a: Neelakesi's pun on the name gains a known moral frame, the denier of common belief as a demon among men.
gains.b: The Kural's unnamed 'what the world holds' gets a content, ghosts and rebirth, and a case where the denier is won back rather than condemned.

note: The Kural says pain perishes when the very names of desire, anger and delusion perish; the teacher names the same three, in the same order, as the cause of all he has taught and gives a separate remedy for each.
teaches: The Kural names the three roots and promises the end of pain but gives no method; the epic, using the same three words, assigns each root its own discipline, contemplation of impermanence for desire, friendliness for anger, hearing and reflection for delusion.

gains.a: the Kural's claim that pain ends wholly when even the names of the three go, a stronger end-state than the remedies alone state
gains.b: a separate practice for each of the three, where the couplet says only that they must perish

note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; Neelakesi 147 says souls sunk in the sea of sorrow, born among beasts and in hells, should take refuge in the guileless great one.
teaches: The epic names what the couplet leaves open: the sea is filled with the births of beasts and hells, and the feet are those of the Jina, so a Jain teacher reads the Kural's refuge as his own.

gains.a: the sage's call to refuge gains the Kural's image of crossing, which shows refuge as escape from rebirth
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed Lord is given a sectarian identity and its sea a list of states

note: The Manimekalai's teacher calls 'paddy seed gives paddy sprout' the naya of own-nature; Neelakesi uses the same fact, that paddy gives only paddy, to argue that the Buddha's example proves sameness of kind.
teaches: One observation serves the Buddhist as a law of causes without a self and the Jain as proof of a persisting kind, so the two epics agree on the fact and differ on what it shows.

note: 83 denies that great penance raises the humans of the small islands; 86 says penance frees the humans of the land of deeds.
teaches: Penance is not a power that works anywhere: in this sermon its fruit depends on the land of one's birth, so the same act frees in one land and fails in another.

note: Both list the same abstentions, killing first, then lying and theft; the Siddhar asks the Lord of Chidambaram to grant him a life without them, while the sage tells householders that keeping them wins the world of the gods.
teaches: The same list of abstentions is a gift begged of the Lord in the Siddhar and the householder's own work with a self-acting reward in the Jain sermon, which is the grace-against-effort divide in miniature.

gains.a: the sermon's silent assumption, that the hearer can keep the vows unaided, is brought out by a text that asks for them as grace
gains.b: the Siddhar's petition is seen against a rival ethic that needs no giver for the same virtues

note: Kural 1233: the shoulders that swelled on the day of union now announce loudly that he has gone. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 14: because he is said to be good, her shoulders have forgotten to waste even if he leaves.
teaches: On a plain reading the two make incompatible claims about the same sign: the Kural takes wasting shoulders as the body's certain witness to separation, while the venba says trust in the man's goodness can stop the body from giving that witness at all.

note: The couplet calls taking bad even if it were a good path and giving good even without heaven; Manimekalai cites the learned that for an alms-seeker both taking and giving are duty, and going to give is better still.
teaches: The couplet's flat ranking of giving over taking leaves no place for the mendicant, while the epic makes taking a duty when it serves giving, so the beggar's bowl is let in under the couplet's rule rather than condemned by it.

gains.a: Her maxim gains a sharp statement of the view it must answer: that taking is bad whatever the path.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case it does not cover, the one who takes only in order to give.

note: The preface says Senguttuvan, son of the Chola Manakkilli, felled Pazhaiyan's neem and made nine heirs of the Chola house fall at the gate; Maadalan praises him for destroying the nine umbrellas that would not bear his cousin Killi's young rule and for felling Pazhaiyan's neem.
teaches: Read together, the preface's nine Chola kin felled at the gate are given a cause in the epic, a war over the succession of a young Chola who was the Chera's cousin through his Chola mother, so the Sangam list of victories becomes a family quarrel among the crowned houses.

gains.a: Maadalan's allusions gain the record of the same deeds and of the Chola mother that explains the word மைத்துனன்
gains.b: the preface's bare list gains a reason for the war on the nine and a sense of why a Chera would fight in Chola affairs

note: The Kural says pain perishes when the names of desire, anger and confusion perish; the Neelakesi names anger, pride, deceit and attachment as the very pains of the unrestrained.
teaches: Both make the passions the root of suffering, but they count them differently: the Kural's three (desire, anger, confusion) against the Jain four (anger, pride, deceit, attachment), so pride and deceit, absent from the couplet, are for the Jain teacher as basic as anger.

gains.a: the Jain list is seen against an older Tamil triad and shows what it adds, pride and deceit
gains.b: the couplet's triad is shown to be one count among rival counts of the passions, not the only Tamil one

note: The Udayana Kumara Kaviyam tells how Yugi, feigning madness and sense by turns, passed along the great streets with crowds about him to the prison where the Vatsa king was held; the Manimekalai likens the crowd's pity for Manimekalai with her bowl in the great street to the pity felt for Yugi's feigned sickness when he freed the Vatsa king.
teaches: The simile reads the nun's garb as a disguise like Yugi's, pitied by onlookers yet hiding a purpose of release, and the later Jain epic's street scene shows the crowd and the prison that the Manimekalai's one-line allusion assumes its hearers know.

note: Kural 218 says the discerning do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even without means; the Innaa line counts a man without wealth desiring to be liberal as painful. Not a tension on our reading: the Innaa line names a cost, not a fault.
teaches: The pair shows the pain hidden inside the Kural's praise: giving steadily in want is admirable, and the wish to give without means is also an ache.

note: Kural 230 says death is sweet when one can no longer give; Neelakesi 218 says a death known to achieve nothing is no virtue, and draws the wife on the pyre as the absurd consequence.
teaches: The Kural's rank of giving above life is hyperbole about value; the Jain argument shows where taking it literally leads, and limits the praise of self-loss to a death that does something.

gains.a: the epic's limit on self-sacrifice is seen answering a Tamil maxim that ranks giving above living
gains.b: the couplet's hyperbole is shown needing a boundary once epics told of givers who literally died

note: In the Purananuru poem the bard hears the noise of eating (ஊணொலி அரவம்) at Pannan's house and asks where the house of the physician of hunger (பசிப்பிணி மருத்துவன்) is; the epic closes with the same noise of eating (ஊண் ஒலி அரவத்து ஒலி, 97) at the public hall, after Kayasandigai has called Manimekalai physician of life (மருத்துவி, 15).
teaches: The epic borrows the Sangam scene of the hunger-healer's feast word for word but moves it from a patron's house, reached by a bard's praise, to a public hall with a gate open to all where anyone who will receive is called in.

gains.a: the epic scene gains a Sangam lineage: the girl with the bowl takes the old title of physician of hunger and the very sound of the patron's feast
gains.b: the poem's question of where the healer's house is, near or far, gains an answer the Sangam world lacked: a public hall that needs no patron and no praise-song

claims.gist: lifeless things such as hide also shrink and change, so wilting does not prove that plants live
craving, clinging and becoming are the fault and the deed within the course of feeling
the gods are five classes of embodied beings, the Bhavana gods being ten in kind
karma is of eight kinds and is burned away by the ascetic
qualities such as colour are the substance itself
a quality changes while its substance remains, so the two are not identical
trees are among the fixed beings, as common usage itself says
the Buddha's scripture, its meaning and his conduct are free of fault
a prince's death is honourable only when he dies guarding his own land or seizing another's
imprisonment does not befit one who has turned to wisdom and given up youth's pleasures
a thing taken apart from its qualities could never appear
the Buddha's gifts in former births of his eyes, body, wife, child and land prove his compassion
a power passes from one moment of the aggregates to the next
such a power is either a sixth thing beyond the five aggregates or there is total destruction
the formless unmanifest cause brings forth the world with form
what is formless cannot produce gross things with form
a woman's beauty is not in the body itself, since lovers, ascetics and jackals see the same body as different things
meat is pure for a monk when three conditions show it was not killed for him
the eater who neither kills nor sells still shares the killing, like a middleman who profits from both sides
hell-beings are neuter and know no pleasure of union
a teacher's instruction, like a physician's, finds the disease, its root and its fitting medicine
the gods grant boons to those who ask
no being within the world-system, god or Brahma, can give back a departed life
sound belongs to space
sound has form and so cannot belong to formless space
a hard deed brings its fruit back on the doer, so one should leave the ways of harm
the learned do not despair when they eat the fruit of their deeds, while the unlearned are bewildered by it
the pains of parting, union and desire belong to those joined with women, not to the strong who live alone
those who hold women and food to be pleasure meet a suffering they did not reckon on
if the doer gets no fruit, the Bodhisattva's self-giving in former births gained him nothing
the soul is only apparently modified, as crystal takes the colour of what is beside it
the crystal image explains only an appearance and does not say what the one soul is
the king's protection is the only fence a woman left alone needs
a king of the true line punishes his own body for a fault against his subjects
the Lord is the one free of rebirth who has gained endless knowledge and is worshipped by the twelve assemblies
when the ruler's sceptre swerves, the planets leave their course, rain fails and living beings perish
a king keeps the standing of being the life of all beings only while his rule holds them alive
to set desire on a woman who has taken up tapas is a wrongful intent a ruler must give up
if the robe brought release, release would come without knowledge
the robe has a small use: it lets the monk's form be known
substance, quality and action have one reality
meditating on the feet of the compassionate lord dispels darkness
of the four states of birth, the human's suffering is partly the fruit of lacking restraint and partly common to all
the Buddha destroyed fault, curbed hatred, knew all things fully and is the first
the Buddha passed beyond Kama and is a refuge
the quality of one thing passes into another, as heated water takes on fire's heat
the omniscient one's knowledge of all things is not acquired by hearing or learning
only the five aggregates are real, and space is no entity
the soul is only a name for the union of the aggregates
if the self is only a name, the title Buddha names no one who awoke
an effect is of the same kind as its cause, so formless awareness cannot come from elements with form
covering the body is a sign of an unfirm mind; restraint lies in guarding the eyes, which disturb the mind
the Vyantara gods are of eight kinds
the place of the released is known from scripture, as the Buddha himself named six destinies
when a king's sceptre bends or a judge leans to one side, the wrong is such that even a statue weeps
since the Lord's teaching is truth, the categories and their workings stand without error
a cruel deed done for the sake of the one served is not shielded by him
a violent deed keeps its strong karma even when done out of love of dharma
the karma of a deed returns on its doer in a later birth

note: Fragment 1 says enemies cannot escape except by heaping rare jewels with elephants and speaking submissively (யானையொ(டு) அரும்கலம் ... பணிந்துவழி மொழிதல்); Akananuru 124 opens with the same formula (நன்கலம் களிற்றொடு ... வணங்கினர், வழிமொழிந்து) as the condition on which a soldier waiting in camp may go home to his wife.
teaches: The submission the praise poet demands as the enemy's only course is, in the akam poem, the event a homesick soldier waits for, so the formula of tribute served both genres and the end of the king's war was imagined from the camp as the start of a lover's return.

note: Sivavakkiyar uses the banyan folded in its own seed as the image of Parabrahman grown within a man; Neelakesi mocks the tall palm said to be already in its seed.
teaches: The tree-in-the-seed image that a Siddhar offers as an insight was, for a Jain debater, the weak point of the doctrine that effects pre-exist, so one image carries a mystic's claim and a logician's refutation.

gains.a: the epic's reductio is shown to bear on a living image of Tamil devotion, not only on a school's technical thesis
gains.b: the Siddhar's image meets an objection it never answers: if the tree is in the seed, why is the hand that holds the seed not holding a tree

note: 295 says that without dharma and adharma the room of souls and matter would spill past the world's edge; 759 says space itself runs on through the world into the non-world.
teaches: Read together, the two verses show why the Jain account needs a limit beyond space: space has no edge, so the world's bound must come from the conditions of motion and rest.

note: Aputhiran lets the bowl go into the Gomukhi pool to rise one day a year into the hands of one who wears compassion and dharma; in kaathai 11 it rises from Gomukhi into Manimekalai's hands as she circles the pool with Deepatilakai.
teaches: The receiving scene is the fulfilment of a test set by the bowl's first owner, so the bowl's coming to Manimekalai is a verdict on her compassion as well as a gift.

note: In 243 Neelakesi charges that the bodhisattva gave away his wives and took that as dharma; in 398 the narrator names the Buddhist debater as great in the dharma that gives away women.
teaches: A charge made once in argument has become the narrator's standing epithet for the Buddhist side, so the poem's narration takes Neelakesi's part even in describing the speaker.

note: Mokkalan demands that substance and quality be declared either one or different; the Manimekalai's teacher gives a naya of oneness and a naya of difference as two valid ways of seeing cause and effect.
teaches: Mokkalan's either-or is stricter than the Buddhist doctrine the Manimekalai sets out, which itself allows a thing to be viewed as one with its cause under one naya and as different under another, close to the Jain answer he rejects.

note: The patikam's morals are that dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship and that an old deed comes to make its doer eat its fruit; the blessing names the old deed as the cause of her suffering and hails the king dharma killed.
teaches: The closing blessing keeps both of the patikam's causes but changes the moral's tone: the king to whom dharma became death is not left as a warning but praised with his whole line, because he died of it.

note: The third kaathai says a sage's curse on Indra's son and a celestial woman was lifted at the dance stage, and introduces Madhavi; here a celestial dancer is cursed to earth for failing before Indra, and Madhavi is of her line.
teaches: Madhavi's art is given a heavenly genealogy rooted in a fall: the courtesan's dancing on earth is the continuation of a curse that her first performance was said to end.

note: Kovalan reports a Madurai free of evil whose kings' sceptre is straight (கோலின் செம்மை, தீதுதீர் மதுரை); the Pandya, after killing him, declares himself the thief and his guarding failed.
teaches: The straightness of the Pandya sceptre is first vouched for by the man it will kill, on the day before his death, so the epic lets the victim's trust in the city's justice set the measure by which the king condemns himself.

note: Purananuru 43 praises a Chola as descendant of the king of limitless giving who entered the scales to save a dove from a hawk; Neelakesi says no living person asks for another's flesh, eyes or head.
teaches: The gift of one's own flesh to a creature in distress, a dynastic boast in Sangam praise and a credential of compassion for the Buddhist, is denied any worth by the Jain debater's test of need, so Tamil tradition did not hold it as a settled virtue.

gains.a: the debater's objection is seen to reject a gift that Tamil royal praise held up as the summit of bounty
gains.b: the poem's ancestral boast is shown to have met a reasoned challenge in a later work

note: The sermon's hell names 'the sin of eating flesh' beside 'the sin of killing'; in 163 Neelakesi's first charge against the Buddha's way is that he does not call eating flesh a fault.
teaches: The hell scene supplies the doctrinal ground for the first debate: because eating is a sin apart from killing, a school that permits meat not killed by the eater stands accused before any metaphysics is argued.

note: The Kural says the king who does justice and protects is set apart as இறை for the people; Senguttuvan says birth into a line that guards the people is suffering and nothing to be revered.
teaches: Read with தொழுதக as 'worthy of reverence', the two judge the same office oppositely: the couplet awards the protector divine standing, while the epic king, speaking after a just king's fall, denies that the office deserves reverence at all.

gains.a: the lament gains a sharp opposite: the standard honour of the just king that it refuses
gains.b: the couplet's conditional honour gains the view from inside the office, where the same duty of protection is felt as fear and suffering

note: The quatrain calls good and bad caste mere words and makes lineage depend on austerity, learning and effort; Aputtiran cites the brahmins' own seers born of cow, deer, tiger and jackal.
teaches: The quatrain denies birth rank from outside by naming what truly makes a line, while Aputtiran denies it from inside the brahmins' tradition, so the critique becomes a charge of inconsistency rather than a rival standard.

gains.a: Aputtiran's retort is given the general principle that his examples only imply.
gains.b: The quatrain's bare assertion gains an argument that defenders of birth rank cannot dismiss as foreign to their own books.

note: The Vedic logician lists eight false semblances of knowledge, errors of seeing and remembering; the Buddhist teacher ends with the semblances of inference, errors in a stated proof.
teaches: The two catalogues of error divide the ground differently: the logician locates falsehood in a mistaken cognition, the Buddhist teacher in a badly built argument, which can be checked rule by rule.

note: Kannaki says that if she is truly a pathini she will not let the king and Madurai live; the city's housewives, keepers of household dharma, declare her breast-battle no cruelty and worship the fire.
teaches: Her conditional oath is answered not by a god but by the wives of the city she burns, so her standing as a pathini is confirmed by the very household virtue she claimed.

note: In the Manimekalai the materialist answers the question whether some have known a former birth by saying that the minds of those deluded by a god or by dreams are changed and such knowledge is mere doubt; in the last kaathai of the Silappathikaram former births are shown through a god possessing a woman and a sprinkled water, before a king's whole court.
teaches: The materialist's objection names exactly the means the Silappathikaram uses to prove former birth, a god's possession, so the sister epic records the reply a sceptic would make to this scene, and the scene offers as public proof what that sceptic rejects as the delusion of the possessed.

note: Manimekalai asks the materialist whether some have not known a former birth, and he waves it off as the delusion of dreams or possession; Neelakesi points instead to the newborn seeking the breast.
teaches: Set beside the Manimekalai, the Jain choice of evidence shows its point: an infant's instinct cannot be dismissed as dream or a god's delusion, the very escape the materialist used against memory of past births.

note: The beaten Aryan kings escaped as ascetics and as dancers (ஆடு கூத்தர்) in a changed guise (விச்சைக் கோலம்); Maadalan tells their conqueror that the soul too is like dancers who change their கோலம்.
teaches: The kings' change of costume to save their lives, mocked by the king's rivals, returns in the sermon as the image of every soul's passage from body to body, so the mockery of the disguised kings recoils on the mocker.

note: 445 defines the Lord by the burning of the eightfold seeds; 458 uses the burnt seed that never sprouts to explain why the released soul is never reborn yet remains.
teaches: The same image does two jobs: first it defines what made the Jina Lord, then it answers whether release is extinction, so the seed shows that what is destroyed is karma while the soul persists.

note: Kovalan tamed a rogue elephant that had seized an old Brahmin; his daughter's pursuer Udayakumaran tames his own elephant gone mad in Puhar.
teaches: The father's deed of rescue returns as the prince's feat of strength on his way to chase the daughter, so the same heroic act is shown serving compassion once and desire the second time.

note: Tirumular keeps the body because without it true knowledge cannot be won; Neelakesi cites as common knowledge that the body lives by food and awareness by the body.
teaches: The same chain, food to body to knowledge, serves opposite ends: Tirumular uses it to justify cultivating the body, while Neelakesi uses it to say the renouncer needs food and nothing more.

gains.a: Neelakesi's proverb is shown to be a premise other traditions also build on, not her private argument
gains.b: Tirumular's case for nurturing the body is shown limited by a rival use of the same premise, where it licenses only bare food

note: In the Silappathikaram Kannaki says she raged at the city as one without fault (சீறினேன் குற்றமிலேன்) and the fire god burns Madurai at her command; in the Manimekalai the same Kannaki says she destroyed the city in anger (சீற்றம் கொண்டு ... சிதைத்தேன்) and calls it the sin of murderous anger, whose fruit awaits her.
teaches: The two epics judge the same act in the same woman's words in opposite ways: the earlier makes the burning the faultless power of chastity, the later makes it a sinful deed that will ripen, and the conflict turns on whether provoked anger can be free of karmic fruit.

note: The Siddhar verse names the Lord as the one who opened his fire-eye and burned Kama; the Neelakesi's hymn says the sage in anger reduced Ananga to white ash.
teaches: A Jain hymn takes the Saiva god's signature deed and gives it to a human ascetic, so the victory over desire that the Saiva texts reserve for the Lord is claimed as something a man achieves by penance.

gains.a: the Jain epithet is seen as a borrowing from the Saiva stock of praise, pointed against it
gains.b: the Siddhar's image of the Lord is shown contested by a school that gives his deed to the ascetic

note: In Puhar's festival warriors set their own heads on the altar praying that the offering be a bulwark of the king's strength, and the narrator does not judge it; Champapathi says lives have been given for kings, yet the burning ground holds a thousand kings' shrines.
teaches: On the plainer reading of lines 164 to 166, the second epic denies what the first epic's rite assumes, that a life given for the king protects him, and it does so in the same city.

note: Purananuru 66 praises Karikal Valavan's victory at Venni but says the defeated king who fasted to death for shame at his back wound is better than he; the epic's Valavan is checked by no rival, only by the Himalaya.
teaches: The Purananuru sets a moral limit on the victor through the vanquished man's honour, while the epic removes every human limit and lets only a mountain halt him, so the later memory of the Chola has lost the Sangam poet's check on royal glory.

gains.a: the epic's war-lust with no rival left gains a contrast that shows what its praise omits
gains.b: the poem's lesson that the defeated may be the better man gains a later portrait in which no such man remains

note: Paripadal 5.9 names the split hill only by its crane name (குருகொடு பெயர் பெற்ற மால் வரை); Thiruppugazh 38 names it க்ரவுஞ்சம் and has it split together with the drying of the sea.
teaches: The Sangam poet renders the Sanskrit name Krauncha by its Tamil meaning, a hill named with the crane, while Arunagirinathar uses the Sanskrit name outright, so the pair shows the same deed passing from a translated to a borrowed name across a thousand years.

note: The couplet says the sweet words of women who seek a man's wealth and not his love bring him harm; here a courtesan writes to a man who has lost his wealth, asking only what her fault was, and he judges her blameless and himself at fault.
teaches: The pair sets the Kural's rule that a courtesan's sweet words are for wealth against a courtesan's letter written after the wealth is gone, so the epic tests the rule on the one case it cannot explain and has the man himself withdraw the charge.

gains.a: Kovalan's verdict that Madhavi is faultless gains force from the rule it overturns: he clears her against the expected judgment of her class
gains.b: the couplet gains its limit case, a courtesan whose plea comes when the man has nothing left to give

note: The hymn in the Kundalakesi sarukkam says the Lord never says 'I will speak' yet has a voice like a drum, and has no mind to harm; the Ajivika holds that a knower who speaks falls into longing and anger.
teaches: The hymn's paradox of a Lord who speaks without willing to speak turns out to be the Jain answer to the Ajivika's dilemma, so a line that reads as devotion is doctrine aimed at this debate.

note: Kural 226 says relieving the destroying hunger of the destitute is where one with wealth should store it; the verse says that if one gives, one should give food.
teaches: The couplet says where wealth is best stored and the verse which gift is best, so together food given to the hungry is both the best gift and the safest store.

note: The Kural calls the tie of body and life a friendship that ends as a bird leaves its nest; the Neelakesi's sage knows a scripture that cuts the deeds entangled in the soul's oneness with and difference from the body.
teaches: Set beside the Kural, the Jain verse turns the body-soul tie from a bond death simply ends into a knot of deeds that a discipline can cut while one still lives.

gains.a: the sage's knowledge is placed against the Tamil commonplace of body and life as passing companions
gains.b: the couplet's bird-and-nest friendship gains a doctrinal account of what holds the two together

note: Kural 380 says nothing is stronger than oozh, which arrives before any device; Kannaki blames the strong deed that pressed on her but also names herself the woman of cruel deeds.
teaches: Kannaki grants karma the force the couplet gives oozh yet keeps the burning of Madurai as her own act, so the epic holds fate and the agent's deed together where the couplet speaks only of fate's priority.

gains.a: her double phrase (வல்வினை, கடுவினையேன்) is set against a flat statement of fate's power, which brings out that she does not hide behind it
gains.b: the couplet's abstract fate is shown working through a person who still owns what she did

note: The couplet says a wife who worships her husband rather than a god can bid the rain fall; Kavunthi calls Kannaki a deity fairer than any she has seen and quotes a saying that where chaste wives live the sky never fails and kings' victory never decays.
teaches: Where the couplet keeps the wife below the gods yet gives her command of the rain, Kavunthi makes the chaste wife herself the deity and extends her power from rain to the king's victory, which is the very extension the epic will turn against the Pandya when that power destroys his city.

gains.a: Kavunthi's saying gains a source for its rain clause in a couplet that ties the wife's power to her refusal of other gods
gains.b: the couplet gains a reading in which the chaste wife's power reaches past nature to the fortunes of kings, and so becomes a threat as well as a blessing

note: Both speakers refuse to be swayed by praise of a woman's beauty because they have seen bones in the burning ground: the Naladiyar's speaker has seen the scattered teeth, the Neelakesi's sage lives among the bones.
teaches: The quatrain's resolve rests on having once seen the burning ground; the sage's rests on dwelling there, so the pair shows the same defence held as a memory and as a way of life.

gains.a: the sage's boast gains the quatrain's precise point that beauty praised as jasmine and pearl ends as scattered teeth
gains.b: the quatrain's resolve is shown put to a real test, a supernatural temptress who chose the burning ground's own sage

note: In 203 Neelakesi told Kundalakesi that a power passing between moments is either a sixth thing beyond the five aggregates or total destruction; here she tells the Buddha the lac is a further thing, and the aggregates have none.
teaches: The same dilemma defeats the disciple's power and the teacher's lac, which shows Neelakesi's case is one argument: every Buddhist carrier of karma is either a soul under another name or nothing.

note: Kural 350 bids one cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging in order to let clinging go; the two Naga kings, unable to let go of their great attachment to the seat each calls 'ours', stop their war when the great sage calls it 'ours' and preaches from it.
teaches: The couplet's paradox, giving up attachment by attaching to the unattached one, is staged as a scene: the sage does not tell the kings to own nothing but sets his own claim, 'this is ours', in place of theirs, and their war ends because a claim of the one without clinging displaces a claim of clinging.

gains.a: a doctrinal key to why the sage answers the kings with the very words of possession they used, instead of a call to give the seat up
gains.b: a concrete case of the clinging the couplet means (kin kings at war over an object neither can lift) and of the moment the substituted clinging takes hold

note: A Kundalakesi fragment praises a man who stood unmoved, saying all that had befallen him was the fruit of deeds; Neelakesi cites that same Buddhist tenet to argue the Buddha's sufferings were his own karma.
teaches: A tenet shared by both schools, that suffering ripens from one's own deeds, cuts against the Buddhist claim that the teacher suffered for others.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher says the mind arises like lightning (சித்தம் உற்பவித்தது மின்போல்); Neelakesi asks how, if the mind perishes wholly with what it knew, its perishing could be known.
teaches: The Buddhist offers the lightning-flash mind as a manner of speaking about what has no lasting being, while the Jain treats it as a claim about a knower and asks who is left to witness the flash's end.

note: The decade's preface lists among Senguttuvan's deeds that he sought the stone of the goddess-pathini (கடவுள் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள்) and bathed in the Ganga; the epic opens this kaathai with the same phrase and the same river.
teaches: Set beside the preface, the epic's நீர்ப்படை is seen to rest on a Chera tradition that already called the pathini a goddess and joined her stone to the Ganga, and the epic's contribution is the story that makes her one: who she was and why a king would march north for her.

gains.a: the bathing gains outside witness: a Chera praise tradition that names the pathini's stone among the king's conquests
gains.b: the bare line of the preface gains the woman behind the title and the reason the stone was wanted

note: Lines 66-67 repeat the formula of Madhavi's training (பதினோர் ஆடலும் ... விதிமாண் கொள்கையின் விளங்க) from the third kaathai, now as the dances a heavenly watcher sees her perform.
teaches: The repeated formula marks what was learned as a girl's curriculum turning into a public festival performance watched even by beings of the sky.

note: In 313 Neelakesi rejects the Buddhist rule that sin joins only where there is intention, using meat-eating; in 595 she argues in general that wherever mind is there action is, so action cannot be left out of karma.
teaches: The particular quarrel over the meat-eater's guilt rests on a general thesis about intention and act, which the Jain debater states only when she faces the Buddha himself.

note: 39 says only what flows from virtue is pleasure, so virtue is the source. 760 makes rightly made wealth the ground from which virtue and pleasure both come easily.
teaches: The order of the three aims differs by book.

note: At 59 she takes the form of the princess Kamalekai to tempt the sage; at 134 she casts off that illusory form, takes her own, and asks pardon as a demon.
teaches: The disguise put on to break his vow is the first thing she gives up, so conversion begins with the end of deception and confession of her real nature, before any doctrine is taken.

claims.gist: the Buddha taught ten perfections, from giving and conduct to strength and knowledge
right knowledge is faultless knowing of the real categories beginning with the soul
the omniscient Lord stays silent, since speaking would draw him back into the round of births
food given to a holy one does not go to waste but will in time cut off the giver's rebirths
a love carried over from a former birth can waste the merit one has earned, as seed is lost on saline ground
birth is the ground of disease and dharma is the medicine that cuts it
desire confuses even the gods
evil deeds lead to birth as beasts, hell-beings and ghosts, and avoiding them leads to birth as gods, men and Brahmas
none escape painful birth except those who hear the dharma of the all-knowing one who is to come
dharma must be practised before death, which cannot be turned back, arrives
a king's power, however great, must not scorn the path of dharma
the person pervades the whole world, and primal nature lasts
qualities and actions are other than the substance that has them
a soul without knowing of its own would be no different from a corpse
one reborn can show his kin what he hid in a former life
there is no soul in any form
monks cultivate friendliness toward all beings
one who meditates on friendliness toward beings and then eats their flesh acts like a madman
there is no doer apart from the doing
whatever has arisen will perish
whether a dead man is reborn depends on whether he has ended clinging
chaste wives whose merit brings rain themselves worship the wife whom fire would not burn
quality and qualified substance are both different and one, and holding both is no contradiction
the soul has bodily form
what has form can be cut into parts and destroyed
the Buddhist book secretly allows one disguised in purity to frequent courtesans unpunished
all things are impermanent
those who teach impermanence while building great dwellings belie their teaching
anger, pride, deceit and attachment are themselves the suffering of the unrestrained, as well as the door to evil deeds
a meeting with a holy man is the fruit of one's own good deeds
there are two kinds of soul, and action comes from the soul bound with deeds
to take captive in war those who fled the field in the guise of non-killers is no victory
the Buddha in a former life gave away his own wife and toiled only for others
the one who eats flesh, not only the one who kills, incurs evil karma
worshipping a relic of the Buddha's body, on hearing his story, becomes merit later
if acts toward a body that one did not make bear fruit, killing and eating also bear fruit
on the Buddhist account a deed cannot be joined to its fruit
a gift to a holy man in a former birth ripens as a means of giving in this one
the prosperous enjoy the fruit of dharma sown before
the bowl yields only for those who feed out of compassion, with dharma as witness
a thing that both lasts and changes, and is one and different in different respects, escapes the faults of either one-sided view
harm a god who is all things does to beings is harm without reason done to himself
reality is set out in six categories: substance, quality, action, generality, particularity and inherence
fixing the heart on the hill god's feet, not on the pools' boons, brings the joy that ends sorrow
seed and lac are each made of eight material constituents
the guileless great one is the refuge of all beings, freeing souls from the births of beasts and hells and giving the high state
adharma is the medium of rest as dharma is of motion, not the cause that makes things stay
if the persisting material makes things the same, mixtures with other matter would share each other's nature
scent passes because pot and flower are present together
the perishing of one moment and the birth of the next are not simultaneous, so nothing joins them
to die in vain, knowing nothing will come of it, is the excellence of the Bodhisattvas

note: Kural 256 argues that no one would sell flesh if no one killed to eat; 260 presses the same point against a Buddhist who says he only eats what another killed.
teaches: The Kural's demand argument is put to work against a named defence, the eater's pure intention, and becomes a claim about karma: the buyer's deed joins the butcher's.

gains.a: the retort to the monk gets a general reason why eating implies killing, which the verse only asserts
gains.b: the couplet's abstract buyer is given a real opponent, a monk who claims his mind keeps him clean

note: Kannaki's left eye throbs at the festival; in Kaathai 9 a servant announces that Kovalan has come home.
teaches: The good omen is fulfilled in Kovalan's return, but the return leads at once to the journey to Madurai, so the sign of reunion is also the first step toward his death.

note: Both picture life in a house: the Kural asks whether life, a lodger in the body, has no home of its own; the Neelakesi's sage likens beings across the states of birth to people who live together in one house and do not fear each other.
teaches: The same lodging image serves the Kural to make the soul homeless and the Jain sage to make all souls housemates, so it can teach unrest or fearlessness depending on whether one looks at one body or at all lives.

gains.a: the sage's housemates image is seen to rework a known Tamil figure of the soul as a lodger
gains.b: the couplet's lonely lodger gains a counter-image in which every being shares the house

note: Both praise the Chola land of Puhar through its water; the Pattinappalai grants that the sky may fail and makes the Kaveri the river that never fails, while the epic's summary sets the divine Kaveri beside a sky that itself never fails (பொய்யா வானம்).
teaches: The Sangam poem rests Puhar's plenty on the river precisely because the sky can fail, and the epic's summary removes that concession, making the sky unfailing too in a line it reuses unchanged for the Pandya land, so the pair shows a Puhar-specific boast about the Kaveri turning into a stock praise that any crowned line receives.

gains.a: the summary's unfailing sky gains a point of contrast: in the older praise of the same city it was the river, not the sky, that could be trusted
gains.b: the Pattinappalai's claim about the Kaveri gains a later form in which the river's distinction has been levelled into a formula shared by the three kingdoms

note: Kural 255 says hell does not open its mouth to release one who eats flesh; 473 says the Buddha, by permitting flesh, will lead himself and his disciples into the burning hell.
teaches: The Kural's hell takes the single eater; the Jain polemic widens it to a teacher and his whole following, so a permission given in doctrine becomes a collective path to hell.

gains.a: the ironic praise of the Buddha's 'kindness' gets the Kural's plain sentence on where flesh-eating leads
gains.b: the couplet's punishment is shown to reach the teacher who permits as well as the one who eats

note: The Kural makes the herdsman's flute evening's envoy and killing weapon; Madhavi's heroine says evening has struck the fishers' palai and bids it, if so skilled in melody, take her life.
teaches: In both the music of dusk is the instrument that kills the parted woman, but in the epic the song is sung on a yazh by a musician, so the deadly melody of evening is the singer's own art turned on herself.

gains.a: the epic stanza gains a precedent for evening's music as a weapon, which explains why the singer offers her life to a melody
gains.b: the couplet's image gains a second landscape, the fishers' shore in place of the herders' pasture, and a singer who is herself the musician

note: Thirikadugam 36 names among the self-deceived the one who eats flesh and claims compassion and the one who says the deed is done without his consent; 474 answers that defence with the middleman who profits from a trade he does not perform.
teaches: The Thirikadugam only lists the excuse 'it was not done with my consent'; the Neelakesi gives the reason it fails, since the eater stands to the killing as a middleman to a sale, profiting from both sides.

gains.a: the attack on the monk's threefold excuse is shown to be a known type of self-deception in the ethical manuals
gains.b: the verse's bare list gets an argument and a target, the Buddhist rule of meat not killed for the eater

note: At the end of the Kaanal Vari the narrator says Kovalan let go of Madhavi because his ஊழ்வினை rose to bear fruit (line 289); here the same departure is recalled as Kovalan sulking and leaving without union (கோவலன் ஊடக் கூடாது ஏகிய).
teaches: One act is given two causes a kaathai apart, past karma ripening and a lover's pique, so the epic's fate does not replace Kovalan's own temper but works through it.

note: Kural 221 defines giving as giving to those who have nothing; Neelakesi 214 argues that a gift of flesh or an eye cannot become the receiver's and so fills no lack.
teaches: The Kural fixes a gift's worth by the receiver's want; the debate adds that the gift must also be usable by the receiver, which rules out the heroic gifts of the body.

gains.a: the Jain objection gains a recognised Tamil definition of giving to argue from
gains.b: the couplet's want-based test is extended to what is given, not only to whom

note: Maadalan reports that Kovalan's father, grieving, gave great gifts and renounced in Puhar's Indra viharas before the sky-walkers; in the Manimekalai the same man, in a Vanji monastery likened to an Indra vihara of sky-walkers, gives his own reason.
teaches: The Silappathikaram tells his renunciation as a grief-driven act seen from outside; the sequel gives it from inside as doctrine, home as illusion and wealth and body as passing, so one renunciation is told first as a mourning and then as a conversion.

note: 739 says a land that makes you labour for riches is no land. 619 says bodily labour pays its wage even where the divine does not help.
teaches: The ideal of the place and the ethic of the person pull in opposite directions.

note: The Naladiyar's wife sets her ever-renewed shyness against women who join many chests for wealth; the Valayapathi says those women serve their payers like பத்தினிப் பெண்டிர்.
teaches: Together they put the difference between wife and courtesan not in the service given, which the fragment says can look the same, but in what the Naladiyar's wife names: a shyness that never wears off and a bond that wealth did not buy.

note: Against Kundalakesi, Neelakesi folded feeling, perception and volition into knowing; against the Buddha she folds feeling into activity.
teaches: The Jain reply to the five aggregates is the same in both debates: reduce them until only knowing and form remain, which is the Jain pair of soul and non-soul.

note: In 134 Neelakesi likens the sage to a mother who nurses her infant even when it hurts her, and drops her false form; in 891 and 892 she, the demoness, calls herself a mother to the frightened Pisasikan and makes him kin through dharma.
teaches: The work closes its debates by repeating its opening conversion one step down: the demoness who was mothered into dharma now mothers a man into it, so conversion is shown as a lineage passed on.

note: Both epics answer a materialist who accepts only perception: Manimekalai shows him that he knows his own parents only by inference; Neelakesi grants his rule and gives him a perception, the sight of a ghost.
teaches: The Buddhist and the Jain epic meet the same Lokayata rule in opposite ways: one turns the rule against itself and leaves the materialist answered, the other satisfies the rule and leaves him converted.

note: The Patitruppattu preface to the fifth decade lists among Senguttuvan's deeds that he went for a stone for the goddess Pattini and bathed it in the Ganges; the epic shows him choosing the Himalaya stone over the one from Pothiyil.
teaches: The preface records the stone as one conquest among many, while the epic gives its reason, a king's honour that refuses the near southern stone, so the pairing shows the pathini's cult being written into the Chera king's record of war.

gains.a: the king's resolve gains independent witness that the stone for Pattini belonged to the tradition of Senguttuvan's deeds
gains.b: the preface's bare phrase கடவுள் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள் gains a scene, a debate over which stone and why

note: In the Vazhakkurai the queen trembles and falls at the dying king's feet; Saathan reports that she resolved to go where the king went and died with him.
teaches: The scene of the verdict leaves the queen's end open, and the report to another court completes it as a chosen death, which is what lets the Chera queen weigh her against Kannaki in the next units.

note: The couplet says that without rain neither giving nor austerity lasts; the ascetic reports that Kanchi's ascetics, finding no almsgivers in the drought, have left for Vanji.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's rule as a chain: the drought ends giving first, and austerity, which lives on gifts, then has to leave the land.

gains.a: the monks' migration gains a stated principle that explains why drought drives out ascetics
gains.b: the couplet gains the mechanism it leaves implicit, that austerity fails because giving fails

note: Madhavi's line is traced to heavenly women freed from a sage's curse, shared with Indra's son, at the place of the talaikkol; the talaikkol staff she later receives is worshipped as Jayanta, Indra's son.
teaches: The staff of honour Madhavi wins is the figure of the curse's release that her own descent goes back to, so her investiture re-enacts that release at the very moment she enters the bond that will undo Kovalan.

note: Both epics give the materialist the liquor figure for awareness arising in combined elements; Manimekalai's lets awareness die like a drum's sound, Neelakesi's sends each element back to its kind and counts space among five elements.
teaches: The liquor analogy was the stock materialist argument in both traditions, but only the Jain epic answers it on its own terms (866, 868), while Manimekalai leaves the doctrine and attacks only its theory of knowledge.

note: At 55 the narrator tells how her terrors of elephant, tiger and lion failed to frighten him and she gave up; at 137 she herself sings that he stayed unshaken when she made the forest rise against him.
teaches: The failed assault becomes, in the attacker's own mouth, a title of praise, so the story's earlier defeat is retold as the ground of her devotion.

note: In the Silappathikaram the Bhuta of the crossroads nooses and devours unchaste women who hide their wrong and men who desire others' wives; here the same Bhuta tells Maruthi its noose will not bind her and that it acts only after the king's seven days.
teaches: Read together, the two show the spirit's justice as a reserve behind the king's: it binds the hidden offender, spares the woman who was only desired, and waits seven days for the king to punish the man before acting itself.

note: The patikam's third moral is that the former deed comes in wrath and makes one eat it; the goddess says ஊழ்வினை came to her king as well as to Kannaki's husband.
teaches: The patikam keeps karma for the story's sufferers and the death-dealing dharma for the king, but the goddess applies ஊழ்வினை to the king himself, so the first and third morals meet in one person.

note: Verse 1 offers the book as rain that ends a great famine; the payiram calls the author's hand rain that ends the famine of not learning.
teaches: Together they show the famine pun is the book's own gloss on its title: the five roots cure, and the rain they bring is learning.

note: In Puhar, Kannaki offered her anklets and Kovalan resolved to recover his lost wealth with them as capital in Madurai; here he takes one anklet to exchange.
teaches: The plan made in the bedchamber as a fresh start is carried out here and leads straight to the goldsmith, so the means of recovery chosen in Puhar becomes the instrument of his death.

note: The Kural advises not to do harm in hostility even when others act against you; the drummer bids the schools' debaters part without hatred or quarrel even from those who do not accept their view (பற்றாமாக்கள்).
teaches: The epic carries the Kural's rule of non-retaliation from private enmity into public doctrinal debate, making civility between rival schools a law of the city's festival.

gains.a: the herald's rule for debaters gains an ethical ground beyond festive peace: hostility harms the one who nurses it
gains.b: the couplet's counsel gains a concrete arena, the debating hall where disagreement is expected but enmity is forbidden

note: Kovalan dreams of his wife's distress, his seized garment and a death-ride, then release and his daughter's renunciation; the Pandya queen dreams of the umbrella and sceptre falling and the sky in disorder.
teaches: The same ruin is dreamed from both sides of the verdict: the victim's dream runs past death into release and his daughter's turn to the Buddha, the queen's stops at the fall of the sceptre, so the dreams divide between them the epic's two morals of ripening deeds and failed kingship.

note: The epic tells Siva's burning of the three cities as an event (the gods asked, the fiery arrow obeyed) and the origin of a dance staged at a city festival; Tirumular calls those who say Siva burned the three cities fools and makes the cities the three impurities.
teaches: The same myth stands in one text as a literal victory reenacted by a courtesan for a crowd and in the other as an inner allegory whose literal telling is folly; the conflict depends on reading the epic's account as a statement of event.

gains.a: the epic's festival myth is shown to be one available reading, the literal and performative one, which a Saiva yogic text explicitly rejects
gains.b: Tirumular's 'fools' get a concrete target: a public culture in which the Tripura burning was danced on a stage as history
