note: The prince leaves saying Manimekalai may yet come to him through Chithirapathi; in kaathai 18 Chithirapathi vows to put the girl in the prince's golden chariot or be shamed among the dancers.
teaches: The prince's passing remark becomes the grandmother's public vow, so the plot against the girl is shown to be carried by her own family's trade rather than by the prince alone.

note: Pattinappalai opens on the Kaveri that does not fail though the white star strays south and the sky withholds rain; the patikam calls the Kaveri the Tamil maiden who does not leave her course though the planets stray and summer lengthens (கோள் நிலை திரிந்து கோடை நீடினும் தான் நிலை திரியா).
teaches: The epic takes the Sangam praise-formula for Puhar's river and turns it into a person, a Chola daughter who bows to the city's goddess and gives the city its second name, so a boast of the land's yield becomes a founding story.

gains.a: the epithet in line 24-25 is shown to be an inherited Sangam formula, placing the epic's Puhar in the Chola praise tradition of Karikalan's city
gains.b: the idyll's unfailing river gains a myth of origin (Agastya's pot, the king's request) and a person who acts, which the idyll's description does not have

note: Kovalan sings the girls' blame of a man who swore by the sea god and broke his word; when Madhavi answers in song, he decides she is the deceiver and leaves her.
teaches: The singer who voiced the charge against the oath-breaking man ends the kaathai by abandoning his woman and calling her the one full of lying tricks, so the story turns the song's accusation back on the one who sang it.

note: Purananuru 35 counsels Killivalavan that in a land of just rule, where the humble can reach the king when they seek முறை, rain comes when sought, and that if he protects his people the unsubmitting will bow; 99 states the bare rule that security needs just order.
teaches: The poem shows to a named Chola what just rule looks like and what it brings, the king reached by the humble and the enemy bowing, and the line reduces the same counsel to a maxim any ruler can carry.

note: The couplet names tending the ancestors and the gods among the householder's five chief duties; Neelakesi argues that merit done in the name of the eminent dead cannot reach them, or the released would be bound again.
teaches: Set beside the Jain reductio, the Kural's duty to the ancestors is seen to say nothing on whether anything reaches them, which is the question on which the Vedic and Jain views divide.

gains.a: Neelakesi's argument gains a respected text whose duty to the ancestors her opponent would cite, so the reductio is seen to strike at ordinary household piety too
gains.b: the couplet gains a sharp question its list leaves open: whether tending the ancestors benefits them or only disciplines the householder

note: The patikam opens with the Chera prince Ilango, who gave up kingship and lives at the eastern gate; here a Chera king is told that body and wealth do not last and is led to a sacrifice, not to the forest.
teaches: Within one royal house the epic shows the two answers to impermanence, the prince who left the throne and the king who is counselled to stay on it and sacrifice, without saying which is right.

note: In the Manimekalai the Vedic brahmin states that the Veda has no cause, beginning or end, and Manimekalai simply judges that it agrees with no way of truth; here the same thesis is put by Bhutikan as a challenge and answered with five inferences.
teaches: The Buddhist epic records the Veda's beginninglessness and dismisses it without argument, while the Jain epic makes it the hinge of a full debate, showing which of the two heterodox poets chose to argue the point.

note: Aravanar called the Amudhasurabhi life-medicine (ஆர் உயிர் மருந்து) and said many events would come to the city through her; she tells the king the bowl is life-medicine (உயிர் மருந்து) and the prison becomes a house of dharma.
teaches: Her words to the king repeat her teacher's phrase, and her first public act fulfils his prophecy of events in the city, so the epic shows the teaching passing into civic change through the disciple's voice before she has formally taken the dharma.

note: The vow to bring a stone for a god on the northern kings' heads is kept when the king takes the Himalayan stone after capturing Kanakan and Vijayan.
teaches: The vow names only a god to be carved and a royal insult to be avenged, and the close names the stone as the pathini's, so the epic joins a war of royal honour to the worship of Kannaki only once the vow is kept.

note: The couplet bids one do virtue without putting it off, because when one perishes it is the companion that does not perish; the epic bids its hearers not wait on their remaining days but seek the true companion for the land they will go to.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the epic's உறுதுணை is aram, the Kural's undying companion, and the epic adds that the companion must be sought before youth, wealth and body fail, after a story in which the dead carried only their deeds and loves into their next births.

gains.a: the epic's unnamed companion gains its identity from the couplet: it is virtue, not a person or a god
gains.b: the couplet's companion at the hour of perishing gains a destination, the land one goes to, which the epic has just shown as a new birth shaped by deeds and attachments

note: The Kural calls craving the seed that gives unceasing births to all beings; in the chain craving (வேட்கை) gives clinging, karma and birth, but itself arises from feeling and contact and ceases only when ignorance ceases.
teaches: Both make craving the seed of birth, but the chain gives the seed its own seed: craving depends on feeling and, eleven steps back, on ignorance, so the Buddhist cure begins with knowledge where the Kural's chapter begins with cutting craving.

gains.a: evidence that the Tamil ethical tradition placed craving, not ignorance, at the root, which shows the chain's order as a doctrinal choice
gains.b: an account of where craving comes from and how it is stopped, which the couplet's image of the seed leaves out

note: Both turn from the noise of the schools to a teacher; Arunagiri asks Murugan for an upadesam and a vision past the logicians' quarrel, while Manimekalai's teacher answers with the rules of valid argument.
teaches: The pair shows two answers to the same fatigue with the schools: the Buddhist epic trains the hearer to argue rightly, the Saiva hymn asks to be lifted beyond argument by grace, and the tension holds as long as the logic is read as a path and not only as a tool.

gains.a: the epic unit gains a contrast showing that its turn to a teacher leads into more reasoning, not out of it
gains.b: the hymn's list of quarrelling schools gains a case where one of those schools, the Buddhist, is seen from inside, offering method rather than clamour

note: Madhavi lists what pathinis do when a husband dies (give up life in grief, enter the fire, or wear the body down in vows) and says Kannaki was of none of these kinds; Manimekalai, praying at the image, says her mother neither held to the debt of love nor took the way of penance but took on the debt of chastity.
teaches: The daughter repeats her mother Madhavi's typology in her own prayer, so that the family keeps Kannaki outside every ordinary path of the widow, and the next lines let Kannaki herself call the path she did take a sin.

note: 327 promises to establish that refusing flesh is a good deed; 331 completes it by turning the Buddhist view that image-makers and worshippers share merit into the view that killers and eaters share sin.
teaches: Neelakesi's proof against meat is built from the opponent's own devotional practice: once merit can pass to those who stand at a distance from the act, sin can too, and the eater cannot claim to stand clear of the killing.

claims.gist: compounded things are unreal though the cognition of them is real
the victory the goddess grants is bought with blood offered to her as the hunters' due
no knowing grasps all things in one act; what looks simultaneous is successive
one sound tenet does not make a doctrine sound when the rest of it is faulty
if every moment perishes entirely, release is that perishing and comes alike to the ascetic and the vicious
a man may die because his own former deed has ripened and come to take his life
one who kills does a cruel deed that will not leave him, even when the death was the victim's own ripened deed
a war won under a just sceptre makes the battlefield a field of dharma
without a soul beyond the elements, penance and its gear are futile and teaching is deception
beings of the animal state are either fixed or moving, and the fixed are of five kinds
if existence and non-existence hold of one thing at once, the calf must already be the bull
the Veda was given by Brahma, son of the discus-bearing lord
one who scorns the Veda is no son of the brahmins and fit to be called a cow's son
birth from an animal does not debase a lineage, since revered seers were so born
the soul's existence abides through each of its states, from austerity to divine birth
there is no soul at all
to deny a thing only by a constructed designation is to concede that it exists
the royal city was burned because the king's just order failed
the pathini is one whom chaste wives themselves worship
God our lord created all living beings in due order
the one who has no form of his own and makes the other forms is God
painful austerity cuts the bond of deeds and seats the soul at the summit of the world of bliss
all things are combinations of the transformed elements
there is no God, the dead are not born again, and dharma serves nothing
knowledge of a former birth is a dream-delusion sent by a deity
the teacher of dharma is the physician of the disease of birth
dharma is heard only when the stains of anger and of mind have been cleansed
there is no soul at all
a being who relieves others' suffering stands as the means to release from deeds
men without a chaste wife do not reach the world of the gods however many good deeds they do
the Buddha prescribed the ascetic practices called dhutanga
when the time for a deed to ripen comes, even a king fails to inquire
a man who bears the marks of good birth is not one to be put to death
good and bad deeds and their ripened fruits are qualities of the soul itself
if deeds were separate from the soul, rebirth and release would be meaningless
without an enduring knower, recollection cannot be accounted for by likeness, karma, yoga or any other means
deeds are wholesome or unwholesome and are done by mind, speech and body
shape is the substance itself and nothing other
the body is bone, flesh and blood
only one of the six cognitions occurs at a time
if cognitions can exist without appearing, the soul can be affirmed by the same reasoning
what passes entire from one moment to the next is a persisting thing, not a trace
the omniscient one sees all existing things together without the eye
the omniscient one takes no food yet keeps a radiant body
when the time for a deed to ripen comes, even a king fails to judge rightly
a chaste wife's power can bring ruin on a king who wronged her
a thesis can fail in nine ways even before any reason is given
the eight constituents of matter are always found together
a doctrine that puts water within fire is contradicted by what is seen
a quality can pass from its own substance into another, as a flower's scent into a pot
a scent must belong to some bearer; if the flower's scent perished with it, the trace in the water belongs to nothing
the monks' recitation, conduct and food are pure
one who calls all things impure cannot call his own practice pure
each of the five senses is made from one of the five elements
some beings, like the conch, have fewer senses though their bodies hold all the elements
a Buddha's appearance sets the heavens, the seasons and all creatures right and frees even the beings of hell from torment
those who hear a Buddha's dharma of grace pass beyond painful rebirth

note: Sirupanchamoolam 69 binds the sin of a killing on five: the killer, the one who consented, the one who took the carcass, the cook and the eater; 475 mocks a master who sorts sin so that the killer bears it and the eater does not.
teaches: Held together, the two show the Jain account of shared guilt as a deliberate counter-rule: the Sirupanchamoolam's five sharers are the answer to the very division of guilt the Neelakesi's Buddha is said to make.

gains.a: Neelakesi's mockery gets a full rule of who shares a killing, which the verse only implies
gains.b: the manual's list of five is shown to be aimed at a rival doctrine that confined guilt to the killer

note: The patikam's three morals are that dharma becomes death to kings who err, that the great praise a pathini, and that former deeds come to fruit; here the pathini gives three lessons, one to each crowned king.
teaches: The epic's late summary turns the patikam's morals into lessons addressed to the three kings and drops karma for the Chera's fulfilled vow, so the story's close weighs kingship more than the former deed the patikam put among its causes.

note: In 194 Neelakesi argued that feeling, perception and formation are not other than knowing, so the five aggregates collapse; in 481 the Buddha concedes that many of his divisions of the five do not fit but holds the aggregates real.
teaches: The objection made against the disciple is half admitted by the master, which lets the poet show the Buddhist defence retreating from the five divisions to a bare claim that the aggregates exist.

note: Kundalakesi states the five aggregates; in 194 Neelakesi answers that perception, feeling and formation are not other than consciousness, so five collapses to two.
teaches: The aggregate doctrine set out here is refuted by reduction later in the debate, which is why its claim is marked refuted here and not merely reported.

note: Sudhamathi, carried off by a vidyadhara, became unfit for the brahmins yet her father kept her; Maruthi, only desired by a youth, declares herself unfit for her husband's fires.
teaches: The epic twice lets the brahmin purity rule fall on a woman who did nothing; in Sudhamathi's case the father stays by her, while Maruthi excludes herself before anyone else does, so the rule is shown working inside the woman's own conscience.

note: The Kalittokai's herders open their bull-catch by praising the Pandya who removed the tiger and the bow and set his fish in their place; the epic's herders open their kuravai on the Pandya whose fish is inscribed on the Himalaya beside the tiger and the bow.
teaches: The same herders' praise of the Pandya emblem is kept in the epic but with the boast of conquest removed, so a work that follows all three kingdoms keeps the mullai custom of beginning with the king while setting the three emblems side by side.

gains.a: the opening's praise of the king gains a precedent: Sangam herders already began the bull-catch songs with the Pandya and his fish
gains.b: the poem's claim that the fish displaced the tiger and the bow gains a later telling that does not keep it, so the claim reads as praise rather than settled history

note: The couplet says a brahmin's birth is ruined when his conduct fails; the brahmin witness declares the boy an outcaste because his mother confessed she acted unlike a brahmin wife.
teaches: The couplet lets a man's own conduct unmake his birth, and the witness stretches this into a son's birth unmade by his mother's conduct, a step the couplet does not take and one Aputtiran then turns back on the Vedic seers' own mothers.

gains.a: The witness's verdict is seen as a twisting of a recognised rule rather than plain prejudice.
gains.b: The couplet's rule is shown to be open to use as hereditary taint once conduct is read through a mother.

note: The Pandya named himself the thief and died; Senguttuvan reads that death as the dying life straightening a sceptre bent by strong former deeds.
teaches: A second king supplies the interpretation the Pandya scene leaves unstated: the fault is laid on வல்வினை, yet the remedy is the king's own death, so karma and royal responsibility are both kept in one verdict.

note: Manimekalai asks whether some have not known a former birth, and the materialist dismisses such knowledge as the delusion of the god-struck or the dreamer; Neelakesi offers the reborn man who leads his kin to the treasure he hid.
teaches: The reborn man's found treasure is a check outside his own mind, so it meets the very objection the materialist raised against Manimekalai's appeal to remembered births.

note: The quatrain's speaker, having seen teeth and bones scattered in the burning ground, will not listen to talk of teeth like pearls; the demon woman eats the eyes without asking 'tooth or pearl', and Sarngalan, seeing it, dies of fright.
teaches: The sight of the burning ground that steadies the Naladiyar's renouncer kills an unready boy, so the contemplation of the dead body is shown to need a prepared mind and not merely a sight.

gains.a: Sarngalan's death is read as a failed contemplation of the body, not only a ghost story.
gains.b: The quatrain's confident resolve gets a counter-case in which the same evidence destroys the one who sees it.

note: The Silappathikaram's hunters offer the goddess blood as the price (விலை) of the victory she gives; the Neelakesi's worshippers offer a goat for the child she gave, and the sage denies that she gave anything.
teaches: Both epics show worship to the fierce goddess as an exchange of blood for a boon; the Jain sage attacks the exchange at its first term, the boon, which the hunters' song takes for granted.

gains.a: the sage's argument is seen to strike at the logic of a widespread kind of worship, not at one family's vow
gains.b: the hunters' price-for-victory is shown to rest on a premise another epic set out to deny

note: Freshly aware of her past birth, Manimekalai hails the Buddha at his seat as a young sun risen over a world that had lost its light; Aravanar foretells the next Buddha as a sun rising to clear the stain of minds.
teaches: The sun image moves from praise of a Buddha already come to prophecy of one yet to come, so the epic places its heroine between two dawns, in the age of mist that Aravanar describes at 63 to 65.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher says there is no arising for a hare's horn, the mode of denial resting on what is not; Neelakesi says there is no perishing for what does not exist, as there is no size to a crow's tooth.
teaches: Both schools grant the same rule for the non-existent, and the Jain uses it against the Buddhist: if a perished moment is as unreal as a hare's horn, it cannot also be the thing whose perishing gives rise to the next.

note: Here Kovalan refuses Madhavi's letter, filing her every sign of love as a dancing woman's role; reading her second letter in the forest he decides she is without fault and the fault is his (தன்றீ திலளென ... என்தீ தென்றே, 13:94-95).
teaches: Kovalan's verdict that a dancer's grief is only art is withdrawn by Kovalan himself once he is ruined and far away, so the story shows the judgment came from his sulk and not from anything in her.

note: The goddess foretold that Manimekalai would hear the false teachings of many schools and gave her the mantra to take another form; here Manimekalai reports having heard them so, in Vanji.
teaches: The tour of the schools in kaathai 27 was a prescribed stage, not a chance encounter: the goddess set it up so that Manimekalai would reject the schools herself before the teacher speaks.

note: Arkkachandra, defeated, named Mokkala, the Buddha's first disciple, as his teacher; Mokkala, defeated, names the one in Kapilapuram who first gave him his delusion.
teaches: Each defeated Buddhist names the teacher above him, so the debates climb a chain of transmission from Kundalakesi to the Buddha himself, and the epic's route is the lineage read backwards.

note: The couplet likens a king's lack of kindness to the world's lack of rain; the epic likens travellers waiting out the scorching sun to subjects waiting for a cruel king to set.
teaches: The Kural pictures the bad king through the weather and the epic pictures the weather through the bad king, so the pair shows the image of misrule running both ways, and the epic placing it, unprompted, at the first step into the Pandya's land.

gains.a: the simile gains the couplet's moral weight: the cruel king is a drought to all that lives, not just a passing discomfort
gains.b: the couplet gains a hope its subjects do not voice: that a cruel reign, like a summer day, has an end to wait for

note: The drummer proclaims the good day of the island's rite of peace (தீவகச் சாந்தி); in kaathai 24 a charana tells the king that on the day the rite is not performed his city will enter the sea, by Manimekala deity's word and Indra's curse.
teaches: The same rite named in the festival proclamation becomes, twenty-three kaathais later, the condition on which the city's survival hangs, so the decorations of the opening are already the terms of a covenant the city will break.

note: The couplet makes understanding the power to find the true substance in whatever one hears from anyone; Manimekalai has heard every school and judged them wanting, but asks a teacher for the true doctrine.
teaches: The epic shows the limit of the couplet's test: a hearer can reject what she hears from many mouths and still lack the means to find the truth, so the teacher gives her a method of knowing rather than an answer.

gains.a: Manimekalai's refusal of the schools gains a general standard by which her judgment is measured
gains.b: the couplet gains a case showing that discernment can stop at rejection, and needs the means of knowledge to go further

note: The Silappathikaram tells Madhavi's seven years of training to be shown to the king; in the Manimekalai, Vasantamalai lists her arts item by item, opening with the same pair வேத்தியல் பொதுவியல், and reports the town saying her turn to tapas is shameful.
teaches: The accomplishment that the first epic crowns with the king's title becomes, in the sequel, the inventory of what Madhavi has given up, so the length of her training is what makes the town read her renunciation as a disgrace.

note: The image on the pillar (கந்தின் ... பாவை) of the Ulaka Aravi proclaims Visakai chaste here; in kaathai 20 the same image tells Kanchanan that the woman before him is Manimekalai in disguise.
teaches: The pillar image is the city's witness for women: it once cleared a slandered virgin by declaring her a rain-bringer, and later declares the truth about a disguised renunciant, but in the second case its word comes after the sword has fallen.

note: The preface to the fifth decad names Senguttuvan, who drove back the sea, as the king who went north to take a stone for the goddess Pattini, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed it in the Ganga; the epic's summary names him by the same epithet (கடல்பிறக் கோட்டி) and the same Ganga, and says nothing of the stone.
teaches: The decad's preface and the epic's summary give the same king the same two marks, the sea driven back and the Ganga reached, but only the Sangam preface keeps the Pattini stone as the purpose of the march, so the epic, which tells the stone's story at length, lets its own summary remember the expedition as the preface's bare royal conquest.

gains.a: the summary's epithet gains its source: கடல்பிறக் கோட்டி is the name under which a Patitruppattu decad was sung for this king, which shows the summary closing the book in the older praise-poets' terms
gains.b: the preface's brief clause on the Pattini stone gains the epic's full account of why and for whom the stone was sought, and a case where the epic's own closing formula leaves that clause out

note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives exactly four bad deeds of speech in a closed list of ten; 535 says there are many more, such as talking alone with a woman.
teaches: Neelakesi quotes the Buddhist list faithfully and attacks its closure, not its content: her additions come from a renouncer's code of conduct, which a list of ten deeds for all people does not try to cover.

note: Evvi is the unsparing giver (ஓம்பா ஈகை மாவேள் எவ்வி) in the Purananuru poem and the lord who gives toddy to the fishermen to end a brawl in 366.
teaches: The Purananuru names Evvi's giving as a title, while the akam simile shows it as a scene of keeping peace between farmers and salt-makers and makes his shade a measure of a woman's comfort, so a patron's fame for protection became an akam image of shelter.

note: Both praise the highest being as victor over Death: Siva kicked Death and became king of the south; the Jina passed beyond Death (காலனைக் கடந்தாய்) along with desire, aging and birth.
teaches: The same victory over Death means a deed of force against another being in the Saiva invocation and a leaving-behind of one's own mortal condition in the Jain hymn.

gains.a: the hymn's war imagery is seen as borrowed from a praise tradition that told the victory as combat
gains.b: the kick of the invocation is set against a victory that requires no enemy outside the self

note: The couplet says evils will not touch a man for seven births if he has children of good character; Visakai says sons do not give heaven.
teaches: On the reading that the seven births are the parent's own, the couplet credits good children with protecting the parent beyond this life, which Visakai flatly denies, so the pair marks a point where the epic's teacher rejects a household hope the Kural endorses.

gains.a: Visakai's denial gains its target: a recognised claim that children carry merit to their parents.
gains.b: The couplet gains a direct contrary in a text that counts only one's own virtue.

note: Perunkoppendu argues for her place on her husband's pyre against the elders who hold her back; Neelakesi 218 cites the wife who burns with her guardian husband as the futile death no one should call virtue.
teaches: The Sangam queen gives the pyre a reason, escape from the widow's diet and gravel bed, that the Jain reductio ignores when it calls such death one that achieves nothing; the two disagree on what the wife's death is for.

gains.a: the epic's 'nothing comes of it' is tested against a widow who says exactly what comes of it
gains.b: the queen's choice is seen being cited later as the standard case of a death a moral argument rejects

note: Aputhiran, stranded on Manipallavam, let the bowl into Gomukhi bidding it rise once a year and enter the hand of anyone who keeps compassion and guards lives; here it rises into Manimekalai's hand on that day.
teaches: The bowl's arrival is not a goddess's gift but the meeting of a condition laid down by its last owner, so the kaathai tests Manimekalai before the reader is told what the test was.

note: Kundalakesi listed the Buddha's gifts of eyes, flesh, wife and body as his glory; here Neelakesi lists the same gifts to ask how, on his doctrine, he could ever reap them.
teaches: The Jataka gifts are turned from praise into a refutation: if no doer reaps, the Bodhisattva's sacrifices were made for a fruit his own teaching denies him.

note: In Puhar she appears with the bowl like a rain cloud over a scorched bamboo forest; in Kanchi the chamberlain says she has come like a great rain cloud.
teaches: The simile becomes literal: in Puhar the cloud is only food for the hungry, while in Kanchi her coming brings real rain to a land in drought.

note: The Chera vowed that unless he took a stone for the goddess on the heads of the northern kings his sword should be counted shameful; here the narrator says the pathini taught the western king that kings' anger does not cool until their vow is fulfilled.
teaches: The Chera's vow, made in anger at reported scorn, is in the end credited to the pathini as one of her lessons, so the king's campaign is retold as her teaching rather than his own design.

note: Naladiyar 16 says the fleeting pleasures of youth, like a sacrificial lamb nibbling its garland, are not found among the wise; Natrinai 126 says no wealth surpasses youth and that love must be taken in youth because wealth cannot buy it later.
teaches: Both start from the shortness of youth and draw opposite duties from it: the Naladiyar to refuse youth's pleasure, the Natrinai hero to refuse wealth for its sake, so the same premise of impermanence served the akam poets as an argument for love and the didactic poets as one against it.

note: 444 calls greater people as support the chief of all strengths; 497 says no support is needed but fearlessness, if the thinking and place are right.
teaches: Five chapters later, the book seems to qualify its own superlative.

note: In 163 Neelakesi resolves to strike down the Buddha's way, which does not call flesh-eating a fault; in 190 she makes that charge before the court.
teaches: The plan made alone at the shrine is carried out in the debate, so the charge of flesh-eating is the purpose of the whole sarukkam, not a passing taunt.

note: Tirumular says that when steadfast Brahmins pour the oblation sky, earth, the quarters and their gods flourish; Neelakesi says that rites cannot drive off disease or demons and that gods who delight in killing cannot remove the killer's karma.
teaches: Where the Saiva verse gives the rite power to sustain the world and its gods, the Jain debater denies it any power over karma at all, so the two disagree on whether ritual acts on the moral order.

gains.a: the verse gains the full Vedic-Saiva claim for the rite that it denies, which shows how much it is rejecting
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains an opponent who asks what the oblation can do against a deed already done, a question it does not take up

note: Akananuru 26: the wife recalls that lately her husband held back from embracing her for fear of spilling the milk meant for their son. Thinaimalai 152: the wife herself refuses his embrace, saying her milk would spoil his garland.
teaches: In the Akananuru it is the husband who fears the milk and the wife who is hurt by his caution; in the Thinaimalai the wife takes up the same fear as her weapon, so together they show the nursing mother's milk standing on either side of the quarrel, as his excuse or as her refusal.

note: The teacher's ten bad deeds include killing, theft, lust and lying, as Tirumular's yama does, but the epic sorts them by body, speech and mind and counts coveting, anger and wrong view as deeds, while Tirumular adds sharing food and shunning drink.
teaches: Set side by side, the two lists of ten show the same core abstentions serving different ends: for the epic they decide the next birth, for Tirumular they are the first step of yoga toward Siva, and only the epic counts states of mind as deeds.

gains.a: a Saiva counterpart showing the same abstentions used as the first limb of yoga rather than as the ledger of rebirth
gains.b: the epic's body, speech and mind sorting, which shows that the yama list has no item for coveting or wrong view

note: Sivavakkiyar's man, having taken a woman for her form, would cut down any rival who desires her, though his own body will stink and be handed to the cremation keeper; Kanchanan cuts down the prince over a form that is not even his wife's, whose body is already gone.
teaches: The epic gives the Siddhar's jealous husband a case where the form (வடிவு) he guards belongs to another woman and his wife's body has already perished, so the jealousy is shown wrong both about whose body it is and about its lasting.

gains.a: Kanchanan's killing gains a general diagnosis: it is jealousy over a body, the most perishable of possessions.
gains.b: The Siddhar's hypothetical gains a narrated case in which the rival is actually killed and the killer's price is named as a deed that clings, beyond the body's decay.

note: Kural 1042 calls poverty 'a sinner' (இன்மை எனவொரு பாவி) that comes with this world and the next both lost; Deepathilakai calls hunger 'the sinner' (பசிப் பிணி என்னும் பாவி, 80) that destroys birth, learning, modesty and beauty.
teaches: The Kural speaks to the poor man about what poverty takes from him, even merit for the next world; the epic speaks to the one who can cure it, so the merit the poor man loses becomes the giver's highest dharma.

gains.a: the list of hunger's ravages is seen to extend a Kural formula, which places the sermon within the ethics books' account of want
gains.b: the couplet's loss of the next world gains a remedy outside the poor man, in another's gift

note: Both tie the cattle raid to toddy: in the Purananuru the jar is kept for the raider who will bring a herd; here the toddy seller's refusal sends the hunter out.
teaches: Read together they show toddy as the raid's credit: the poem's kept jar is advance pay, and the epic's refusal is the unpaid debt the seized herd later settles in the seller's yard.

gains.a: the epic's brief motive (a refused drink) gains the Sangam custom behind it, where the raider is paid in toddy before he goes
gains.b: the Purananuru poem gains the other side of the trade: a seller who will not pour and is paid afterwards in cattle (lines 132-135)

note: Paripadal 3 says the god is everything and the essence within everything and calls him one full of maayam (மாயமார் அனையை); the kuravai asks whether the churner of the sea bound by Asodhai's churning rope is maayam, for it bewilders.
teaches: The hymn treats the god's maayam as a doctrine to be stated, his being all things at once, while the herdswomen meet it as an unanswered question in a domestic scene, so the same paradox is shown both as learned theology and as village wonder.

gains.a: the kuravai's question gains an answer it does not give: the hymn's account of why one god can be both the cosmic churner and a bound child
gains.b: the hymn's abstract claim gains a concrete case, a single hand that churned the ocean and was tied with a butter-churn's cord

note: The Buddha offered paddy and sugarcane as a continuity that is neither same nor other; Neelakesi answers that paddy never comes from cane's line, so the example shows each kind giving only itself.
teaches: The seed example cuts both ways: what the Buddhist uses to show change without identity the Jain uses to show a kind that persists, so the dispute is over which feature of the seed counts.

claims.gist: release comes only when the inner mind and outward conduct agree
the kinds are many and unmixed yet are the one substance
if all beings are the one Lord, the difference of ruler and ruled vanishes
heaven is where deeds done on earth are only enjoyed, and no one there does dharma, austerity or strives to cut attachment
one who can feed all who come has nothing to gain from heaven's rewards
whether an act brings merit or fault depends on what the mind took its object to be
one who holds the means to feed a starving land is bound to go and protect it
there is no earth apart from hardness and no soul apart from cognition
dispositions such as theft, lust and generosity are not qualities of any element
one who dies with a being held unwavering in mind is reborn from that being's womb
feeling, cognition, perception and volition belong to a single subject
space is one, formless and non-sentient, and extends through the world and the non-world
a knowledge of infinitely many things can never be completed, so no one knows all things
deeds and their fruits exist, but there is no doer
none of the aggregates lasts beyond a moment
a reason found in only part of the similar and part of the dissimilar instances is inconclusive
a king's bounty sustains the world as the rain does
the soul is spoken of in four ways beginning with the soul in name, and these do not allow its existence to be denied
a courtesan leaves a man when his merit is spent, as Fortune does
an ascetic's dress on a courtesan is a thing for everyone to laugh at
a conquering king must protect the Veda-keeping Brahmins of the conquered land
the goddess is the woman's form in the half of Shiva's body, praised by the Veda
one who lacks the merit of penance cannot grasp what a dream foretells
if mistaken belief excused the deed, a man could carry off another's wife without fault
the dead man's death was his own cruel karma coming to ripeness
two beings meet in many births in changing relations, so the present relation is no ground for grief
those who preach dharma yet eat flesh bought in the market do evil, since the creatures were killed for that market
a soul is only the name for the five aggregates taken together, as 'hand' is for five fingers
perception is of six kinds, one for each of the five senses and the mind
one who keeps the dharma of compassion through births, born a man, becomes the chief disciple of the Buddha and is freed by cutting dependence
killing is a sin punished by burning in hell
eating flesh is a sin of its own, punished in hell like killing
earth is known by its marks of hardness and support
if earth is established by its marks, the soul is established by its marks of knowing and seeing
as gold persists while the pot perishes and the crown arises, the soul persists through births as man or god
there is nothing but mind
what is called evil conduct is not evil karma when the mind is pure
eating a creature that died of itself and eating one killed by another both bring evil
souls never enter one another and each has its own length and breadth
if souls cannot share room, beings crowded together would leave their souls no place
giving to everyone alike is good
a gift of the body that destroys the lives within it is a fault

note: Mokkalan says Kundalakesi conquered every rival creed on her naaval-branch vow; in 228 the narrator shows the same Kundalakesi, who planted the naaval branch, beaten with drums and driven out of the city gate.
teaches: Mokkalan's praise is refuted by the epic's own earlier scene, so the reader sees him defending a champion the story has already disgraced, and his charge of lying falls back on him.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says gain, loss, birth and death are mixed in at conception and the fate laid down before brings what follows; Neelakesi tests this with the infant girl whose womanhood must then already be present.
teaches: The Buddhist epic records the claim that a life's course is fixed at conception and walks away from it; the Jain epic answers it with a concrete reductio, the grown woman's features absent from the infant.

note: Naladiyar 48 says those who praise sandal paste and garlands have not seen what the body is; 557 treats 'those who wear garlands and sandal have not found the path' as the absurd outcome of the Buddhist claim that nothing is pure.
teaches: A Jain anthology and a Jain epic part ways on impurity: the Naladiyar finds it in the body and condemns the garland, while the Neelakesi attacks the Buddhist 'nothing at all is pure' because extended to everything it erases the difference between path and no path.

gains.a: the epic's reductio is shown to aim at the word 'all', since its own tradition accepts the body's foulness in the same image of sandal and garland
gains.b: the quatrain's contempt for adornment is marked as a claim about the body, which the Jain debater would not let grow into a claim that everything is impure

note: The officers seize Vaarthikan because his son wears jewels a stranger gave; the goldsmith tells the king that the stranger with the anklet is the thief of the palace anklet.
teaches: The goddess's precedent is the same case as Kovalan's, a man holding valuable jewels wrongly taken for a thief by the king's men, chosen so that the old king's remedy can be measured against the present king's haste.

note: 528 tells a king not to look at all alike but by rank; 541 says to show no favour to anyone.
teaches: Household management and the court of justice have different requirements, though they are only two chapters apart.

note: The bard of the puram poem hails Athiyaman as the ploughman who yokes white-mouthed donkeys on the bloody fields of captured forts and sows white varagu and horse-gram; the Chera's ploughmen sing their king as the donkey-plough ploughman who sowed kavadi on the northern kings' forts.
teaches: The terror title that a Sangam bard gives a patron at his gate is in the epic sung by real ploughmen in their field song, beside their oxen's holiday, so the conqueror's mock ploughing of enemy ground is absorbed into the farming folk's festival of his return.

gains.a: the ploughmen's epithet gains the rite behind it: ploughing a ruined fort with donkeys and sowing it with poor seed
gains.b: the bard's title gains a later setting where the king's own ploughmen own it as a song of joy

note: Purananuru 56.1-8 gives four gods four banners: the bull, the palm (பனைக்கொடி) of the conch-white one with the plough, the bird of the sapphire-dark one, the peacock; Paripadal 4.37-41 gives the dark god the bird, the palm, the plough and the elephant, and says there is no banner that is not his. On the plain reading the palm banner belongs to a different god in one poem and to Mal in the other.
teaches: The puram poet needs four separate gods so that the king can match each in one excellence, while the devotional poet folds the elder brother's palm and plough into Mal's own emblems, so the pair shows how a hymn's claim of sole lordship rearranged the very iconography the court poets used as a fixed set.

note: Madurapathi appears before Kannaki here; in the next kaathai she names herself and tells her that the harm came to her husband as ஊழ்வினை, a deed come to fruit.
teaches: The goddess who comes because she cannot bear the fire is the one who will give karma as the cause, so the poem brings in its karmic account only after the pathini's justice has run its course.

note: Against Kundalakesi, Neelakesi said that if nothing of one moment is in the next, knowing and speaking are impossible; against the Buddha she says that if will perishes at each arising, knowledge cannot grow.
teaches: The argument against momentariness moves from memory to learning: the first debate asked how anything is known, this one how anything is learned.

note: The sage foresees that Neelakesi, once she learns the arts of meaning, will come to the path of dharma; the invocation says she took the great one's dharma and turned the world from violence.
teaches: The invocation's report of her conversion is planted in the story as the sage's own foreknowledge at the moment of her attack, so the conversion is his aim from the start, not a later turn.

note: The Silappathikaram lists Kama's eunuch dance and the pot dance in Bana's city among the eleven dances Madhavi performs at Indra's festival; here a street performer dances the eunuch dance, named in nearly the same words (வாணன் பேர் ஊர் மறுகிடை ... நீள் நிலம் அளந்தோன்), as her daughter passes in robes.
teaches: The dance that was Madhavi's art on the royal stage at one festival is a street show at the next, watched by the crowd while her daughter walks past it to the Buddha's grove, so the repeated formula marks how far the family has moved from that stage.

note: The painted image on the pillar of the hall speaks at night to frightened Sudhamathi; later the same image speaks to Kanchanan just after he has killed the prince, telling him the woman he sought was Manimekalai in disguise.
teaches: The pillar's voice comes once in time, to comfort with knowledge of past births, and once too late, to tell a killer what he did not know, so the same speaking image marks both the gift and the failure of right knowing.

note: Kaathai 3 says the crystal pavilion lets no voice out but shows the body outside (விளிப்பு அறைபோகாது மெய் புறத்து இடூஉம்); Sudhamathi hides Manimekalai in it.
teaches: The hiding place was announced as one that hides speech but shows the body, so the shelter Sudhamathi picks is the one that will display the girl to the prince while she preaches against the body.

note: The couplet ranks the strength of enduring hunger below the strength of removing others' hunger; the goddess gives Manimekalai the first strength by mantra, and the patikam (manimekalai:0:51-68) says the bowl for feeding others comes next.
teaches: The epic follows the couplet's order of rank but removes the effort from the lower strength: enduring hunger is granted as a gift, so the renouncer is freed for the higher task the couplet values, feeding others.

gains.a: The hunger mantra is seen as a step in a known scale of virtue rather than a magic convenience.
gains.b: The couplet's ranking is shown worked out in a life, where the lesser strength is a means to the greater rather than a rival to it.

note: Kannaki before the Pandya recalls the Chola who relieved a bird's distress and the one who crushed his son under the wheel for a cow, to accuse a king who did not inquire; the ammanai sings the dove-king and the cow's justice as the glory of Puhar, after Kannaki has declared the Pandya blameless.
teaches: The same two Chola precedents change use across the story: in Madurai they are Kannaki's weapon against a Pandya, and in Vanchi, once she has cleared him, they are a girls' refrain beside ball songs hailing that same Pandya, so the standard of justice survives the verdict while losing its edge.

note: Sivavakkiyar mocks those who bathe daily crying 'pollution', since the body itself took form from pollution; 561 tells those who hold all things impure to bathe in the gutter, as if that conclusion were absurd.
teaches: The Siddhar draws the very conclusion the Jain debater uses as a reductio: if everything is born of impurity, the ritual bath is pointless, so the same premise ends in mockery of ritual in one text and in mockery of the premise in the other.

gains.a: the epic's reductio meets a poet who accepts its consequence, showing that the argument holds only for one who still values the clean over the foul
gains.b: the Siddhar's attack on bathing is seen to rest on a premise a Jain epic thought no sane teacher could hold

note: 36 tells the besieging king that to have fought a rival who sits at ease behind his walls is a matter of shame; Naladiyar 241 says the worthy, seeing their enemies humbled, feel shame and do not advance.
teaches: The Naladiyar's maxim about shame before a humbled foe is in 36 an actual plea to stop a siege, which shows the poets used this sense of honour to bring wars to an end, and that the shame was felt to fall on the victor.

note: Ainkurunuru 250 tells the beads that the one who afflicted the girl is not Vel, lord of their valli forest; the friend here tells the lover that he comes with kadamba and spear but has no six faces, no peacock and no kurava bride.
teaches: The Sangam friend's bare denial that the god caused the sickness is worked out here as a point-by-point comparison of the man with the god's attributes, which shows the denial leaning on an iconography of Murugan already settled.

gains.a: the friend's list gains a precedent: denying the god's seizure was a set move of the friend's speech
gains.b: the short poem's 'not Vel' is spelled out in the god's own marks, making plain what the girl's lover is being measured against

note: Kundalakesi's invocation praises the lord who kept nothing for himself and laboured only for others' good (பிறர்க்கேயுறு திக்கு ழந்தான்); 587 tells the Buddha that because he laboured for others (பிறர்க்கே உழந்தாய்), by his own rule that a pain-bringing deed is evil, he must himself suffer those deeds.
teaches: The Jain epic lifts the Buddhist poem's central praise almost word for word and recasts it as a karmic debt, so the same self-giving reads as perfection in one sect and as a self-inflicted evil deed in the other.

note: The couplet says that if the king bends justice the sky withholds rain; the bhutas say that on the day the king errs in the order of rule the city is eaten by fire.
teaches: Both bind nature's order to the king's justice, but the epic replaces the slow withdrawal of rain with an immediate fire on the city and gives the city's own guardian spirits the knowledge of the rule, so the couplet's consequence becomes a sentence carried out the same night.

gains.a: the bhutas' rule gains a recognised doctrine: misrule upsets the order of nature, which the Kural already states
gains.b: the couplet gains a sharper instance where the penalty falls at once on the city as a whole, and the guardians themselves stand aside for it

note: The prince follows Manimekalai like a shadow (நிழல் போல், 185); the couplet says ruin stays at the evildoer's feet like his shadow.
teaches: The epic inverts the couplet's shadow: the prince makes himself Manimekalai's shadow, but his own evil deed is the shadow at his own feet, and it catches him in the hall where he followed her.

gains.a: The prince's pursuit gains the couplet's image of what was following him.
gains.b: The couplet's shadow gains a scene where the pursuer is himself pursued, so the image shows how the ruin comes.

note: Kural 256 says no one would sell flesh for a price if the world did not kill to eat; 471 makes the market's beasts say the buyers' money sends the netter out to kill them.
teaches: The couplet's demand argument is given a voice and an opponent: in the Buddha's own town the dead animals accuse the buyer, so the rule becomes a charge against a monastic order that buys rather than kills.

gains.a: the verse's picture of the protesting beasts gets the Kural's general law of price and killing behind it
gains.b: the couplet's abstract buyer becomes a named religious community, which shows whom the argument was useful against

note: In the Silappathikaram Kannaki lists the chaste wives of Puhar and their wonders as she turns on Madurai; here Kayasandigai names Athirai as the one who stands alone among Puhar's rain-giving wives.
teaches: The pathinis of the same city serve the twin epics in opposite ways: Kannaki calls on them to back a curse that burns a city, while Manimekalai seeks one of them to give the first food to a bowl that feeds it.

note: Both are a sage's warning that a city will sink: Brahmadharma gives Attipathi a fixed day and the king leads his people out, while the charana makes Puhar's sinking hang on a rite that must never be forgotten and that the goddess cannot override.
teaches: The pair shows the epic's two kinds of prophecy of ruin: a Buddhist sage's fixed fact that is escaped by leaving, and a curse tied to Indra's festival that is escaped only by unbroken observance, which is why the city's fate turns on the king's memory.

note: Madurai's gem street is full of men who tell gems apart by the flaws the treatises name; before the king Kannaki says her anklet holds gems, the queen's holds pearls, and when she breaks it a gem flies to the king's mouth and he declares himself the thief.
teaches: The city Kovalan admires is one where every stone is judged by rule, yet the king condemns him on a goldsmith's word without testing the anklet, and the truth comes only when Kannaki breaks it, so the pairing shows the failure was not of the city's knowledge but of the king's will to use it.

note: The Vaisheshika of kaathai 27 counts space among the nine substances and sound among the qualities; here 'space is a substance by its quality of sound' is a thesis whose subject an opponent may deny.
teaches: The doctrine stated as settled fact in kaathai 27 is shown here to rest on a subject not every school grants, so the teacher answers the Vaisheshika by the form of debate rather than by contrary doctrine.

note: At 148 the sage gives as her atonement the task of making the Jina's path clear; at 163 she chooses the Buddha's path, which does not call flesh-eating a fault, as the first to subdue.
teaches: The debates of the rest of the poem are her penance: the commission given as expiation for her violence is carried out first against the school she charges with tolerating killing for food.

note: The couplet gives the chaste wife power to bid rain fall; the king asks whether failed chastity among women withheld it.
teaches: The pair shows the couplet's power run in reverse: if a wife's chastity can command rain, the community's women can be suspected when it fails, and the epic records the suspicion without confirming it.

gains.a: the king's third cause gains the couplet's claim that underlies it
gains.b: the couplet gains its darker corollary, that drought can be laid at women's door

note: In Akananuru 56 the wife tells the bard who blundered into her house 'இம்மனை அன்று; அஃது உம்மனை'; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 22 she tells him 'நெறிஅதுகாண் எங்கையர் இற்கு'.
teaches: The same retort appears as a told comic incident in Akananuru and as a direct taunt in the four-line venba, which shows that pointing the bard to the other house was a fixed refusal move the later poet could use bare, without the story.

note: To Ilango, Saathan explains the former-birth curse behind the deed; to the king he tells only the anklet, the case, the vow and the burning.
teaches: Saathan tailors the story to his hearer: the renouncer is told the karmic cause, the king is told the public case of a bent sceptre, so the epic keeps its two explanations of the disaster apart by audience.

note: The couplet makes the householder the support of renouncers, the needy and the dead; Kannaki says that without her husband she lost giving to the virtuous, tending Brahmins, receiving ascetics and welcoming guests.
teaches: The couplet speaks of the householder as one person, while Kannaki shows that a wife alone could not keep those duties, so the householder's dharma the Kural assigns depends on the pair being together.

gains.a: Kannaki's list gains its standing: what she lost is the very support the Kural makes the householder's office
gains.b: the couplet gains its cost when the house is broken: the wife left at home cannot be the support it describes

note: The goddess's dream foretold a creeper of tapas that would leave Kama helpless; in the Silappathikaram's last kaathai Madhavi gives her daughter to the dharma at the Bodhi seat while Kama throws his bow and arrows on the bare ground.
teaches: The earlier epic's closing image of Kama disarmed turns out, read with this dream, to be the fulfilment of a prophecy spoken at the child's naming.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain speaker says space gives room to all things; Neelakesi says space is one, formless, non-sentient and extends through world and non-world.
teaches: The Buddhist epic's report of Jain space matches the Jain epic's own voice on its function, while only the Neelakesi adds the non-world beyond the world, the part an outside report left out.

note: Thuvathikan foretells famine in Kanchi and Manimekalai's coming with the bowl; when she arrives, the Kanchi king says all the pillar image's words have come true (கந்திற்பாவை கட்டுரை எல்லாம் வாய் ஆகின்று).
teaches: The epic closes its own prophecy by having a king cite the pillar image by name, so the deity's claim at 112 to 129 that installed gods speak true is confirmed inside the story, not only asserted.

note: In 49 the sage knows she may try to frighten him with her transformations (விகுர்வணை) and fail; in 888 she uses the same power of transformation to frighten the materialist into belief.
teaches: The demon's power to change shape, useless against the Jain sage at the start, becomes at the end the Jain debater's proof of unseen beings, so the same faculty passes from assault to teaching.

note: Aiyai and her mother likened Kannaki to the one of their clan who relieved the gem-coloured god's distress in the Yamuna; here the girl cast as Pinnai garlands the girl cast as Mayavan while Kannaki looks on.
teaches: Because the herdswomen had already seen Kannaki as Pinnai and Kovalan as the dark god, the dance's Pinnai garlanding Mayavan plays out before Kannaki the union that has, unknown to her, already ended.

note: The opening sermon praises a land where Brahmins and the rest make up the four flawless varnas, none straying from its path; here the same heroine argues that high and low birth is not real, since no sense can detect it.
teaches: The Jain epic holds two views of caste at once: as a social order it can praise the four varnas, but as a claim of inborn rank it denies it, so its quarrel is with birth as worth, not with the order of occupations.

note: Kural 25 makes Indra the witness to the power of one who has quenched the five senses; in the epic Indra's throne trembles at a beggar's feeding of all creatures, and he comes in person to reward it.
teaches: The epic moves the test that brings Indra down from the ascetic's restraint to a giver's feeding, and then shows the witness turning rival, since the god's reward will undo the giving it acknowledges.

gains.a: the known Tamil rule that Indra's disturbance testifies to a human's power, so the shaken throne reads as a verdict on Aputhiran
gains.b: a story in which Indra's witness is followed by Indra's interference, which the couplet's bare 'witness enough' does not foresee

note: In 574 the Buddha denied any doer; here he says the doer is the doer and the reaper the reaper.
teaches: Neelakesi's pressure forces the Buddha from 'no doer' to 'the doer is the doer', which is the point at which she can make the doer the reaper and he falls silent.

note: The goddess gave her a mantra to take another form and travel the sky so that no one would refuse her teaching for her youth; here she first uses the other form to evade the prince and enter a prison with the bowl.
teaches: The power given so she could hear doctrine as an adult is first spent on escaping desire and feeding prisoners, so the epic puts charity and self-protection before debate in the order of her training.

note: The quatrain says the harlot's love is like a lamp that dies when its oil is spent; here Madhavi, a courtesan, gives Kovalan union and sulking and herself asks for the outing, and in the story it is Kovalan, not she, who breaks off (silappathikaram:7:286-300).
teaches: The epic's courtesan breaks the quatrain's rule from the other side: the love ends, but by the man's suspicion on the shore, not by her turning away when his wealth runs out.

gains.a: Madhavi's devotion in this unit is set against the moral literature's verdict on her class, which makes it pointed rather than merely decorative
gains.b: the quatrain's general rule meets a counter-case in the classical story most read by Tamil readers, which limits it to a type rather than every courtesan

note: Both see the king's white umbrella as the moon; the benediction praises the moon for resembling the Chola's sheltering umbrella, the quatrain says every king under such an umbrella has been carried off as dead.
teaches: The same moon-umbrella serves the epic's opening as a sign of rule that shelters the world and serves the Naladiyar as proof that such rule ends, so the pair shows the epic beginning in the confidence the ethics book was written to undercut.

gains.a: the hymn's royal moon gains a shadow: the image it uses for lasting shelter is the Naladiyar's stock image of the king who dies
gains.b: the quatrain's umbrella gains an instance of the praise it answers, the court poet's moon that is meant to outlast the king

claims.gist: an atom that touches another must have an inside and sides, and so cannot be indivisible
the released soul, like a burnt seed, is never born again and abides eternally in perfection with eight qualities
the bond that brings rebirth can be destroyed
every real thing has arising, perishing and lasting together
an omniscient Lord without organs cannot speak, and one with organs is only the fruit of past good karma
the sin of killing falls on the one who killed, not on the one who eats
karma binds only when all five conditions of the deed are met
nothing could bind in the round of births a soul that is pure, pervading and changeless
earth, water, fire and air are four distinct substances
the four elements are of one kind and change into one another
those who only take part after the killing, as by drawing out the arrow, are not bound by its deed
dharma itself becomes death to rulers who go wrong in kingship
the exalted praise a pathini of great renown
the deed of a former time comes in wrath and makes its doer eat its fruit
the Anga and Purva scriptures were proclaimed by the omniscient Jina himself
whether the soul is said to move between births or not, the Sankhya account fails
the soul's own twofold deeds accompany it through births
no one knows the fixed span of his life
hell-beings have bodies of vast measure, five hundred bows tall
unbroken moral discipline (சீலம்) keeps a future Buddha from harm and moves the gods to help him
a future Buddha must complete the perfections over many births before he turns the wheel of dharma
killing in sacrifice to gods and ancestors brings a heavy deed upon the sacrificers
a woman trained in the arts of the dancing women shames herself by taking up tapas
suffering through countless births implies evil deeds of the same measure
a dissimilar example must lack the property to be proved; one that keeps it fails
a dissimilar example must lack the reason; one that keeps it fails
a cause must pass something into its effect, as water must flow down the channel to fill a tank
the twelvefold penance cuts the chain of births
a scent in a pot remains the flower's, carried by particles of the flower
a thing's number and qualities are known only as belonging to it
the absence of a perceivable thing is proved by its not appearing where it would appear
a fault in the worthy shows as plainly as the spot on the moon
the five senses and their five objects arise from the five elements joined together
a reason proves its conclusion through a real tie of nature or causation, not through observed co-presence or co-absence alone
the ascetic can close the doorway by which karma enters
atoms combine and part but never enter one another
what is called the universal is only the likeness of things to one another
the categories are six
the Sankhya's twenty-five categories are faulty
there is no soul
the soul is conscious
the soul is the cause of pleasure and the other qualities
a thesis the opponent already holds is not a thesis to be proved
one who dies holding the purpose of sustaining lives is born again where that purpose can be carried out
since nothing carries the soul, the doer of good cannot travel to the world of the gods
deeds move the soul to its next birth as the wind turns a whirligig
a careless step that harms even small creatures like the crab and the snail is a grief to be guarded against
a mind set on eating flesh is itself enough to earn evil deed
silence alone cannot be what makes one an omniscient Lord
on the Buddhist account the one who reaches heaven is other than the one who earned it
there are sixteen Kalpa heavens and above them further heavens in groups of nine, nine and five

note: The ஊழ்வினை that drives the couple out of Puhar before dawn is the deed whose ripening time (வினைவிளை காலம்) the patikam gives as the reason the Pandya failed to inquire.
teaches: The epic names the past deed both at the first step out of the house and at the hour of the killing, so the whole journey is framed as one deed's ripening, while the travellers themselves give wealth as their reason.

note: The couplet says a ruler who does not examine (ஓரா) and do justice falls by himself; the patikam has the Pandya fail to examine (தேரானாகி) and fall, but says he failed because the time of the deed's ripening had come.
teaches: The couplet treats the failure to examine as the king's own fault and the ruin as its consequence, and the epic keeps the consequence but places the failure itself inside a karmic order, which raises the question the couplet does not face of how a fated lapse can still be the king's guilt.

gains.a: the epic's double cause gains a precise rule from outside the story against which the king's lapse is a fault in law and not only a misfortune
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case in which the lapse it condemns is said to have been brought on by a past deed, so its self-caused ruin is shown with a second cause behind it

note: The goldsmith names Kovalan the thief (கள்வன்) of the anklet; in the Vazhakkurai Kaathai the king, seeing the gem fly from the broken anklet, says that he, who heard the goldsmith, is the thief (யானே கள்வன்).
teaches: The word thief passes in the course of the poem from the accused stranger to the goldsmith's own hidden act and finally to the king's mouth about himself, so the patikam's first accusation is set up to be reversed by the one who acted on it.

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out the one who did it as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Neelakesi makes 'the doers themselves reap' the point that silences the Buddha.
teaches: The proverb that a deed finds its doer turns out to presuppose a doer who lasts until the fruit comes, which is exactly what the Buddhist no-self denies and what Neelakesi defends.

gains.a: the debate's decisive answer gets a common-sense image of karma that ordinary hearers already trusted
gains.b: the quatrain's untroubled image is shown to carry a metaphysical premise, a persisting self, that one school rejects

note: Tirumular makes knowledge of the First, the meaning of the Veda, together with Parashakti abiding in his half, the mark of the one in niyama; the vari makes the hunters' war goddess the woman's form in the half of the forehead-eyed god, praised by the Veda, while carrying Vishnu's conch and discus.
teaches: The half-woman form that Tirumular holds as an object of contemplative knowledge is, in the hunters' song, a goddess with Vishnu's weapons on a fighting mount, so the pair shows the same Saiva image serving yogic discipline in one text and a war cult that will not keep her to one god in the other.

gains.a: the stanza's line on Shiva's half is shown to be the Saiva doctrinal image, and its addition of Vishnu's weapons stands out against it
gains.b: the verse's பாதியுள் மன்னும் பரசக்தி gains an early witness outside the Saiva canon, worshipped by hunters with offerings rather than known in niyama

note: Puram 9's Pandya warns cows, Brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter before he attacks; Kannaki tells the fire to spare Brahmins, the virtuous, cows, chaste women, elders and children.
teaches: The protected classes of the just king's war reappear as the limit a wronged woman sets on her own vengeance against a Pandya city, so the code meant to restrain kings now restrains the one punishing a king, and is applied to his own capital.

gains.a: her list of the spared gains a precedent: it is the established rule of righteous attack, not a sudden mercy
gains.b: the poem's battle rule gains a case where it binds a non-king and is turned against the Pandya line whose ancestor proclaimed it

note: Against the Ajivikas Neelakesi argued that a Lord who never spoke left no scripture; here she argues that a school with no teacher freed from deeds has no first book at all.
teaches: Her test of a school's scripture is constant across the debates: authority runs only from an omniscient speaker, and the materialist fails it more completely than the Ajivika, having no such teacher even in claim.

note: Manimekalai's Jain says only that the atom, matter (புற்கலம்), is the outward form of things; Neelakesi 395 to 397 defends how atoms become form against the objection that touching atoms must have parts.
teaches: The bare formula in the Buddhist epic hides a live problem, how indivisible atoms can join, which the Jain epic answers with many atoms sharing one place.

note: The Buddha here says deed and fruit exist but no doer; Manimekalai 30's teacher says the chain has no maker, no I and no mine, and is itself deed and fruit.
teaches: Set against the Buddhist epic's own teaching, the Jain poem's Buddhist thesis turns out to be stated fairly, so Neelakesi's reply in 575 attacks a view the school holds, not a straw figure.

note: The couplet says sulking is love's pleasure and its pleasure is to come together and embrace; the venba has the cuckoo proclaim love's command to all who have sulked (ஊடினீர்) to unite (கூடுமின்), and chides the one who spurned the letter.
teaches: The couplet's pleasure rests on a condition, that union follows, and the venba shows that condition failing even under love's own command, so the sulk the Kural treats as seasoning becomes the start of a separation.

gains.a: the venba's command gains a stated rule of love, so Kovalan's refusal is a breach of love's own order and not only of Madhavi's hope
gains.b: the couplet's closing condition பெறின், 'if one gets to', gains a case where one does not get to, and what follows then

note: The epic opens saying the learned speak of Puhar only as standing unshaken, never of its decline; the Manimekalai tells how the city was swallowed by the sea when the Indra festival was neglected and Manimekala Deivam cursed it.
teaches: Taken together, the two epics make the city whose permanence the wise affirm at the first wedding the city the sea takes in the next generation, so the opening's confidence becomes the first instance of the impermanence the sequel preaches.

note: Neelakesi says the Buddha himself spoke of six kinds of destinies; in the Manimekalai Aravanar teaches that beings are of six kinds (humans, gods, Brahmas, hell-beings, animals, ghosts), born by good and bad deeds.
teaches: Neelakesi's retort works because Buddhists did teach six realms on their master's word, as the Buddhist epic confirms, so her appeal to scripture for the place of release matches their own practice.

note: Aravana Adigal told Manimekalai that Chintadevi gave Aputhiran the bowl on a rainy night saying it would not fail though the land did; the reborn king, his birth shown him by the seat, recalls the same night and the goddess's words almost word for word.
teaches: The teacher's story and the seat's revelation agree to the word, so the king's restored memory works in the epic as proof that the seat shows births truly.

note: The sun's voice says bright fire will eat this city; in the vow, the fire god appears and says he was ordered long ago to eat the city on the day it wronged the great pathini.
teaches: The burning of Madurai is announced twice by gods, first by the sun as witness and then by the fire as agent, so Kannaki's act fulfils a sentence already spoken from above rather than a private revenge.

note: The Kural says giving alone is good even if there were no higher world; in 416-417 both debaters take the giver's reaching heaven as what makes giving worth doing, and Neelakesi calls the identity of giver and god the truth of giving (தானத்தின் உண்மை).
teaches: The Kural's 'even if there were no higher world' is a position neither the Jain nor the Buddhist debater will hold here, since both stake the worth of alms on a rewarded doer.

gains.a: The epic's grounding of giving in reward is shown to be a choice that another ethics declined.
gains.b: The couplet's hypothetical is seen against a real debate in which a giver without a future was taken to make giving void.

note: Tirumular nurtures the body because its perishing ends the life before true knowledge is won; when the queen wishes Aravanar's aged body long life, he answers that ageing and death are the nature of the born and turns to teaching.
teaches: The pair sets the Saiva siddha's body kept alive for knowledge against the Buddhist teacher's body let go because knowledge has been reached and must be passed on, so the worth of a long life depends on whether knowledge is still to be won.

gains.a: a contrary view that makes Aravanar's refusal of the blessing a position, not just an old man's modesty
gains.b: a teacher who has the knowledge and still declines the body's prolonging, which tests whether nurturing the body is a means or an end

note: In the court the Pandya calls himself the thief and dies; here the narrator says he gave his life for the bent sceptre and so showed the earth a straight one.
teaches: The narrator turns the king's self-condemnation into his last act of just rule, so the same death that proves the sceptre bent is counted as straightening it.

note: The Bhuta quotes the couplet to Maruthi and explains her lost power by her worship of gods, festivals and talk.
teaches: The couplet states the wife's power as a fact; the epic uses it as a test a chaste woman fails, reads தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் literally as a ban on worshipping gods, and adds festivals and gossip, so the couplet becomes a rule with conditions that can be broken.

gains.a: Maruthi's loss of power gains a named authority, the poet who never lies, behind the Bhuta's verdict.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case that spells out what not worshipping a god excludes and what happens to the power when it is not kept.

note: The couplet says a Brahmin's birth is ruined when conduct fails though the Veda can be relearned; Neelakesi says the Veda itself teaches that birth yields nothing yet fixes the four classes and shuts out the Sudra.
teaches: Both put conduct above birth, but the Kural keeps birth as a rank that conduct can lose, while Neelakesi finds the Veda caught between those two and calls the mixture confusion.

gains.a: the verse gains a well-known saying that already ranks conduct above the Brahmin's birth, which makes the contradiction she alleges in the Veda visible in a familiar text
gains.b: the couplet gains a reader who notices that it still assumes a Brahmin's birth as something to be lost, which the Jain argument treats as the very confusion

note: The couplet says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and those of the six duties forget their books; in burning Madurai the Vedic chant and the fire offering cease.
teaches: The couplet's warning that Vedic learning lapses under an unguarding king is shown happening in a single night, and with the cows spared, so the epic keeps one half of the couplet's penalty and lets the other fall.

gains.a: the stopping of the rites gains its doctrinal reading: it is the Kural's named sign of a king who failed to guard
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene in which its two penalties are separated, the cows spared by the pathini's command while the books' recitation still falls silent

note: The Brahma-vadin says the world is an egg laid by one god; the teacher says the chain is made by no maker and is not a made thing (பண்ணுநர் இன்றிப் பண்ணப் படாதாய்).
teaches: The pairing shows that the creator Manimekalai dismissed without argument in Vanji is excluded here by the structure of the doctrine itself, since a chain in which each link supports the next leaves no place for a maker outside it.

note: Bhoothapandiyan's queen rebukes the elders who hold her back and chooses the pyre over the widow's austerities, calling fire and a lotus pond one to her; the summary sets the Pandya Nedunjeliyan's queen of flawless chastity lying with him on the throne-couch, her death having come at once at his feet.
teaches: Both remember a Pandya queen who would not outlive her husband, but the Puram queen must argue her way to the pyre against counsel, while the epic's queen dies without fire or argument and the summary counts that death as flawless chastity, so together they show the widow's death moving from a chosen and contested act to a sign of karpu that needs no choosing.

gains.a: the summary's praise of the queen gains the older Pandya precedent of a wife who refused widowhood, which shows what kind of chastity புரைதீர் கற்பின் is honouring
gains.b: the Puram poem gains a later version of its scene in which no elders object and no pyre is needed, which shows the queen's resolve becoming an ideal assumed rather than argued

note: Manimekalai remembers the camp at Kayangarai as a day of worship and the sage's compassionate teaching; the deity of the pillar in kaathai 21 tells that on that same visit Rahulan killed the cook who stumbled with the sage's food.
teaches: The recovered memory is partial: what the seat restores to her is the piety of that day, and the deed that will kill her husband has to be supplied later by a god, so knowing one's birth in this epic does not yet mean knowing one's karma.

note: The rumour says he stole an anklet from the palace; in the next kaathai Kannaki tells the women of the city that he was no thief and was killed for the price of her own anklet.
teaches: Kannaki turns the private news she received into a public counter-charge, correcting the one fact the rumour got wrong (whose anklet it was), which is the fact the trial will turn on.

note: The couplet says griefs that never let go hold those who hold attachment and do not let go; Maadalan says those whose hearts are full of love go where their attachment leads, and the mothers, held by love for Kannaki, are reborn near her temple.
teaches: The epic agrees with the couplet that attachment binds one to birth, but shows what the couplet does not: a bond of love that leads to a new birth beside the one loved, told without blame, so attachment's hold is the cost the mothers pay for staying near the pathini rather than only a grief.

gains.a: the epic's phrase பற்றுவழிச் சேறல் gains from the couplet the warning that the same hold is what keeps a soul from release, which Maadalan's calm statement does not say
gains.b: the couplet gains a case of attachment that is love for a virtuous woman and whose fruit, a rebirth near her, is told as a mercy, which tests its flat equation of holding with grief

note: The Manimekalai's teacher says the Buddha came down leaving the Tushita world (துடிதலோகம் ஒழியத் தோன்றி); Neelakesi asks how the ascetic who perished could be a god in the Tushita palace at all without a self to carry him.
teaches: The Buddhist epic tells the Tushita descent as sacred history, and the Jain epic takes the same episode as its test case against rebirth without a self.

note: Both describe flesh-eating as feeding flesh with flesh (ஊனைப் பெருக்குதல், ஊன் பெருக்கற்கு); the Kural asks how such a person can hold அருள், the Innaa line ranks the act as the first of pains.
teaches: The pair shows one image doing two jobs: in the Kural it proves the loss of compassion, in the Innaa verse it is a pain ranked above even soured honey and kingless armies.

note: The Vaigai hides tears as if knowing the young wife's fate; in the court the king, called the lord of the Vaigai, loses his life at the hearing of her words.
teaches: The pair shows the river grieving at the entry for the wife and the river's lord dying at her word in the court, so the Vaigai frames Madurai's story from the woman's arrival to the king's death, siding with her in silence before he hears her.

note: The Kural says that when evening comes the whole town reels and suffers; Madhavi's heroine says the world shuts its eyes and, if evening and her husband are such, the world has become poor.
teaches: Both widen one woman's evening grief to the whole settlement, and the epic adds the lover himself to the cause, so the poverty of the world is laid as much on the husband's nature as on the hour.

gains.a: the epic stanza gains a Kural precedent for making the world share the lament
gains.b: the couplet's reeling town gains a named cause in the husband, which the couplet leaves out

note: 785 makes acquaintance unnecessary, while a whole chapter on old friendship opens at 801.
teaches: Parimelazhagar's gloss on 801 eases this by saying that பழைமை is not elapsed time but a certain kind of friendship.
