note: Both summaries open with the same frame (aram, maram, the old city, festivals, the gods' visits, the land's wealth); the Madurai summary keeps the river and the unfailing sky and ends with the Pandya who lay dead on his throne-couch with his chaste queen, the Vanchi summary drops river and sky and ends with Senguttuvan's army at the Ganga, adding valour fitted to aram.
teaches: The shared frame lets the difference show: the Pandya book is summed up in a king undone by a wrong verdict, the Chera book in a king whose war is declared righteous, so the epic's last word on aram passes from the court of justice to the battlefield, and neither summary names the woman both books turn on.

note: Neeli cried through the halls and streets asking whether this was justice and cursed the killers to suffer her sorrow; Kannaki cries through Madurai asking whether there are women, wise men or a god in the city.
teaches: Neeli's curse asked for the same sorrow, and Kannaki's lament fulfils it in form as well as fact, a widow's public cry against an unjust killing repeated in a new birth.

note: 216 says the friend, known by hearing alone and never met for many years, will come; Kural 785 says neither meeting nor long acquaintance is needed, feeling alone gives the claim (கிழமை) of friendship.
teaches: The Kural's rule and the king's wager share the technical word கிழமை, so the couplet's claim that friendship needs no meeting has a famous royal case behind it, one staked on a seat kept for a man never seen.

note: Mokkalan says exposure, fasting and sleeplessness bring nothing; Neelakesi replies that the Buddha's own perfections and ascetic rules bring many hardships.
teaches: The Buddhist attack on Jain penance is met not by defending pain but by showing the Buddhist path also prescribes sleeping in the open and eating once, so the quarrel becomes one of degree rather than of principle.

note: Madhavi tells how the teacher Aravanar taught her that suffering comes of attachment and freedom from it of letting go; here, a renouncer, she sits like a body without life because her daughter has not come.
teaches: The pair shows the epic letting its own renouncer fall short of the teaching she received, so taking robes does not by itself end attachment to a child.

note: Kuruntokai 135: the friend tells the heroine not to cry: the man himself said work is life to men and men are life to women of the house, so he will put off his going. Thinaimalai 82: the friend says a man's duty makes him go for wealth, so she should not grieve. On the plain reading the two friends draw opposite conclusions from the same premise.
teaches: Both friends begin from the maxim that work belongs to men, but the Kuruntokai adds that men are women's life and concludes he will stay, while the venba stops at the man's duty and concludes he will go, so the outcome turns entirely on whether the maxim's second half is said.

note: The Kural argues that no one would sell flesh if no one killed to eat; Saathuvan, told the Nagas cannot live without meat, lets them keep only the flesh of beasts that die of age and bids them harm no living thing.
teaches: The couplet treats the eater as the cause of all killing, while Saathuvan finds the one flesh no killing supplies and so gives people who cannot give up meat a way to keep the Kural's end without its whole demand.

gains.a: Saathuvan's concession gains the reasoning that makes it a principle: what is wrong is the killing that eating causes
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its rule must bend to what a people can bear, and a shape the bending can take

note: The Ainthinai Ezhupathu heroine asks whether the sea, like her, does not sleep because the same shore lord took his fill of it and left; Madhavi's woman tells the neythal that, unlike her, it sleeps free of pain.
teaches: The two neythal women look to the shore for company in sleeplessness and reach opposite answers, one finding in the restless sea a fellow sufferer, the other finding in the closed flower only a sleeper who does not share her pain, so the pair shows the same evening shore read as sympathy and as indifference.

gains.a: the stanza's envy of the flower gains a contrast with the older convention in which the shore suffers with the woman
gains.b: the Sangam poem's consoling fellow-sufferer gains a counter-case in which nature sleeps and the woman is alone

note: The materialist says that when the elements part, all comes to nothing; the Siddhar says he saw the five elements die and fall and the five senses burn and fall.
teaches: The Siddhar describes as his own experience the parting of elements and senses that the materialist says must end awareness, and he remains to report it, which is the case Neelakesi argues for and does not show.

gains.a: Neelakesi's bare rejection gains a first-person witness who outlasts the falling away of the elements.
gains.b: The Siddhar's vision gains its doctrinal stake: it is the very event the materialist claims would leave no one to see it.

note: Perunkoppendu tells the elders holding her back that for her, her husband dead, a lotus pond and the pyre's fire are one, and scorns the widow's life of sparse food and bare ground; Madhavi's second kind of pathini enters the blazing fire as into a cool-water pool, and her third wears the body down in vows.
teaches: The queen's single act of defiance, in which the pyre is a cool pond and the austere widowhood she refuses is worse than fire, becomes in the epic a ranked typology of the chaste wife where entering the fire is only the second kind and the vowed austerity she despised is admitted as the third, and all three are then set beneath Kannaki.

gains.a: the source of the fire-as-cool-pool figure in a widow's own speech against the elders, so that Madhavi's kinds are seen to be drawn from remembered acts and not invented as a scheme
gains.b: a later frame in which the queen's choice is one recognised option among three, with the widow's austerity she scorned now counted as a path of chastity, which shows how the poem's personal refusal was absorbed into a norm

note: Both list Saturn smoking, a comet showing and Venus running south; Kapilar credits the rain that never failed in Pari's land to the king's straight sceptre, while the epic credits the Kaveri's flood to the river.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the same omen formula assigning the land's safety to different powers: to a just king in Purananuru 117, and to the river itself in the epic.

gains.a: the epic's omens gain their weight as signs that normally ruin a land unless something stronger holds
gains.b: Kapilar's poem gains a counter-case where the formula is used without any king's virtue as the cause

note: The Manimekalai's Jain counts space (ஆகாயம்) as a substance that gives room to all things; in 794 Neelakesi says the Vaisheshika's direction comes down to space.
teaches: Neelakesi's denial of direction is not a denial of space: the Jain list keeps space as a substance, so she can fold direction into it rather than abolish it.

claims.gist: the aggregates are impermanent, painful and impure, and there is no soul
those who understand these four truths reach release whatever they do
the courtesan's life is the lowest, one the noble, the learned and the discerning cast off as a disease
dream, mantra, thought, life-span, astrology and bird-omen are real yet are not elements
a guardian king's umbrella is cool shade to those joined to him and burns those who are not
a thing stays one and unchanged through all its states
the twelve links fall across three times: past, present and future
the Buddha's dharma, which pities not one's own life and protects the lives of others, does not leave a suffering world to seek a higher world for oneself
one who has done evil deeds has no good destiny left
the son of a brahmin wife who broke her conduct is an outcaste and must not be touched
the five categories are earth, water, fire, wind and soul, each with its own qualities
soul and nature combine like a lame man riding a blind one, the one seeing and the other acting
atoms bind by qualities of their own and build compounds upward from the two-atom unit
the five aggregates are impermanent, without self, suffering and impure
what has perished cannot report its own perishing
old enemies meet in hell and wound each other without end
the Bodhisattva's patience that yields to the one who strikes him is a mark of his greatness
a teacher who has passed into release can no longer act in compassion
if every moment perishes wholly, knowledge cannot grow by accumulation
the teaching is set out in three scriptures, the Sutra, the Vinaya and the Shastra
a god who must test a giver to learn his heart cannot read minds and is god only in name
there are five organs of knowing, five of action and the mind, eleven in all
the Buddhist scriptures teach the great sorrow of wandering through births
eating flesh bought in the market is not blameworthy
things are both permanent and arising and perishing, and the omniscient knows them all as plainly as a gem in the palm
karmic stain returns only through the activity (yoga) of body, speech and mind; the freed soul without it is not bound again
a woman's adornments lead those who attach themselves to them into hell
the bodies of hell-beings cannot be killed before their time
one enters the Buddha's path of dharma when the cause for it has ripened
an example that lacks both the property to be proved and the reason fails, whether the example exists or not
living beings are produced by the elements alone, with no knowing principle
the differences among the young of one litter come from their own deeds
it is not right to refuse the word of one's husband from a former birth
the human body is a vessel of suffering marked by birth, ageing, disease and death, and knowing this one should turn to dharma
the goddess of the stag grants victory in war only to those who pay her due offering
the evil one has done is atoned for by making the Jina's path clear to others
the Buddha's doctrines contradict one another in every way
earth and the other elements are the bodies of souls

note: The narrator says the queen hid her grief with helpless heart (கையாற்று) and false conduct (பொய்யாற்று ஒழுக்கம்); Manimekalai's maxim says those who take falsehood as their way never pass beyond helpless grief (பொய்யாற்று ஒழுக்கம், கையாற்று அவலம்).
teaches: Read together, the maxim is not general advice but the queen's own conduct described back to her in the narrator's words, so the teaching names her deceit without accusing her.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives the collective name (body, water, country) as a Buddhist mode of speech; the Neelakesi's Buddha calls the soul such a name, like 'hand' for five fingers.
teaches: The Jain poet gives his Buddha a doctrine the Buddhist epic itself states, so here the polemic reports Buddhist teaching recognisably before answering it.

note: Kannaki cited the Chola who killed his own son under the wheel when the cow's tears burned his heart (நெஞ்சுசுட); the goddess answers with a Pandya who cut off his own hand when a woman's reproach burned his heart (நெஞ்சஞ் சுடுதலின்).
teaches: The two speeches match self-punishment for self-punishment, son for hand, showing that the argument over Kovalan's death is being fought with rival royal legends of the same pattern.

note: Naladiyar 24 ends with the dying carrying the dead; Kundalakesi 9 says the foetus, child, youth and young adult have each died in us and we die daily.
teaches: The quatrain makes the mourners already dying in the moment of a funeral; the fragment moves death inside each life, as a series of deaths of one's own former selves, so the bearer is also already a corpse many times over.

note: The Kural asks what other ties (தொடர்ப்பாடு) can remain for those cutting off birth, when even the body is excess; the Neelakesi defends those who teach that at death every tie, even to dharma (அறத்தொடர்ப்பாடு), must go.
teaches: The Kural's list of ties ends at the body, while the Jain teaching carried into the hour of death adds dharma itself to what must be let go, so renunciation's last step is dropping the merit that led there.

gains.a: the Jain teaching of letting go at death is seen to extend a rule the Tamil ethics book already states for the renouncer
gains.b: the couplet's 'further ties' is given a hard case it does not name: the tie to dharma, and a moment, the time of dying

note: The Kural has the five elements laugh inwardly at a deceiver's hidden conduct; Neelakesi argues that no element has theft, lust or generosity as a quality.
teaches: Read together, the Kural's laughing elements must be a figure of moral witness, since the Jain debate shows that moral traits are exactly what the elements cannot bear, and her 'thieving element' mocks any literal reading.

gains.a: her sarcastic 'thieving element' gains a target: a familiar way of speaking in which elements do take moral notice
gains.b: the couplet gains a test of its figure: whether the elements could literally judge conduct is a question the schools argued

note: The Purananuru poem describes the same burning ground of owls, corpse-eating jackals and dancing demon women, which has taken even conquerors, and urges the patron to give freely and win lasting fame; the goddess draws from it that revelling in wealth instead of desiring dharma is the height of folly.
teaches: The same memento mori leads the puram poet to gift and fame that outlast the body, and the Buddhist epic to dharma, with no word of fame: the cemetery's lesson changes with what each tradition thinks survives.

gains.a: The goddess's verdict is seen to drop the fame and the patron that the older use of the scene required.
gains.b: The poem's turn from the burning ground to fame is shown to be a choice, since the same scene could argue for renunciation.

note: Kannaki sprinkles water on the ground as if to clear the earth-woman's distress (மண்ணக மடந்தை, line 40); at the killing the earth-woman's grief grows as Kovalan's blood pours over her (line 215).
teaches: The earth that Kannaki soothes with water at his last meal is soaked with his blood the same day, so the poet makes one figure measure the distance between her care and his death.

note: Tirumular says that saying Siva Siva makes evil deeds die and brings the state of Siva (சிவகதி); Neelakesi says that praising the Aptha destroys both kinds of deed and brings the undivided state of Siva (சிவகதி).
teaches: The two verses share the formula of praise, deeds destroyed and சிவகதி, but for Tirumular the word names Siva and only evil deeds must go, while for the Jain hymn it names a godless auspicious state and good deeds must go too.

gains.a: the hymn's Saiva-sounding vocabulary is seen as a contest over shared words, not a borrowing of Saiva belief
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's சிவகதி is shown to be a term a rival school used for release without a creator god

note: The Kural ranks not killing first and not lying second; the sage lists killing, lying, theft, going to others' wives and craving for wealth, and promises the world of the gods.
teaches: The Kural's ranking of not killing above not lying is the head of a fixed Jain list of five householder abstentions, which the epic gives whole with a heavenly reward rather than release.

gains.a: the sage's list is seen keeping the same order of the first two goods that the Kural argues for
gains.b: the couplet's two-term ranking is shown as the opening of a longer five-part code

note: Saalini, possessed, calls Kannaki a goddess and the jewel of the world, and Kannaki hides behind her husband; at the Pandya's gate the gatekeeper can describe Kannaki only by saying she is not Kotravai on the bleeding pedestal, nor Kali who tore Daruka's chest.
teaches: The divinity a hunter priestess proclaims in a desert shrine, and which Kannaki herself laughs off as confusion, becomes visible to a stranger at the palace door, so the pair shows the story turning Saalini's words into what others see, and the shy wife into a figure that can only be named by the war goddess she is denied to be.

note: The couplet ranks those who fast below those who bear the harsh words of others; Kavunthi, whom the mockers address by her fasting body, curses them, and it is the insulted couple who ask that the words be taken as ignorance.
teaches: The epic splits the couplet's two figures between two people: the faster answers insult with a curse, and the forbearance the couplet ranks higher comes from the young couple who were insulted.

gains.a: the couple's plea gains a ranking: by the couplet their forbearance stands above the nun's austerity
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene showing that fasting and forbearance can come apart, with the insult aimed at the ascetic's wards and not at herself

note: The couplet says the wife who worships her husband and not a god can bid the rain fall; Kayasandigai praises Athirai as standing alone among the house-dwelling wives of rain-giving chastity (வான் தருகற்பின் மனை உறை மகளிரின்) and so the right giver of the bowl's first alms.
teaches: The epic takes the couplet's rain-giving wife as a known type and makes it a rank, one supreme among many, and a qualification for feeding a Buddhist bowl, so domestic chastity is set to work for the renouncer's charity.

gains.a: Kayasandigai's phrase is shown to rest on the Kural's claim, so her choice of Athirai appeals to a test the hearers already accept.
gains.b: The couplet, which speaks of any such wife, gains a use: chastity's power over the rain becomes a standard for whose alms are worthiest, a ranking the couplet does not make.

note: The Kural sets abstaining from one killing above a thousand fire sacrifices; the Neelakesi's sage does not ask the worshippers to drop their vow but to offer a clay goat in its place.
teaches: Between the Kural's flat preference for not killing over ritual and outright refusal of the rite lies a third course the epic shows a teacher using: keep the vow, replace the victim with an image.

gains.a: the clay-goat advice is seen as a practical form of a principle the ethics books already state
gains.b: the couplet's comparison is shown applied to a vowed village offering, where giving up the rite has a social cost the couplet does not weigh

note: The beaten Aryan kings fled the field disguised as matted, ash-smeared ascetics, singers and dancers; here the Chola names that disguise கொல்லாக் கோலம் and denies the Chera any glory for taking them.
teaches: The ruse that saved the northern kings' lives in battle becomes, in the rival Tamil kings' mouths, the reason the Chera's triumph counts for nothing, so the escape and the taunt together show a victory spoiled by the vanquished's change of dress.

note: Both are a friend comforting a woman whose man has crossed the desert, and both argue that no gain could keep him: 201 says not even the Chola rice country, 213 not even the world of the worthy with its nectar.
teaches: Side by side they show the friend's reassurance as a scale that can be pushed from an earthly kingdom to heaven, always measuring his love by what he would refuse rather than by any promise he made.

note: The couplet likens a king's killing of the cruel to weeding the crop; the new Pandya kills a thousand goldsmiths in one day as an offering of lives to the pathini.
teaches: The couplet's punishment by death is of the cruel, one by one, as care for the crop, while the epic's new king kills a whole craft for one goldsmith's lie and calls it an offering, so the pair shows royal punishment sliding from justice into collective sacrifice to restore a king's standing.

gains.a: Cheliyan's act gains a measure from the ethics of the sceptre against which its scale and its form as offering stand out
gains.b: the couplet gains a case that asks who counts as the weed when a king must atone for a predecessor's wrong

note: Avvaiyar at the gate of Athiyaman (390) and of his son Ezhini (392): the same stripping of rags, new cloth, toddy and food.
teaches: Father and son receive the same bard with the same ritual of rags exchanged for cloth, which shows the reception as an inherited house custom of the Athiyar rather than one chief's whim, while the son's poem adds conquest as the source of what is given.

note: Kovalan buys Madhavi's garland at the price of the king's 1008 kazhanju and forgets his home; returning to Kannaki, he says that sporting with a deceiver (சலதி) has wasted the mountain of wealth his line gave him.
teaches: The narrator tells the purchase as a rule-bound custom and blames no one, and only later does Kovalan himself call Madhavi a deceiver and the purchase a ruin, so the epic lets the buyer, not the poet, put the blame on the seller.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher counts the collective name (the body, water, a country) as a true mode of speech; 533 says naming collections one holds unreal makes every such word a lie.
teaches: The Jain charge of lying presupposes that a name must match one real thing, which is the very premise the Buddhist account of conventional naming in the Manimekalai rejects.

note: Maadalan, finding no cause for Kovalan's suffering in his good deeds of this life, asks whether it is the fruit of a former birth; the patikam's goddess names that cause, a curse from a former birth.
teaches: The epic reaches its doctrine of former deeds by elimination: a witness who knows only Kovalan's good acts can explain his ruin only by a past birth, and the patikam later confirms the guess with a named curse, so the karmic cause is offered as what remains when the visible life acquits the sufferer.

note: The crossroads spirit of Puhar announces that it seizes false witnesses and others with its noose and devours them; here it seizes one and refuses Kovalan's offer of his own life in exchange.
teaches: The spirit's announced punishment proves rigid in practice: it will not take a good man's life even when he offers it, so the pair shows its justice as exact matching of deed to doer, with no place for the substitution that Kovalan's generosity proposes.

note: Earlier the Buddha likened the aggregates, arising and perishing in one moment, to the tip of a lamp's flame; here Neelakesi refuses the flame as an example of continuity because two real things are in it.
teaches: The flame the Buddha offered as the very picture of momentary arising is claimed by the Jain for her own side, since a lamp shows a lasting fuel beside its passing tip, so one image serves both doctrines depending on which of its two parts is looked at.

note: 864 says one who doesn't let go of anger is easy prey for anyone. 899 makes the anger of the exalted able to bring down a king.
teaches: Anger is weakness or supreme power depending on who has it, and 306 warns that it burns the one who has it.

note: In 202 Neelakesi grants that the pathiri scent stays in the new pot after the flower decays, to argue a soul outlasting the body; in 422-423 Mokkalan cites the scent in the sherd as a quality leaving its substance, and she answers that the flower's particles stay and carry it.
teaches: The same pot-and-scent example cuts both ways in the Jain debater's hands: against Kundalakesi it shows something that endures, against Mokkalan she must deny that the scent ever left its substance.

note: The patikam promises to show that the high praise a renowned pathini (உரைசால் பத்தினிக்கு உயர்ந்தோர் ஏத்தல்); here the gods of heaven worship her and the hill women sing her praise.
teaches: The second moral is first fulfilled among the gods and the hill girls of a love song, before any king hears of her, so the praise of the pathini begins at the margin of the kingdom and travels to the Chera court in the next kaathai.

note: The sermon lists killing for spirits and gods among the beasts' deaths; in the Veda debate Neelakesi tells the Vedic disputant that killings for the Vasus, Rudras and ancestors bring hard karma on the killers.
teaches: The sermon counts the sacrifice from the victim's side and the later debate from the sacrificer's, so the Jain case against the rite is made twice: the beast suffers, and the deed returns on the one who kills.

note: The patikam's goddess says Kannaki will see her husband only in the form of the gods; here he rises among a host of immortals (பல்லமரர் குழாத்துளான்) on the day of his death.
teaches: The vision anticipates the reunion the goddess limits to divine form, and Kannaki's refusal to join him until her anger cools shows the reunion withheld by her own choice, not only by the curse's term.

note: Kannaki threw the Chola who relieved the bird's distress at the Pandya as a reproach; Maadalan offers the same ancestor to the Chera as proof that the Chola sceptre cannot bend.
teaches: The one exemplum works in two directions within the epic, as an accusation of a king who failed and as a guarantee for a king who has not been tested, which shows how the ancestor's deed stands in for an inquiry into the living king's justice.

note: The couplet says all of keeping a house is for tending guests and doing good; the epic's household is set up so that its charity and hospitality may be seen, and the story later takes both away.
teaches: The epic founds Kannaki's household on exactly the couplet's purpose, then lets a husband's absence and exile empty it, showing that the householder's dharma the couplet assigns to the house depends on the pair staying in it.

gains.a: the narrator's brief line on the household's purpose gains the weight of a stated rule, so its later loss reads as the loss of the household's whole reason
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a case of its failure: a wife ready to keep it who cannot once her husband leaves the house

note: The invocation praises as god only the one who knows all (எல்லா முணர்ந்தான்); verse 193 denies that the Buddha knew without remainder (ஒழிவின்றி யுணர்கலான்).
teaches: The invocation's definition of god by omniscience is not only praise but the premise of the debate: it becomes the test by which the rival teacher's book is ruled out as scripture.

note: Pattinathar's verse begins its list of the world's reversals with the born dying and the dead being born and turns from them to Siva, who frees from coming and going; Maadalan says the born die and the dead are born and calls it nothing new, the ancient way of life.
teaches: The same saying about the born and the dead serves the epic as a reassurance that the order of deeds holds and the Siddhar as a reason to loathe that order and seek Siva, so the line itself carries no verdict and its meaning depends on whether release or a good rebirth is the goal.

gains.a: the epic's law gains from Pattinathar the reminder that a round of births ordered by deeds is still a round, so the mothers' reunion is not release
gains.b: the Siddhar's formula gains a setting where it is said without disgust, as the Brahmin's comfort to a king, which shows that its horror in the Siddhar comes from his frame and not from the saying

note: The couplet asks whether the host who feeds guests need even sow his field; the epic likens the bowl's plenty to alms in ascetics' hands and to seed sown with the right water, soil, season and tools.
teaches: Both make feeding others a kind of sowing, but the couplet promises the giver's field yields unsown, while the epic makes the yield depend on conditions, the worth of the receiver among them.

gains.a: the epic's image gains a contrast that shows how conditional its sowing is
gains.b: the couplet's unconditional promise gains a rival view in which a gift's fruit depends on where and how it is sown

note: The hunters owe the goddess a bali as a debt; Tirumular, having nothing to show the god who eats oblations, offers a song as his food offering.
teaches: The vari is itself a song sung over the bali, so the hunters give both the blood and the song that Tirumular offers in its place, which shows the song offering was a companion of the blood rite before it was a substitute for it.

gains.a: the hunters' debt-offering gains a contrast that shows its song as a second offering, not mere accompaniment
gains.b: Tirumular's song-oblation gains a scene of the older rite in which song and blood were offered together

note: Kakandhan, though grieving, kills his elder son with his own sword for seizing Visakai's garland; the present Chola says the vidyadhara did to his son what he himself should have done.
teaches: The ascetic's stories prepare the king's verdict: Kakandhan executes his sons with his own hand, and the Chola, faced with a son already dead, claims that act as his own duty, while also hiding the body from other kings, which Kakandhan never did.

note: The shrine set up for the demon-mother among flesh-eating hosts is where, in 35, people come to cut a lamb's head for the goddess and the sage forbids the killing.
teaches: The description of the shrine as a place of demons who eat bodies is the moral setting of the first act: the sage's reform begins by ending blood offering at that very shrine.

note: The couplet says those sick with love cannot know the dignity of not going after one who has turned hostile; Manimekalai says her heart went after the stranger who had scorned her, and asks if this is the nature of desire.
teaches: The couplet's lovesick woman knows her loss of dignity and keeps loving, while Manimekalai, meeting the same fact in herself on a single sight, answers it with a curse on desire (91), the renunciant's reply the love chapter never gives.

gains.a: Manimekalai's question is shown to have a known answer in the Tamil love tradition, so her surprise marks how new desire is to her.
gains.b: The couplet's diagnosis is applied to a girl vowed to austerity, which shows it holding even where the speaker has renounced the love it describes.

note: The couplet calls a head that does not bow to the eight-qualitied one as useless as a sense organ without sense; Kavunthi vows each organ, ears, tongue, eyes, body, hands, head and mind, to the Arhat alone.
teaches: The couplet's single comparison between the bowing head and a dead sense is worked out by the nun into a vow for every sense in turn, and the eight-qualitied one is named in the preceding sermon as the Jain Lord (எண்குணன், line 188).

gains.a: the nun's vow gains its root: a sense not turned to the Lord is as if it did not work
gains.b: the couplet's எண்குணத்தான் gains a reading in which a Jain voice claims the title for the Arhat

note: Against the Buddha, who denied a soul, she asked who he then was that taught; against the materialist she asks which element is the one debating with her.
teaches: The same self-reference argument serves against both deniers of the soul: the debater's own presence is the counterexample, whether the denial is the Buddhist's no-self or the materialist's mere elements.

note: Kural 4 sets the Lord apart as one without liking or aversion; Puranan argues that a knower who speaks must fall into longing and anger, and Neelakesi denies that speech implies them.
teaches: The Kural defines its Lord by the absence of liking and aversion without asking whether such a Lord can teach; the Ajivika debate shows that the absence was contested, since a rival held that any speaking Lord must have them.

gains.a: the epic's debate gains a well-known Tamil statement of the passionless Lord that Neelakesi's position needs and the Ajivika's denies
gains.b: the couplet gains a live dispute over whether its Lord could speak at all without losing the very freedom from liking and aversion it praises

note: In the last kaathai the town's talk, brought by Vayantamalai, calls Madhavi's tapas shameful; here the festival crowd says it to Manimekalai's face and calls the mother cruel.
teaches: The gossip that reached Madhavi indirectly becomes a crowd around the daughter, and its charge shifts from the mother's shame to her cruelty to the girl, so the town's judgment follows the renunciation from one generation to the next.

note: Tirumular says the soul reaches the saving state by seeing through the twenty-five principles, prakriti and maya; 763 says listing the principles can do nothing for a soul that never changes.
teaches: The pair shows what the Saiva use of the twenty-five needs and the Sankhya lacks: a soul that can be bound and freed, so that seeing through the principles is a real change of state.

gains.a: The Neelakesi verse gains a case where the twenty-five lower principles are in fact used as a path to release, which is the use its objection says is impossible.
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a pointed objection it must meet: that seeing through the principles changes nothing if the soul who sees is unchangeable.

claims.gist: spirits, men and beasts are the three living sources of outside harm
a death that befalls one's own is the fruit of old deeds and is not to be grieved
the Lord's single speech is understood by every hearer according to his kind
a killing counts as killing only when there is a living being, knowledge that it lives, the intention to kill, the act, and death
release is a void
a release that is mere void can be no goal, since people fear even a death that leads to heaven
those of good conduct stretch themselves out for others even to their own death
the beam is one only by an assigned name; nothing stands besides the motions of its ends
feeling is of three kinds: pleasant, painful and neither
the neutral feeling arises from deed that is neither good nor evil
seeing and knowing belong to the soul that abides joined with the body
Kovalan and Kannaki perished in sorrow through the evil deeds they themselves had done
household life is an illusion, and wealth and the body do not last even a moment
a scent is received by some thing, and the Buddhist must name what receives the trace
keeping a charge entrusted by ascetics, however small, brings very great joy
bodily diseases are curable, incurable, or such as pass by subsiding rather than by medicine
killing, lust and theft are the deeds that arise in the body
no deed of the body is done without a mind that does it
generality, higher and lower, gathers things into classes and particularity marks each as distinct
inherence is what makes qualities and actions belong to their substance
all that the scripture treats comes down to atoms of five kinds
protecting the Brahmins who keep the Vedas is a king's duty
there is never death for the soul
wanting what is good is not a fault; coveting must be judged by its object
the soul and its qualities are to be known through placing, standpoints, means of knowledge and the categories of search
if kinds are not different from substances, naming them separately is only synonymy
in a round of births without beginning no teacher can be great 'from the first'
contact without intention brings no karma
drinking coconut toddy kills nothing, so an ascetic of non-harm may drink it
toddy gives this world, the next and endless joy
all the Buddhas of past ages taught one and the same truth
things arise in dependence: where this is not, that is not; where this is, that is
seeing fault, deed and fruit as unstable, empty and suffering is the sure way to release
the infant already contains all it will later have
a cubit-long infant cannot hold the many parts and powers it will later have
eating flesh is not a fault
there is no abiding soul
enduring bodily austerity is not a vow
mahat comes forth from prakriti
no good comes of speaking falsely
Pandya kings do not live on once their sceptre bends
the effect is not now but exists later
every thing is both existent and non-existent according to its time
a doctrine with no teacher freed from deeds has no first scripture, and so is invention
a dancing woman's signs of love are performances of her art, not true feeling
birth is suffering and freedom from birth is bliss, as the first teacher of dharma taught
a caitya to the Buddha is raised to end the distress of all who come after
lying, harming living trees and quarrelling over meat lead without doubt to the burning hell
a king should clear his prison and give it over, with compassion, to those who practise dharma

note: The Neelakesi's sage says the hells are seven (ஏழாய்) and spread into eighty-four hundred thousand dwellings; the Manimekalai's goddess summons the eight kinds of hell-beings (எண் வகை நரகர்) within the Chakravala.
teaches: The two epics count the hells differently, seven earths stacked below the world against eight kinds of hell-dwellers within one world-system, so hell's shape is itself a point of sectarian difference.

note: The venba says gods worship the woman who worships her husband and that Kannaki has become the guest of the women of heaven; Kannaki here says she reached heaven by former good deeds and will leave it when that merit is spent.
teaches: The Manimekalai accepts the Silappathikaram's heavenly welcome for Kannaki but makes it a stay that ends, so the earlier epic's final honour becomes one stage of a samsaric account whose real end is still to come.

note: Nettimaiyar wishes the Pandya years more than the sands of the Pahruli river of the ancient Pandya; the epic's blessing says the sea took the Pahruli river (பஃறுளி யாற்றுடன்) with the Kumari peak.
teaches: The Sangam poet measures a king's life by a river that still flows, while the epic remembers the same river as drowned and makes its loss the occasion of a northern conquest, so the river turns from a figure of endurance into a figure of loss.

gains.a: the epic's legend gains evidence that Pahruli was a living name in Pandya praise before it was told as lost
gains.b: the Purananuru blessing gains a later memory in which the river it swore by has vanished, sharpening its wish for long life

note: Manimekalai's Jain states that every thing takes on origination, persistence and destruction in each instant; Neelakesi 392 has the Buddhist ask what bears those three if they are qualities.
teaches: Manimekalai lets the Jain triad stand unanswered, while the Jain epic shows the Buddhist's actual objection to it, the missing bearer, and the Jain reply in 393 that quality and bearer are one and different.

note: Kovalan sang the girls' charge that a man who swore by the sea god and broke his oath is without virtue; Madhavi's last song bows to the sea god and asks it to bear a false oath.
teaches: The two singers take opposite stances to the same broken oath before the same god, his to condemn and hers to plead for pardon, and the plea, left without a named oath-breaker, is what Kovalan hears as her guilt.

note: The anklets Kannaki leaves off in grief (அணிசிலம்பு ஒழிய) are the anklets she offers with a smile when Kovalan returns ruined and sees her wasted body (சிலம்புஉள கொண்மின்).
teaches: The epic's fatal anklet enters the story as an ornament set aside in loneliness, and that unworn state is what lets it become the capital for the journey to Madurai.

note: Kannaki, appearing in the sky to Senguttuvan, says the Southerner is blameless and has become a guest in the palace of the king of the gods, and that she is his daughter; the ball songs that follow hail the Southerner with the gods' necklace at every stroke.
teaches: The ball songs are the public form of Kannaki's acquittal: only because she has called the Pandya blameless can the women of the Chera city hail the king who killed her husband, and his old title of the gods' necklace now reads as his place in Indra's hall.

note: The couplet calls stealth a dark knowledge (காரறிவாண்மை) absent in those who love measure; the goldsmith, the real thief, lectures the guards on the eight arts of thieves as an unmatched skill.
teaches: The Kural grants that stealth is a kind of knowledge, and the epic shows that knowledge turned from taking goods to taking a life, as the thief's expertise in theft persuades the guards to kill an innocent man.

gains.a: the goldsmith's lecture gains a name for what it displays: cleverness that is still darkness
gains.b: the couplet's dark knowledge gains a use it does not mention, deceiving those who keep the law

note: Sivavakkiyar mocks the ochre-wearers with matted hair, water-pots and yoga staffs who leave their wives and beg from house to house; Neelakesi mocks the monk who boils and dyes his cloth as though he had only given up cooking rice.
teaches: Jain and Siddhar both ridicule the ochre-robed renouncer, but for opposite failings: Sivavakkiyar faults him for abandoning home duties, Neelakesi for carrying them on in the monastery.

gains.a: Neelakesi's joke is seen to belong to a wider Tamil satire of the ochre robe, aimed here at its labour rather than its begging
gains.b: Sivavakkiyar's charge that the renouncer abandons home is set against a charge that he never left it

note: Both set the ascetic's ஆற்றல் against கூற்றம்: the Kural says those who gain the power of penance can leap even Death; here a demoness likened to Death owns that the fire of the sage's penance would destroy her.
teaches: The couplet's abstract boast that penance outruns death becomes a scene in which Death's likeness itself gives up the fight, and the victory comes without the ascetic acting at all.

gains.a: the demoness's surrender is read as the outcome the Kural promised for true penance
gains.b: the couplet's claim gains a dramatised instance in which the threat is a being, not the end of life

note: The couplet says anger left unguarded kills the one who holds it; Kannaki says her anger at Madurai, though it followed a just grievance, is a sin that will reach her after her heavenly merit ends.
teaches: Kannaki is the hardest case for the couplet, a woman whose anger an earlier epic praised as just, and the Manimekalai applies the rule to her anyway while stretching its reach across births: the self that anger kills is a future self, after heaven.

gains.a: Kannaki's confession gains a stated rule that anger turns on its holder, which explains why a goddess fears her own deed
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case of righteous anger and a time scale beyond one life, which its two lines do not give

note: The Kural says that one who restrains the five senses as a tortoise draws in its limbs is protected through seven births; Neelakesi says the monk should guard the eyes that stir the mind instead of covering his limbs.
teaches: The tortoise image of drawing in the limbs is exactly what Neelakesi denies is restraint when done with cloth: she moves the Kural's withdrawal from the body to the senses, against the robe.

gains.a: her charge gains a standard of restraint the Buddhist side would also grant, so the robe can be judged by it
gains.b: the couplet's figure is shown to need a reading, since hiding the limbs literally is what she calls weakness

note: Kural 929 says reasoning with a drunk is like searching with fire under water; here the drunk reasons with a sober ascetic, arguing that toddy kills nothing.
teaches: The epic reverses the couplet's direction, letting the drunk be the one who argues, and his argument from non-harm shows that the drunkard's reasons can borrow the ascetic's own principle and still be worthless.

gains.a: the rule that makes the drunk's reasoning absurd without the narrator having to answer it
gains.b: a scene where the drunk himself offers reasons, showing the futility runs both ways

note: The Kundalakesi's invocation opens 'he stood in greatness from the first' (முன் தான் பெருமைக்கண் நின்றான்); Neelakesi asks what 'first' can mean in a beginningless round of births.
teaches: A word of praise in the Buddhist invocation is read as a doctrinal claim and put to a dilemma, showing how the Jain debater turns devotion into a proposition that can be refuted.

note: The hill kuravar's report of the one-breasted woman taken to heaven, made to Ilango in the patikam, is made here to the reigning king.
teaches: The same witnesses tell the same wonder twice, to the prince who renounced and to the king who rules, and only the king's hearing turns it into a cult and a war, so the epic's frame and its last book answer each other.

note: The couplet's woman lives because she sees in dreams the man who gives no grace awake; Madhavi's woman, whose eyes cannot sleep in the evening, asks the sleeping neythal whether it sees the cruel man coming in its dreams.
teaches: The Kural's comfort depends on sleep, and the song removes it: the sleepless woman is shut out of the dream that keeps the couplet's speaker alive and can only ask a flower for it, so the pair shows the dream-comfort as a privilege of those who can sleep.

gains.a: the stanza's question gains its stake: in the Kural the dream is what keeps a deserted woman alive
gains.b: the couplet gains a limit it does not state, that its consolation fails the woman who cannot sleep at all

note: Visakai vows in youth to be her cousin's wife only in the next birth; at sixty she tells him again she will not come to his feet in this birth but will serve him in the next.
teaches: The vow made to silence a slander outlives the slander by forty years, so what began as a defence of her name becomes the form their love takes, kept apart in body and joined in shared charity.

note: Kural 334 says what shows itself as a day is a blade sawing through life; Kundalakesi 10 says each day's step takes us to lay our heads at the edge of Death's sword.
teaches: The couplet makes the day itself the blade; the fragment makes the day a step toward a blade held by Death and adds the condemned man's walk, so time becomes not only the cutting but the procession to execution with no reprieve.

note: In 260 Neelakesi tells Arkkachandra that the eater shares the butcher's karma whatever his mind; in 344 she meets Mokkalan's same plea of innocent intention with the seller who kills for the price.
teaches: Against two Buddhist teachers the Jain debater answers the defence by intention in two ways, by the butcher's act and by the merchant's motive, so the epic builds a consistent case that the buyer's purpose is the cause.

note: The couplet defines the good path (நல்லாறு, நெறி) as the way that keeps not killing anything in view; Kavunthi's road counsel makes that literal, warning that a careless step on the shore may harm the crab and the snail.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's path metaphor turns into an actual walk where every footfall must be watched, and the nun counts harm to a snail as a grief equal to the dangers to the traveller herself.

gains.a: the nun's warning gains its principle: the attention she asks for is the couplet's சூழும், a constant watch
gains.b: the couplet's யாதொன்றும் gains a case showing it reaches even crabs and snails underfoot

note: Here a pleasant word beats a gladly given gift. In 225, relieving hunger is a power above the ascetic's.
teaches: A hungry person's view of 92 might differ, which suggests the ranking in 92 assumes someone who isn't in need.

note: Kannaki names a strong deed of the past and her own cruel deed as the cause of Madurai's ruin; the hill women sing that she burned Koodal because the royal order failed.
teaches: Within one kaathai the burning is put down to karma in the victim's voice and to the king's broken justice in the worshippers', so the chapter repeats the patikam's two morals as two voices rather than choosing one.

note: The couplet says fate outruns any other plan; the narrator puts ஊழ்வினை behind a journey Kovalan plans, by his own word at line 51, to win back wealth.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's claim working from inside a person's own scheme: the plan to recover wealth is not overtaken by fate but is the road fate travels.

gains.a: its passing word ஊழ்வினைக் கடைஇ gains the force of a stated rule that no counter-plan can outrun the deed
gains.b: the couplet's abstract 'it gets there first' gains a case where the victim's own design is the vehicle

note: The couplet's spy goes in the guise of renouncers to get in and see; the defeated northern kings put on the guise of ascetics and performers to get away.
teaches: The couplet treats the renouncer's dress as a tool of the king's intelligence, and the epic shows the same dress used by kings themselves to escape a lost battle, so the guise that hides a spy's purpose also hides a king's shame, and it works because no one strikes a man who looks like a renouncer.

gains.a: the kings' flight gains a known device, the renouncer's dress as cover for passing through hostile ground, rather than a chance escape
gains.b: the couplet's technique gains a case where it is used not by a servant to enter but by the defeated to leave, turning a spy's skill into a mark of a king's disgrace

note: Aputhiran dies on Manipallavam with the purpose of sustaining lives and is born in Savakam, where he had meant to carry the bowl against a famine; in kaathai 25 the minister tells the king that before his birth Savakam lost its rain for twelve years, and that since he was born the sky has not failed and no creature has known hunger.
teaches: The famine Aputhiran set out to relieve with the bowl is ended by his birth instead, so the purpose held at death is fulfilled by what he becomes rather than by what he carries.

note: The kuravar's report of a one-breasted woman taken to heaven under a flowering vengai by the retinue of the king of the gods is the event the Katturai Kaathai narrates at its close, where Kannaki climbs the hill, stands under the vengai and boards the heavenly car with Kovalan.
teaches: The patikam gives the ascent as seen by strangers who call it a wonder, while the kaathai gives it from inside, with Kannaki naming herself one who did the deed of fire, so the pair shows the poem framing as a marvel what its heroine felt as guilt.

note: Both use the phrase of Karikal 'taking the cool water' (தண்பதம் கொள்ளும் / தண்பதம் கொண்டு): in the Akananuru a courtesan recalls how at Karikal's water festival at Kazhar the Kaveri carried off the dancer Atthi, and likens her lover's loss to it; the epic likens the joyful crowd on the shore to the first day of that festival.
teaches: The festival the epic uses as a simile of joy is, in the Sangam poem, the scene of a dancer lost and a courtesan abandoned, which is what this shore day will become for Madhavi.

gains.a: the simile carries a buried memory of loss at the same festival, so the epic's joyful shore is shadowed before the songs begin
gains.b: the Akananuru's water festival gains a fuller picture of its crowds, costumes and noise and of its standing as a byword for Puhar's festivity

note: Both tell a death by refusing food: the Chera Perunjeralathan, ashamed of a wound in his back, sits facing north with his sword; Kavunthi, after the deaths of her wards, gives up life by the vow of not eating.
teaches: The fasting death that the Sangam poem shows as a warrior king's answer to shame is in the epic taken up by a Jain nun as an answer to failed guardianship, so the same act carries the honour code into the renouncer's vow.

gains.a: Kavunthi's brief death gains a Tamil precedent that makes it read as an answer to dishonour, not only as grief
gains.b: the king's death gains a counterpart outside the warrior class, showing the act could be chosen by a renouncer for a failure of care rather than of valour

note: The couplet says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; Kannaki, though a goddess in heaven, says she must swim the hard sea of births (40) until she hears the Buddha's dharma and leaves birth.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the epic shows that even a deified woman is still in the sea, and it names the means of crossing as hearing a teacher's dharma, which the couplet's 'Lord' leaves unnamed and which here replaces devotion with understanding.

gains.a: Kannaki's prophecy gains the Kural's image of the sea of births as the frame for her long passage to release
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed Lord gains a rival reading in which the crossing is made by hearing the Buddha's teaching, and in which gods too are swimmers

note: Tirumular says the wise gave up logic and debate (தர்க்க வாதம்), recited the Veda and gained release; the Buddhist teacher folds scripture into inference and makes logic the first part of the true doctrine.
teaches: The two disagree on the same question, whether scripture stands as its own source of truth above argument, and the Buddhist answer explains why the epic's road to release passes through debate rules that the Saiva verse tells the wise to leave behind.

gains.a: the epic's quiet reduction of all other means to inference gains a clear statement of the position it denies
gains.b: the verse's dismissal of தர்க்க வாதம் gains a concrete instance of the logic it dismisses, taught as a path to release

note: The assemblies warn that a forgotten festival will bring the guardian spirit's affliction on the city; in kaathai 25 the king, searching for his lost son, neglects the festival and Manimekala deity curses the city to the sea.
teaches: The opening warning is the plot's first prophecy, but its fulfilment shifts the punisher from the city's guardian spirit to Manimekala deity, so the epic keeps the civic threat while giving the punishment to its own Buddhist-protecting goddess.

note: The couplet calls the tears of those who cannot bear their suffering a weapon that wears away wealth; here a widow's tears and words take the king's life.
teaches: The couplet's slow wearing-away of a bad king's wealth by the people's tears becomes, in the epic, the instant death of the king at one wronged woman's tears and words.

note: The Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Neelakesi asks whether rules for shaving heads and eating are the path of dharma.
teaches: The couplet's neutral rule that outward marks do not make the renouncer becomes in the epic a weapon against a rival order's rule-book, and the pairing shows the rule cuts against every order with marks, the Jain one included.

gains.a: the challenge is seen to rest on a principle Tamil readers already granted, not only on sectarian scorn
gains.b: the couplet's general rule is shown in use in inter-sect debate, where it decides which order's discipline counts as dharma

note: Parasaran hails the Chera who cut the kadamba in the sea (கடற்கடம் பெறிந்த) and carved his bow on the hill; Patitruppattu 11 tells the felling of the guarded kadamba after reaching the sea by Imayavaramban Neduncheralathan, whom the Himalaya marks.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam Chera's signature deed as a blessing formula in a brahmin's mouth, and strings it with Mantharam Cheral and the Porunai's Poraiyan, so the separate Cheras of the decades become one praised house.

gains.a: the brahmin's blessing gains a real deed and a named king behind its epithet
gains.b: the decade's battle gains an afterlife as a stock title, cited in a Pandya village by a Chola-land brahmin as the Chera's fame

note: Aravanar, in Thuvathikan's foretelling, blesses her with வாய்வதாக நின் மனப்பாட்டு அறம்; at Kanchi she says it of herself, வாய்வது ஆக என் மனப்பாட்டு அறம்.
teaches: The teacher's blessing becomes the pupil's own vow in the same words, marking the point where she stops being foretold and begins to will her path.

note: The herdswomen pray that the Pandya's drum bring victory day after day; the same day that king's verdict has killed Kovalan, and the next morning he names himself the thief and dies.
teaches: The closing blessing is the stock wish of a herders' song, but placed on the day the sceptre has bent it becomes a prayer for a king already doomed, so the reader hears the epic's justice theme inside a rite meant only to save the cattle.

note: The Brahmin who opened in anger, calling her an unbeliever, is at the close urged to speak truly, concedes, and is praised by the onlookers as one of the true.
teaches: The Jain poem converts its opponent rather than humiliating him: the man who began by denying her standing ends with standing of his own, praised for yielding to the truth.

note: The couplet says the fire-disease of hunger seldom touches one who habitually shares food (பாத்தூண்); the unit opens on a bowl first filled with a chaste wife's share (பாத்தூண், 1) and on a woman with the elephant-fire disease whose hunger came from old deeds.
teaches: The couplet's protection covers only the sharer's own body, while the epic shows a fire-hunger that no habit of one's own sharing could have kept off because a former deed sent it, so the cure has to come from someone else's share.

gains.a: the epic's alms bowl gains the Kural's name for hunger as a fire-disease that sharing holds off, which makes the bowl a medicine
gains.b: the couplet gains a case beyond its reach: hunger sent by karma, curable only by another's gift and not prevented by one's own

note: Puram 173 praises Pannan's house, where the noise of eating (ஊணொலி அரவம்) sounds like birds in a fruiting tree, as the home of the doctor of hunger; the epic uses the fruit-tree birds for the crowd at Aputhiran's hall (26 to 27), then tells how the hall's noise of eating (ஊண் ஒலி அரவம், 60) fell silent once rain removed hunger.
teaches: The epic takes the Sangam praise of a patron's noisy kitchen and shows its condition: the sound that proves a giver's fame lasts only as long as others are hungry, so the doctor of hunger is unmade by a world without the disease.

gains.a: the phrase ஊண் ஒலி அரவம் is shown to be the Sangam patron's formula, so its silencing marks the end of Aputhiran as a patron of the poor
gains.b: Pannan's praise gains a counter-case in which the same sound stops, exposing that the patron's glory depends on the hunger he cures

note: The couplet says the wife who worships her husband rather than a god commands the rain; the patikam says that because Kannaki was a pathini she burned Madurai and brought down its king.
teaches: The power the couplet gives the devoted wife is a blessing on the world through rain, and the epic turns the same power into fire against a city once her husband is wronged, so the pair shows the chaste wife's word as a force that can destroy as well as nourish.

gains.a: Kannaki's burning of the city gains a source in the ethics book's claim that a wife's devotion commands nature
gains.b: the couplet's promise gains its dark counterpart: the same command over nature used for punishment, which the couplet's rain never suggests

note: Kural 557 likens the king's lack of grace to the world's lack of rain; Kalittokai 10 likens the drought-dried waste to a world under a crooked-sceptred king whose men rob and kill.
teaches: The comparison runs both ways: the ethics book explains tyranny by drought and the love poet explains drought by tyranny, so the bond between bad rule and failed rain was common enough to be used as vehicle or as tenor.

note: The quatrain has the best of people renounce home and wealth after slow reflection on impermanence; the ascetic renounces when the news of his son's death by evil deeds reaches him.
teaches: The pairing shows impermanence learned two ways: the quatrain's sage reasons his way to it, while the epic's merchant has it forced on him by bereavement and only then states it as the doctrine.

gains.a: the ascetic's turn gains a known ethical type, the renouncer who sees nothing stands, against which his grief-driven timing stands out
gains.b: the quatrain's unhurried reflection gains a case where the same insight comes suddenly, through a son's ruin

claims.gist: a king who strays from justice is better dead before the word of it spreads
strong former deeds bent the king's sceptre and his dying straightened it
a protecting king lives in fear of the rain failing and greater fear of any life being wronged
to be born to a line that guards the people is suffering, not a thing to be revered
the sin of killing is removed by raising the hand and declaring it gone
speech is produced by effort through letters and words, so the Veda is not natural or eternal
the merit of great giving does not fail and brings rescue in disaster
a monk does not share in a killing when the animal was not marked out for him
the eater of flesh is the equal of the robber on the road
what one gained in past births can be known in this birth, as a scripture taught by Indra shows, without entering the cave
nothing is beyond the reach of those who never swerve from truth and who protect living beings
a king must punish his own son's wrong as he would any other's
without the guardian's protection there are no ascetics' vows and no women's chastity
an action that has ceased persists as a capacity in its bearer and returns when needed
an effect does not come without a cause
a cause has no mind that intends its effect
there is nothing but aggregated things
the threefold remedy of knowledge, clear faith and conduct ends the disease of birth and brings great joy
it is wrong to keep back a means of ending the world's hunger, as the gods kept back the leftover nectar
the chain of dependent arising has no maker and no fixed fate
in the chain there is no I and nothing that is mine
those who know the twelve links gain the great reward; those who do not know them fall to hell
ignorance is forgetting what reasoning has established and holding as clear what is only heard, as that a hare has horns
living beings are of six kinds: humans, gods, Brahmas, hell-beings, animals and ghosts
the adorned body is skin covering a vessel of filth
giving away one's own body and wives is a virtuous gift on the way to buddhahood
a man who gives away his wives has shown that no bond restrains what he will do next
if mind and action are identical, the merit and demerit that settle in the doer cannot be accounted for
the store the Buddhist posits is the soul the Jain teachers teach
lying, slander, harsh words and idle talk are the four evil deeds of speech
a curse laid in grief binds those who caused the grief and comes to fruit in a later birth
a deed of a former birth rises in wrath and does not fail to reach its doer
a reason found only in the subject leaves the conclusion in doubt
when the elements part at death all is scattered and nothing remains
the soul does no action of any kind and is without the qualities
the soul is eternal, all-pervading, a seer and an experiencer
a soul that does nothing and without which things go on serves no purpose, and cannot be the enjoyer
the sin of a killing done for the gods passes to the gods
each person's deed comes back to that person, whoever it was meant for
the burning of Madurai and the fall of its king were foretold to a fixed day
without liquor and meat the life in this body cannot be kept
dharma may be fitted to what a person can keep: spare the shipwrecked, eat only what dies of age, and harm no living being
deeds that harm whoever happens to meet them bring blame and sin though no particular victim was intended
earth, water, fire, wind and all made things are unreal
a thing serves any use only through the qualities joined in it
at the time of death every bond, even the bond to dharma, must be let go
an ascetic's penance gives her curse the power to take hold
the wrong words of those who have left the right path should be taken as ignorance and pardoned
the whole and its parts do not exist together
a whole that does work cannot be denied while its parts are granted
a king's unjust killing bends his sceptre and turns the shade he gives his people into heat
for one who lives on alms, both receiving and giving are duties, and going out to the needy to give is the higher act
the base humans of the intermediate islands have beastlike forms and are untouched by right conduct and right vision
an ascetic's curse can fall on one who has given no cause
those who take faith, knowledge and conduct together pass through heavenly enjoyment and, free of clinging karma, reach the single bliss of release

note: In 302 Neelakesi asked the Buddhist how formless consciousness could touch or be bound to a body with form; in 745 she asks the Sankhya how a formless soul with no contact with nature can see or experience.
teaches: One Jain objection, that the formless cannot touch the formed, is aimed at two opposite opponents, the Buddhist who denies a soul and the Sankhya who makes it untouched, which shows the Jain body-sized soul is meant as the middle that both lack.

note: The Naladiyar's new pot gives its water the scent of pathiri flowers, an image of the unlearned gaining sense from the learned; Neelakesi attacks the same image as the Buddha's proof of a trace that outlives the flower.
teaches: The ethical image of borrowed fragrance only works if the scent has a lasting bearer, the flower-dust in the pot, so the Jain debater's demand to know whose the scent is shows what the Naladiyar's figure quietly assumes about company and influence.

gains.a: the debate verse is seen to be contesting a well-worn Tamil figure, not a stray example, which explains why the Buddhist chose it and why the Jain must dismantle it
gains.b: the quatrain's simile of good company is shown to rest on a theory of how a quality passes, which the epic makes an open question between schools

note: The preface to the Patitruppattu's fifth decade says Senguttuvan, seeking a stone for the goddess-pathini, went through the forests, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed it in the Ganga; the last kaathai has the Chera endow the pathini's temple and the freed Aryan kings and Gajabahu of Lanka beg her to come to their lands.
teaches: The Sangam preface records the pathini stone as one deed among a king's conquests; the epic carries the story past the conquest, to the defeated kings themselves asking for the goddess, so the war for the stone becomes the way her worship spreads beyond the Chera land.

gains.a: the epic's scene gains from the preface an independent record that a Chera named Senguttuvan was remembered for fetching a pathini's stone from the north, though the preface itself is late
gains.b: the preface's single phrase about the pathini gains the cult that the epic says grew from it: a temple, a daily festival and a boon asked by foreign kings

note: The couplet warns that the sweet words of bangled women who want wealth and not love bring harm; in the epic the garland priced at the king's reward is sent into the street by the doe-eyed woman, Madhavi speaks no word, and Kovalan buys it of his own infatuation.
teaches: The epic splits the couplet's single figure into a household that sets the price in the king's own coin and a dancer who is silent, so the harm the couplet lays on the woman's sweet speech here comes from a public custom and from the buyer's own desire.

gains.a: the scene gains a rule against which Kovalan's purchase can be judged, which the narrator withholds
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which no sweet word is spoken and the harm still follows, so its warning must reach the custom and the buyer, not only the woman's speech

note: The Akananuru friend asks the lord of the shore whether the oath he swore when his chariot crushed the girls' sand dolls was false too, with the sea as witness; the vari asks how simple girls could know that the man who swore by the sea god would break it.
teaches: The pair shows the epic lifting the neithal friend's charge, an oath with the sea as witness and the girls' sand-play spoiled, out of the courtship plot where it pressed for marriage and into a sung entertainment, where the charge of broken faith is performed by the man who will himself walk out at the song's end.

gains.a: the stanza gains its source situation: the sea-oath and the spoiled sand-play were a friend's demand for marriage before they were a song for a courtesan
gains.b: the Akananuru poem gains evidence that its situation had become a fixed piece of Puhar song, recognisable enough to be sung by a merchant at the shore festival

note: Both call birth a sickness with a medicine: the Neelakesi's sage names the medicine as dharma that cuts the diseases of birth; Pattinathar names it as never forgetting the lotus feet of the Lord of the Tillai hall.
teaches: The two traditions agree on the diagnosis and part on the cure: the Jain medicine is a dharma one takes up oneself with no god named, while the Siddhar's medicine is remembrance of the Lord's feet.

gains.a: the Jain sermon's medicine is set against a Saiva one, showing that it names no saviour
gains.b: the Siddhar's medicine of the feet is seen as one answer among rival cures for the same disease

note: Both use gram cooked into a mash (கும்மாயம்) as the Jain example of a kind that persists while its form passes; the Manimekalai lets the Jain state it unanswered, the Neelakesi puts it under a Buddhist's attack.
teaches: The same stock example served the two traditions differently: the Buddhist epic records it as the Jain's own illustration and moves on, while the Jain epic has a Buddhist demand to be shown the persisting thing, so the example's weak point is named by the side that wrote it down.

note: The Vedic logician listed false appearances of knowing (shell for silver, post or man); the Buddhist teacher lists false theses, reasons and examples.
teaches: Set side by side, the two lists show the Buddhist teacher moving error from the senses to argument: what goes wrong is less a mistaken seeing than a thesis put in terms the other side cannot grant.

note: Two claims about the sharpest edge (எஃகு). In 759 wealth is the sharpest steel for cutting an enemy's pride. In 773 the edge of valour is helping that enemy when he falls.
teaches: Cutting and sparing are both called sharpness.

note: 534 mocks the teacher who calls earth, water, fire and city false; Pambatti Siddhar bids the reader be clear that the world is false and dance.
teaches: The Jain realist's retort, that one who calls all things false leaves no ground for his own truth, falls on the Siddhar's world-is-false as much as on the Buddhist's, though the Siddhar makes it a release-giving insight, not a doctrine to defend.

gains.a: the verse's attack is shown to reach beyond Buddhism to a Tamil Saiva-Vedantic saying that also calls the world false
gains.b: the Siddhar's flat statement meets the objection it never answers: how one who calls the world false still claims his own words are true

note: Kural 139 says those with conduct cannot speak evil even by a slip; Nanmanikkadigai says deceitful words do not appear in the mouths of the learned even if they die.
teaches: The Kural rules out the accident, a slip; the quatrain rules out the extremity, death, so between them neither chance nor pressure draws evil speech from the good.

note: The Silappathikaram's last line calls it the work whose story's matter is completed in Manimekalai; the Manimekalai patikam closes by saying that Saathan set out Manimekalai's renunciation (மணிமேகலை துறவு) in thirty songs, with Ilango hearing it, reversing the Silappathikaram patikam, where Ilango sang and Saathan heard.
teaches: Each work's frame names the other's author as its listener, and the Silappathikaram declares its own story finished only in a sequel whose subject is a daughter's renunciation, so the pair presents the two epics as one story whose tale of justice and chastity reaches its end in the turn from household life to the robe.

note: Saathuvan tells the Naga chief that the faultless forbade liquor and the killing of living beings; Neelakesi argues that those who shun toddy should for the same reason shun flesh.
teaches: The Buddhist epic's own ban joins liquor with killing, not with eating meat, and the Jain debater exploits exactly that gap, asking why the reasoning that forbids toddy stops before flesh.

note: Kural 1203: a sneeze that seems to come and then dies away makes her think he seems about to think of her and does not. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 41: sneezes come one after another, so he is thinking of her. On the plain reading the same sign gives opposite verdicts.
teaches: Both women read the sneeze by the same folk belief, but the Kural uses its failure for a wry doubt while the venba piles it up as proof, which shows the belief was firm enough to support either despair or hope depending on what the body did.

note: Saathuvan is ruined by a courtesan and by dice and cast off penniless; among the Nagas he refuses the woman and liquor offered him, and comes home with treasure.
teaches: The couplet names double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has left, and the story runs the rule both ways: two of the three strip Saathuvan of wealth, and his refusal of a woman and liquor on the island is what brings fortune back.

gains.a: the tale's two halves gain a single rule that ties his ruin to his later refusal
gains.b: the couplet gains a reversal it does not state, that leaving the three restores what keeping them lost

note: Kayasandigai sends Manimekalai to Athirai's house as the one wife of rain-giving chastity; the next kaathai ends with Athirai putting the first food, the 'medicine for life', into the bowl (ஆதிரை இட்டனள் ஆருயிர்மருந்து).
teaches: Manimekalai's rule that the bowl's first alms must come from a pathini is carried out at once, and the giver chosen is a wife whose husband had left her for a courtesan, so the courtesan's daughter's bowl is first filled by such a wife.

note: The benediction hails the moon because it is like the Chola's cool white umbrella sheltering the world; the venba makes the moon like a guardian king's white umbrella that is shade to the joined and heat to the rest.
teaches: The umbrella that the opening praised as sheltering everyone is here given its second edge, and the edge falls on Kannaki: royal protection, like love, covers only those inside the bond.

note: The blessing பசியும் பிணியும் பகையும் நீங்கி வசியும் வளனும் சுரக்க is uttered in both: here by possessed old women at the spirit's altar, in Manimekalai by the royal drummer announcing the festival.
teaches: The same two lines pass from the trance speech of warrior women at a spirit's altar to the official proclamation of the king's crier, showing the sequel turning a possessed blessing into the festival's civic formula.

note: The couplet says the ruin of evil-doers stays at their feet like a shadow; the pillar tells Kanchanan his cruel deed will not leave him, even though the prince died by his own former deed.
teaches: The couplet considers only the doer, while the epic adds that being the instrument of another's ripened karma does not lift the deed from the one who kills, so karma explains the victim's death without excusing the killer.

gains.a: The pillar's warning gains the couplet's image of a consequence that never leaves its doer's feet.
gains.b: The couplet gains a hard case, a killing the victim's own deed called for, in which its rule still holds.

note: The couplet asks why those who take good fortune as good grieve when ill fortune comes; Kavunthi says the learned do not despair when they eat the fruit of their deeds, while the unlearned are bewildered when the evil deed ripens.
teaches: The couplet's argument for calm rests on consistency between good and bad fortune, while the nun rests it on learning and adds a cause, desire for women and food, so the pair shows the Kural's equanimity before fate being turned into a renouncer's diagnosis of where suffering comes from.

gains.a: Kavunthi's counsel gains a compact general rule behind it, so her talk of the learned not despairing reads as a recognised teaching rather than private comfort
gains.b: the couplet gains a hearer and an occasion, a ruined husband in a strange city, and a second argument for calm that it does not make, that the suffering was earned by desire

note: Patitruppattu 43 praises Kuttuvan whose army broke kings from the Himalaya to Kumari; Villavan Kothai argues that because of such victories none in the world will resist him.
teaches: The Sangam poem praises conquest as done, while the epic minister uses the same fame as a reason no new conquest is needed, so the reputation of past war is offered as the means of a bloodless one.

gains.a: the minister's claim that none will resist gains the Sangam record of conquest it rests on
gains.b: the poem's praise gains a political use, fame as a weapon that spares battle

note: The couplet says a ruler endures by just rule and without it his lustre does not endure; the Vanchi women sing that Pandyas do not live once the sceptre bends, and praise the Pandya for that.
teaches: The epic grants the couplet's link between a bent sceptre and the king's end but reverses its outcome for fame: the Pandya's dying of his own injustice is exactly what makes his line's glory endure and be sung by a rival kingdom.

gains.a: the women's saying gains a general rule behind it, so the Pandya's death reads as the law of kingship and not a private collapse
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where losing life for a bent sceptre restores the lustre it says is lost, a limit on its simple equation

note: Both call the cure of the soul a medicine that leaves it clear: in the Neelakesi the soul takes the three remedies of knowledge, clear faith and conduct; in Tirumular the mind becomes clear when Nandi gives grace, like a madman cured by medicine.
teaches: The shared image of medicine and clarity hides opposed accounts of who heals: for the Jain sermon clarity is one of the remedies the soul swallows itself, for Tirumular it is the effect of the Lord's grace, and on the Jain reading no giver of grace is needed.

gains.a: the sermon's godless remedy is seen as a real alternative to a Tamil account of release by grace that uses the same image
gains.b: the verse's claim that clarity is given, not achieved, is sharpened by a rival who makes clarity something the soul takes

note: Kundalakesi praised her teacher as one who suffered only for others; Neelakesi addresses the Buddha as the compassionate one who toiled for others through every aeon, in a verse that charges him with contradiction.
teaches: The Buddhist's chief title of praise returns in the Jain's mouth as an ironic address, so the founder's compassion is set beside the incoherence of his doctrine.

note: The couplet calls virtue the companion that does not perish when one perishes; Visakai calls great virtue the true companion (விழுத் துணை) in place of youth, body, wealth and sons.
teaches: Visakai uses the couplet's idea of virtue as companion to replace the wife-companion the brahmin demanded, so a teaching about virtue outlasting death becomes an answer to the claim that a man needs marriage for heaven.

gains.a: Her answer gains the couplet's reason why virtue alone survives.
gains.b: The couplet's companion gains a concrete rival it displaces: the wife and the sons a householder is told he must have.

note: Kovalan sang of a conch that ploughed through a girl's sand-play and left her grieving; Madhavi sings of a man who came by the backwater, spoiled their sand-play and went.
teaches: Madhavi takes Kovalan's own image and puts a man in place of the conch, so the spoiled sand-play changes from a picture of a girl's charm into a charge of desertion, the answer-song turning his playful scene against the lover.

note: Kural 35 sets aside envy, craving, anger and harsh words as the four that virtue avoids; 529 names anger, pride, deceit and greed as the faults of the mind.
teaches: Both make anger and greed central, but each completes the list from its own school: the Kural adds envy and a fault of speech, the Jain debater pride and deceit, so the shared pair is common ground and the rest is sectarian.

gains.a: the Jain list of passions is shown to share its core with a widely accepted ethical rule, which strengthens her charge that the Buddhists left faults out
