gains.b: the couplet's list is shown not to be the only fourfold reckoning; a Jain debater would count pride and deceit where it counts envy and harsh speech

note: 143 asks who the weeping woman at the door was (யார்கொல் அளியள்) without answering; 144 tells the same kind of scene and lets the woman answer that she is no kin of Pekan's and that he goes to another woman.
teaches: Read in sequence, the Pekan poems work as a cycle in which each poet adds what the last withheld: Kapilar leaves the woman unnamed, Paranar gives her a voice and names the cause, so the reproach of a patron was built up by several poets in turn.

note: Kural 244 says one who sustains lives (மன்னுயிர் ஓம்பி) and holds to grace need fear no deed for his own life; the minister says the Buddha's dharma is not to pity one's own life and to protect other lives (பிற உயிர் ஓம்பும், 116), and charges the king with seeking a higher world for himself.
teaches: The couplet promises the protector of lives safety for his own; the minister makes indifference to one's own life the protector's mark, so a king's wish for his own release counts against his grace.

gains.a: a Tamil rule that makes protecting others' lives the core of grace, so the minister's appeal reads as more than Buddhist piety
gains.b: a reversal of its reward: in the epic the protector of lives is the one who does not seek safety for himself, not the one granted it

note: The Buddha says those who know the four truths reach release whatever they do; the monk in 259 says only the mind counts and evil conduct is not evil karma.
teaches: The monk's excuse in the earlier debate is given a source in the Buddha's own words here, so the poet makes the founder answerable for the disciple's conduct; this rests on reading எவையே செய்தும் as 'whatever they do'.

note: Pattinattar calls the body the enjoyment of deeds, gone the moment deeds end, and sends the mind to Siva's feet; Sudhamathi calls it born of deeds and the field where they ripen, and asks only that it be known and turned from.
teaches: The two share the premise that the body exists to eat karma but part on the remedy: the Saiva poet needs Siva's feet, while the epic's speaker names no god and puts release in seeing the body truly.

gains.a: Sudhamathi's godless remedy stands out once set beside a Saiva statement of the same premise.
gains.b: Pattinattar's appeal to Siva's feet is shown to be an addition to a premise that a Buddhist epic holds without it.

note: The quatrain warns men not to desire the spear-eyed woman because she too will stoop and walk with a staff; Manimekalai, the woman desired, points her pursuer to an old woman and shows him eyes and face already changed.
teaches: The quatrain's warning against desire is spoken by a man to men about a woman, while the epic puts it in the mouth of the desired woman as her own defence, turning the lesson on aging into a refusal.

gains.a: Manimekalai's demonstration gains a recognized ethical topos, so her act reads as instruction rather than mere evasion.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the warned man ignores the lesson and dies of the desire, which tests what the warning can do.

note: Tirumular says there is no dharma that leaves out the Veda, and the wise gave up disputation and recited it to gain release; Neelakesi argues by inference that the Veda is made and, being joined to killing, drives its followers to evil births.
teaches: The two verses disagree both on the Veda and on method: Tirumular sets recitation above argument as the way to release, while Neelakesi makes argument the test that the Veda fails.

gains.a: the verse gains a clear statement of the Veda's claim to contain all dharma, the claim her inferences are built to break
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a concrete instance of the disputation it tells the wise to give up, and of what that disputation says about the Veda

note: Maadalan once praised Kovalan as the compassionate hero who entered the rogue elephant's trunk to free an old Brahmin; in the last kaathai Maadalan says that this man, who entered the elephant's trunk to end the Brahmin's distress, has won the form of the gods.
teaches: The poem names one deed of Kovalan's, the elephant rescue and not his life with Madhavi or his wasting of wealth, as the deed whose fruit is his heavenly form, so the man the story often blames is judged at the end by his single act of risking his life for a stranger.

note: In 199 Neelakesi says Kundalakesi's two kinds of continuum destroy her own case; in 603 she presses the Buddha on what a feeble continuum can do once the aggregates have wholly perished.
teaches: The epic makes the same objection to continuity defeat the disciple first and the master later, so the Buddhist doctrine is shown failing at one point from both its spokesmen.

note: The king declares it good to renounce kingship wholly, crediting Manimekalai as the cause; Manimekalai, whose call woke him, sends him back to rule and tells him a king's dharma is food, clothing and shelter for all.
teaches: The epic of renunciation turns its heroine against a king's renunciation: the waking she causes is meant to make him a giver on a throne, not an ascetic, so renunciation is not the right end for everyone it moves.

note: Kannaki declines to worship at Kama's shrine for her husband; the Katturai venba says the gods themselves worship her who worships her husband and no god.
teaches: The early refusal and the later venba make one arc: the wife who would not seek her husband through a god ends as one the gods receive, so the poem pays out the refusal in the Kural's own terms.

note: The venba says husband and wife, joined like coiled serpents, never parted; in the next kaathai Kovalan buys Madhavi's garland, cannot leave her and forgets his home.
teaches: The closing praise of a union that never parts is reversed within one kaathai, and the venba's own hint of impermanence turns out to be about the marriage itself rather than about the world.

note: The couplet ranks not taking one creature's life above a thousand oblations; the boy takes the cow from a sacrifice and is caught, beaten and called a thief.
teaches: The couplet weighs abstention against sacrifice as a private choice of merit, while the epic shows what acting on it costs inside a sacrificing community: the rescuer is branded a thief and expelled from his caste.

gains.a: The boy's theft gains a recognised ethical rule behind it, which the brahmins' charge of theft leaves out.
gains.b: The couplet's comparison gains a case where refusing the sacrifice carries a social price, which the couplet does not count.

note: The Kural says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one avoids what the world condemns; Mokkalan grants the robe only the small use of making the monk known, and Neelakesi asks what such a sign is for.
teaches: The Kural's dismissal of ascetic marks becomes a live weapon between sects: the Jain debater uses it against the Buddhist robe, while her own tradition's nakedness is a mark of another kind.

gains.a: Neelakesi's question about the robe is seen to rest on an accepted Tamil maxim that outward marks are not the test of renunciation
gains.b: the couplet's general maxim is shown being turned by one order against another's dress, a use it does not foresee

note: The quatrain mocks one who sees a corpse carried to the burning ground yet marries and thinks there is joy here; the venba says the newly married couple enjoyed every pleasure like people who had seen the world's impermanence.
teaches: The same knowledge that nothing on earth lasts is, for the Naladiyar, a reason to give up marriage and its joys and, in the epic's venba, a reason to take them while they last, so the pair sets out the two lessons impermanence can teach.

gains.a: the venba's last line gains a rival reading of its own premise, so its haste for pleasure is seen as a choice the ethics book condemns
gains.b: the quatrain gains the voice it argues against: not a fool blind to death but lovers who claim to have seen it and draw the opposite lesson

note: In 203 Neelakesi argued that a power passing across the moments would be a sixth thing beside the five aggregates; in 478 and 480 the Buddha's teaching posits a person (pudgala) besides the aggregates.
teaches: The 'sixth thing' that Neelakesi forced on Kundalakesi as an absurd consequence turns up as the master's own tenet, the person, so the earlier argument becomes the charge of contradiction here.

claims.gist: only the workings of the five elements need be stated, without any distinction of substance and quality
atoms that combine into gross things must either interpenetrate or stay apart, and either way the Jain account fails
kinds distinguished only by name and not by examination give no ground for a doctrine
only humans of the land of deeds can shed their karma by penance and reach the highest bliss
a chaste wife does not gainsay her husband even when his conduct is unworthy
the plain natures everyone perceives, such as the heat of fire and the cold of water, need no qualification
the five aggregates are momentary
there is no knower that persists from one moment to the next
there is nonetheless a person (pudgala)
the Lord, rid of the inner deeds, knows all things without reasoning his way to them
paying a price for meat is a fair transaction and brings no sin
the buyer who pays the fisherman every day wants the killing
wives whose word brings rain never enter another man's heart
a wife who has entered another man's heart may no longer tend her husband's three sacred fires
the other religious paths are base paths to be overcome
gentle speech is a good deed
soft words that plot harm are not good, so speech is not good by its gentleness
penance done by one who kills is destroyed by the killing
a god who destroys and then creates shows no wisdom
what is plainly present before one cannot be called non-existent
to know past and future things is to know what does not exist, which is a fault in knowledge
if the released soul is the same one that was bound, karma can bind it again, so release by a lasting soul is not final
whatever is born grows old, falls ill and dies by nature
birth runs through twelve linked conditions from ignorance to the fruit of deeds
those who know the twelve links gain the great reward and those who do not go to deep hell
ignorance is trusting hearsay over what is seen, like believing a hare has horns
beings are of six kinds, born by good and bad deeds, which ripen as joy and sorrow
a wife who rises worshipping her husband rather than a god can bid the rain fall
a wife given to festivals, gossip and the worship of gods loses the power to command rain
the spirit's punishment follows only when the king's justice has failed within seven days

echoes.words: தெய்வம் தொழா அள் கொழுநன் தொழுது எழுவாள்

claims.gist: urging another to give is a wholesome deed of speech
bondage and release are the two states of the soul that the teacher expounds
the three delusions are to be known and avoided
if all eight constituents are present everywhere, nothing can be named as one element rather than another
the self is distinct from the body
a vowed living offering is discharged without sin by offering its image in clay
past and future qualities belong to the nature of a substance, so the omniscient knows them without knowing non-existents
nose, tongue and body know their objects only on contact with them
a formless knowing cannot receive contact
a reflection never remains after its original has perished, so the moon example cannot show rebirth after death
a deed must yield its fruit either while it persists or after it has wholly perished
a deed, like every existent, has persistence, arising and destruction together
merit done in the name of others reaches them and not the doer
if deeds passed to those they were aimed at, the released could be bound again
undergoing bodily hardship yields nothing, and leaving it brings the soul bliss
evil deeds are ten: three of the body, four of speech and three of the mind
those who do the ten are reborn as animals, ghosts and beings of hell
those who avoid the ten, keep the precepts and give are reborn as gods, humans and Brahmas and enjoy the fruit
if every part is momentary, the balance and its two ends do not exist and the image ends in nothing
direction is space named by convention from the sun's rising and setting, not a substance of its own
in the land of a king whose sceptre is straight, even wild beasts, demons and thunder do no harm to those who rely on it
the deed of killing does not reach one who eats meat when the killer and the giver are hidden from him
those who swell attachment while appearing free of it and seize deposits are reborn as ghosts or dragged into hell
the life of herders who tend cows and give their yield has no crookedness
from the standpoint of the bearer qualities are not separate, and from the standpoint of the quality the same holds
since a meritorious king's birth the rain has not failed and no disease has struck his people
a direction is one quarter for one person and another for the next, so it has no nature of its own
the feet of the Supreme are attainment and the final end
the sin of killing does not attach where there is no intention to kill
if killing is a sin, it reaches also the one who eats what was killed

note: In Paripadal 19 maidens who do not eat the leftover of the god's elephant at Parankunram fail to win husbands; the hill girls pray to Murugan not for marriage in general but that their friend be spared another's match and given her own lover.
teaches: The temple poem treats Murugan as giver of husbands to all maidens who honour him, while the kuravai bends the same belief to the akam crisis of the secret union, asking him to prevent the family's match.

gains.a: the girls' prayer is seen to rest on an established belief that Murugan grants marriages
gains.b: the hymn's general belief is shown turned to one lover and against one feared marriage (அயல்மணம்)

note: Akananuru 296 makes the husband's bathing in the great Vaigai with a dark girl the gossip of Koodal; Paripadal 6.26-43 shows the whole town, young and old, rich and strong, going down to play in the same river.
teaches: Read against the Paripadal's crowd at the fords, the Akananuru friend's charge cannot be that he bathed in the Vaigai, since everyone did; the scandal lies in whom he bathed with, so the akam reproach depends on a public festival that the akam poem itself never describes.

note: The drunk calls toddy-drinking a yoga whose fruit the ascetic should taste; Tirumanthiram 566 says breath-control gives the intoxication of toddy without drinking it.
teaches: The equation of drink and yogic ecstasy runs in opposite directions: the Tirumanthiram borrows toddy's joy as an image for breath-discipline, while the epic's drunk borrows yoga's name to sell toddy, so the pair shows the figure was common enough to be turned either way.

gains.a: evidence that 'the yoga of drink' was a live figure the epic could parody
gains.b: a satirical counter-use that shows the risk in its image of yoga as intoxication

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Kovalan's former deed reaches him through a goldsmith's lie, a king's hasty word and a drunken guard's sword.
teaches: The quatrain's deed finds its doer by itself, while the epic shows it arriving through other people's free and blameworthy acts, so karma here does not excuse the hands it works through.

gains.a: Kovalan's death gains the quatrain's image of the deed that cannot miss its doer, which explains why every escape fails
gains.b: the quatrain's calf gains a path: the seeking deed travels through other people's lies and violence

note: The Pattinappalai's fishermen count the coloured lights of Puhar's mansions at night; the epic counts the shore's lamps by trade, from perfume-sellers and hawkers to the lighthouse, fishing boats and foreign traders.
teaches: The idyll's lights are a spectacle watched from the boats, while the epic's are a roll of the port's livelihoods, showing how the later poem turns the same harbour of lights into a social survey.

gains.a: the epic's catalogue gains a Sangam precedent for Puhar as a city known by its lights, which marks it as a set piece of the port, not a passing detail
gains.b: the idyll's anonymous lights gain owners: the epic names who keeps each lamp, filling in the trades behind the glow

note: The Purananuru poem says the world endures because there are those who strive not for themselves but for others (தமக்கென முயலா ... பிறர்க்கென முயலுநர்); Sudhamathi calls the Buddha one who lives not for himself but belongs to others (தனக்கு என வாழாப் பிறர்க்கு உரியாளன்).
teaches: The epic takes the Sangam formula for a class of honourable men who hold the world up and makes it the mark of one being whose living for others is the turning of the dharma wheel, moving the ideal from social honour to religious compassion.

gains.a: The epithet at 73 is heard as a Tamil ideal already named in puram poetry, so the Buddha is praised in terms a Tamil audience held as the highest human worth.
gains.b: The poem's unnamed many who strive for others are given a single founder as exemplar, whose motive is compassion for all beings rather than fear of blame and love of fame.

note: The Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker derives the ear and sound from space (line 214); 760 says sound has form and cannot belong to formless space.
teaches: The derivation the Buddhist epic lets the Sankhya state unanswered is the very step the Jain epic attacks, so the two polemics differ less in what they report of Sankhya than in what they choose to contest.

note: The quatrain says that because a wife cannot be put away even if she lacks virtue and bears no child, the learned called marriage கடி; Kavunthi says the pains of parting and union belong only to those joined with women, not to the strong who live alone.
teaches: Both make marriage a source of suffering from which the solitary are free, but the Naladiyar argues it to recommend renunciation while Kavunthi states it to a married man and then sends him on with his wife, so the pair shows the renouncer's diagnosis offered without its prescription.

gains.a: the nun's claim gains the ethical tradition's own argument for why the bond brings pain, that it cannot be undone
gains.b: the quatrain gains a case where its view is spoken to a husband who is not told to leave his wife, which limits how far the ascetic diagnosis is meant to bind a householder

note: Purananuru 18 tells a Pandya king that those who give food give life (உண்டி கொடுத்தோர் உயிர்கொடுத் தோரே) and that land waiting on the sky does not serve its ruler, so he must build tanks; Deepathilakai gives the same line (96) after a famine ended only by a god's rain.
teaches: The maxim moves from a king's public works to a renunciant's alms-bowl, and the remedy for a failing sky moves from tanks a ruler digs to a god's gift and a bowl that never empties.

gains.a: line 96 is shown to be a borrowed Sangam maxim, so the goddess's sermon carries the authority of old royal counsel
gains.b: the poem's maxim gains a later life in which the duty to feed passes from the state to a single compassionate giver

note: In both a Buddhist ascetic foretells that a city will be swallowed, Idavayam by earthquake and Kaveripattinam by the sea, and those who trust the word act on it and are saved from the ruin.
teaches: The epic repeats the drowned city as a test of trust in a seer's word: the survivors in both are those who believed a forecast before any sign, which makes heeding the ascetic the epic's form of escape from a city's fate.

note: Kural 52 says that if the wife lacks household excellence the life is nothing whatever else it has; saying 42 says the same in the அல்ல form.
teaches: The Kural's claim that a wife's excellence decides the household survives the move into a book of bare definitions, where it becomes one of the tests by which a thing earns its name.

note: Flesh eaten by birds: the Kundalakesi fragment shows vultures and dogs tearing the desired body; Neelakesi 214 says flesh cut off as a gift feeds only crows.
teaches: The same carrion image serves the Buddhist as a reason to stop desiring the body and the Jain as a reason not to throw it away, so contempt for the body and refusal to waste it come from one picture.

note: The townsfolk say Kovalan is a thief (கள்வனாம்); the sun's voice answers கள்வனோ அல்லன்.
teaches: The kaathai sets the hearsay of men, which the king acted on, against the testimony of the all-seeing sun, so the case against Kovalan is answered by a higher witness before it ever reaches the king's court.

note: On Manipallavam the bowl rises from the Gomukhi pool before the Buddha's seat once a year into a fit hand; in Kanchi the king builds a copy of the pool and seat and she sets the bowl on it for all beings.
teaches: The holy island is reproduced in a royal city, and the bowl that came out of it to one worthy hand is now placed on the copy of the seat and offered to everyone.

note: The goddess says only that the cause for the girl's entry into dharma has ripened; at the jewel seat Manimekalai learns that in her birth as Lakshmi a sage foretold that on the day of her trouble the goddess Manimekala would carry her to an island in the south.
teaches: The bare 'ripened cause' of this kaathai is revealed later as a prophecy made in a former birth, so the goddess is fulfilling an old word, not deciding afresh.

note: The invocation says Neelakesi was a demoness of harm whose heart turned; the teacher, describing demons as fire to all, exempts her from her own kind.
teaches: Her conversion is acknowledged inside the sermon itself, which uses her former kind as its example of harm while addressing her as one already changed.

note: The goddess Manimekala warned the prince that a swerving sceptre ruins rain and life and told him to drop his wrongful intent toward one who has taken up tapas; here he resolves to seize her even against the wise and the king.
teaches: The prince's death is set up as the end of a refused warning: he was told in advance that his desire for an ascetic was a fault of the sceptre, and he now names the king's anger as one more thing he will override.

note: Kavunthi told Maadhari that a charge held for the ascetics, however small, yields very great joy; Maadhari, who could not guard that charge, gave up her life.
teaches: The promise of joy from keeping a trust is reversed into death from failing it, and the failure was not hers: the pair shows the epic laying on a guardian the full weight of a duty that the king's act made impossible to keep.

note: The sage's prophecy, recalled in kaathai 9, bids her go to the radiant seat where the healer of the disease of birth sits and preaches, where the Naga kings cleared anger and the stain of mind, and worship it, and that very day know her birth.
teaches: The seat that the narrator first presents as the prize of a war over 'ours' is named in the prophecy by what it did to the warring kings, purging their anger and opening their ears to dharma, so the place that cured possession becomes the place where a grieving girl recovers her past.

note: Aravanar's four lines to Madhavi set suffering for the born, bliss for the unborn and attachment as the cause; in kaathai 30 he sets out the twelve links, with attachment (பற்றே) one link among them, and says the born who know them gain the great reward.
teaches: The same teacher gives the grieving mother a single cause and five precepts, and the daughter the full twelve-link chain, so the epic shows the doctrine scaled to its hearer: consolation and lay discipline first, the analysis of release later.

note: The Buddha of the Neelakesi offers seed, sprout and branch as a continuity in which release lies; the Manimekalai's teacher uses seed, sprout and stalk as the example of the continuity name, one word for a series.
teaches: The Buddhist epic uses the seed series as a rule of naming, while the Jain epic puts it in the Buddha's mouth as an account of what passes on to release, which is the stronger claim its heroine can then attack.

note: The deity foretells that the materialist will call her knowledge of a former birth a dream sent by a deity; in Vanji he says those deluded by a god or by dreams have changed minds.
teaches: The prophecy foretells the opponent's very objection, so when the debate comes the reader already knows the materialist's charge is aimed at a real divine intervention that the epic itself narrated.

note: Saathuvan tells the Naga chief that the dying of the born and the birth of the dead are like sleeping and waking, the simile of Kural 339 in other words, and draws from it that good deeds lead to a good world and ill to hell.
teaches: The couplet's simile is a calm statement of impermanence, but Saathuvan turns it into the premise of an argument against liquor and killing, showing that the image of sleep and waking implies a self that wakes again and must answer for its acts.

gains.a: Saathuvan's premise gains a formulation already familiar as a saying, which is why he can offer it to a sceptic without proof
gains.b: the couplet gains a moral consequence it never draws, that what one does before sleeping decides where one wakes

note: In the Ainkurunuru the friend says the girl's sickness is not the ford-spirit's doing but the man's oath; Madhavi's heroine asks the sea god not to punish the false oath sworn in the grove.
teaches: Both rest on the belief that a water deity punishes a false love-oath, but where the Sangam friend turns that belief against the man, the epic's heroine asks the god to spare him, so the same belief serves blame in one and loyal forgiveness in the other.

gains.a: the epic song gains the background belief that makes its plea meaningful: an oath sworn at the water draws the god's affliction
gains.b: the Ainkurunuru poem's belief gains a second use, as something a wronged woman can ask the god to withhold

note: 388 says a king who rules justly and protects is held to be a god among people: the title is earned. On Parimelazhagar's reading of 698, the divinity belongs to any king, young or kin, and the courtier mustn't ask.
teaches: Other readings of ஒளி remove the conflict.

note: In Puhar Aravanar asks whether Indra or the king of the just sceptre is at fault for the famine, in the words அலத்தல்காலை ஆகியது; the Kanchi king uses the same words about his own land and adds women's chastity.
teaches: The question first put by the teacher about another's kingdom is put by a king about himself, and both times the epic's answer is the bowl, not a judgment on the ruler.

note: Mokkalan argued that on the Jain view an ascetic's soul would not exist in the time to come and keeping the precepts would be wasted toil; here Neelakesi argues that on the Buddha's view nirvana comes alike to the ascetic and the vicious.
teaches: Each side charges the other's metaphysics with making austerity pointless, which shows that in these debates a doctrine of time and persistence was tested by whether it could still reward discipline.

note: Kural 579 calls it the highest disposition to show kindly regard to and bear with even those whose way is to hurt one; the Neelakesi's sage is likened to a mother who in excess of kindly regard (கழிகண்ணோட்டம்) suckles the infant that hurts her.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's high virtue an image and a result: the forbearance is maternal, and it converts the one who came to harm, which the couplet's rule does not promise.

gains.a: the mother simile gains a name in the ethics books, கண்ணோட்டம் extended to those who harm
gains.b: the couplet's virtue is shown working on an attacker who then gives up her violence

note: Freed of her hunger, Kayasandikai told Manimekalai she would go to her city in the sky; the pillar image reveals she was seized over the Vindhya on the way and swallowed by its goddess.
teaches: The cure that Manimekalai's bowl gave Kayasandikai did not bring her home: the release she announced ends in a second death, and her husband's search ends in a killing over her likeness.

note: Akananuru 355: in spring bees hum on the budding branches like the strings of a paalai lute touched by a master, the season in which the heroine fears her man's going. Thinaimozhi 16: bees hum the paalai melody as the man leads the girl away.
teaches: The same sound of bees playing the paalai mode marks the spring of a parting in the Akananuru and the spring of an elopement in the venba, so the image does not carry a fixed mood but takes its grief or its promise from the uri it serves.

note: The Manimekalai's Vaisheshika makes generality the first common being that lets substance, quality and action work; 813 says the universal is only likeness between things.
teaches: What the Vaisheshika in one epic treats as the ground of all working, the Jain in the other reduces to resemblance, so the dispute is over whether the common is a thing or a relation.

note: The Ajivika says all gain, loss, pleasure, pain, birth and death are fixed at conception by fate laid down before; the teacher says the chain has no fixed fate (ஊழ்பாடு இன்றி) and runs by conditions that can be reversed.
teaches: Kaathai 27 leaves the Ajivika's fixed fate unanswered, and this line supplies the Buddhist reply: the same goods and ills are conditioned links, so cutting a condition can stop them, which fixed fate rules out. The tension depends on reading ஊழ்பாடு as fixed fate.

note: Silappathikaram's patikam ends with Ilango graciously telling and Saathan the grain merchant hearing (அடிகள் அருள ... சாத்தன் கேட்டனன்); Manimekalai's ends with Ilango graciously hearing and Saathan setting out the work (இளங்கோ வேந்தன் அருளிக் கேட்ப ... சாத்தன் ... அறிய வைத்தனன்), each in thirty parts.
teaches: The two patikams frame the twin epics as one exchange between the same two men, each the listener of the other's poem, so the tradition joins them by their frames and not only by Madhavi's daughter continuing the story.

note: The Madurai goddess told Kannaki that a deed of the former birth had come and pressed (உம்மை வினைவந் துருத்த காலை) and that after fourteen days she would see her husband only in a god's form; here Kannaki uses the same words of herself and the gods bring her husband.
teaches: Kannaki takes the goddess's karmic account into her own mouth when strangers ask who she is, so the explanation offered to her in Madurai becomes the one she gives of herself, and the prophecy is fulfilled before witnesses outside the city.

note: The Silappathikaram tells how the stone for the pathini goddess, taken from the Himalaya, was set on the crowns of Kanaka and Vijaya and the goddess bathed in the Ganga; the Manimekalai names the same stone on the same crowns in a line of praise for Senguttuvan's city.
teaches: The stone that in the Silappathikaram makes Kannaki a goddess becomes in the Manimekalai a mark of the king's glory and the name of the city where Kannaki's daughter will learn that her mother's goddesshood is not release.

note: Sudhamathi told the prince in the grove that the human body is born of deeds, ages, dies and holds disease and grief; Manimekalai now tells him in nearly the same words why she renounced.
teaches: The lesson that did not reach the prince's heart from the companion (4:122-123) is repeated by Manimekalai herself as her own reason, and she expects it to fail again, so the teaching is a test the prince keeps failing rather than an argument he has not heard.

note: Kural 327 says not to take another's life even at the cost of one's own; the island goddess tells Aputhiran that by starving he killed his own life and that the merchants who came back and died where he lay died for his sake, so that he is a killer.
teaches: The couplet treats giving up one's own life as a price that may be paid to avoid killing; the epic counts giving up one's own life as itself a killing, and one that draws others to die.

gains.a: a known Tamil rule against which the goddess's charge reads as a judgment about killing, not only grief for the dead
gains.b: a case its two lives cannot keep apart: one's own death that becomes the cause of others' deaths

note: The sage promised that the goddess who brought her would appear and say 'this is your husband'; in kaathai 10 Manimekala comes and names Rahulan as Udayakumaran, telling the story of Lakshmi's past.
teaches: The husband she longs to be shown turns out to be the prince she has been hiding from, so the promised reunion is delivered as a reason to understand her pull toward him and turn from it.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain says gram keeps its nature when cooked into a dish; the Neelakesi's Jain asks how milk, curd and buttermilk could fill the vessels if nothing lasts.
teaches: Both epics give the Jain the same proof from the kitchen, a substance that persists through its changes; the Buddhist epic reports it unanswered there, and the Jain epic aims it at the Buddha's momentariness.

note: The Kural says one who denies what the world holds to be will be counted a demon (அலகை); the epic names its materialist Pisasakan, a name that sounds like பிசாசு, and ends the sarukkam by showing him a demon (887-892).
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's label into a plot: the man who denies spirits carries a demon's name and is converted by meeting one, so the Kural's 'demon' becomes both insult and refutation.

gains.a: the name Pisasakan gains an ethical frame, as the stock word for the denier of what all accept
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed blank, what is denied, is filled with a case: the denial of soul, rebirth and spirits

note: The verdict scene ends with the Pandya saying 'am I king? I am the thief', falling dead, and his queen falling at his feet saying there is nothing to show those who have lost their husbands; the summary recalls this as the king who slept on his throne-couch with his queen of flawless chastity.
teaches: The summary turns the king's self-condemnation and his wife's instant death into one dignified image of a royal pair at rest, and gives its only epithet of chastity to the queen and does not name Kannaki, so the book's official memory honours the Pandya's atoning death as the thing its whole story is viewed with.

note: The narrator in 48 says the sage Munichandra knew without limit the things of the three times; in 435 Neelakesi argues that if virtuous gods can show the three times, the Lord must know them.
teaches: Her a-fortiori argument for the Lord's knowledge of the three times rests on lesser knowers the epic had already shown, including the human sage who converted her.

claims.gist: silence is no evidence of knowledge, since infants, trees and mountains are silent too
the Lord's silence after declaring that he knows all shows his perfect knowledge
a king should hold to the path of dharma
whoever distinguishes floating from sinking things has already given up their identity
the goddess is the hidden truth above the Vedas and the shoot of wisdom
if the soul does nothing, the speaker's own words are not his doing and his doctrine is not his
the labour of sewing, dyeing and perfuming robes yields no fruit for one who has renounced
material form is made of octads, units of eight things joined inseparably
the one who reaps a deed's fruit is neither the doer, nor another, nor both, nor no one
the consciousnesses not now manifest are kept in a store-consciousness
a lasting store of consciousness is the soul under another name
the Lord's feet destroy the darkness of karma
the gods worship the wife who worships her husband rather than a god
harm from outside comes either from living beings or from lifeless things, the four elements
a sage's curse that falls on a person is the fruit of that person's old deed
austerity that cuts evil deeds is to be undertaken while one has a human body
thieves work by eight aids: mantra, deity, drug, omen, technique, place, time and tool
from the formless unmanifest arise the great principle, the sense of self, its sixteen products and the five elements
an ascetic needs no magic: his virtue alone makes him unassailable
a gift that meets no stated need of the receiver is folly, not generosity
the non-perceptual means of knowledge are five: memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and the word of the sages' scripture
refusing flesh out of fear of the deed of killing is a good deed
the soul's good needs one enduring bearer, not a series of aggregates
what is not the same must be other; there is no third case
anger is a fault of the mind
deceit, pride and greed are faults of the mind as evil as anger
flood, wind, rockfall, poison, weapons, fire and thunder harm without any living agent
a wife who takes on the duty of chastity discharges in it what she owes
giving away one's eyes, body, wife and child is the conduct of the deluded and the possessed, not of the compassionate
the monk may take up ascetic rules such as living at a tree's foot, in the open and in the burning ground, and wearing cast-off cloth
in all three times the world is only the combining of the elements
outer cleanness does not make the mind pure
the four great elements are known by hardness, moisture, heat and motion, and act by bearing, binding, drying and stirring
the Buddha's tales of former births establish his compassion
one who speaks of the truth without knowing it is not a fit authority
whatever a being will have is already present in it, since what does not exist cannot come to be
bodily parts such as breasts, teeth, hair and nails come into being later and were not there before
the principles unfold in a chain from prakriti through mahat to the elements
trees grow, fold and change as living beings do, and so they have life
a king does well to give up kingship and its pleasures wholly for renunciation

note: The Kural warns that honouring a spy openly lets out the king's secret; Azhumbil Vel counts on the enemy's spies at Vanchi's gate to carry the proclamation.
teaches: The couplet treats exposure to spies as a leak to be prevented, while the epic court makes the leak its instrument, so the pairing shows intelligence used as a channel of open threat.

gains.a: the counsel gains the norm of secrecy that it deliberately inverts
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where a king wants his purpose known, which marks the limit of its rule

note: In Puhar Madhavi received by the king's rule the thousand and eight kalanju (ஆயிரத்து எண்கழஞ்சு ... எட்டுக்கடை நிறுத்த) with the talaikkol, and Kovalan bought her garland; in Madurai the talaikkol dancers receive the same sum (எட்டுக் கடைநிறுத்த ஆயிரத் தெண்கழஞ்சு) every day by fixed rule, and both passages praise the house as வடுநீங்கு சிறப்பின்.
teaches: The price that marked Madhavi's debut as a singular royal honour, and began Kovalan's ruin, turns out in Madurai to be the standing daily fee of a whole profession, and Kovalan walks past it as a man who has already paid it.

note: The dream's plea before the king (காவலன் முன்னர் யான் கட்டுரைத்தேன்) is fulfilled when Kannaki stands before the Pandya and argues her case.
teaches: Set beside the plea, the dream shows that Kannaki's speech before the king was foreseen as her own act from the start, not a chance turn of grief, and that she already knew it would bring harm to the city.

note: The quatrain says that when people who know what should be known still do blameworthy things, it comes from their own former deeds; the epic says the king inquired into nothing because it was the time for a deed to ripen.
teaches: The quatrain traces the knowing man's wrong to his own deeds, while the epic leaves open whose deed ripens, the king's or Kovalan's caught in its net, so one man's karma may be what makes another man err.

gains.a: the king's failure gains a received explanation: knowing men do wrong when former deeds press them, and blame still attaches
gains.b: the quatrain gains a case where the deed that ripens may not be the wrongdoer's own, which its wording does not consider

note: Kavunthi quotes the saying that where chaste wives live the kings' victory does not decay; the patikam says that because Kannaki was a pathini she burned Madurai and the Pandya fell.
teaches: The saying Kavunthi offers as a pledge of the king's safety is reversed in the same city, where a pathini's presence ends the king, so the pair shows that the epic makes the chaste wife's power conditional on the king's justice rather than a blessing that protects any throne.

note: The kuravai is danced so that the coming distress may pass; at the dance's end an uproar from the town brings the news of Kovalan's death.
teaches: The rite meant to turn the sorrow away becomes the frame in which the sorrow arrives, so the herders' remedy is shown powerless against a deed already done.

note: The Maduraikkanchi's courtesans of Madurai drain the wealth of rich young men and leave them like bees leaving a spent flower; the epic's courtesans of the same city are masters of the two styles of dance and its treatises, paid a fixed fee by rule, before whom kings bow.
teaches: The Sangam poem sees Madurai's courtesans as the drain on the young rich, while the epic sees them as an institution of learned art with a royal tariff, so the pair shows the epic recasting a city's vice as its high culture, the very shift that made Madhavi's art and Kovalan's ruin the same thing.

gains.a: the epic's dancers' quarter gains its older picture, in which the same women of the same city appear as takers of wealth, which the epic's praise silently suppresses
gains.b: the Sangam poem's courtesans gain an account of their art and its rules, which the poem, seeing them only from the side of the spent lover, does not give

note: The couplet ranks the strength of those who endure hunger below that of those who remove it; Viruchikan eats once in twelve years, and when his fruit is crushed his fasting power becomes a curse of hunger on another, which Manimekalai's bowl removes.
teaches: The story stages the couplet's ranking and adds a reason for it: the endurer's power, once offended, can itself manufacture hunger in others, so only the giver's power ends suffering rather than moving it about.

gains.a: the epic's sage and girl gain a stated rule that ranks them, the faster below the feeder
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the endurer's strength is not merely lesser but harmful, causing the very hunger the giver must remove

note: Thirikadugam 96 names the knowing wife, the ascetic who keeps his vow and the good king as three at whose word rain falls; the verse makes rain rest on ascetics, ascetics on the king, the king on householders.
teaches: Both books make human virtue the cause of rain, but Thirikadugam sets three causes side by side while the verse lines them up, so one gives co-equal powers and the other a chain of dependence ending in the household.

note: The Chera king washes the charanas' feet and serves them six-flavoured food of four kinds; Manimekalai washes Aravanar's feet and serves the same.
teaches: The lay gift that founded Buddhism in Vanji is repeated by Manimekalai in Kanchi, so her entry into the order is staged as the same act of royal hospitality to monks.

note: Kural 882 says to fear the enemy who seems like kin; Thirikadugam counts taking by the hand a man formerly enraged against one as the conduct of one about to die.
teaches: The couplet warns against the hidden foe in general; the verse names the concrete act, taking back a former enemy, and states its outcome as death.

note: The Charana says the strong deed cannot be put off once it clings and that release from births comes through the Jina's spoken teaching; Tirumular says that by Siva's grace deeds do not cling at all.
teaches: The two give incompatible accounts of whether a ripening deed can be stopped: for the Charana only the cycle of births can be ended, by teaching, while the deed must still be eaten; for Tirumular grace prevents the deed from clinging.

gains.a: the Charana's sermon gains a clear rival: what it denies is precisely the grace that removes karma
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a contemporary opponent for whom no god's grace stops a deed once sown

note: Tirumular lists the goddess's names (Tripurai, Sundari, Narani, Manonmani and others) and says by them the great one stands as many; the vari lists Amari, Kumari, Gauri, Samari, Shooli, Neeli and others for the hunters' goddess of the stag.
teaches: Both pile names on one goddess, but the hunters' names come from her weapons, mounts, hides and battle with the asura and end in a rite where a girl wears them, while Tirumular's end in the doctrine that one power stands as many, so the pair shows the same device of the name-chain serving a public rite of costume and possession in one text and an inner theology of a single Shakti in the other.

gains.a: the vari's chain of names is seen to make no doctrinal claim of oneness; it names a goddess to be worn and worshipped
gains.b: Tirumular's doctrine that the one stands as many gains an older, folk chain of names (குமரி, கவுரி, நீலி) that it gathers into his single Shakti

note: Here Kannaki names only the king's error as the cause; before the king she says her husband came to the city driven by ஊழ்வினை.
teaches: In private grief Kannaki blames the king alone, but in court she joins karma to his fault, so the two causes the patikam names are shown held by one speaker at two moments, not only by narrator and character.

note: The patikam's second moral, that the great praise a renowned pathini, begins to be enacted when the Chera queen proposes worshipping her.
teaches: The moral is fulfilled first by a queen's judgment that sets the Pandya queen's death aside for heaven and chooses Kannaki for worship on earth, so the praise of the great begins in a comparison of two wives.

note: Kural 282 says even thinking of stealing another's goods is wrong; 547 holds that the burglar, the would-be killer and the would-be adulterer carry the karma of their intent even when the act fails.
teaches: Read beside a debate that also condemns the unintended killing, the couplet's thought-crime proves to be only half of the Jain position, which binds karma both to the intent without the deed and to the deed without the intent.

gains.a: the verse's claim that a failed intent binds finds a rule in the Kural that gives the same verdict on theft without any doctrine of karma
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'thinking is wrong' is set inside an account of why: the intent itself binds karma, and a deed done in error binds it too

note: 333 says wealth is by nature unstaying; 753 calls it the unfailing lamp that drives out darkness wherever one intends.
teaches: The chapter on impermanence and the chapter on acquiring wealth describe the same thing in opposite terms.

note: Neelakesi rejects the Buddhist rule that the sin of killing attaches only where there is intention; the Kural argues that if none killed to eat, none would sell flesh for a price.
teaches: The Kural's buyer-and-seller argument is the reply the intention defence needs: the eater need intend no killing for his eating to cause one, so a rule that weighs only intention misses the chain from buyer to slaughter.

gains.a: Neelakesi's bare charge that the sin reaches the eater gets a causal argument behind it
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed opponent is identified as a live doctrine, that sin requires the intent to kill

note: 251 charged the monk Arkkachandran with preaching compassion while eating fish and flesh; 470 brings the same charge to the Buddha's own town and its market, before the teacher himself.
teaches: The flesh charge moves from the disciple's conduct to the master's city and then (472-473) to the master's teaching, so the poem traces a monk's fault back to the rule that permits it.

note: The quatrain's renunciant refuses talk of teeth like jasmine buds and pearls because he has seen fallen teeth and bones in the burning ground; Manimekalai shows teeth once like a row of pearls now loosened in a living mouth.
teaches: The quatrain needs the cremation ground to refute the pearl simile, while the epic finds the refutation in a living old woman, so the argument against the body moves from death to aging that every lover can see in the street.

gains.a: Manimekalai's catalogue gains the Naladiyar's frame of rejected similes, showing it answers the praise-poets' language point by point.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a version of its proof that does not wait for death, which widens it from the funeral ground to ordinary life.

note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of the kindly to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of a town; 199 likens suppliants to birds that return to a fruiting banyan.
teaches: The Kural sees the fruiting tree from the owner's side, as wealth placed where all can reach it, while Perumpadhumanaar sees it from the birds' side, as a place to return to daily, so together they give both halves of the gift relation and make the asker's return a sign of the giver's worth.

note: The Kural states that when the king bends justice the sky withholds rain; the drummer's blessing wishes three rains and an unswerving king in the same sentence, as things the festival must secure.
teaches: The Kural makes rain follow from the king's justice alone, while the festival treats both rain and just rule as gifts to be prayed for from the gods, so the epic's city does not leave the causal chain to the king.

gains.a: the paired wish in lines 33-34 gains its logic: the Kural explains why rain and the sceptre belong in one blessing
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a ritual setting in which a city, not trusting the king alone, asks the gods for both ends of it

note: The couplet says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules with the sceptre as it should be; the summary lists the Chola line's righteousness beside the unfailing sky and abundant food, and the Madurai summary gives the same lines to the Pandya line.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the summaries' line of unfailing rain reads as the Kural's sign of just rule, yet the epic grants it equally to the line whose king it shows killing an innocent man, so the pair shows the epic keeping the sign as ceremony while placing the real test of the sceptre in a single verdict.

gains.a: the formula's rain line gains the political meaning the couplet gives it, as a claim that the realm is justly ruled
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its sign of good rule is ascribed to a kingdom whose sceptre the story will show bent, which shows that the sign alone cannot vouch for the king

note: Kannaki's vow to see her husband and hear a faultless word from him is kept in the vision, where he speaks only of her faded face and bids her stay.
teaches: The vow is fulfilled in form but not in substance: the dead husband's word clears no one, so the proof of innocence has to come from Kannaki's own plea at court.

note: Silappathikaram 16 tells how a drunken guard's sword cut Kovalan down as the king's sceptre bent and his former deed came in wrath; his daughter's lament on the island recalls the sword on his chest and the cruel deed ripening.
teaches: The earlier epic gives two causes for Kovalan's death, the bent sceptre and the ripened deed, but his daughter's memory keeps only the deed and stretches it over her own plight, so the sequel's first word on the killing drops the king's guilt and makes karma something a family suffers together.

note: Both curses are told in the same formula, a curse given (இட்ட சாபம்) that took hold (கட்டியது); the former-birth curse on Kovalan has no term and ends in his never again being seen in human form, Kavunthi's has a term of twelve months and a return to former shape.
teaches: Just before Madurai the epic shows a curse that the wronged can soften and that ends in a restored body, so the reader meets the bounded curse first and the unbounded one, which no plea can term, at the story's end.

note: 246 sets out the no-soul doctrine against the Buddhist talk of a being who relieves pain and wins release; 248 cites a Buddhist assembly that recites that a person exists.
teaches: Neelakesi answers the no-soul claim not with Jain doctrine but with a split inside Buddhism, so the debate uses the opponent's own schools as witnesses.

note: Mokkalan raised the faults of holding a thing both to stand and to perish; the Buddha now makes the same objection, and Neelakesi calls it one-sided.
teaches: The same objection recurs from the disciple to the master, and the reply sharpens from 'each in its respect' (378) to the charge of ekanta, naming the error the Jain sees in every Buddhist objection.

note: The Neelakesi's Buddha calls impermanence, suffering, impurity and no-soul his four truths; the Manimekalai's teacher gives the four truths as suffering, its cause, release and release's cause.
teaches: Holding the two lists together shows the Jain epic replacing the Buddhist's path of cause and cure with four bare marks of things, so that release seems to follow from seeing alone; this depends on reading நான்மை in 493 as the four truths.

note: The Purananuru poem tells Killivalavan that the land of the just sceptre on the Kaveri gets rain when it asks, and that kings are blamed when rains fail; Madhavi's stanza reads the Kaveri's easy flow as proof that the Chola sceptre does not bend.
teaches: The Sangam counsel makes plenty a duty the king must earn and warns he will be blamed for drought, while the epic song takes the river's plenty as already proving his justice, so the pair shows the counsel hardened into a courtly praise that can no longer imagine the failure the older poem warns of.

gains.a: Madhavi's figure gains its political doctrine, that a straight sceptre shows itself in the land's fertility, from an older address to a named Chola
gains.b: the poem's conditional warning gains a later reception in which the same link between sceptre and Kaveri is sung as settled fact, the form the epic later breaks with the Pandya

note: Both give an account of where a child comes from: the Neelakesi's sage assigns the body to the parents' blood and the life to its own former deeds, leaving the deity nothing to give; Tirumular has the Lord sit in the womb and form the embryo, knowing what it will become.
teaches: On the same question, the making of a child, the Jain sage removes every divine agent while Tirumular puts the Lord inside the womb, so karma alone and karma shaped by the Lord are opposed answers, not one view in two idioms.

gains.a: the sage's denial is seen to cut against a Tamil theology in which a god does make the child, not only against a village vow
gains.b: Tirumular's embryology is seen as a position a rival school in Tamil openly argued against

note: Both tell Neeli's curse and close it with the same words, உம்மை வினை வந்து உருத்தல்; the Silappathikaram adds that penance does not help the unrighteous when the old deed comes and calls Bharatan a vow-breaker, while the Manimekalai calls him a doer of evil work and Sangaman faultless.
teaches: The later epic keeps the karmic verdict word for word but moves it into Kannaki's own mouth and sharpens the contrast of guilty and faultless, so the explanation that consoled her in Madurai becomes in Vanchi her own testimony against her husband's former self.

note: In kaathai 9 the sage foretold that on the island seat she would know her birth and find his word clear; at her second visit Manimekalai says the sage's word of that day has come true today, after recalling his account of why the seat reveals births.
teaches: The second visit adds the ground of the seat's power, Indra's order made for the coming Buddha, so the fulfilment rests on the Buddha's future presence and not on the seat itself.

note: In 238 Neelakesi hears the Vinaya rule of how to shave the head recited in Arkkachandra's monastery; in 318 she cites the same tonsure (தலைமழி) against Mokkalan's claim that bodily hardship is a fault.
teaches: The Vinaya rules she overheard as ritual detail at Ujjain become her evidence that the Buddhist middle way still imposes discipline on the body, so the earlier scene was gathering ammunition.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives the joined name as a valid mode of speech: many letters coming together appear as a word; 518 says a momentary mind could never put the letters together.
teaches: The two epics take the same example, a word made of letters, to opposite ends: the Buddhist treats it as a correct conventional name, the Jain as proof that something must last to join the letters.

note: At the palace gate Kannaki called the Pandya a king of ruined sense who strayed from right rule (இறைமுறை பிழைத்தோன்); in the sky she calls him faultless (தீதிலன்) and herself his daughter.
teaches: The same speaker gives opposite verdicts on the same king, and the epic means both: the turn shows that in its eyes the king's death of his own sentence has cancelled the fault she rightly charged him with.

note: The Manimekala goddess foretold that Manimekalai would hear the false words of many schools and gave her the mantra to take another form because no one would tell a young girl the truth (79-80); here the same two lines are recalled and she chants the mantra and becomes an ascetic.
teaches: The disguise is set off by two voices together: the Manimekala goddess supplied the means long before, and Kannaki now supplies the order of study, so the Buddhist sea goddess and the Tamil pathini goddess both direct the girl to the debates.

note: In the Manimekalai the Jain's account of things as lasting and passing at once is heard and left among the doctrines Manimekalai sets aside; in the Neelakesi the Buddha himself is made to praise that account.
teaches: Each epic stages the same Jain doctrine before the other side and gives it the opposite fate, so the debate scenes show how each school wanted the meeting to end.

note: The song praises a wife who does not sulk at her husband's other love; Madhavi hears in Kovalan's songs a hidden intent and takes up the yazh in a sulk disguised as pleasure.
teaches: The song's ideal of the wife who never sulks is answered at once by the courtesan's sulking, so the kaathai shows the praise of patient chastity working as a provocation on the one woman who is not his wife.

note: The goddess gives Manimekalai a mantra to travel the sky and another that cuts hunger, since the body is a lump of food; Kayasandigai has lost the mantra for going through the sky (55, and அந்தரம் செல்லும் மந்திரம் 43) and suffers a hunger no food fills.
teaches: The two women are drawn as mirror images: the very powers granted to Manimekalai by mantra, flight and freedom from hunger, are those the curse stripped from Kayasandigai, and Manimekalai restores the second to her by charity, not by mantra.

note: The prince goes at midnight to the hall to take Manimekalai and dies; the next kaathai's report to the king sets his death among those of men who approached chaste wives or ascetic women and died as their evil deed ripened.
teaches: The midnight approach is later read as one case in a city's record of such deaths, so the narrative's private intrigue becomes a public precedent that the court uses to explain a prince's death to his father.

note: In 263 Neelakesi grieves for the Buddha who taught a void release; in 512 she argues that his account of will ends in the void through infinite regress.
teaches: The void is charged twice, once as a goal no one could want and once as the end of a regress, so the Jain treats Buddhist emptiness as both a bad hope and a failed argument.

claims.gist: one person continues across births, and the jewel seat lets her know her former birth
the highest humans are the founders of the ford, the wheel-bearing kings and the sky-going Vidyadharas
object, perception and consciousness arise together and perish together
on that account nothing is ever known
every occurrence is fixed by niyati
a vessel that sustains all lives must not be used to sustain the life of the one who holds it
his lone suffering comes where his merit is exhausted
the bowl should pass only to those who wear compassion and dharma and sustain lives
the Lord's knowing is one and present to all things at once, as one moon is in every water
the five aggregates as the Buddha teaches them do not exist
there is no time beyond the risings of the heavenly bodies
the ear grasps sound without contact
sound is heard after the thing is seen because it must travel to the ear, so hearing is by contact
there is no principle beyond the twenty-five
one should worship the feet of the Jina
a creator can neither create himself nor be created without an endless regress of creators
a soul that rises by its own nature could not remain bound in a body to die and do deeds
the Lord speaks and answers through a body, which karma by itself cannot do
the river's unfailing gift that sustains all life is the grace of the ruler of the wheel
those caught by desire for a woman's adorned body meet deep sorrow, as fish meet the hook
the Buddha's feet are a ship that carries beings off the great sea of births
those who keep the vow of the Buddha's dharma and worship the seat come to know their former births
plants take food and die without it, which only living things do
spirits and demons do not take a life; a former deed ripens and takes it, with fright only as its occasion
the fruit of a deed falls on its doer as poison works on the one who eats it
no thing persisting through the change of gram into mash can be shown, so it does not exist
without women and food there is no gain for men in this world
the faultless have forbidden liquor and the killing of living beings
death and birth follow one another as sleep and waking do
those who do good reach a good world and those who do ill reach hell
from birth come aging, sickness, death, grief, lament, care and despair, an unending sorrow
when ignorance ceases action ceases, and each later link ceases with the one before
there are two kinds of continuum, the separate and the unseparated
the human body comes from past deeds and is the place where deeds bear their fruit
stripped of its adornments the body is only flesh fit to be thrown out, subject to age, death and disease
one who knows the body for what it is should turn his back on it
a king of the right line can bind the clouds and make the harvest unfailing
seed gives its own kind, so the paddy example proves sameness of kind, not a reaper who is neither same nor other
one who takes the faultless dharma becomes kin of those who keep it
wonders such as a cloudless rain of flowers belong to the time when a Buddha appears on earth
even the gods' heavenly life comes to an end
what bears the fruit is neither the same nor other but another in the same line of continuity
the soul that gives and keeps vows is the same soul that later dwells in heaven, which is what makes giving true
a thesis that contradicts one's own accepted scripture is false
sound is impermanent
nothing perishes
if a thing exists only in its own time, the ascetic's soul will not exist in the future and keeping precepts is vain
showing two properties together in one instance, without stating the general rule, does not establish the connection
the rule must run from the narrower property to the wider; stated the other way it fails, since the wider occurs without the narrower
whatever is made is impermanent

note: On the road the brahmin blesses the Pandya line as one of faultless fame (தீதுதீர் சிறப்பின் தென்னனை); in Madurai the reigning Pandya pronounces himself the thief (யானோ அரசன் யானே கள்வன்) and falls dead.
teaches: The journey to Madurai opens with a blessing of a flawless lineage, so the king's self-condemnation reads as a fall from inherited fame and not only as one wrong verdict.

note: Kural 2 asks what learning is worth if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Manimekalai says learning that is merely learned is not learning, and names the learned as those who curb hatred, end hunger and love all creatures.
teaches: Both refuse learning its own worth, but the couplet completes it in worship while the epic completes it in compassion and the ending of others' hunger, so the pair shows two answers to the same question of what learning is for.

gains.a: a classic statement that learning needs a further end, against which her list reads as a choice of ends
gains.b: a Buddhist answer to its question that puts the further end in conduct toward beings rather than in reverence to a lord

note: 533 holds that naming a thing one thinks unreal is a lie; Kural 292 holds that even a falsehood stands as truth if it yields faultless good.
teaches: Neelakesi's charge only works on a test of truth by match with things; on the Kural's test by effect, the Buddhist's conventional names, harming no one, would not be lies at all.

gains.a: the verse's assumption about what truth is becomes visible as an assumption, one a widely read ethics book does not share
gains.b: the couplet's measure of truth by its fruit is shown to settle a philosophical dispute about speech that it never names

note: The Naladiyar's old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the deity says the cook's killing came 'here' to strike the man reborn as the prince.
teaches: The quatrain's deed that seeks out its doer becomes in the epic a deed that crosses a death and a new body, so the 'doer' it finds is a person with another name who does not remember the act.

gains.a: an image for the deed's active search, which the deity states only as a bare claim
gains.b: a case that sets the search across births, which the quatrain does not say

note: The Naladiyar says an old deed seeks out the one who did it (தற்செய்த கிழவனை) as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the Buddha in 602 says the doer has perished and the continuum running on from him receives the fruit.
teaches: The quatrain's image needs a doer who is still there to be found, while the Buddha's answer removes him, so the pair shows that the Tamil ethical common sense about karma assumes a lasting self.

gains.a: the Buddha's continuum is seen against the common Tamil picture of a deed finding its owner, which it has to replace
gains.b: the quatrain's calf-and-mother image is shown to carry an assumption, a persisting doer, that a Buddhist would deny

note: The couplet says unguarded anger kills the one who has it; Kanchanan's anger, kindled by misread signs, kills the prince, and the pillar then tells him the deed will cling to him.
teaches: The epic traces how anger turns on its owner: it begins in a misreading of another's signs, kills someone else first, and returns as a deed that will not leave the angry man, which the couplet states as a single blow.

gains.a: Kanchanan's rage gains the couplet's judgment that the angry man is his own first victim.
gains.b: The couplet gains the route by which anger kills its owner: through the deed done to another and its clinging consequence.

note: Manimekalai's Ajivika spokesman, Puranan, gives as god a knower without limit present everywhere, and five categories, soul and four atoms; Neelakesi's Puranan gives Makkali as god, the nine Kathir books as scripture, and five categories.
teaches: A Buddhist and a Jain polemic agree on the Ajivika spokesman's name and the five categories, which points to the Ajivikas' own teaching, but only the Jain account makes Makkali the god, which sets up its attack on a silent omniscient whose books no one heard.

note: The couplet asks whether the young woman's look is Death, an eye or a doe and finds all three in it; the vari asks whether her eyes are fierce Death and answers that Death has become an innocent girl.
teaches: Where the Kural holds Death and the doe's innocence side by side in one look, the song makes one the form of the other, so the innocent girl is Death in disguise, a step from mixture to transformation.

gains.a: the stanza's turn gains a reference point: it resolves into one being what the couplet leaves as three natures
gains.b: the couplet's list gains a storytelling form in which its opposites are joined by the god of death taking a girl's shape

note: The couplet's man says sulking is love's sweetness and the embrace after it sulking's sweetness; the epic says Madhavi gave Kovalan both union and sulking, after he had sat in a sulk.
teaches: In the epic the two halves of the couplet's cycle are things a trained woman gives, so ūdal becomes an art supplied to a lover rather than only a mood that lovers fall into.

gains.a: Madhavi's giving of ஊடல் and கூடல் is placed in the Kural's account of love, where sulking followed by union is love's fullest pleasure
gains.b: the couplet's private cycle is shown inside a courtesan's house, where it can be practised and offered, which raises the question the couplet does not ask, whose feeling it is

note: Puranan likens the Lord's unseen form to a rainbow that no bound contains; Neelakesi answers that a rainbow is made when sunlight falls on rain-cloud.
teaches: The simile chosen to set Makkali beyond causes is turned into an example of a thing produced by conditions, so the Ajivika's own image testifies against a Lord without cause.

note: The couplet says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than begging, even water for a cow; Manimekalai enters the street with a begging bowl and, at 71-74, calls receiving a chaste wife's alms a thing of great worth, while the crowd grieves at the sight.
teaches: The town's grief voices the Kural's shame of asking, and the nun's claim answers it with a begging that asks nothing for herself and seeks the worthiest giver, so the two disagree about whether all asking shames the asker.

gains.a: The crowd's pity (சிந்தை நோய் கூர) is shown to rest on the ethics books' contempt for begging, which the nun's alms round has to overcome.
gains.b: The couplet's limit case, begging even for a cow, meets a beggar whose bowl came down from a cow-born king and feeds others, a case its absolute rule does not consider.

note: The Neelakesi praises those who strive (முயல்வார்) with knowledge to wear away their deeds; the Tirumanthiram says deeds end when grace comes as the guru and one's own doing ceases (தன்செயல் அற்றால்).
teaches: Both make knowledge the solvent of deeds, but they disagree on whose act it is: for the Jain land it is the striver's own effort, for Tirumular the end of one's own agency under grace; the tension holds if முயல்வார் is read as self-reliant effort.

gains.a: the passing praise of strivers is shown to carry the Jain view of self-wrought release
gains.b: the verse's stress on the end of one's own agency stands out against a tradition that makes that agency the means

note: The king of Kampili asked the debaters for their first teacher, his scripture, its matters and their workings; Neelakesi now puts the same heads (ஆத்தன், நூல், பொருள், நிகழ்ச்சி) to the Ajivika.
teaches: The heads that a king imposed on the first debate have become Neelakesi's own method, so the epic shows the convert taking over the judge's role as well as the debater's.

note: The patikam's second moral, that the great praise a renowned pathini, begins to be acted out when the Chera takes the stone for the pathini from the Himalaya.
teaches: The patikam promises only that the high will praise the pathini, and this kaathai shows the praise has to be won by humbling northern kings, so the honour paid to Kannaki and the Chera's conquest are made one act.

note: At Kannaki's shrine in Vanji the maid asks the pathini whether she has heard of Madhavi's and Manimekalai's renunciation; Manimekalai here resolves to go to Vanji and do good deeds for the great pathini.
teaches: The two epics meet at the Vanji shrine from both sides: the Silappathikaram brings news of the girl's renunciation to the pathini, and the Manimekalai sends the renounced girl to make merit for her.

note: The couplet says that taking what is not a thing for a thing breeds an unworthy birth; the teacher gives a test for absence, that a thing which exists appears like a gooseberry in the hand, and the hare's horn does not.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's warning into a procedure: what would appear if it were there and does not appear may be judged absent, which gives the confusion the couplet fears a check in method.

gains.a: the logic of non-appearance gains a moral stake, since the couplet ties the error it guards against to rebirth
gains.b: the couplet's மருள் gains a means of correction, a rule for deciding what is not there

note: The patikam promises that the deed of the past comes in wrath to be eaten and that the great praise a pathini; Maadalan uses the same verb (ஊழ்வினை உருத்தெழ) and says the woman has risen onto the crowns of the northern kings.
teaches: The patikam's morals are fulfilled here in a messenger's words: the praise of the high is made literal as kings carrying her stone on their crowns, and the wrathful deed is placed at a courtesan's song, a smaller and more human moment than the former-birth curse the patikam gives as its cause.

note: The 'good' that would be laughed at if told is the ending in which Kannaki, after fourteen days, rises to heaven with Kovalan.
teaches: The pairing explains why Kannaki calls the dream's ending laughable: a reunion that comes only after death and in the form of gods sounds absurd as a blessing to a living wife.

note: Puhar has an image that weeps when the sceptre bends; in Madurai the Pandya's sceptre bends and he himself declares 'I am the thief' and dies.
teaches: Puhar's check on a bent sceptre is an image that can only weep, while Madurai has no such image and the king must find and judge his own fault at the cost of his life, so the epic moves from a ritual sign of injustice to its full price.

note: The Purananuru raider takes herds yet his own pot shows no curd; the epic names whose yards the seized herds fill.
teaches: The poem's pitied raider who keeps nothing is explained by the epic's list: the herd goes to smith, drummer, bards, augur and toddy seller, so a raid's wealth is a gift economy that leaves the raider poor.

gains.a: the list of yards gains its point: giving the herd away is the raider's honour, as the poem's empty curd-pot shows
gains.b: the poem's riddle (why a cattle-taker has no curd) gains the epic's answer in named receivers

note: Madhavi's right eye throbs at the festival; at the end of the Kaanal Vari Kovalan, his former deeds come to fruit, lets go of her and leaves.
teaches: The bad omen given to Madhavi on Indra's festival is fulfilled at the seashore at the festival's end, where the story names former deeds as the cause, so the omen and the karma explanation frame the same parting from two sides.

note: The quatrain says the best renounce home and wealth after slowly seeing that nothing lasts; here Kannaki's father and Madhavi renounce on hearing of deaths, and the two mothers simply die of the same news.
teaches: The quatrain's renunciation comes from calm reflection on impermanence, while in the epic it comes from the shock of bereavement and is only one of two outcomes of the same grief, so the pair shows the distance between the ethics book's ideal path to renunciation and the way the story's people actually reach it.

gains.a: the epic's renunciations gain a standard by which they look sudden and grief-driven rather than reasoned
gains.b: the quatrain's ideal gains a case showing that the same knowledge of loss can end in death as well as in renouncing

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika gives water its own coolness and taste and fire its burning; the Neelakesi's gives every sensible quality but sound to earth alone, and Neelakesi argues the other elements would then be imperceptible.
teaches: Set beside the Buddhist report, the Jain objection is seen to strike the version of the doctrine that gives the senses' objects to earth alone; the Manimekalai's Ajivika, who gives water a taste, would be harder to hit.

note: 491 says the five aggregates arise together in one moment; 506 gives them an order in which cognition makes activity and activity makes feeling.
teaches: Neelakesi uses the Buddhist's own causal chain against his doctrine of simultaneity: if one aggregate produces another, they cannot all be born and die in the same instant.

note: The festival bids the debaters of the schools mount Puhar's debating hall and part without quarrel; in kaathai 27, after Puhar is lost, Manimekalai goes among the schools of Vanji in disguise and hears each in turn without dispute.
teaches: The public hall of debate promised at the opening is never shown in Puhar; it returns only in another city as one renunciant's quiet hearing of the schools, so the epic moves doctrinal inquiry from civic festival to private search.

note: The venba wishes Puhar, made by fame for the earth whose moat is the sea, to live like the sun and the moon; the Manimekalai tells that when the king, searching for his lost son, left off the Indra festival, Manimekala Deivam bade the sea take the city.
teaches: The sea the venba names only as the earth's protecting moat is the agent that takes the city in the sequel, and the festival the summary counts among Puhar's glories is the rite whose neglect brings it, so the blessing of lasting life holds the terms of its own reversal.

note: Mokkala argues that infinite things cannot be known to their end; the hymn answers that the Lord's knowledge is not sensory and does not go in order (முறைபடும் அறிவிலன்).
teaches: The infinity objection assumes knowing means counting through objects one by one, and the hymn's answer is to deny that the omniscient's knowledge is sequential at all, which shows where the two sides really part.

note: 1018 sees shame as the condition of virtue, with virtue itself ashamed to approach the shameless. 1075 is a kind of counter-case: the base still have conduct, with fear and desire in place of shame.
teaches: Their conduct looks alike and differs in its source.

note: The couplet defines a gift by its receiver: what goes to those who have nothing. Neelakesi tests a gift by what is given: persons handed over as alms make their taker a thief.
teaches: A gift can satisfy the couplet's test of the receiver's want and still fail, because the thing given must be the giver's own, which the couplet takes for granted.

gains.a: Neelakesi's objection gains a householder's definition of giving that does not mention property, showing her test adds a condition
gains.b: the couplet gains a limit it leaves unstated: one may give only what is one's own, and persons are not

note: Both refuse the promise of a quick return: the girl quotes his 'we will come right away' against the spring, the Kural says tell your quick return to those who will be alive.
teaches: Read together they show the same refusal of comfort in two registers, the Kural as a sharp retort before parting and the Akananuru as proof gathered afterwards from the season's signs.

note: The venba says both deeds will reach their doer and bids men turn to good dharma; Tirumular says that when the two deeds stand balanced, grace comes as the guru and frees the soul from them.
teaches: The venba's remedy for the two deeds is to do more good, which on its wording still returns to the doer, while Tirumular's is grace that comes when good and evil are balanced and ends them, so the pair sets merit-making against release by grace; the conflict holds if நல்லறம் is read as producing good fruit.
