gains.a: the venba's moral gains a contrast that shows it offers no escape from deeds, only better ones
gains.b: Tirumular's balancing of the two deeds gains a plain statement of the view it moves beyond, that good deeds are the answer to karma

note: Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounced in childhood; 191 says grey hair has not come to the poet because of his good wife, children, servants, king and the worthy men of his town. On the reading that both speak of how to meet old age, one counsels leaving the household and the other credits it.
teaches: The Naladiyar's answer to ageing is renunciation, while Pisirandhaiyar's is a good household and good company, so the pair shows two Tamil remedies for the same fear, one by leaving the world early and one by living well in it.

note: The townspeople's bent sceptre and cool umbrella breeding heat are the omens the queen sees falling in her dream in the next kaathai.
teaches: The same signs of ruin appear first as the street's verdict in waking speech and then as the palace's dream, so the city knows the king's fall before the court does.

note: Against Mokkalan (389) Neelakesi held that a thing's modes perish and arise while the thing stays; against the Sankhya (777) she says a thing is non-existent now and existent later, both at once.
teaches: One Jain doctrine is turned two ways: against the Buddhist's momentary things she stresses what lasts, against the Sankhya's lasting effects she stresses what is not yet, and each answer depends on the other.

note: The quatrain asks whether spices, flowers in the hair and false finery can remove a foulness the great saw and gave up; Manimekalai says the flowers, paste, cloth and jewels that hide the flesh are a deceit 'those of old' devised.
teaches: The quatrain credits the great of the past with seeing through the body's adornment, while the epic blames those of old for building it, so the same disguise is a personal vanity in one and an inherited social custom in the other.

gains.a: The epic's charge against custom gains a parallel in which tradition is on the side of seeing through adornment, which sharpens how unusual its blame of 'those of old' is.
gains.b: The quatrain gains an account of where the false finery comes from, which it treats only as something individuals put on.

note: In 74 the sage promised to tell birth, its disease, and the medicine that cuts that disease; 86 names the medicine as penance that drives out the dark karma.
teaches: The promised medicine for birth turns out to be penance, and it is offered only to humans of the land of deeds, so the cure is narrower than the promise first sounded.

note: The Kural likens men without kindly regard to trees fixed in the soil; Neelakesi argues that trees feel heat and cold and change as living bodies do.
teaches: Read with the Jain argument, the couplet's tree is not a dead thing but a living being that feels by touch yet has no eye to look with, which makes the comparison exact for a man who has eyes and does not use them kindly.

gains.a: the Jain claim that trees feel is seen against a Tamil commonplace that used the tree as the very type of the unfeeling
gains.b: the couplet's simile gains a precise sense under the Jain scale of senses: the tree lacks sight, not life

note: Murinjiyur Mudinagarayar praises Uthiyan Cheralathan as the one who gave the great feast without limit while the Five and the hundred fought until the hundred fell; the swing song gives the feast at the war of the Five and the twice fifty to the Chera, Poraiyan, Malaiyan, by house names only, and pairs it with the kadamba deed.
teaches: The Puram poem binds the feast to one named king, while the epic gives it to the Chera house in general and sets it beside another king's deed, so the pair shows a single patron's distinction becoming an heirloom any Chera can be sung by.

gains.a: the swing song's line gains its source and the king it belonged to, Uthiyan Cheralathan, whom it does not name
gains.b: the Puram poem's claim gains a measure of its fame: generations later it is still the Chera line's mark, though detached from the king it praised

note: Verse 4 says women's hearts melt for another as fish delight in new floodwater; verse 46 says a divided woman's mind can no more be made one than oil spread on water gathered.
teaches: The fragment moves from women's hearts straying to their being past recall once divided, which completes its case for giving them up.

note: 201 argues that if nothing of the first moment remains in the next, knowing is impossible; 518 tests this on hearing a word letter by letter.
teaches: The general continuity objection becomes a concrete test the opponent cannot dodge: no one could even understand the word 'Buddha' if each letter's knower perished before the next.

note: Madhavi reads a hidden intent into Kovalan's songs and sings as if she had one too; at the end Kovalan says she sang with her mind on another, and leaves her, the narrator saying his former deed had come to fruit.
teaches: Set together, the two passages give the break two causes: a pair of mutual misreadings of songs that the poet marks as seeming, and the ஊழ்வினை the narrator names when Kovalan goes, so choice and karma are both offered for the same parting.

note: When the Chera Perunjeralathan sits north to die, the ploughmen's cry is forgotten and the village festival forgotten; when Senguttuvan returns, the ploughmen's song and the bathing festival fill the land.
teaches: Holding the two Chera poems together shows the ploughmen's song as the land's own measure of its king, silenced by a king's shameful death and loud at a king's triumph, so the epic's return scene answers the Sangam lament with its exact reverse.

gains.a: the field songs gain a Sangam frame in which the ploughmen's voice is a sign of the king's fortune
gains.b: the lament gains its opposite case, showing what the forgotten songs were when the king lived and won

a curse laid in a former birth binds and comes to fruit in this one

insects like lice and ants have three senses, and bees and wasps, which lack hearing, have four

if souls were finite in number the round of births could not be without end

meat is no more impure than cow's milk
flesh, made of semen and blood, is impure as milk is not
the later states of a being already exist, unsprouted, in its beginning

kings who will not bow to the Chera's feet cannot long prosper
Aravanar teaches austerity, dharma, dependent arising and the path that cuts off becoming

a thing is non-existent from another place and existent where it is, and both are said together

if a teacher's greatness was only won by coming to know dharma, any who know dharma, even the lowest, would equal him
the soul is without any change

birth as a beast is full of suffering from weather, war, hunting and the snare

those who take falsehood as their way of gain never escape helpless grief
the sufferings that follow these deeds are not for thieves alone; all who live in the world must renounce them
for those born in the royal line, to die of old age without a wound is a shame
